afoqt-va.title: Verbal Analogies
afoqt-va.blurb: 25 analogies in 8 minutes. Learn to turn the first pair into a precise sentence, recognize the classic relationships (part and whole, tool and job, cause and effect, degree, opposite, symbol, sequence), dodge reversed pairs and still score when a word is new to you.

units.title: Find the relationship: the sentence method
units.objective: Turn the first pair into a precise sentence, then test every option in that same sentence until only one fits.

steps: The AFOQT gives you 25 analogies in 8 minutes, about 19 seconds each. Each item shows a pair (A is to B) and asks for the word or pair that relates in the same way. Five options, one best answer.
Before you look at the options, link A and B in a short sentence: 'A cartographer draws maps.' The sentence is the relationship; what the words are about doesn't matter.
Make the sentence specific. 'A cartographer is connected with maps' fits almost anything. 'A cartographer makes maps as a profession' rules most options out.
Drop C into the same sentence, in the same position, and try each option: 'A lexicographer makes ___ as a profession.' Dictionaries fits; words, spelling and libraries don't.
If two options still fit, sharpen the sentence again: add degree (slightly or extremely), kind (a type of, a part of) or purpose (used to). The tighter sentence leaves one answer.
Wrong options are usually linked to C in some other way: its tool, its material, its place, its opposite. They feel right because they belong with C. Ignore the feeling and test the sentence.
teach.formula: A ___ B, so C ___ ? (same sentence, same order, as specific as it can be)

worked.stem: Odometer is to distance as tachometer is to —
steps: Sentence for the first pair: an odometer is an instrument that measures distance.
Same sentence with C: a tachometer is an instrument that measures ___.
A tachometer reads how fast an engine's shaft is turning, in revolutions per minute.
Tempting wrong picks: speed (that's the speedometer), engine (what it's attached to, not what it measures) and fuel (another gauge entirely).

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: An analogy is a matching game. The first two words are linked in some way, and you must find another pair linked the same way.
Cover the options with your hand. Look only at the first two words.
Say a sentence out loud that joins them: 'A pilot flies an airplane.'
Now put the third word into the very same sentence: 'A captain sails a ___.' The blank is now easy: a ship.
Uncover the options and test each one in your sentence. Only one should make it true.
If more than one works, your sentence was too loose. Add a detail and test again.
Say A and B as a sentence
Make it specific
Drop C into the same sentence
Two fit? Sharpen it

practice.stem: Ornithologist is to birds as entomologist is to —
practice.explain: An ornithologist studies birds, so an entomologist studies insects, the whole class. Words is the trap from the look-alike etymologist, fossils belong to a paleontologist and fungi to a mycologist. Bees are insects, but they are only one group, while birds is a whole class, so bees is too narrow.

practice.stem: Anthology is to poems as atlas is to —
practice.explain: An anthology is a book that collects poems, and an atlas is a book that collects maps. Geography is the subject an atlas covers, not what it is a collection of, and the cartographer is the person who draws the maps. A globe is a different object showing the same thing, and a journey is something an atlas might be used for.

practice.stem: Preamble is to constitution as foreword is to —
practice.explain: A preamble is the introductory statement at the start of a constitution, and a foreword is the introductory section at the start of a book. An appendix comes at the end, so it reverses the position. A chapter is a part of a book but not its introduction, and the author and publisher are people, not the document being introduced.

practice.stem: Embargo is to trade as quarantine is to —
practice.explain: An embargo is an official ban on trade, so the answer is what a quarantine officially bans: contact, or movement in and out. Medicine is what treats an illness, not what a quarantine bans; that pick comes from a loose 'is related to' sentence. Isolation is roughly what a quarantine is, a synonym rather than the thing banned, and cure and hospital are merely associated with illness.

practice.stem: Arbiter is to dispute as physician is to —
practice.explain: An arbiter's job is to resolve a dispute, and a physician's job is to resolve an ailment by treating it. The patient is the person treated, not the problem resolved. A remedy and a diagnosis are things the physician produces, like an arbiter's ruling, and a hospital is the workplace.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Think of the first pair as a job description you fill in.
steps: Every analogy hides a short sentence. Find it before you look at the options.
Use a fill-in frame: 'A is a part of B', 'A is a kind of B', 'A is used to B', 'A makes B', 'A is an extreme B', 'A is the opposite of B'.
Pick the frame that fits A and B best, then fill it in with C.
Test every option, even if the first one looks good. A word that merely goes with C is often placed early to catch people who rush.
If two survive, add one detail to the sentence until only one fits.
Choose a frame for A and B
Fill it in with C
Test all five
Two left? Add a detail

example.stem: Conductor is to orchestra as editor is to — (newspaper, ink, reporter, article, printer)
steps: Loose sentence: a conductor works with an orchestra. Reporter, article and newspaper all seem to fit.
Sharper sentence: a conductor directs the whole orchestra.
An editor directs the whole newspaper. A reporter is one member, and an article is one piece of work, not the whole.

reteach.hook: No sentence, no answer.

check.stem: Author is to novel as composer is to —
check.explain: An author writes a novel, so a composer writes a symphony. The orchestra plays it and the conductor leads the performance, so both are performers, not the work. A piano is an instrument and the audience listens.

check.stem: Glossary is to definitions as index is to —
check.explain: A glossary lists terms with their definitions, and an index lists topics with their page references. Both are in alphabetical order, so alphabet describes their order rather than their contents. Chapters and footnotes are other parts of a book, and the book is the whole that contains the index.

check.stem: Sentry is to guard as scout is to —
check.explain: A sentry's job is to guard, and a scout's job is to reconnoiter, to explore ahead and gather information. The enemy is who a scout watches and the camp is where a sentry stands. A weapon is equipment, and retreat is the opposite of a scout's forward work.

check.stem: Pediatrician is to children as geriatrician is to —
check.explain: A pediatrician is a doctor who specializes in children, and a geriatrician specializes in the elderly. Infants are a pediatrician's patients again, the trap for anyone who matches the first pair instead of the third word. Diseases, nurses and hospitals go with every kind of doctor, not with this specialty.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down: one pair, one sentence.
steps: An analogy says: these two words are linked the same way as those two.
Read only the first two words. Ask how they are linked, and say it as a short sentence.
Example: 'Bird is to nest.' Sentence: a bird lives in a nest.
Put the third word into the very same sentence: 'Bee is to ___.' A bee lives in a hive.
Check each option with the sentence. Only one should make it true.

example.stem: Key is to lock as password is to — (account, keyboard, secret, letters, screen)
steps: Sentence: a key opens a lock.
Same sentence: a password opens an ___.
A password opens an account. It is typed on a keyboard and made of letters, but those don't fit the sentence.

reteach.hook: Say it, swap it, check it.

check.stem: Bird is to flock as wolf is to —
check.explain: A bird is one member of a flock, and a wolf is one member of a pack. A den is a wolf's home and the forest its habitat, places rather than groups. A howl is its sound and a cub is a young wolf.

check.stem: Hammer is to carpenter as stethoscope is to —
check.explain: A hammer is a tool used by a carpenter, and a stethoscope is a tool used by a physician. The heart and pulse are what the stethoscope listens to, the patient is who it is used on, and the hospital is the workplace.

check.stem: Chapter is to book as scene is to —
check.explain: A chapter is one part of a book, and a scene is one part of a play. The actor performs it, the stage and curtain are parts of the theater, and the audience watches.

check.stem: Thirsty is to drink as tired is to —
check.explain: When you are thirsty, you drink to fix it; when you are tired, you rest to fix it. A yawn is a sign of tiredness, not the cure, and a bed is where you rest. Weak is another feeling, and awake is the state being lost.

units.title: Part to whole and category to member
units.objective: Tell 'a part of' from 'a kind of', keep the levels in the right order, and match the size of the step.

steps: Part to whole: A is one piece of B. A chapter is part of a book; a fuselage is part of an aircraft. The sentence is 'A is one of the parts that make up B.'

Category and member: A is a kind of B, or B is a kind of A. A sloop is a kind of sailboat; a falcon is a kind of raptor. A part is not a kind: a wing is part of a bird, but a sparrow is a kind of bird.
Group pairs are part to whole too: a juror is one member of a jury, a star one member of a constellation, a player one member of a team. A player is not a kind of team.
Match the level. If A is one of many small repeated units (a brick in a wall, a stitch in a seam), the answer must also be a repeated unit, not a single big section such as the nose of an airplane.
Keep the order. 'Scene is to act' runs small to big; 'act is to scene' runs big to small. An option with the right two words in the wrong order is wrong.
Watch near-miss categories: 'sparrow is to bird' is member to category, so 'salmon is to fish' matches, but 'salmon is to school' (one member of a group) does not.
teach.formula: Part: A is one piece of B · Kind: A is a type of B · Same level, same order

worked.stem: Brick is to wall as — (skull is to skeleton, plank is to boardwalk, wall is to brick, mortar is to brick, mason is to brick)
steps: First sentence: a brick is a part of a wall. Too loose: a skull is also a part of a skeleton.
Sharpen it: a brick is one of many identical units laid together to build a wall.
Skull is to skeleton fails: a skeleton has only one skull. Wall is to brick is reversed. Mortar joins bricks, and a mason lays them.
Plank is to boardwalk passes: a boardwalk is built from many identical planks laid together.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: There are two ways one thing can belong to another.
It can be a PIECE of it, like a slice of a pizza. You could cut it off.
Or it can be a KIND of it, like pepperoni pizza is a kind of pizza. It's a type in a group.
For the first pair, ask: piece or kind?
Then ask: which comes first, the small one or the big one?
The answer must be the same type (piece or kind) and in the same order.
Piece of, or kind of?
Small first or big first?
Same size of step?
Choose the match

practice.stem: Platoon is to soldier as fleet is to —
practice.explain: A platoon is made up of soldiers, so a fleet is made up of ships; the pair runs from the whole group to one member. Navy is a bigger group that contains fleets, so it points the wrong way. An admiral commands a fleet, a harbor is where it anchors, and sailors belong to the crews of the ships rather than being the fleet's units.

practice.stem: Violin is to strings as oboe is to —
practice.explain: A violin is a member of the string family, so an oboe is a member of the woodwind family. Bow is what you play a violin with, a trap from the first pair, not a family, and orchestra is the larger group both play in. Brass is the wrong family, and flute is another member of the woodwinds, a fellow member rather than the category.

practice.stem: Paragraph is to essay as —
practice.explain: A paragraph is one of the sections that make up an essay, and a verse is one of the sections that make up a song. Sentence is to word runs the other way, whole to part. Author is to book and editor is to manuscript pair a person with a piece of writing, and ink is a material applied to a page.

practice.stem: Mammal is to bat as —
practice.explain: A bat is a kind of mammal even though it flies, and a penguin is a kind of bird even though it doesn't. A dolphin is a mammal, not a fish, and a spider is an arachnid, not an insect, so those pairs state false memberships. Ocean is to whale is habitat, and a bird is one member of a flock, not a kind of flock.

practice.stem: Tile is to mosaic as —
practice.explain: A tile is one of many small, repeated pieces that together form a mosaic, and a bead is one of many that form a necklace. A nucleus is part of a cell, but it is a single central part, not one of many repeated units. A frame surrounds a painting, a seed grows into a tree, and necklace is to clasp runs whole to part.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Use two quick tests: is it a piece of, or is it a kind of?
steps: Piece test: can you say 'A is one piece of B'? A keel is a piece of a ship. That's part to whole.
Kind test: can you say 'A is a kind of B'? A frigate is a kind of ship. That's member to category.
A frigate is not a piece of a ship, and a keel is not a kind of ship. Run both tests and the relationship becomes clear.
Then check the direction: is the small one first or the big one first? The answer must go the same way.
Last, check the size of the step: a repeated building block (brick) matches another building block (plank), not one big section.
Piece test
Kind test
Direction check
Size-of-step check

example.stem: Frigate is to warship as falcon is to — (raptor, feather, sparrow, hunt, nest)
steps: Kind test: a frigate is a kind of warship. Yes, so this is member to category.
A falcon is a kind of raptor, a bird of prey. That passes.
A feather is a piece of a falcon (piece, not kind), a sparrow is a different bird, and hunt and nest are what it does and where it lives.

reteach.hook: Piece of, or kind of? Then which way round?

check.stem: Spoke is to wheel as rung is to —
check.explain: A spoke is one of several identical parts of a wheel, and a rung is one of several identical parts of a ladder. Climb is what you do on it and height is what you gain. Step is a near-synonym for rung, not the whole it belongs to, and rope is a different object.

check.stem: Trout is to fish as eagle is to —
check.explain: A trout is a kind of fish, and an eagle is a kind of bird. A feather is a piece of an eagle, a hawk is another kind of bird, and a nest and the sky are its home and its setting.

check.stem: Chapter is to novel as —
check.explain: A chapter is one of the main sections of a novel, and a movement is one of the main sections of a symphony. A library holds books, a conductor leads an orchestra and an author writes a novel. A ticket gets you into a concert but is not part of it.

check.stem: Juror is to jury as —
check.explain: A juror is one member of a jury, and a senator is one member of a senate. Crew is to sailor is the same idea in reverse, group first. A judge delivers a verdict, a lawyer serves a client and a witness gives testimony.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's take it one picture at a time.
steps: Think of a pizza. A slice is a PART of the pizza.
Think of food. Pizza is a KIND of food.
Part means a piece you could cut off. Kind means a type inside a bigger group.
For the first pair, ask: is the first word a slice (part) or a type (kind) of the second?
Then pick the answer that is the same: slice with slice, type with type.

example.stem: Page is to book as leaf is to — (tree, green, root, autumn, forest)
steps: A page is a part of a book.
A leaf is a part of a tree.
Green is its color, a root is another part, autumn is when it falls and a forest is made of trees, not leaves.

reteach.hook: Slice or type? Match it.

check.stem: Toe is to foot as finger is to —
check.explain: A toe is a part of a foot, and a finger is a part of a hand. A nail is a part of the finger itself, and the arm is a larger part farther up. A glove and a ring are things you wear.

check.stem: Oak is to tree as rose is to —
check.explain: An oak is a kind of tree, and a rose is a kind of flower. A thorn and a petal are parts of a rose (parts, not kinds), a garden is where it grows and red is a color.

check.stem: Wheel is to car as —
check.explain: A wheel is a part of a car, and a wing is a part of an airplane. A pilot flies an airplane, fuel goes in a tank and a runway is where a jet takes off. Sky is to cloud is the wrong way round for a part, and a cloud is not really a piece of the sky.

check.stem: Wolf is to pack as fish is to —
check.explain: A wolf is one member of a pack, and a fish is one member of a school. Fins and gills are parts of a fish, the ocean is where it lives and a net is used to catch it.

units.title: Tools, users, actions and functions
units.objective: Decide whether the pair is worker and tool, tool and action, thing and purpose, or worker and product, and refuse the material, place and product traps.

steps: Worker and tool: a plumber uses a wrench, a glazier uses a glass cutter, a blacksmith uses an anvil. Sentence: 'A uses B to do the job.'
Tool and action: a bellows blows air, a winch hauls, an auger bores. Sentence: 'A is used to B.' The answer must be the tool's actual job, not something near it.
Function and purpose: a muffler quiets an engine, a splint holds a broken bone still, a filter removes impurities. Sentence: 'A exists to do B.'
Worker and product: a vintner makes wine, a potter makes pots, a milliner makes hats. Don't confuse what a worker MAKES with what they WORK ON or WORK WITH.
Traps: the worker's material (marble for a sculptor), the workplace (a studio), the finished product when the pair asks for the tool, and the tool when the pair asks for the product.

Learn the specialist trades, because they appear precisely because they're hard: farrier (shoes horses), wainwright (wagons), milliner (hats), chandler (candles or ship supplies), glazier (glass), cartographer (maps).
teach.formula: Worker USES tool · Tool DOES action · Thing EXISTS TO do purpose · Worker MAKES product

worked.stem: Plumb line is to vertical as level is to —
steps: Sentence: a plumb line is a tool used to check that something is truly vertical.
Same sentence with C: a level is a tool used to check that something is truly ___.
A spirit level's bubble centers when a surface is flat across, so it checks horizontal.
Traps: bubble (a part of the tool), carpenter (its user) and flat surface sounds close, but the parallel to 'vertical' is the direction, horizontal.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Lots of analogies are about work. There are four common links.
WHO uses it? A chef uses a knife.
What does it DO? A knife cuts.
What is it FOR? An oven mitt is for protecting your hand.
What does the worker MAKE? A baker makes bread.
Find which link the first pair uses, then pick the option with the same link.
Who uses it?
What does it do?
What is it for?
What does the worker make?

practice.stem: Cobbler is to shoes as cooper is to —
practice.explain: A cobbler is a craftsman who makes and mends shoes, and a cooper is a craftsman who makes barrels. Copper is a sound-alike, and chickens comes from the look-alike word coop. Horses belong to a farrier and wagons to a wainwright.

practice.stem: Whetstone is to sharpen as sieve is to —
practice.explain: A whetstone is used to sharpen, so a sieve is used to strain. Flour is something you might put through a sieve, the material rather than the action, and mesh is what a sieve is made of. A colander is a similar tool, not an action, and pour is a different kitchen action.

practice.stem: Engraver is to burin as —
practice.explain: A burin is the steel cutting tool an engraver uses, so the answer pairs a worker with the tool of the trade: a welder uses a torch. Canvas and clay are materials that a painter and a potter work on, a novel is what an author produces, and a kitchen is a workplace.

practice.stem: Fuse is to overload as —
practice.explain: A fuse exists to protect a circuit against an overload, and sunscreen exists to protect skin against sunburn. Fire is to extinguisher has a protective pair in the reverse order. A thermometer detects a fever rather than preventing it, a symptom is a sign of an illness, and a lock is opened by a key.

practice.stem: Lapidary is to gems as fletcher is to —
practice.explain: A lapidary is a craftsman who cuts and shapes gems, and a fletcher is a craftsman who makes arrows. Feathers are the material a fletcher fits to the arrows, bows are made by a bowyer, and archery is the sport the arrows serve. Letters is a look-alike trap from the word's ending.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Ask one question: what does the first word DO with the second?
steps: Worker and tool: the worker USES it. A pilot uses a yoke; an engraver uses a burin.
Tool and action: the tool DOES it. A saw cuts, a drill bores, a sieve strains.
Thing and purpose: it EXISTS TO do something. A muffler exists to quiet an engine.
Worker and product: the worker MAKES it. A vintner makes wine; a cooper makes barrels.
Uses, does, exists to, makes: four verbs. Choose the right verb for the first pair and keep it for the answer.
USES (worker, tool)
DOES (tool, action)
EXISTS TO (thing, purpose)
MAKES (worker, product)

visual.caption: Pick the verb, keep the verb

example.stem: Vintner is to wine as brewer is to — (hops, beer, barrel, tavern, grapes)
steps: The verb is MAKES: a vintner makes wine.
A brewer makes beer.
Hops are the brewer's material, a barrel is a container, a tavern is a place and grapes are the vintner's material.

reteach.hook: Uses, does, exists to, makes: pick the verb.

check.stem: Plow is to till as scythe is to —
check.explain: A plow is used to till soil, and a scythe is used to reap, cutting grain or grass. Grain is what the scythe cuts, the object rather than the action, and the blade is part of the tool. The field is the place and the farmer is the user.

check.stem: Cartographer is to map as —
check.explain: A cartographer makes maps, and an architect makes blueprints. A pilot uses a chart and a sailor uses a compass, so those pairs are user and tool, not maker and product. A teacher teaches students, and a reader reads a book someone else made.

check.stem: Lock is to secure as alarm is to —
check.explain: A lock exists to secure something, and an alarm exists to warn. A bell is a part of some alarms, a clock may contain one, and fire is one thing it warns about. Sleep is what an alarm clock interrupts, not its purpose.

check.stem: Blacksmith is to hammer as —
check.explain: A blacksmith uses a hammer as a main tool, and a tailor uses a needle. Anvil is to iron pairs a tool with a material, and a recipe is instructions rather than a tool. A doctor treats a patient and a painter produces a portrait.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Two questions do most of the work: what is it for, and who uses it?
steps: Many analogies ask what a thing is FOR. A knife is for cutting. A pen is for writing.
Or WHO uses it. A chef uses a knife. A writer uses a pen.
Or what a worker MAKES. A baker makes bread.
Find which question the first pair answers.
Then answer the same question for the third word.

example.stem: Broom is to sweep as needle is to — (thread, sew, sharp, tailor, cloth)
steps: What is a broom for? Sweeping.
What is a needle for? Sewing.
Thread goes through it, sharp describes it, a tailor uses it and cloth is what it sews.

reteach.hook: What's it for? Who uses it?

check.stem: Scissors is to cut as shovel is to —
check.explain: Scissors are used to cut, and a shovel is used to dig. Dirt is what it moves, a garden is where it's used, a handle is part of it and planting is a different job.

check.stem: Painter is to brush as writer is to —
check.explain: A painter uses a brush, and a writer uses a pen. A book and a story are what the writer makes, paper is the material written on and the reader is the audience.

check.stem: Oven is to bake as freezer is to —
check.explain: An oven is used to bake, and a freezer is used to freeze. Ice is what it makes, cold describes it, food is what goes in and the kitchen is where it stands.

check.stem: Baker is to bread as —
check.explain: A baker makes bread, and a tailor makes a suit. A farmer uses a tractor and a miner wears a helmet, which are tools and gear. A hospital and a desk are places where people work.

units.title: Cause and effect, sequence and stage
units.objective: Tell 'A causes B' from 'A comes before B' and 'A grows into B', and match both the direction and the size of the gap.

steps: Cause and effect: A brings about B. A spark ignites tinder; overwork causes fatigue; a flood causes damage. Sentence: 'A leads to B.'
Check the direction. 'Smoke is to fire' runs effect to cause, so the answer must also put the effect first (puddle is to rain), not the cause first.
Sequence: A comes before B in a fixed order. Dawn before noon, takeoff before landing, draft before final copy. Sentence: 'A comes before B.'
Stage of development: A grows or turns into B. A bud becomes a flower, a fawn becomes a deer, a cadet becomes an officer. Sentence: 'A grows into B.'
Check the gap. If A is immediately before B (Monday to Tuesday), the answer should be next in line too, not two or three steps apart.
Traps: things that merely happen together, the right pair in reverse order, a later stage skipped to, and cause confused with prevention.
teach.formula: Cause → effect · Earlier → later · Young → grown · Keep the arrow's direction and length

worked.stem: Scar is to wound as — (fire is to ash, ash is to fire, bandage is to wound, burn is to blister, smoke is to chimney)
steps: Sentence: a scar is what a wound leaves behind. The pair runs from effect back to cause.
Fire is to ash and burn is to blister are cause to effect: the right link, wrong direction.
A bandage covers a wound, and smoke rises through a chimney. Neither is cause and effect.
Ash is what a fire leaves behind: effect first, cause second, just like the stem.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Some word pairs tell a little story in time.
Cause: one thing makes the other happen. A spark starts a fire.
Order: one thing simply comes first. Morning comes before evening.
Growing: one thing turns into the other. A seed becomes a plant.
Picture an arrow from the first word to the second. Which way does it point?
Your answer's arrow must point the same way and be about the same length.
Cause or order or growth?
Which way does the arrow point?
Next step or a big jump?
Match all three

visual.caption: Draw the arrow, then match it

practice.stem: Inoculation is to immunity as irrigation is to —
practice.explain: Inoculation produces immunity, so irrigation produces growth in crops. Water is what irrigation supplies, the means rather than the result, and a canal is the channel that carries it. Drought is the problem irrigation answers, and the farmer is the person who does it.

practice.stem: Indictment is to trial as —
practice.explain: An indictment, the formal charge, comes before a trial, and a verdict comes before sentencing. Appeal is to verdict runs the other way, because an appeal follows a verdict. A jury sits in a courtroom, a judge uses a gavel, and the defendant and plaintiff are opposing parties, so none of those is a sequence.

practice.stem: Sapling is to oak as —
practice.explain: A sapling is a young tree that grows into a mature oak, and a cygnet is a young swan that grows into an adult swan. An acorn is food for a squirrel, a leaf is part of a branch and a calf is one member of a herd. Seed is to soil names where something is planted, not what it becomes.

practice.stem: Erosion is to wind as —
practice.explain: Erosion is an effect produced by wind, so the pair runs effect to cause, and rust is an effect produced by moisture. Virus is to fever, glacier is to valley and river is to delta are all cause to effect, the right link in the reverse order. Shade prevents sunburn rather than causing it.

practice.stem: Insolvency is to bankruptcy as —
practice.explain: Insolvency, being unable to pay one's debts, can progress to bankruptcy, the more serious legal stage, and an infection can progress to sepsis, its more dangerous stage. Bankruptcy is to debt points back toward a cause, and wealth is to poverty is a pair of opposites. A creditor and a debtor are counterparts, and an audit is carried out by an accountant.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Draw an arrow in your head from the first word to the second.
steps: Ask: does A MAKE B happen, does A just come FIRST, or does A GROW INTO B?
Cause: a spark makes a fire. Order: Monday comes before Tuesday. Growth: a seed grows into a plant.
Now look at the answer. Does its arrow point the same way? A pair with the arrow backwards is the most common trap.
Check the length of the arrow too: next step matches next step. Monday to Tuesday matches March to April, not March to June.
Cause, order or growth?
Which way does the arrow point?
How long is the arrow?
Match all three

example.stem: Tuesday is to Wednesday as Friday is to — (Saturday, Thursday, Sunday, weekend, Monday)
steps: The arrow: Tuesday comes immediately before Wednesday.
Friday comes immediately before Saturday.
Thursday points backward, Sunday and Monday are too far ahead, and weekend is not a single day.

reteach.hook: Draw the arrow; match its direction and length.

check.stem: Friction is to heat as —
check.explain: Friction causes heat, and gravity causes falling: cause first, effect second. Sweat is to exercise and smoke is to fire both run from effect to cause, the reversal. A thermometer measures heat, and sail is to wind puts the thing pushed before the force that pushes it.

check.stem: Cub is to bear as —
check.explain: A cub grows into a bear, and a kitten grows into a cat. Cat is to kitten has the same words with the arrow reversed. A petal and a stem are parts of a plant, a tree is part of a forest and an egg sits in a nest.

check.stem: Overeating is to indigestion as overexertion is to —
check.explain: Overeating causes indigestion, and overexertion causes exhaustion. Exercise is the activity itself, not its result, and energy is what gets used up. A gym is a place, and rest is the cure, not the effect.

check.stem: Third is to fourth as —
check.explain: Third comes immediately before fourth, and seventh comes immediately before eighth. Second is to fifth skips two steps, first is to last spans the whole list and ninth is to eighth goes backward. Half is to quarter is about size, not order.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Some word pairs tell a little story in time.
steps: Cause: one thing makes the other happen. Rain makes the ground wet.
Order: one thing comes right before the other. Morning comes before afternoon.
Growing up: one thing turns into the other. A puppy grows into a dog.
Find the story in the first pair.
Pick the answer that tells the same story, in the same order.

example.stem: Puppy is to dog as kitten is to — (cat, milk, litter, mouse, purr)
steps: Story: a puppy grows up into a dog.
A kitten grows up into a cat.
Milk is what it drinks, litter is a group of kittens, a mouse is what a cat chases and purr is a sound.

reteach.hook: Same story, same order.

check.stem: Rain is to flood as wind is to —
check.explain: Heavy rain can cause a flood, and wind can cause erosion, wearing away soil and rock. A breeze is a kind of wind, not something it causes. A cloud is moved by wind, a kite is flown in it and an umbrella is used in rain.

check.stem: Caterpillar is to butterfly as tadpole is to —
check.explain: A caterpillar turns into a butterfly, and a tadpole turns into a frog. A pond is where it lives, it looks like a fish but isn't one, an egg is the earlier stage and swim is what it does.

check.stem: January is to February as —
check.explain: January comes right before February, and June comes right before July. March is to May skips a month, April is to March goes backward, winter and summer are seasons and a month is part of a year.

check.stem: Sunlight is to sunburn as —
check.explain: Too much sunlight causes sunburn, and too much cold causes frostbite. Shade prevents sunburn rather than causing it. The sun and moon are a pair in the sky, a beach is covered in sand and lotion goes on skin.

units.title: Degree, opposites and lack
units.objective: Spot when B is a stronger form of A, its opposite or its absence, and match the exact size of the step.

steps: Degree: B is a stronger (or weaker) form of A. Damp to saturated, irritate to infuriate, tap to pound. Sentence: 'B is an extreme A.'
Match the size of the step. If the stem goes from mild to extreme, the answer must too. A word that is only a little stronger, or the same strength, is the classic wrong option.
A good quality pushed too far: cautious to timid, firm to rigid, proud to vain. The second word is the same trait gone bad, not its opposite.
Antonym: A is the opposite of B. Lavish and austere, garrulous and taciturn, ephemeral and enduring. The answer must be a true opposite, not a weak contrast or a different quality.

Lack: A means without B. Listless lacks energy, penniless lacks money, tactless lacks diplomacy. Sentence: 'Something A has no B.' Don't confuse lacking with having too much (verbose has too many words).
Traps: the right direction but the wrong degree, a synonym when the pair needs an opposite, and an excess when the pair needs a lack.
teach.formula: Degree: B is extreme A · Opposite: A is the reverse of B · Lack: A has no B

worked.stem: Damp is to saturated as hungry is to — (peckish, full, thirsty, ravenous, appetite)
steps: Saturated means soaked through, the extreme of damp. So the answer is the extreme of hungry.
Peckish is only slightly hungry: right direction, wrong degree.
Full is the opposite, thirsty is a different need, and appetite is the feeling itself, not a degree of it.
Ravenous means extremely hungry, the same jump as damp to saturated.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Picture a volume dial that runs from zero to ten.
Some pairs turn the dial up: warm, then hot, then scorching.
Some pairs flip to the other end: generous and stingy.
Some pairs sit at zero: an empty glass has no water.
For the first pair, ask: turned up, flipped, or at zero? And by how much?
Pick the option that moves the dial the same way, by the same amount.
Turned up? (degree)
Flipped? (opposite)
At zero? (lack)
Same jump, same direction

visual.caption: Where is each word on the dial?

practice.stem: Annoy is to enrage as like is to —
practice.explain: To enrage is to annoy to an extreme degree, so the answer is to like to an extreme degree: adore. Dislike is the opposite, and prefer means to like one thing more than another rather than to like it intensely. Tolerate and notice are both weaker than like.

practice.stem: Arid is to moisture as —
practice.explain: Arid means lacking moisture, and callous means lacking sympathy. Verbose and wealthy are the reverse idea, having many words or much money. Humid describes air that holds a lot of moisture, and sour is one kind of taste.

practice.stem: Prodigal is to thrifty as gregarious is to —
practice.explain: Prodigal (wastefully extravagant) is the opposite of thrifty, so the answer is the opposite of gregarious (fond of company): reclusive. Friendly and sociable are near-synonyms of gregarious, the trap for anyone who reads a likeness instead of an opposite. Talkative is a related trait, and generous is linked to the first pair, not to gregarious.

practice.stem: Brave is to foolhardy as —
practice.explain: Foolhardy is bravery pushed to a harmful extreme, and parsimonious (excessively stingy) is thrift pushed to a harmful extreme. Generous is to stingy, proud is to humble and careful is to careless are opposites, not excess. Honest and truthful mean nearly the same thing, so there is no step at all.

practice.stem: Simmer is to boil as smolder is to —
practice.explain: To simmer is to bubble gently below a full boil, and to smolder is to burn slowly without flame, below a full blaze; the pair runs from the held-back form to the full one. Ash and smoke are products of smoldering, and an ember is a smoldering piece of fuel. Extinguish means to put a fire out, which moves the wrong way.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Picture a volume dial and place each word on it.
steps: Degree pairs turn the dial: quiet, loud, deafening.
Ask where each word sits on the dial. 'Chilly is to frigid' goes from a little to the extreme, so the answer must jump the same way.
Opposites flip the dial to the other end: generous and stingy.
Lack means the dial is at zero: arid has no water, mute has no speech.
For each pair ask: up the dial, flipped, or at zero? Then match it.
Up the dial: degree
Flipped: opposite
At zero: lack
Match the move

visual.caption: Three ways a pair can move

example.stem: Breeze is to gale as drizzle is to — (downpour, shower, mist, puddle, umbrella)
steps: A gale is a very strong wind; a breeze is a light one. The dial goes from low to very high.
Drizzle is light rain. A downpour is very heavy rain, the same jump.
A shower is only moderate, mist is even lighter, and a puddle and an umbrella aren't amounts of rain at all.

reteach.hook: Up the dial, flipped, or at zero?

check.stem: Chuckle is to guffaw as —
check.explain: A chuckle is a quiet laugh and a guffaw a loud, hearty one, and a whisper is quiet speech while a bellow is a loud roar. Shout is to whisper turns the dial the other way. Laugh and cry are opposites, a song is what you sing and listening is the other side of speaking.

check.stem: Odorless is to scent as —
check.explain: Something odorless has no scent, and something silent has no sound. Fragrant, loud and bright all describe having a lot of something, the reverse of lacking it. Smell is to nose pairs a sense with its organ.

check.stem: Ally is to adversary as praise is to —
check.explain: An ally is the opposite of an adversary, so the answer is the opposite of praise: criticism. Compliment, applause and flattery are all forms of praise, near-synonyms rather than opposites, and a reward is something given for good work.

check.stem: Content is to ecstatic as uneasy is to —
check.explain: Ecstatic is the extreme of content, so the answer is the extreme of uneasy: terrified. Nervous and worried are about the same strength as uneasy, so the dial doesn't move enough. Calm is the opposite, and bored is a different feeling.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Three simple ideas: more, opposite, or none.
steps: Some pairs are about HOW MUCH. Warm and hot: hot is more.
Some pairs are opposites: up and down.
Some pairs are about having NONE: an empty glass has no water.
Look at the first pair and ask: more, opposite, or none?
Then find the answer with the same kind of change.

example.stem: Big is to enormous as small is to — (tiny, little, short, large, few)
steps: Enormous is much more than big: the 'more' kind.
So we need much more than small: tiny.
Little is about the same as small, short is about height, large is the opposite and few is about number.

reteach.hook: More, opposite, or none?

check.stem: Cool is to freezing as warm is to —
check.explain: Freezing is the extreme of cool, and scorching is the extreme of warm. Mild and pleasant are about the same as warm, sunny describes the sky and cold is the opposite.

check.stem: Hungry is to famished as tired is to —
check.explain: Famished means very hungry, and exhausted means very tired. Sleepy is about the same as tired, awake is the opposite, a bed is where you rest and a yawn is a sign of tiredness.

check.stem: Day is to night as —
check.explain: Day and night are opposites, and so are victory and defeat. Morning comes before noon, a cloud is in the sky, a week is shorter than a month and a lamp gives light.

check.stem: Bald is to hair as toothless is to —
check.explain: Bald means having no hair, and toothless means having no teeth. A dentist cares for teeth, and the mouth, smile and gums are related to teeth without being what is missing.

units.title: Symbols, sources and places
units.objective: Recognize 'stands for', 'comes from' and 'is found in' pairs, and choose the idea, source or place rather than a fact about the object.

steps: Symbol: A stands for B. A laurel wreath for victory, a white flag for surrender, an olive branch for peace, a skull and crossbones for poison. Sentence: 'A is a symbol of B.'
The answer is the idea the symbol stands for, not a fact about the object. An owl symbolizes wisdom; that it hunts at night or eats mice is irrelevant.
Product and source: B is where A comes from or what A is made from. Linen comes from flax, leather from hides, cork from tree bark. Sentence: 'A is obtained from B.'
Place and dweller (or contents): A is found, kept or made in B. Grain in a granary, weapons in an armory, wine in a cellar. Sentence: 'B is where A is kept.'
Specialist place words to know: apiary (bees), silo (grain or missiles), corral (horses or cattle), arsenal (weapons), cellar (wine), hangar (aircraft).
Traps: the place a product is stored instead of its source (honey is kept in a hive but comes from bees), material and finished product swapped, and objects that merely appear together.
teach.formula: Symbol: A stands for B · Source: A comes from B · Place: A is kept in B

worked.stem: Granary is to grain as aviary is to —
steps: Sentence: a granary is a building where grain is stored.
Same sentence: an aviary is an enclosure where ___ are kept.
The root avi- means bird (as in aviation, which takes its name from birds).
Traps: airplanes (a hangar holds those), seeds (what birds eat) and cages (what an aviary resembles).

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: This group of analogies asks one of three simple questions.
What does it STAND FOR? A heart stands for love.
Where does it COME FROM? Milk comes from a cow.
Where is it KEPT or FOUND? A car is kept in a garage.
Decide which question the first pair answers.
Then ask the same question about the third word, or of each option pair.
Stands for? (symbol)
Comes from? (source)
Kept in? (place)
Same question, same order

practice.stem: Scales is to justice as —
practice.explain: Scales are a symbol of justice, and a dove is a symbol of peace. A gavel is an object a judge uses, so that pair is tool and user, not symbol and idea. A blindfold covers the eyes, a court is where law is applied, and a blade is part of a sword.

practice.stem: Ivory is to elephant as —
practice.explain: Ivory is a material obtained from an elephant, and down is a material obtained from a goose. Honey is stored in a hive, but the hive is a place, not the animal it comes from. Wool is to sweater and leather is to shoe run from material to product, and a field is where cotton grows.

practice.stem: Quiver is to arrows as scabbard is to —
practice.explain: A quiver is the case that holds arrows, and a scabbard is the sheath that holds a sword. Bow goes with arrows, the first pair's world, not with a scabbard. A knight carries a scabbard and a belt holds it up, and a shield is separate equipment.

practice.stem: Mint is to coins as —
practice.explain: A mint is a factory where coins are made, and a foundry is a factory where metal castings are made. A bank, a wallet and a vault store money, bills or gold but don't produce them, so each is a place of storage, not manufacture. Coin is to mint is the stem in reverse.

practice.stem: Pewter is to tin as —
practice.explain: Pewter is an alloy made mostly of tin, and bronze is an alloy made mostly of copper, so each pair runs from an alloy to its main metal. Copper is to bronze is the same link in reverse order. Gold is a material for jewelry, steel can rust and iron is attracted by a magnet, none of which is alloy and main metal.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Three questions cover this whole family.
steps: What does A STAND FOR? A white flag stands for surrender, a laurel wreath for victory. The answer is an idea, not an object.
Where does A COME FROM? Wool comes from sheep, charcoal from wood, maple syrup from sap. The answer is the source, not what the product becomes.
Where is A KEPT or MADE? Bees in an apiary, grain in a granary, coins in a mint.
Make sure the answer asks the same question, in the same order.
Stands for
Comes from
Kept or made in
Same question, same order

visual.caption: Which question does the pair answer?

example.stem: Amber is to resin as charcoal is to — (wood, fire, black, grill, coal)
steps: Amber is hardened tree resin: it comes from resin.
Charcoal is made by heating wood with little air: it comes from wood.
Fire is the process, black is its color, a grill is where it's used and coal is a look-alike fuel, not its source.

reteach.hook: Stands for, comes from, kept in.

check.stem: Hangar is to aircraft as —
check.explain: A hangar is the building where aircraft are kept, and a garage is where a car is kept. A runway is where takeoff happens, fuel powers an engine, a wing is part of a bird and a driver operates a truck.

check.stem: Maple syrup is to sap as —
check.explain: Maple syrup is made from sap, and a raisin is made from a grape. Juice is served in a glass and bread is toasted in a toaster, which are containers and tools. Sugar is sweet, and syrup goes on a pancake.

check.stem: Kennel is to dogs as coop is to —
check.explain: A kennel is where dogs are kept, and a coop is where chickens are kept. Barrels and cooper are traps from the look-alike word cooper, the barrel maker. Pigs are kept in a sty and cows in a barn.

check.stem: Bee is to apiary as horse is to —
check.explain: Bees are kept in an apiary, and horses are kept in a stable. A saddle and a rider go on the horse, hay is what it eats and a herd is a group of horses, not where they are kept.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Some things stand for ideas, some come from other things, and some live somewhere.
steps: Some things stand for an idea. A heart stands for love. A trophy stands for winning.
Some things come from other things. Milk comes from cows. Eggs come from hens.
Some things live or are kept somewhere. A fish lives in a tank; a car is kept in a garage.
Ask which one the first pair is: stands for, comes from or lives in.
Pick the answer that does the same.

example.stem: Milk is to cow as egg is to — (hen, nest, breakfast, shell, farm)
steps: Milk comes from a cow.
An egg comes from a hen.
A nest is where it's laid, breakfast is when it's eaten, the shell is part of it and a farm is a place.

reteach.hook: Stands for, comes from, lives in.

check.stem: Heart is to love as trophy is to —
check.explain: A heart stands for love, and a trophy stands for victory. A shelf is where a trophy sits, gold is what it may be made of and the team and game are who wins it and where.

check.stem: Apple is to tree as —
check.explain: An apple comes from a tree, and an acorn comes from an oak. Oak is to acorn has the same words in reverse order. A pie is made from apples, a basket holds fruit and green is a color.

check.stem: Bird is to nest as bee is to —
check.explain: A bird lives in a nest, and a bee lives in a hive. Honey is what a bee makes, a flower is where it feeds, a sting is how it defends itself and a garden is somewhere it visits.

check.stem: Pool is to swimmer as rink is to —
check.explain: A pool is where a swimmer performs, and a rink is where a skater performs. Ice covers the rink, a hockey puck is equipment, a coach trains the skater and an arena is the larger building.

units.title: Pick-the-pair items and the reversal trap
units.objective: Answer 'A is to B as' items by matching relationship to relationship, left word to left slot, and reject reversed and same-topic pairs.

steps: In the second format the stem gives only one pair ('Timid is to terrified as') and every option is a full pair. You are matching one relationship to another, so name the stem's relationship precisely before reading the options.
Test each option in your sentence with its left word in the A slot and its right word in the B slot. Never swap an option's words to make it fit.
The reversal trap: the right relationship in the wrong order. If the stem is part to whole (petal is to flower), 'tree is to branch' is whole to part and is wrong.
The same-topic trap: an option that uses words from the stem's subject (an aviation stem with an aviation option) but a different relationship. The topic never matters, only the relationship.
The related-but-different trap: both words in the option are clearly linked, but by another relationship, such as a worker and workplace when the stem is a worker and tool.
If two pairs both fit, tighten the sentence: degree (mild to extreme), direction (expert to novice or novice to expert) or exact action (detects versus prevents). One will drop out.
teach.formula: Name the stem link → slot each pair left to right → reject reversals and same-topic decoys

worked.stem: Splint is to fracture as — (crutch is to ankle, fracture is to cast, doctor is to splint, bandage is to cut, X-ray is to bone)
steps: Sentence: a splint holds and protects a fractured bone while it heals.
Fracture is to cast reverses the order, and doctor is to splint is a user and a tool.
X-ray is to bone is an image of something; it detects rather than protects.

Crutch is to ankle shares the medical topic, but a crutch supports walking, not the injury itself, and ankle is a body part, not an injury. Bandage is to cut fits: a bandage covers and protects a cut while it heals.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: In these items every choice is a pair of words, not a single word.
Say how the question's pair is linked: 'A kitten grows into a cat.'
Read the first choice in the same order and put it into your sentence: 'A puppy grows into a dog.' True!
Now try one that's backwards: 'A dog grows into a puppy.' False, even though the words go together.
Check every choice this way, left word first.
The one that makes your sentence true, in order, is the answer.
Name the stem's link
Left word in the left slot
Reversed? Cross it out
Same topic only? Cross it out

visual.caption: Never flip an option to make it fit

practice.stem: Scene is to act as —
practice.explain: A scene is one of the parts that make up an act, and a paragraph is one of the parts that make up a chapter: small to big. Novel is to chapter is the same link in reverse, the classic trap. Author is to novel is maker and work, stage is to curtain pairs two things in a theater, and drama is to tragedy runs category to member.

practice.stem: Gale is to breeze as —
practice.explain: A gale is a strong wind and a breeze a gentle one, so the pair runs strong to weak; a torrent is a violent flow of water and a trickle a feeble one. Drizzle is to downpour has the right idea in reverse, weak to strong. Wind is part of a storm, a hurricane and a tornado are two kinds of storm, and rain falls from a cloud.

practice.stem: Altimeter is to altitude as —
practice.explain: An altimeter is the instrument that shows altitude, and a compass is the instrument that shows heading. Speed is to airspeed indicator is the same link in reverse, the quantity first and the instrument second. The other pairs share the aviation topic but not the link: a pilot works in a cockpit, an airplane uses a runway and a wing produces lift.

practice.stem: Bibliophile is to books as —
practice.explain: A bibliophile is a lover of books, and a gourmet is a lover of fine food. A misanthrope is the opposite, someone who dislikes humanity. A librarian works in a library and a critic judges films, which is work rather than love, and an insomniac is someone who can't sleep.

practice.stem: Neophyte is to virtuoso as —
practice.explain: A neophyte is a beginner and a virtuoso a highly skilled performer, so the pair runs from novice to expert, as apprentice to master does. Virtuoso is to amateur, veteran is to recruit and mentor is to protégé all run from expert to novice, the reversal trap three times over. A dilettante is someone who dabbles in a hobby, a different relationship.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Finish your sentence before you read a single option.
steps: With pick-the-pair items, write the sentence first: 'A scene is one of the parts of an act.'
Read each option left to right and slot it in: 'A paragraph is one of the parts of a chapter.' True? Keep it.
Never flip an option to make it fit. If you have to read it right to left, it's the reversal trap.
Ignore the subject matter. A stem about theater can be answered by a pair about books, ships or weather.
If two still fit, the sentence was too loose. Add one more detail and test again.
Sentence first
Slot each pair left to right
No flipping
Ignore the topic

example.stem: Seed is to tree as — (tree is to seed, egg is to bird, root is to soil, nest is to egg, leaf is to branch)
steps: Sentence: a seed grows into a tree.
Tree is to seed is the reversal. Root is to soil and nest is to egg are about where things are.
Leaf is to branch is part to whole. Egg is to bird passes: an egg develops into a bird.

reteach.hook: Left word in the left slot. No flipping.

check.stem: Colt is to stallion as —
check.explain: A colt is a young male horse that grows into a stallion, and a filly is a young female horse that grows into a mare. Mare is to foal runs from adult to young, the reversal. Herd is to horse is group to member, a horse is kept in a stable and a saddle carries a rider.

check.stem: Coward is to courage as —
check.explain: A coward is someone who lacks courage, and an ignoramus is someone who lacks knowledge. A hero, an athlete and a scholar are all known for HAVING bravery, strength or learning, the opposite link. A miser hoards wealth rather than lacking it.

check.stem: Captain is to ship as —
check.explain: A captain is in charge of a ship, and a conductor is in charge of an orchestra. A pilot sits in a cockpit, which is a place, not something commanded. A passenger rides a train, crew is to captain is people under the leader rather than the leader and what is led, and a sailor works at sea.

check.stem: Whisper is to scream as —
check.explain: A whisper is a soft, small use of the voice and a scream an intense one, and a glance is a brief look while a stare is a long, fixed one. Roar is to murmur goes from strong to weak, the reversal. Look is to see, ear is to sound and voice is to song are different links.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Every choice is a pair. Read each one in the same order as the question.
steps: In these questions, every choice is a pair of words.
First say how the question's pair is linked: 'A kitten grows into a cat.'
Read each choice in the same order: 'A puppy grows into a dog.' That works.
'A dog grows into a puppy.' That's backwards, so it's wrong, even though the words go together.
Pick the pair that works in the same order.

example.stem: Kitten is to cat as — (dog is to puppy, puppy is to dog, cat is to mouse, milk is to kitten, bark is to dog)
steps: Sentence: a kitten grows into a cat.
Dog is to puppy is backwards. Cat is to mouse, milk is to kitten and bark is to dog are other links.
A puppy grows into a dog, in the right order.

reteach.hook: Same link, same order.

check.stem: Glove is to hand as —
check.explain: A glove covers a hand, and a sock covers a foot. Foot is to sock is the same pair backwards. A hat and a coat are two pieces of clothing, a ring may be made of gold and a lace is part of a shoe.

check.stem: Teacher is to student as —
check.explain: A teacher trains a student, and a coach trains an athlete. Patient is to doctor puts the person helped first, the reversal. A student attends a school, a page is part of a book and a player belongs to a team.

check.stem: Small is to tiny as —
check.explain: Tiny is much smaller than small, and huge is much bigger than big, so both pairs step up in strength. Huge is to big steps down, the reversal. Tall and short are opposites, small and little mean the same, and giant and dwarf are opposites.

check.stem: Egg is to chick as —
check.explain: An egg becomes a chick, and a seed becomes a plant. Chick is to egg is the reversal, and a hen lays an egg rather than turning into one. A bird lives in a nest, and a barn is part of a farm.

units.title: When you don't know a word
units.objective: Score on items with an unfamiliar word by fixing the answer slot, decoding roots and eliminating the options you do understand.

steps: The AFOQT uses college-level words on purpose. Meeting one you don't know is normal, and it rarely means you can't get the item right.
Fix the slot first. From the words you do know, decide what kind of word the answer must be: a person, a place, a product, an extreme, a lack. Strike any option that isn't that kind of word.

Decode word parts. -phile means lover, -phobia fear, -cide killing, -ology study of, a- or an- without, avi- bird, hydr- water, mis- hatred, anthrop- human. One part is often enough to fix the relationship.

If an option word is unfamiliar, don't pick it or reject it for that reason alone. Eliminate the known options that fail your sentence. If one known option fits, choose it; if none do, the unfamiliar option is your best bet.
In pick-the-pair items, if you can name a different relationship for an option pair, it's out, even if you can't name the stem's relationship exactly.
There's no penalty for guessing on the AFOQT. Never leave an item blank: eliminate what you can, choose, and move on within about 19 seconds.
teach.formula: Fix the slot · Decode the roots · Cut the known misfits · Unknown survivor wins · Never leave a blank

worked.stem: Oenophile is to wine as — (philatelist is to stamps, cartographer is to maps, glutton is to diet, vintner is to grapes, aviator is to birds)
steps: Oenophile looks strange, but -phile means lover, so the sentence is 'an oenophile is a lover of wine.'
Cartographer is to maps and vintner is to grapes are makers and their work or materials, not lovers. Out.
A glutton overeats, but a diet is not what a glutton loves. Aviator is to birds uses the avi- root as a trap: aviators fly aircraft. Out.
Only philatelist is to stamps remains. A philatelist collects and loves stamps, so the unfamiliar survivor is right.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: A strange word doesn't mean a lost point. Take a breath.
Look at the words you DO know. What sort of answer is needed: a person, a place, a feeling, a thing?
Cross out every option that isn't that sort of word.
Look inside the strange word for a piece you know, like 'aqua' (water) or 'phobia' (fear).
Test the options you understand. Cross out the ones that don't fit.
Choose from what's left and move on. Never leave a blank.

visual.caption: One familiar part can unlock the word

practice.stem: Hydrophobia is to water as acrophobia is to —
practice.explain: Hydrophobia is an abnormal fear of water, and acrophobia, from Greek akron (peak or top), is a fear of heights. Acrobats is a look-alike trap built on the same opening letters. A fear of spiders is arachnophobia, of crowded or open places agoraphobia, and of darkness nyctophobia.

practice.stem: Herpetologist is to reptiles as —
practice.explain: A herpetologist studies reptiles, and an ichthyologist studies fish. A philologist studies language and literature, not philosophy, so that pair is a look-alike with a false link, and a botanist studies plants, not animals. A cardiologist specializes in the heart rather than in surgery as such, and a geologist studies rocks, not maps.

practice.stem: Loquacious is to words as —
practice.explain: A loquacious person pours out words, far more than needed, and a prodigal person pours out money in the same way. A taciturn person is sparing with speech and a miser with wealth, the opposite direction. Verbal is to grammar is only a topic link, and keeping to a budget is restraint, not excess.

practice.stem: Sinecure is to effort as —
practice.explain: A sinecure is a paid position that requires little or no work, so it is defined by a lack of effort, and anarchy is a state defined by the absence of government. Insomnia is a lack of sleep, not of dreams, so that pair has the wrong second word. A monarchy has a king, a regime holds power and labor earns wages, which are all presence, not absence.

practice.stem: Apiarist is to bees as ostler is to —
practice.explain: An apiarist looks after bees, and an ostler looks after horses, traditionally at an inn. Inns and stables are where an ostler works and where the horses are kept, places rather than the animals cared for. Oysters and hostels are sound-alike traps.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Work backwards from the blank before worrying about the strange word.
steps: Decide what KIND of word the answer must be: a place, a tool, a product, a victim, an extreme.
Strike any option that isn't that kind of word. Often only two survive.
Look inside the unknown word for a part you know: -phobia fear, -phile lover, -cide killing, -ology study of, a- or an- without, hydr- water.
If you still aren't sure, pick the option that fits the slot and move on. A wrong answer costs nothing; a blank wastes a free chance.

visual.caption: Split the word, read the parts

example.stem: Regicide is to king as fratricide is to — (brother, father, poison, crime, sister)
steps: -cide means killing, so regicide is the killing of a king and the answer is the victim.
Strike poison and crime: they aren't victims. That leaves brother, father and sister.
Frater- means brother, as in fraternity. Fratricide is the killing of one's brother.

reteach.hook: Know the slot, cut the misfits, crack the root.

check.stem: Matricide is to mother as patricide is to —
check.explain: Matricide is the killing of one's mother (mater), so patricide is the killing of one's father (pater). Country and patriot are traps built from the same root, which also gives patriotism. Sister and family are other relatives, but the root names the father.

check.stem: Ichthyology is to fish as ornithology is to —
check.explain: Ichthyology is the study of fish, and ornithology is the study of birds. Rocks belong to geology and teeth to odontology. Eggs and flight are about birds but are not the whole subject of the field.

check.stem: Bibliophile is to books as anglophile is to —
check.explain: A bibliophile loves books, and an anglophile loves England and English things. Angles and geometry are look-alike traps, and fishing comes from the word angler. Languages is too broad a guess from 'English'.

check.stem: Amorphous is to shape as —
check.explain: Amorphous means without shape (a- not, morph shape), and anhydrous means without water (an- not, hydr water). Shapely, colorful and famous all describe having a lot of something, the reverse. A hydrant supplies water, a look-alike trap that keeps the root but loses the 'without'.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: A strange word doesn't have to cost you the point.
steps: Don't panic when you see a word you don't know.
Step one: look at the words you DO know. What sort of word does the answer need to be?
Step two: cross out options that aren't that sort of word.
Step three: look for a small piece you know inside the hard word, like 'aqua' (water) or 'auto' (self).
Step four: choose, and move on. Never leave it blank.

example.stem: Aquarium is to fish as aviary is to — (birds, water, planes, cages, zoo)
steps: An aquarium is where fish are kept, so the answer is an animal that is kept somewhere.
Water, cages and zoo aren't animals. Planes aren't animals either.
Avi- means bird, so an aviary is where birds are kept.

reteach.hook: Cross out, look inside, choose.

check.stem: Telescope is to far as microscope is to —
check.explain: A telescope helps you see things that are far away, and a microscope helps you see things that are very small (micro- means small). A lens and light are parts of how it works, science is where it's used and a doctor may use one.

check.stem: Biology is to life as geology is to —
check.explain: Biology is the study of life, and geology is the study of the earth (geo- means earth). Maps belong to geography and geometry is math, both look-alikes. Plants are part of biology, and weather is meteorology.

check.stem: Monologue is to one as dialogue is to —
check.explain: A monologue is spoken by one person (mono- means one), and a dialogue is between two (di- means two). Many and none are the wrong numbers, and speech and talk describe both words rather than the number.

check.stem: Pedal is to foot as manual is to —
check.explain: A pedal is worked by the foot (ped- means foot), and something manual is worked by hand (manu- means hand). Book is a trap from the other meaning of manual, a handbook. Machine, worker and gear go with manual work but are not the body part.

afoqt-ar.title: Arithmetic Reasoning
afoqt-ar.blurb: No-calculator word problems: distance, rate and time with wind, fuel and range, work rates, percents, ratios and map scales, averages, mixtures and interest, and unit and time-zone conversions. Learn the method, then prove it on exam-standard questions.

units.title: Distance, rate & time
units.objective: Use D = R × T with wind, head starts, closing and catch-up speeds, and find a true average speed.

steps: Every motion problem runs on one relation: distance = rate × time. Rearranged, time = distance ÷ rate and rate = distance ÷ time.
Keep the units matched. Knots are nautical miles per hour, so time must be in hours: 45 minutes is 0.75 hour, 20 minutes is 1/3 hour, and 2.5 hours is 2 hours 30 minutes.
Wind changes ground speed, not airspeed. Ground speed = airspeed − headwind, or airspeed + tailwind. Distance and time over the ground always use ground speed.
Two craft heading toward each other close the gap at the SUM of their speeds. One chasing another on the same track closes at the DIFFERENCE.
If one starts earlier, first find its head start: its speed × the extra time. Then divide that gap by the closing speed to get the time to meet or catch up.
Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, stops included. Never average the two speeds: you spend longer at the slower speed, so the true average is below the midpoint.
teach.formula: D = R × T · ground speed = airspeed ± wind · catch-up time = head start ÷ (fast − slow)

worked.stem: A tanker leaves base at 0900 flying at 300 knots. A fighter leaves the same base at 1000 on the same track at 500 knots. At what time does the fighter catch the tanker?
steps: Head start: by 1000 the tanker has flown 300 × 1 = 300 nautical miles.
Same direction, so the gap closes at 500 − 300 = 200 knots.
Time to close 300 nautical miles at 200 knots: 300 ÷ 200 = 1.5 hours = 1 hour 30 minutes.
1000 + 1 hour 30 minutes = 1130.
Check: tanker 2.5 h × 300 = 750; fighter 1.5 h × 500 = 750. Same spot ✓.

visual.caption: Cover what you want: time = distance ÷ rate

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Start with a car at 50 mph. In 1 hour it goes 50 miles; in 3 hours, 150 miles. That is D = R × T.
Going backward: 150 miles at 50 mph takes 150 ÷ 50 = 3 hours.
Minutes must become hours before you multiply. Divide by 60: 30 minutes = 0.5 hour, 15 minutes = 0.25 hour, 40 minutes = 2/3 hour.
A headwind is like walking up a down escalator: it takes speed away. A 200-knot aircraft in a 30-knot headwind covers ground at 170 knots.
Two aircraft flying at each other: each hour the gap shrinks by both speeds added. One chasing another: the gap shrinks only by the difference.
For any trip with several legs, add up all the miles and all the hours, then divide once. That is the only true average speed.

practice.stem: A helicopter with an airspeed of 140 knots flies into a steady 20-knot headwind for 2 hours 15 minutes. How far does it travel over the ground?
practice.explain: Ground speed is 140 − 20 = 120 knots and 2 hours 15 minutes is 2.25 hours, so 120 × 2.25 = 270 nautical miles. 315 ignores the wind, 360 treats it as a tailwind, 258 reads 2 hours 15 minutes as 2.15 hours, and 240 drops the 15 minutes.

practice.stem: A supply truck drives 180 miles to a depot at 60 mph, spends 1 hour unloading, then drives the 180 miles back at 36 mph. What is its average speed for the whole trip, including the stop?
practice.explain: The legs take 180 ÷ 60 = 3 hours and 180 ÷ 36 = 5 hours, plus the 1-hour stop, for 9 hours in all; 360 miles ÷ 9 hours = 40 mph. 48 mph averages the two speeds, 45 mph leaves out the stop, 20 mph uses one leg's distance over the whole time, and 36 mph is just the slower leg.

practice.stem: A search aircraft leaves base at 1415 flying at 180 knots. A jet leaves the same base at 1445 on the same track at 300 knots. How far from base is the jet when it catches the search aircraft?
practice.explain: By 1445 the search aircraft is 180 × 0.5 = 90 nautical miles out, and the jet closes at 300 − 180 = 120 knots, so it needs 90 ÷ 120 = 0.75 hour and flies 300 × 0.75 = 225 nautical miles (check: 1.25 h × 180 = 225). 90 is only the head start, 135 multiplies the catch-up time by the slower speed, 375 uses the search aircraft's whole flight time at the jet's speed, and 180 assumes a full hour.

practice.stem: A transport flies 480 nautical miles into a steady headwind in 3 hours, then flies the same route back with the wind behind it in 2 hours. Its airspeed is the same both ways. What is the wind speed?
practice.explain: Ground speeds are 480 ÷ 3 = 160 knots out and 480 ÷ 2 = 240 knots back, so airspeed − wind = 160 and airspeed + wind = 240. Subtracting gives 2 × wind = 80, so the wind is 40 knots (airspeed 200). 80 forgets to halve the difference, 20 halves it twice, 200 is the airspeed, and 160 is the outbound ground speed.

practice.stem: An aircraft must cover 840 nautical miles and land 3 hours 20 minutes after takeoff. It flies the first 2 hours at a ground speed of 300 knots. What ground speed must it hold for the rest of the flight?
practice.explain: After 2 hours it has flown 600 nautical miles, leaving 240 to cover in 1 hour 20 minutes = 4/3 hours, and 240 ÷ 4/3 = 180 knots. 200 reads 3 hours 20 minutes as 3.2 hours, 252 is the average speed for the whole trip, 240 assumes exactly one hour is left, and 405 subtracts only one hour's 300 nautical miles.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Let's put every motion problem into a small table so nothing gets lost.
steps: Draw three columns: rate, time and distance. Give each aircraft (or each leg of a trip) its own row.
Fill in what you know. Any row with two of the three filled gives you the third, because distance = rate × time.
Wind goes in the rate column: always write the ground speed, never the airspeed.
Meeting head-on: the two distances add up to the starting gap. A chase: the two distances are equal at the moment one catches the other.
Average speed: add the distance column, add the time column, then divide the totals.

example.stem: Two jets 1,050 nautical miles apart fly toward each other at 320 knots and 380 knots. How long until they meet?
steps: Rows: jet 1 covers 320t and jet 2 covers 380t in the same time t.
Head-on, the distances add to the gap: 320t + 380t = 1,050, so 700t = 1,050.
t = 1.5 hours = 1 hour 30 minutes. Check: 480 + 570 = 1,050 ✓.

reteach.hook: Toward each other, add. Same way, subtract. Average = total miles ÷ total hours.

check.stem: An aircraft with an airspeed of 210 knots flies 540 nautical miles with a 30-knot tailwind. How long does the flight take?
check.explain: Ground speed is 210 + 30 = 240 knots, and 540 ÷ 240 = 2.25 hours = 2 hours 15 minutes. 2 hours 25 minutes reads 0.25 hour as 25 minutes, 3 hours treats the wind as a headwind, about 2 hours 34 minutes ignores the wind, and 2 hours adds the wind twice.

check.stem: Two trucks start 300 miles apart at the same time and drive toward each other at 55 mph and 45 mph. How far has the slower truck gone when they meet?
check.explain: They close at 55 + 45 = 100 mph, so they meet after 3 hours; the slower truck has gone 45 × 3 = 135 miles. 150 assumes they meet halfway, 165 is the faster truck's distance, 100 is the closing speed for one hour, and 45 is the slower truck's first hour only.

check.stem: A cargo aircraft leaves base at 0900 at 240 knots. A second aircraft leaves the same base at 1000 on the same course at 320 knots. At what time does the second aircraft catch the first?
check.explain: The head start is 240 nautical miles and the gap closes at 320 − 240 = 80 knots, so the catch-up takes 3 hours after 1000: 1300. 1200 adds the 3 hours to 0900, 1045 divides the head start by the faster speed, 1026 divides it by the sum of the speeds, and 1600 doubles the head start.

check.stem: A pilot flies 240 nautical miles at 120 knots and then 240 nautical miles at 240 knots. What is the average speed for the whole 480 nautical miles?
check.explain: The legs take 2 hours and 1 hour, so the average is 480 ÷ 3 = 160 knots. 180 averages the two speeds, 80 divides one leg's distance by the total time, and 120 and 240 are just the two leg speeds.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's go right back to what a speed means, one hour at a time.
steps: A speed tells you how far you go in ONE hour. 60 mph means 60 miles every hour.
Two hours at 60 mph is 60 + 60 = 120 miles. That is why distance = speed × time.
To find the time, ask how many hours of 60 fit into the distance: 180 miles ÷ 60 = 3 hours.
Part hours: 30 minutes is half an hour, so at 60 mph you go 30 miles. 15 minutes is a quarter hour: 15 miles.
Wind just changes the speed number. A 100-knot aircraft with a 20-knot headwind really covers 80 nautical miles each hour.
Last step every time: multiply your answer back and see if you get the distance you started with.

example.stem: A boat travels at 24 mph for 1 hour 45 minutes. How far does it go?
steps: 45 minutes ÷ 60 = 0.75 hour, so the time is 1.75 hours.
Check: 42 ÷ 24 = 1.75 hours ✓.

reteach.hook: Speed is distance in ONE hour. Minutes ÷ 60 = hours.

check.stem: A drone flies at 48 mph for 40 minutes. How far does it fly?
check.explain: 40 minutes is 2/3 hour, and 48 × 2/3 = 32 miles. 19.2 treats 40 minutes as 0.4 hour, 1,920 multiplies by 40 without converting, 1.2 divides 48 by 40, and 8 subtracts.

check.stem: An aircraft with an airspeed of 160 knots flies 350 nautical miles into a 20-knot headwind. How long does the flight take?
check.explain: Ground speed is 160 − 20 = 140 knots, and 350 ÷ 140 = 2.5 hours = 2 hours 30 minutes. 2 hours 50 minutes and 2 hours 5 minutes misread 2.5 hours, about 2 hours 11 minutes ignores the wind, and about 1 hour 57 minutes adds it.

check.stem: An aircraft with an airspeed of 180 knots has a 25-knot tailwind. How far does it travel over the ground in 3 hours?
check.explain: Ground speed is 180 + 25 = 205 knots, and 205 × 3 = 615 nautical miles. 465 subtracts the wind, 540 ignores it, 690 adds it twice, and 205 is one hour's distance.

check.stem: Two cyclists 63 miles apart ride toward each other at 12 mph and 9 mph. How long until they meet?
check.explain: They close at 12 + 9 = 21 mph, and 63 ÷ 21 = 3 hours. 21 hours subtracts the speeds, 7 hours uses only the slower rider, 5.25 hours only the faster one, and 6 hours uses their average speed instead of their combined speed.

units.title: Fuel burn, endurance & range
units.objective: Turn fuel load, burn rate and reserve into endurance and range, convert gallons and pounds, and find a radius of action.

steps: Fuel problems are rate problems: fuel used = burn rate × time, and endurance (hours available) = usable fuel ÷ burn rate.
Take the reserve off first. A 45-minute reserve at 2,000 pounds per hour is 0.75 × 2,000 = 1,500 pounds that the trip may not use.
Range = endurance × ground speed. Wind changes range because it changes ground speed; it does not change how fast the engines burn fuel per hour.
Gallons and pounds: the problem gives the weight per gallon (jet fuel is about 6.7 pounds per gallon, avgas about 6). Gallons × pounds per gallon = pounds; pounds ÷ pounds per gallon = gallons.
Radius of action (fly out, come back on the same fuel): split the TIME so the two distances match. With ground speeds a out and b back and T hours of fuel, a × t = b × (T − t).
Always check the reserve, the unit (gallons or pounds, minutes or hours) and whether the question wants one-way or round-trip distance.
teach.formula: endurance = (fuel − reserve) ÷ burn rate · range = endurance × ground speed

worked.stem: A trainer carries 48 gallons of usable fuel, burns 8 gallons per hour and must land with a 30-minute reserve. At a ground speed of 110 knots, what is its maximum range?
steps: Reserve: 0.5 hour × 8 gallons per hour = 4 gallons.
Fuel for the trip: 48 − 4 = 44 gallons.
Endurance: 44 ÷ 8 = 5.5 hours.
Range: 5.5 × 110 = 605 nautical miles.
Check: 5.5 h + 0.5 h = 6 h, and 6 × 8 = 48 gallons ✓.
Take off the reserve
Fuel left ÷ burn rate = hours
Hours × ground speed = range

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of the fuel as money in a wallet and the burn rate as what you spend each hour.
$60 at $10 an hour lasts 6 hours. In the same way, 60 gallons at 10 gallons per hour lasts 6 hours.
A reserve is money you promise not to spend. A 30-minute reserve at 10 gallons per hour is 5 gallons, so only 55 gallons are for the trip: 5.5 hours.
Now ask how far you go in those hours: hours × ground speed. 5.5 hours at 100 knots is 550 nautical miles.
Wind only changes the ground speed number. Into a 20-knot headwind, that 100-knot aircraft makes 80 knots, so 5.5 hours gets only 440 nautical miles.
If fuel is given in gallons but burn in pounds, convert first so both use the same unit.

practice.stem: A helicopter burns 450 pounds of fuel per hour. How much fuel does it burn on a flight of 2 hours 40 minutes?
practice.explain: 40 minutes is 2/3 hour, so the flight is 8/3 hours and 450 × 8/3 = 1,200 pounds. 1,080 treats 40 minutes as 0.4 hour, 1,170 treats it as 0.6 hour, 900 drops the 40 minutes, and 1,350 rounds the flight up to 3 hours.

practice.stem: An aircraft burns 80 gallons of fuel per hour, and the fuel weighs 6 pounds per gallon. How many pounds of fuel does it burn on a flight of 3 hours 15 minutes?
practice.explain: 3 hours 15 minutes is 3.25 hours, so it burns 80 × 3.25 = 260 gallons, and 260 × 6 = 1,560 pounds. 1,512 reads the time as 3.15 hours, 260 forgets to convert gallons to pounds, 1,440 drops the 15 minutes, and about 43 divides by 6 instead of multiplying.

practice.stem: A light aircraft has 54 gallons of usable fuel, burns 9 gallons per hour and must land with a 45-minute reserve. At a ground speed of 120 knots, what is the greatest distance it can fly?
