steps: A function machine: put a number in, apply the rule, read the number out. Use brackets when the input is negative.
Two machines in a row (composition): the inner one works first, and its output feeds the outer one.
Slope is the stair: rise over run. Count up (or down) and across between two points, or use the formula.
y = mx + b: start at b on the y-axis, then climb m for every 1 step right.
Midpoint is just the average of the x's and the average of the y's.

example.stem: If f(x) = 2x − 5 and g(x) = x², what is f(g(3))?
steps: Inner machine first: g(3) = 9.
Feed it to f: f(9) = 18 − 5 = 13.

reteach.hook: Inside machine first. Slope = rise over run.

check.stem: If f(x) = 5 − x², what is f(3)?
check.explain: f(3) = 5 − 9 = −4. 14 adds the 9, 4 computes (5 − 3)², −1 doubles 3 instead of squaring it, and 2 forgets to square.

check.stem: What is the slope of the line through (1, 2) and (4, 11)?
check.explain: Rise 11 − 2 = 9 over run 4 − 1 = 3: slope 3. 1/3 puts run over rise, 13/5 adds the coordinates, −3 slips a sign, and 9 forgets to divide by the run.

check.stem: Which line passes through (0, −2) with slope 4?
check.explain: The y-intercept is −2 and the slope 4: y = 4x − 2. y = −2x + 4 swaps them, y = 4x + 2 slips the intercept's sign, y = −4x − 2 slips the slope's sign, and y = x/4 − 2 uses the reciprocal slope.

check.stem: What is the midpoint of (2, −6) and (8, 4)?
check.explain: Average each coordinate: ((2 + 8)/2, (−6 + 4)/2) = (5, −1). (3, 5) halves the differences, (10, −2) adds without halving, (5, 1) slips a sign, and (6, 10) gives the differences.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's go back to plugging numbers in and reading a line's equation.
steps: f(x) = 3x + 1 is a rule. f(4) means 'use 4 for x': 3 × 4 + 1 = 13.
The slope is how steep a line is: how far up for each step to the right.
In y = mx + b, the number in front of x is the slope and the number on its own is where the line crosses the y-axis.
A point (x, y) is on a line if putting its x into the equation gives its y.
Distance between points: find the across gap and the up gap, then use Pythagoras.

example.stem: If f(x) = 3x + 1, what is f(4)?
steps: Replace x with 4: 3 × 4 + 1.

reteach.hook: Swap the number in for x, then follow the rule.

check.stem: If f(x) = 2x + 7, what is f(5)?
check.explain: 2 × 5 + 7 = 17. 10 forgets the 7, 12 forgets to double the 5, 24 doubles (5 + 7), and 35 multiplies 5 by 7.

check.stem: What is the slope of y = −3x + 8?
check.explain: The coefficient of x is the slope: −3. 8 is the y-intercept, 3 drops the sign, 8/3 is where the line crosses the x-axis, and −1/3 is the reciprocal of the slope, not the slope.

check.stem: Which point lies on the line y = 2x − 1?
check.explain: At x = 3, y = 6 − 1 = 5, so (3, 5) is on the line. At x = 5, y would be 9; at 0, −1; at 2, 3; and at 1, 1, so the others miss.

check.stem: What is the distance between (1, 1) and (4, 5)?
check.explain: The gaps are 3 across and 4 up, so √(9 + 16) = 5. 7 adds the gaps, 25 forgets the root, √7 roots the sum of the gaps, and 3.5 halves 7.

units.title: Angles, polygons, circles, area & volume
units.objective: Chase angles with parallel lines and triangles, use polygon angle sums, find arcs and sectors, and compute and scale areas and volumes.

steps: A straight line is 180°, a full turn 360°, and a triangle's angles add to 180°. Vertical angles are equal. With parallel lines and a transversal, corresponding and alternate angles are equal, and same-side interior angles add to 180°.

A triangle's exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles. In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal. Any side must be shorter than the sum of the other two.
Polygon interior angles add to (n − 2) × 180°. In a regular polygon each exterior angle is 360° ÷ n, so each interior angle is 180° − 360°/n; a regular hexagon's are 120°.
Circles: C = 2πr = πd and A = πr². An arc or sector is a fraction of the whole circle: central angle ÷ 360°.
Areas: rectangle lw, triangle ½bh, parallelogram bh, trapezoid ½(b₁ + b₂)h. Volumes: box lwh, cylinder πr²h, cone ⅓πr²h, sphere (4/3)πr³.
Scaling: multiply lengths by k and areas multiply by k², volumes by k³. Similar figures have equal angles and proportional sides.
teach.formula: interior sum = (n − 2) × 180° · A = πr² · V(cylinder) = πr²h · V(cone) = ⅓πr²h

worked.stem: A cylindrical tank has radius 3 ft and height 8 ft. A cone with the same base and height sits inside it. What volume of the tank lies outside the cone?
steps: Cylinder: πr²h = π × 9 × 8 = 72π cubic feet.
Cone: ⅓ × 72π = 24π cubic feet.
Outside the cone: 72π − 24π = 48π cubic feet.
Name the shape
Write its formula
Substitute and keep π as π
Units: squared for area, cubed for volume

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Half a turn is 180°. So two angles that make a straight line add to 180°, and the three corners of any triangle add to 180°.
When two lines cross, the angles opposite each other are equal. Parallel lines copy those angles everywhere the cutting line crosses them.
Area counts unit squares inside a shape. A 5 × 3 rectangle holds 15 of them; a triangle is half of a rectangle, so ½ × base × height.
For a circle, the radius goes from the center to the edge. Area is π × r × r and the distance around is 2 × π × r.
A slice of a circle (a sector) is a fraction of the whole: 90° is a quarter, 120° a third.
Volume counts unit cubes: base area × height for boxes and cylinders, a third of that for cones.

practice.stem: What is the measure of each interior angle of a regular octagon?
practice.explain: The interior angles add to (8 − 2) × 180° = 1,080°, and 1,080° ÷ 8 = 135° (or 180° − 360°/8 = 135°). 45° is the exterior angle, 1,080° is the total, 120° belongs to a hexagon, and 140° to a nine-sided polygon.

practice.stem: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Two same-side interior angles measure (3x + 10)° and (5x − 30)°. What is the larger angle?
practice.explain: Same-side interior angles add to 180°: 8x − 20 = 180, so x = 25, giving 85° and 95°. The larger is 95°. 85° is the smaller angle, 70° sets the angles equal (x = 20), 25° is x, and 90° just halves 180°.

practice.stem: A sector of a circle with radius 12 has a central angle of 150°. What is its area?
practice.explain: The sector is 150/360 = 5/12 of the circle: 5/12 × π × 12² = 5/12 × 144π = 60π. 10π is the arc length, 144π the whole circle, 5π uses r instead of r², and 240π uses the diameter as the radius.

practice.stem: A cone has a volume of 54 cubic inches. A second cone has twice the radius and half the height. What is its volume?
practice.explain: Volume varies with r²h: doubling r multiplies by 4 and halving h multiplies by 1/2, so the factor is 2 and the volume is 108. 54 assumes the changes cancel, 216 ignores the halved height, 27 halves the volume, and 432 cubes the radius factor.

practice.stem: In triangle ABC, AB = AC. Side CB is extended past B, and the exterior angle formed at B measures 115°. What is angle A?
practice.explain: The interior angle at B is 180° − 115° = 65°. AB = AC makes angles B and C equal, so C = 65° and A = 180° − 130° = 50°. 65° is angle B, 57.5° treats B as the apex angle, 130° is B + C, and 115° is the exterior angle.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Let's mark every angle you know on a sketch and chase the rest one rule at a time.
steps: Sketch the figure, even roughly, and write each known angle or length on it.
Use one rule per step: straight line 180°, triangle 180°, vertical angles equal, parallel lines copy angles.
Write unknown angles in terms of x and set up one equation from a rule.
For circles, decide first whether you need the edge (circumference, arc) or the inside (area, sector).
For solids, find the base area first, then multiply by the height (and by ⅓ for a cone).

example.stem: A triangle's angles are x, 2x and 3x. What are they?
steps: Triangle rule: x + 2x + 3x = 180, so 6x = 180 and x = 30.
The angles are 30°, 60° and 90°.

reteach.hook: Sketch it, label it, one rule per step.

check.stem: What is the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon?
check.explain: (6 − 2) × 180° = 720°. 1,080° uses 6 × 180°, 540° is a pentagon's sum, 360° is the exterior angle sum, and 120° is one angle of a regular hexagon.

check.stem: A circle has an area of 49π. What is its circumference?
check.explain: πr² = 49π gives r = 7, so C = 2π × 7 = 14π. 7π uses πr, 49π repeats the area, 98π doubles the area, and 28π uses the diameter in 2πr.

check.stem: A triangle has a base of 10 and a height of 7. What is its area?
check.explain: ½ × 10 × 7 = 35. 70 forgets the ½, 17 adds, 24.5 uses the height for both, and 50 uses the base for both.

check.stem: A box measures 3 by 4 by 5. What is its volume?
check.explain: 3 × 4 × 5 = 60. 12 adds the edges, 94 is the surface area, 120 doubles the volume, and 47 is half the surface area.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's rebuild the key facts with simple shapes.
steps: Angles on a straight line add to 180°. If one is 70°, the other is 110°.
When two lines cross, the angles opposite each other are equal.
The three angles of a triangle add to 180°.
Area of a rectangle = length × width. Perimeter = the distance all the way around.
A circle's circumference is 2πr and its area is πr².

example.stem: Two angles make a straight line. One is 70°. What is the other?
steps: A straight line is 180°.

reteach.hook: Line 180, triangle 180, full turn 360.

check.stem: Two angles of a triangle are 48° and 77°. What is the third angle?
check.explain: 180° − 48° − 77° = 55°. 125° is the sum of the two given angles, 235° subtracts from 360°, and 103° and 132° subtract only one of the angles from 180°.

check.stem: A circle has a radius of 5. What is its circumference?
check.explain: C = 2πr = 10π. 25π is the area, 5π forgets the 2, 20π doubles the diameter, and 100π squares the diameter.

check.stem: A rectangle is 9 by 4. What is its area?
check.explain: 9 × 4 = 36. 26 is the perimeter, 13 adds the sides, 18 halves it as if it were a triangle, and 72 doubles it.

check.stem: Two lines cross. One of the angles is 38°. What is the angle directly opposite it?
check.explain: Vertical (opposite) angles are equal: 38°. 142° is the angle next to it on the straight line, 52° is the complement, 322° subtracts from 360°, and 76° doubles it.

units.title: Right triangles & trigonometry
units.objective: Use Pythagoras and its triples, the 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 ratios, SOH-CAH-TOA, exact trig values and the basic identities.

steps: Pythagoras: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse opposite the right angle. Learn the triples 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 9-40-41 and their multiples (6-8-10, 9-12-15).
45°-45°-90° triangle: sides x, x, x√2. 30°-60°-90° triangle: the side opposite 30° is x, opposite 60° is x√3, and the hypotenuse is 2x.
SOH-CAH-TOA from the angle you're using: sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan = opposite ÷ adjacent.
Identities: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ, and sin θ = cos(90° − θ).
Angle of elevation problems: draw the right triangle, label what you know relative to the angle, and pick the ratio that links the known side to the unknown.
teach.formula: a² + b² = c² · sin = O/H, cos = A/H, tan = O/A · 30-60-90 = x : x√3 : 2x · 45-45-90 = x : x : x√2

worked.stem: A 20-foot ladder leans against a wall, making a 60° angle with the level ground. How high up the wall does it reach?
steps: The ladder is the hypotenuse (20) and the height is opposite the 60° angle.
Opposite and hypotenuse means sine: height = 20 × sin 60° = 20 × √3/2 = 10√3.
Check with 30-60-90 ratios: hypotenuse 2x = 20 gives x = 10 (the foot of the ladder), and the long leg is 10√3 ✓.

visual.caption: Label the sides from the angle you're using

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Find the right angle first. The side across from it is the hypotenuse, always the longest side.
Pythagoras: square the two short sides, add them, and that equals the square of the long side. 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5².
Now pick one of the other angles and stand at it. The side across from you is 'opposite'; the side next to you that isn't the hypotenuse is 'adjacent'.
SOH: sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse. CAH: cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse. TOA: tangent = opposite ÷ adjacent.
Half a square cut on the diagonal gives a 45-45-90 triangle: legs x and x, hypotenuse x√2.
Half an equilateral triangle gives a 30-60-90 triangle: short side x, hypotenuse 2x, long leg x√3.

practice.stem: A right triangle has legs of 9 and 40. How long is the hypotenuse?
practice.explain: 9² + 40² = 81 + 1,600 = 1,681 = 41², so the hypotenuse is 41 (a 9-40-41 triple). 49 adds the legs, 31 subtracts them, 1,681 forgets the square root, and about 39 subtracts the squares as if 40 were the hypotenuse.

practice.stem: In a 30°-60°-90° triangle, the side opposite the 60° angle is 9. How long is the hypotenuse?
practice.explain: The long leg is x√3 = 9, so x = 9/√3 = 3√3, and the hypotenuse is 2x = 6√3. 18 treats 9 as the short side, 9√3 multiplies instead of dividing, 3√3 is the short side, and 9√2 uses the 45-45-90 ratio.

practice.stem: In right triangle ABC with the right angle at C, sin A = 5/13. What is tan A?
practice.explain: Opposite = 5 and hypotenuse = 13, so the adjacent side is √(169 − 25) = 12 and tan A = 5/12. 12/13 is cos A, 12/5 is tan B (the reciprocal), 13/12 is the hypotenuse over adjacent, and 5/13 is sin A again.

practice.stem: From a point on level ground 120 ft from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation to the top is 30°. How tall is the tower?
practice.explain: tan 30° = height ÷ 120, so height = 120 × (1/√3) = 120√3/3 = 40√3 ft (about 69 ft). 60 ft uses sin 30°, 120√3 uses tan 60°, 60√3 uses cos 30°, and 240 ft is twice the distance, as if 120 were the short side opposite 30°.

practice.stem: If θ is acute and cos θ = 0.6, what is sin θ × tan θ?
practice.explain: sin θ = √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8 and tan θ = 0.8 ÷ 0.6 = 4/3, so the product is 0.8 × 4/3 = 16/15. 0.48 is sin θ × cos θ, 4/3 is tan θ alone, 0.64 is sin²θ, and 3/4 is the reciprocal of tan θ.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Let's label the three sides from the angle before choosing any ratio.
steps: Mark the angle you're given or looking for.
Label the sides from it: H across from the right angle, O across from your angle, A beside your angle.
Circle the side you know and the side you want. That pair names the ratio: O and H → sin, A and H → cos, O and A → tan.
Write the ratio as an equation and solve: opposite = hypotenuse × sin θ, and so on.
With 30°, 45° or 60°, use exact values or the special-triangle ratios instead of decimals.

example.stem: A right triangle has a hypotenuse of 10 and an angle of 30°. How long is the side opposite the 30° angle?
steps: Known: H = 10. Wanted: O. That's sine.
Check with 30-60-90 ratios: hypotenuse 2x = 10 gives short side x = 5 ✓.

reteach.hook: Label O, A, H from the angle; the pair you have picks the ratio.

check.stem: A right triangle has legs of 6 and 8. How long is the hypotenuse?
check.explain: 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100, so the hypotenuse is 10 (a 6-8-10 triangle). 14 adds the legs, 100 forgets the root, 2√7 subtracts the squares, and 48 multiplies the legs.

check.stem: A 45°-45°-90° triangle has legs of 7. How long is the hypotenuse?
check.explain: Hypotenuse = leg × √2 = 7√2. 14 doubles the leg, 7√3 uses the 30-60-90 ratio, 49 squares the leg, and 3.5√2 divides instead of multiplying.

check.stem: In a right triangle, the side opposite angle A is 8 and the hypotenuse is 17. What is cos A?
check.explain: The adjacent side is √(289 − 64) = 15, so cos A = 15/17. 8/17 is sin A, 8/15 is tan A, 17/15 is hypotenuse over adjacent, and 15/8 is adjacent over opposite.

check.stem: What is sin 30° + cos 60°?
check.explain: sin 30° = 1/2 and cos 60° = 1/2, so the sum is 1. √3 and √3/2 use the 60° sine values, 1/2 counts only one term, and (1 + √3)/2 uses cos 30° in place of cos 60°.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's start with the right angle and the longest side.
steps: A right triangle has one 90° corner. The side across from it is the hypotenuse, the longest side.
The two shorter sides are the legs. Square them, add, and you get the hypotenuse squared.
The 3-4-5 triangle is the famous one: 9 + 16 = 25.
If you know the hypotenuse and one leg, subtract instead: leg² = hypotenuse² − other leg².
Tangent is opposite ÷ adjacent, sine is opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent ÷ hypotenuse.

example.stem: A right triangle has legs 3 and 4. How long is the hypotenuse?

reteach.hook: Leg² + leg² = hypotenuse². SOH-CAH-TOA.

check.stem: A right triangle has a hypotenuse of 13 and one leg of 5. How long is the other leg?
check.explain: 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144, so the leg is 12. 8 subtracts the lengths, √194 adds the squares as if 13 were a leg, 18 adds the lengths, and 144 forgets the root.

check.stem: Which set of side lengths forms a right triangle?
In a right triangle, the side opposite angle A is 3 and the side adjacent to A is 4. What is tan A?
check.explain: tan = opposite ÷ adjacent = 3/4. 4/3 flips it, 3/5 is sin A, 4/5 is cos A, and 5/3 is hypotenuse over opposite.

check.stem: What is sin 30°?
check.explain: In a 30-60-90 triangle the side opposite 30° is half the hypotenuse, so sin 30° = 1/2. √3/2 is sin 60°, √2/2 is sin 45°, 1 is sin 90°, and √3 is tan 60°.

afoqt-rc.title: Reading Comprehension
afoqt-rc.blurb: Short passages, several questions each, about 90 seconds a question. Learn to pin down the main idea, find details fast, infer only what the passage makes certain, read words in context, name the author's purpose and tone, apply an idea to a new case, and spot the three traps: true but unstated, too strong and too narrow.

units.title: Main idea
units.objective: State the one point the whole passage is built to make, and reject choices that are too narrow, too broad or off target.

steps: AFOQT Reading Comprehension gives you 25 questions in 38 minutes on short passages, about 90 seconds a question including the reading. Every answer comes from the passage, not from what you already know.
The main idea is the one point the whole passage is built to make. Every sentence either states it or supports it.
Find it in three moves: name the topic (what it's about), name what the author says about that topic, then check that your statement covers every part of the passage.
Watch the turn words: however, but, yet, in fact. The main idea often comes right after a turn, because the author sets up a common view and then corrects it.
Wrong answers are too narrow (one detail, often a vivid one), too broad (the whole field instead of this passage's point) or off target (true and related, but not what the passage argues).
Final test: if the choice were the passage's title or one-sentence summary, would every sentence fit under it?
teach.formula: Topic + what the author says about it = main idea · covers every part, no more

worked.passage: In clear weather a pilot judges the aircraft's attitude mainly by looking at the horizon. In cloud, that reference disappears, and the brain falls back on the balance organs of the inner ear. These organs detect changes in motion well but cannot sense a steady state. If an aircraft enters a gentle, prolonged turn, the fluid in the inner ear soon stops moving relative to the canal walls, and the turn begins to feel like level flight. When the pilot then rolls level, the inner ear reports a turn in the opposite direction, and a pilot who trusts that sensation may bank back into the original turn without realizing it. For this reason, instrument training stresses one rule above all others: when the body and the instruments disagree, believe the instruments.
worked.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
steps: Topic: how pilots sense the aircraft's attitude when they can't see the horizon.
What the author says: the inner ear can't sense a steady turn, so it gives false signals, and the instruments must be trusted instead.
Too narrow: 'The fluid in the inner ear stops moving in a steady turn.' True, but it is one step in the explanation.
Too broad: 'Many accidents happen in bad weather.' The passage never says this, and it's about a much wider subject.
The answer covers both the problem and the rule that follows from it.
worked.answer: Without a visible horizon, the inner ear can mislead a pilot about the aircraft's attitude, so the instruments must be trusted.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Read the whole passage once without worrying about the question.
Ask yourself: what is this mostly about? Say it in two or three words. That's the topic.
Now ask: what does the writer keep saying about that topic? Say it in one sentence.
Look at the first and last sentences again. They often state the point most clearly.
Read the choices. Cross out any that talk about only one small piece of the passage.
Cross out any that talk about something much bigger than the passage. The one left is the main idea.
Name the topic
What does the author say about it?
Does it cover every part?
Reject too narrow, too broad

visual.caption: The main idea covers the whole passage

practice.passage: The white streaks behind high-flying jets are often mistaken for smoke, but they are mostly ice. Jet engines burn fuel and release hot, moist exhaust. At cruising altitude the surrounding air is often colder than minus 40 degrees, and the water vapor in the exhaust condenses and freezes almost at once, much as a person's breath fogs on a winter morning. Whether a contrail vanishes in seconds or spreads into a sheet of cloud depends on the air it forms in. In dry air the ice crystals quickly turn back into vapor and the trail disappears; in air already close to saturation they persist and can widen for hours. Forecasters have long treated the length of contrails as a rough clue to the humidity of the upper atmosphere.
practice.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Jet engines put more water vapor into the upper atmosphere than any natural source of moisture does.
Forecasters depend on contrails as their main tool for measuring how humid the upper atmosphere is.
Contrails are ice trails formed from exhaust, and how long they last depends on the air's humidity.
A person's breath fogs on a cold morning for the same reason that clouds form in the sky.
Contrails last much longer in dry air than in air that is already close to saturation.
practice.explain: The passage explains what contrails are made of and then what decides whether they vanish or spread: the humidity of the air. Saying forecasters depend on contrails as their main tool is too strong, since the passage calls them only 'a rough clue'. Nothing compares engine vapor with natural sources, the breath comparison is a single illustration, and the claim about dry air reverses the passage.

practice.passage: When the Wright brothers' 1901 glider produced far less lift than their calculations predicted, they did not simply conclude that the design was flawed. They suspected the numbers. The figures they had used, published by earlier experimenters, had never been tested systematically. That autumn the brothers built a small wind tunnel in their Dayton bicycle shop and spent weeks measuring the lift and drag of some two hundred miniature wing shapes. The data showed that a widely used coefficient was wrong and that long, narrow wings performed better than the short, deep ones then in favor. Their 1902 glider, built to the new figures, flew well, and the powered airplane of 1903 grew directly from it. The breakthrough at Kitty Hawk, in other words, was won first in a workshop.
practice.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: The Wright brothers built the first wind tunnel that anyone had ever used to study the shapes of wings.
The Wrights' success rested on careful testing that exposed errors in the data they had first trusted.
The 1901 glider failed because its wings were longer and narrower than those of later designs.
Many of the figures published by early aviation experimenters were careless and unreliable.
The Wright brothers ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, where they built much of their equipment.
practice.explain: The passage moves from the disappointing 1901 glider, to the wind-tunnel tests that showed the published figures were wrong, to the successful 1902 and 1903 machines, and its last sentence sums this up. It never says the Wrights' tunnel was the first, and it says long, narrow wings performed better, the reverse of the glider claim. Calling early experimenters careless overgeneralizes from one wrong coefficient, and the bicycle shop is a minor detail.

practice.passage: When the Wright brothers' 1901 glider produced far less lift than their calculations predicted, they did not simply conclude that the design was flawed. They suspected the numbers. The figures they had used, published by earlier experimenters, had never been tested systematically. That autumn the brothers built a small wind tunnel in their Dayton bicycle shop and spent weeks measuring the lift and drag of some two hundred miniature wing shapes. The data showed that a widely used coefficient was wrong and that long, narrow wings performed better than the short, deep ones then in favor. Their 1902 glider, built to the new figures, flew well, and the powered airplane of 1903 grew directly from it. The breakthrough at Kitty Hawk, in other words, was won first in a workshop.
practice.stem: Which of the following would be the best title for the passage?
options: Kitty Hawk, 1903: The Story of the First Powered Flight
Two Hundred Wings: A Catalog of the Models They Tested
From Bicycles to Biplanes: The Business of Early Flight
Won in the Workshop: How the Wrights Fixed the Numbers
A Complete History of Research Into Aerodynamics
practice.explain: The passage's point is that the breakthrough came from testing in the workshop, which corrected the numbers the Wrights had relied on, and its last sentence says so. The 1903 flight is mentioned only as the result, so a title about Kitty Hawk misses the focus. A catalog of models is too narrow, the bicycle business is a passing detail and a complete history of aerodynamics is far too broad.

practice.passage: During the First World War, many British and American ships were painted in bold stripes and jagged blocks of black, white and blue. The scheme, called dazzle, looked like the opposite of camouflage, and in a sense it was. On the open sea a ship could not be hidden; its smoke and silhouette gave it away. Dazzle aimed instead to confuse a submarine commander, who had only seconds at the periscope to judge a target's speed and heading before firing torpedoes that would take minutes to arrive. Broken patterns made the bow hard to find and the angle hard to read, so an error of a few degrees could send a torpedo astern. Whether dazzle actually saved many ships is still debated, since the wartime records are incomplete, but the reasoning behind it was sound.
practice.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Dazzle paint saved large numbers of British and American ships from submarine attack during the war.
Submarine commanders had only a few seconds at the periscope to aim their torpedoes at a target.
Because the wartime records are incomplete, nothing useful can be learned about the effects of dazzle paint.
Navies of the First World War gave up trying to protect their ships from attack by submarines.
Dazzle was meant to confuse an attacker's aim rather than hide ships, though how well it worked is debated.
practice.explain: The passage explains that dazzle could not hide a ship and instead tried to spoil a submarine commander's estimate of speed and heading, then notes that its success 'is still debated'. Claiming it saved large numbers of ships is too strong for a debated question, and saying nothing useful can be learned twists the point about incomplete records. The periscope timing is one supporting detail, and dazzle itself shows that navies were still trying to protect their ships.

practice.passage: It is often said that the Great Wall of China is the only human-made structure visible from the Moon. The claim appeared in print decades before anyone had been to space, and it has survived largely because it sounds right: the wall is thousands of miles long. Length, however, is not what makes an object visible from far away; width and contrast are. Much of the wall is only a few yards wide and built of local stone and earth that blend with the land around it. From the Moon, a quarter of a million miles away, no individual structure can be seen at all, and even from low orbit astronauts have found the wall hard to pick out, while broad highways, airports and city lights at night stand out far more clearly.
practice.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: A popular claim about the Great Wall is false, since width and contrast, not length, decide what is visible.
The Great Wall of China is the longest structure that human beings have ever built anywhere on the earth's surface.
From low orbit, broad highways, airports and city lights are all easier to pick out than the Great Wall.
No structure built by human beings can be seen from space by an astronaut under any conditions at all.
The story about the Great Wall began with astronauts returning from the Apollo missions to the Moon.
practice.explain: The passage states a popular claim, explains why it sounds right and then shows it is wrong because 'width and contrast', not length, make an object visible from afar. The wall's length is described, but the passage never calls it the longest structure. The comparison with highways and lights is a supporting detail, saying nothing can be seen from space contradicts that same comparison, and the passage says the claim appeared in print before anyone went to space.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Try the headline method.
steps: Imagine the passage is a news story and you must write its headline in about ten words.
Your headline needs the topic plus the point the author makes about it.
Check the headline against the first and last sentences: they usually frame the point.
Find the choice closest to your headline. Throw out choices that fit only one sentence, or that would fit a whole book on the subject.
Write a ten-word headline
Topic plus point
Check first and last sentences
Match the closest choice

example.stem: 'Honeybees cannot see red, but they can see ultraviolet light, which is invisible to people. Many flowers that look plain to us carry ultraviolet patterns that guide bees to the nectar.' What is the main idea?
steps: Topic: how bees see flowers.
Point: bees see ultraviolet, and flowers carry ultraviolet patterns that guide them.
'Bees can't see red' is only one detail, too narrow for the main idea.
example.answer: Bees see flowers differently from people, and many flowers carry ultraviolet patterns that guide them.

reteach.hook: Headline it: topic plus point.

check.passage: Road crews spread salt on icy roads because salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes. A layer of salty water stays liquid at temperatures that would turn plain water to ice. Salt stops working well in severe cold, however. Below about 15 degrees Fahrenheit it melts ice very slowly, and crews often switch to sand, which does not melt anything but gives tires something to grip.
check.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Sand melts ice more quickly than salt does once the temperature drops below about 15 degrees Fahrenheit.
Road crews prefer to spread sand rather than salt in every kind of winter weather.
Salt clears roads by lowering water's freezing point, but in severe cold crews may turn to sand.
A layer of salty water stays liquid at temperatures that would freeze plain water.
Winter driving is dangerous for anyone whose car does not have the proper winter tires.
check.explain: The passage explains how salt works and then its limit in severe cold, when crews switch to sand for grip. Sand 'does not melt anything', so the first choice contradicts the passage, and crews switch only in severe cold, not in every weather. The salty-water point is one detail, and tires are never discussed.

check.passage: Road crews spread salt on icy roads because salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes. A layer of salty water stays liquid at temperatures that would turn plain water to ice. Salt stops working well in severe cold, however. Below about 15 degrees Fahrenheit it melts ice very slowly, and crews often switch to sand, which does not melt anything but gives tires something to grip.
check.stem: Which title best fits the passage?
options: The Hidden Dangers of Black Ice
Salt, Sand and the Limits of De-icing
Choosing Tires That Grip in Snow
How Road Crews Are Hired and Trained
check.explain: The passage covers how salt melts ice and when crews switch to sand, so a title naming both and the limit fits. Why water freezes is off focus, black ice and tires are never discussed and nothing is said about hiring crews.

check.passage: Most birds make a noticeable rustle when they flap, but owls fly almost in silence. The leading edge of an owl's main flight feathers has a comb-like fringe that breaks up the air flowing over the wing, and the soft surface of the feathers absorbs much of the remaining sound. Silent flight lets an owl hear its prey while closing in, and keeps the prey from hearing the owl.
check.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Owls hunt only at night, when the animals they prey on cannot see them coming.
The comb-like fringe on an owl's feathers breaks up the air flowing over the wing.
Most other birds are far too noisy in flight to catch prey with good hearing.
Special features of its feathers let an owl fly almost silently, which helps it hunt.
Owls have sharper hearing than any other kind of bird, which is why they hunt well.
check.explain: The passage describes the two feather features that silence an owl's flight and then why silence helps it hunt. Night hunting and the owl's hearing compared with other birds are never stated. The fringe is one detail, and the passage says other birds rustle, not that they can't catch prey.

check.passage: Most birds make a noticeable rustle when they flap, but owls fly almost in silence. The leading edge of an owl's main flight feathers has a comb-like fringe that breaks up the air flowing over the wing, and the soft surface of the feathers absorbs much of the remaining sound. Silent flight lets an owl hear its prey while closing in, and keeps the prey from hearing the owl.
check.stem: The passage is mainly concerned with
options: the hearing of the animals that owls hunt
how and why owls are able to fly quietly
the differences between the feathers of all birds
the way owls choose places to build nests
why owls are so rarely seen during the day
check.explain: Every sentence is about how an owl's feathers quiet its flight or why that matters for hunting. The prey's hearing is mentioned only as part of the reason. The passage doesn't compare all birds' feathers, and nests and daytime sightings aren't discussed.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: The main idea is what the whole passage is about.
steps: The main idea is what the whole passage is about, not just one part of it.
Step 1: Who or what is the passage about? That's the topic.
Step 2: What does it say about that topic, again and again?
Step 3: Put both into one short sentence.
Step 4: Pick the choice that matches your sentence. If a choice only matches one line, it's too small.

example.stem: 'Penguins cannot fly, but they are superb swimmers. Their wings work like flippers, and their smooth bodies slip easily through cold water.' What is the main idea?
steps: Topic: penguins.
What it keeps saying: they can't fly, but their bodies are made for swimming.
'Their wings work like flippers' is only one detail.
example.answer: Penguins are built for swimming rather than flying.

reteach.hook: Topic plus point, whole passage.

check.passage: A cactus is built to save water. Its thick stem stores water after rare desert rains. Its spines are leaves that have become so narrow they lose almost no water. A waxy coating on the stem slows drying even more.
check.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Cactus spines are a kind of leaf.
Deserts receive very little rain each year.
Cacti are the only plants that are able to live in a desert.
A cactus has several features that help it save water.
A waxy coating protects a cactus from animals.
check.explain: Each sentence names a feature that saves water: the stem stores it, the spines lose almost none and the coating slows drying. Spines being leaves is one detail. Desert rainfall is background, the passage never says only cacti live there and the coating slows drying rather than stopping animals.

check.passage: A cactus is built to save water. Its thick stem stores water after rare desert rains. Its spines are leaves that have become so narrow they lose almost no water. A waxy coating on the stem slows drying even more.
check.stem: Which title fits the passage best?
check.explain: The whole passage is about the ways a cactus saves water. Rain is mentioned once, spines are discussed for saving water rather than hurting, plants of the world is far too broad and the waxy coating is only one feature.

check.passage: Before railroads, most towns kept their own time, set by the sun. Noon in one town could be several minutes away from noon in the next. As trains began to run on tight schedules, this caused confusion and even accidents. In 1883 the railroads of the United States and Canada adopted standard time zones, and towns soon followed.
check.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Trains were the most dangerous way to travel anywhere in North America in the 1800s.
Noon was a different time in every single town in the country.
Local sun time caused trouble for train schedules, so railroads adopted standard time zones.
Clocks were first invented to help the railroads run on time.
Canada adopted standard time zones many years before the railroads of the United States did.
check.explain: The passage explains a problem (each town kept its own sun time), why it mattered for trains and the fix: standard time zones in 1883. It never says trains were the most dangerous travel, clocks were not invented for railroads and the two countries' railroads adopted the zones together. Noon differing between towns is one detail.

check.passage: Before railroads, most towns kept their own time, set by the sun. Noon in one town could be several minutes away from noon in the next. As trains began to run on tight schedules, this caused confusion and even accidents. In 1883 the railroads of the United States and Canada adopted standard time zones, and towns soon followed.
check.stem: The passage is mainly about
options: how the first trains were built
the history of clocks and watches
how the sun is used to set noon
why standard time zones were created
check.explain: The passage builds toward the adoption of standard time zones and explains why it happened. Train building and the history of clocks aren't discussed. Accidents are mentioned as part of the problem, not as the topic, and setting noon by the sun is background.

units.title: Detail questions
units.objective: Locate the sentence that answers a detail question, match its meaning rather than its words, and catch details attached to the wrong thing.

steps: Detail questions ask what the passage SAYS: 'According to the passage…', 'The passage states that…'. The answer is written there, usually in different words.
Pull a key word from the question (a name, number, date or unusual term) and scan for it. Then read the sentence that contains it, plus the one before and after.
Expect a paraphrase. The right choice rarely copies the text; wrong choices often do, borrowing the passage's words but changing the meaning.
Watch the small words that flip a detail: before and after, more and less, some and all, cause and result. A choice can use every right word and still reverse the relationship.
The commonest detail trap is a true fact from the passage attached to the wrong thing: something said about mirrors offered as an answer about lenses. Check what the passage says about THAT thing.
For 'EXCEPT' or 'NOT' questions, find the four choices the passage does state. The one left over is the answer.
teach.formula: Key word → scan → read around it → match the meaning, not the words

worked.passage: Structural icing forms when an aircraft flies through visible moisture, such as cloud or rain, at temperatures near or below freezing. Supercooled droplets, which remain liquid below 32 degrees Fahrenheit, freeze on contact with the airframe. Rime ice forms when small droplets freeze instantly; it is rough, milky and brittle. Clear ice forms when larger droplets flow back across the surface before freezing; it is glossy, heavy and much harder to remove. Both kinds change the shape of the wing, reducing lift and increasing drag, and even a thin, rough layer on the upper surface can raise the speed at which the wing stalls.
worked.stem: According to the passage, clear ice differs from rime ice in that clear ice
steps: Key words: clear ice, rime ice. Find the two sentences that describe them.
Rime: small droplets freeze instantly; it is rough, milky and brittle.
Clear: larger droplets flow back across the surface before freezing; it is glossy, heavy and harder to remove.
So the right choice must say, in other words, that clear ice comes from larger droplets that spread before freezing. A choice saying clear ice is easier to remove would reverse the passage.
worked.answer: Clear ice forms from larger droplets that spread across the surface before they freeze.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: A detail question is a treasure hunt. The answer is hidden in the passage.
Read the question and pick out its most unusual word, a name or a number.
Find that word in the passage. Put your finger on it.
Read the whole sentence around your finger, slowly.
Say in your own words what that sentence tells you.
Pick the choice that means the same thing, even if it uses different words.
Pick the key word
Scan for it
Read the sentence around it
Match the meaning

practice.passage: Before 1823, lighthouses relied on mirrors or thick glass lenses to throw their light toward the sea. Mirrors tarnished quickly, and a single lens large enough to gather a powerful lamp's light would have been impossibly heavy. The French physicist Augustin Fresnel solved the problem by dividing a lens into concentric rings of glass prisms. Each ring bent light toward the same direction, so the assembly worked like one huge lens while using only a fraction of the glass. The first Fresnel lens, installed at the Cordouan lighthouse in France, could be seen from about 20 miles out at sea, and within a few decades the design had spread to lighthouses around the world.
practice.stem: According to the passage, why was a single large lens impractical for a lighthouse?
options: Its surface would have tarnished too quickly.
It would have been far too heavy to use.
It would have bent light in too many directions.
It could not be made in France before 1823.
It needed a stronger lamp than any that existed.
practice.explain: The passage says a single lens big enough 'would have been impossibly heavy'. Tarnishing is what the passage says about mirrors, a true detail attached to the wrong thing. Nothing is said about scattering light, about when lenses could be made in France or about lamps being too weak.

practice.passage: Before 1823, lighthouses relied on mirrors or thick glass lenses to throw their light toward the sea. Mirrors tarnished quickly, and a single lens large enough to gather a powerful lamp's light would have been impossibly heavy. The French physicist Augustin Fresnel solved the problem by dividing a lens into concentric rings of glass prisms. Each ring bent light toward the same direction, so the assembly worked like one huge lens while using only a fraction of the glass. The first Fresnel lens, installed at the Cordouan lighthouse in France, could be seen from about 20 miles out at sea, and within a few decades the design had spread to lighthouses around the world.
practice.stem: The passage states that each ring of prisms in a Fresnel lens
options: was made from a different kind of glass than the rings around it
doubled the brightness of the lamp it surrounded
replaced one of the mirrors used in older lighthouses
bent light toward the same direction as the other rings
used more glass than a solid lens of the same size
practice.explain: The passage says 'Each ring bent light toward the same direction, so the assembly worked like one huge lens.' It never mentions different kinds of glass or doubled brightness. The design replaced mirrors and thick lenses, not one mirror per ring, and the rings used 'only a fraction of the glass', the reverse of the last choice.

practice.passage: Despite their popular name, an aircraft's flight recorders are painted bright orange so that they can be found in wreckage. Most airliners carry two. The cockpit voice recorder captures the crew's conversation, radio calls and background sounds such as alarms and engine noise. The flight data recorder stores hundreds or thousands of measurements, including altitude, airspeed, heading and control positions, several times a second. Both are mounted near the tail, the part of the aircraft most likely to survive a crash, and both are built to withstand intense heat, crushing force and deep-water pressure. An underwater locator beacon attached to each unit begins sending a signal when it is submerged, helping searchers find recorders that have sunk.
practice.stem: According to the passage, the cockpit voice recorder captures all of the following EXCEPT
practice.explain: The passage lists the crew's conversation, radio calls and background sounds 'such as alarms and engine noise' for the voice recorder. Control positions belong to the flight data recorder, along with altitude, airspeed and heading. Mixing up which recorder stores what is the trap.

practice.passage: Despite their popular name, an aircraft's flight recorders are painted bright orange so that they can be found in wreckage. Most airliners carry two. The cockpit voice recorder captures the crew's conversation, radio calls and background sounds such as alarms and engine noise. The flight data recorder stores hundreds or thousands of measurements, including altitude, airspeed, heading and control positions, several times a second. Both are mounted near the tail, the part of the aircraft most likely to survive a crash, and both are built to withstand intense heat, crushing force and deep-water pressure. An underwater locator beacon attached to each unit begins sending a signal when it is submerged, helping searchers find recorders that have sunk.
practice.stem: Which statement about the underwater locator beacon is supported by the passage?
options: It is painted bright orange so that searchers can see it in deep water.
It begins sending a signal at the moment a crash is detected by the aircraft.
It starts transmitting once the recorder it is attached to is under water.
It records the final minutes of sound from the cockpit before an accident.
It is mounted apart from the recorders, in a separate housing near the engines.
practice.explain: The passage says the beacon 'attached to each unit begins sending a signal when it is submerged'. The orange paint is a fact about the recorders, not the beacon, and the signal starts on submersion, not at the moment of a crash. Recording cockpit sound is the voice recorder's job, and the beacon is attached to each recorder, not mounted apart.

practice.passage: Sound travels through air at roughly 760 miles per hour at sea level on a standard day, but that figure is not fixed. The speed of sound depends on the temperature of the air, not on its pressure. In the colder air of the upper atmosphere, sound travels more slowly, which is why an airliner cruising at 35,000 feet reaches Mach 1, the speed of sound, at a lower true airspeed than it would near the ground. Pilots therefore track their speed as a Mach number at high altitude: holding a fixed Mach number keeps the aircraft at the same fraction of the speed of sound even as the air temperature changes along the route.
practice.stem: According to the passage, an airliner at 35,000 feet reaches Mach 1 at a lower true airspeed than it would near the ground because
options: the air pressure at that altitude is lower
pilots track Mach number rather than airspeed
jet engines produce less thrust in thinner air
sound waves lose strength at high altitude
the air at that altitude is colder
practice.explain: The passage says the speed of sound depends on temperature and is slower 'in the colder air of the upper atmosphere', and it draws the airliner example from that. Lower pressure is the tempting answer, but the passage says the speed of sound does not depend on pressure. Tracking Mach number is a result, not a cause, and thrust and the strength of sound waves are never mentioned.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Treat it like a scavenger hunt.
steps: Circle the clue word in the question: a name, a number, a place or an unusual term.
Skim the passage for that clue. Don't reread everything.
Read the whole sentence that contains it, plus the one before and after.
Say in your own words what those lines state, then pick the matching choice.
If a choice has the passage's exact words, slow down and check that the meaning hasn't been flipped.
Circle the clue word
Skim for it
Read around it
Say it, then match it

example.stem: 'The base library opens at 0700 on weekdays and 0900 on Saturdays. It is closed on Sundays except during exam weeks, when it opens at noon.' When does the library open on a Sunday during exam week?
steps: Clue words: Sunday, exam week.
The second sentence: closed on Sundays except during exam weeks, 'when it opens at noon'.
0700 and 0900 are true details about other days, the trap.

reteach.hook: Find the clue word, read around it, match the meaning.

check.passage: A hummingbird's heart can beat more than 1,000 times a minute while it flies. To save energy on cold nights, many hummingbirds enter a state called torpor, in which the heart rate falls to a small fraction of that and body temperature drops sharply. In the morning the bird warms itself by shivering before it can fly again.
check.stem: According to the passage, why do many hummingbirds enter torpor?
options: to recover from long migration flights
to hide from predators in the dark
to slow the growth of their feathers
to save energy on cold nights
to warm their bodies before flying
check.explain: The passage says they enter torpor 'to save energy on cold nights'. Warming up before flying is done by shivering in the morning, the reverse of torpor. Migration, predators and feather growth are never mentioned.

check.passage: A hummingbird's heart can beat more than 1,000 times a minute while it flies. To save energy on cold nights, many hummingbirds enter a state called torpor, in which the heart rate falls to a small fraction of that and body temperature drops sharply. In the morning the bird warms itself by shivering before it can fly again.
check.stem: What does the passage say happens in the morning?
options: The bird shivers to warm up before it flies.
The bird's heart rate falls sharply.
The bird feeds before it starts to shiver.
The bird flies off to a warmer place.
check.explain: The last sentence says the bird 'warms itself by shivering before it can fly again'. A falling heart rate and body temperature describe torpor at night, the wrong time. Feeding and moving to a warmer place are never mentioned.

check.passage: The Panama Canal does not cut across the isthmus at sea level. Ships are raised by a series of locks to Gatun Lake, about 85 feet above the sea, cross the lake, and are then lowered by more locks to the ocean on the other side. The locks are filled by gravity from the lake, so no pumps are needed to move the water.
check.stem: According to the passage, how are the locks filled?
options: by pumps that draw water from the ocean
by rainwater collected in large tanks
by water flowing down from the lake
by seawater pushed in by the tides
by pumps that are powered by the lake
check.explain: The passage says the locks 'are filled by gravity from the lake, so no pumps are needed'. Both pump choices contradict that. Rain tanks and tides are never mentioned.

check.passage: The Panama Canal does not cut across the isthmus at sea level. Ships are raised by a series of locks to Gatun Lake, about 85 feet above the sea, cross the lake, and are then lowered by more locks to the ocean on the other side. The locks are filled by gravity from the lake, so no pumps are needed to move the water.
check.stem: The passage states that Gatun Lake
options: is lower than the ocean on both sides
lies about 85 feet above sea level
was dug out to sit at sea level
is crossed after ships are lowered
needs pumps to keep its water level
check.explain: Ships are raised to 'Gatun Lake, about 85 feet above the sea'. So it is higher, not lower, than the ocean, and the canal is specifically not at sea level. Ships cross the lake before they are lowered, and no pumps are needed.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: A detail question asks about one fact.
steps: A detail question asks about one fact.
Look for words like 'according to the passage' or 'the passage says'.
Pick out the key word in the question.
Find that word in the passage and read that sentence slowly.
Choose the answer that says the same thing as the sentence.

example.stem: 'The museum is free on Tuesdays. On other days, tickets cost $12 for adults and $6 for children.' How much does a child's ticket cost on a Friday?
steps: Key words: child, Friday.
Friday is one of the 'other days', and children pay $6 then.
Free is only on Tuesdays, and $12 is the adult price.

reteach.hook: Find it, read it, match it.

check.passage: A submarine dives by letting seawater into large tanks called ballast tanks. The extra weight makes it sink. To rise, it blows compressed air into the tanks, which pushes the water out and makes the submarine lighter.
check.stem: According to the passage, what makes a submarine sink?
options: water being pushed out of its tanks
the weight of its steel hull
check.explain: Seawater let into the ballast tanks adds weight, and 'The extra weight makes it sink.' Compressed air and pushing water out are how it rises, the reverse. Engines and the hull aren't mentioned.

check.passage: A submarine dives by letting seawater into large tanks called ballast tanks. The extra weight makes it sink. To rise, it blows compressed air into the tanks, which pushes the water out and makes the submarine lighter.
check.stem: What does the compressed air do, according to the passage?
options: lets more seawater into the tanks
pushes the water out of the tanks
check.explain: The air 'pushes the water out and makes the submarine lighter'. Letting seawater in and making it heavier describe diving, the reverse. Engines and breathing tanks aren't mentioned.

check.passage: Some kinds of bamboo are among the fastest-growing plants on Earth. In good conditions, a shoot can grow about three feet in a single day. Bamboo is a grass, not a tree, even though some kinds grow taller than many trees.
check.stem: According to the passage, bamboo is
check.explain: The passage says 'Bamboo is a grass, not a tree.' Some kinds grow taller than many trees, which is not the same as being the tallest plant. It grows fast, not slowly, and forests aren't mentioned.

check.passage: Some kinds of bamboo are among the fastest-growing plants on Earth. In good conditions, a shoot can grow about three feet in a single day. Bamboo is a grass, not a tree, even though some kinds grow taller than many trees.
check.stem: How fast can a bamboo shoot grow, according to the passage?
options: about three feet in a week
about one foot in a day
about three inches in a day
about three feet in a single day
as tall as a tree in a day
check.explain: The passage says 'a shoot can grow about three feet in a single day.' The other choices change the number, the unit or the time, or exaggerate it.

units.title: Inference: certain versus likely
units.objective: Pick the statement the passage makes certain (or, for 'most likely', best supports) in one short step, without outside knowledge or stronger wording.

steps: Inference questions ask what the passage suggests, implies or most likely means: 'It can be inferred that…', 'The author would most likely agree…'. The answer isn't stated, but it must follow from what is.
A good inference is one short step from the text. If you can point to the sentences and say 'so this must be true', you have it.
Certain beats likely. When the question says 'must be true' or 'can be inferred', choose the statement the passage makes certain, not one that is merely plausible.
When the question says 'most likely' or 'suggests', choose the best-supported reading, still built only from the passage's own clues.
Reject choices that need outside knowledge, need two or more leaps, or go further than the passage does (from 'many' to 'most', from 'can' to 'always').
Combine statements: 'Every pilot in the squadron is instrument rated' plus 'Lee is a pilot in the squadron' makes 'Lee is instrument rated' certain, though no sentence says it.
teach.formula: Stated + stated → certain · one short step only · no outside facts, no stronger words

worked.passage: Antarctic ice preserves a record of the ancient atmosphere. As snow piles up and is compressed into ice, it traps tiny bubbles of air. Because each year's snow buries the last, ice deeper in the sheet is older, and scientists who drill out long cylinders of it can measure the gases sealed in bubbles that formed hundreds of thousands of years ago. The deepest cores from East Antarctica reach back about 800,000 years. Over that span, the record shows carbon dioxide rising and falling in step with the cycle of ice ages and warmer periods.
worked.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that a sample taken from near the top of an ice core
steps: Find the relevant statement: each year's snow buries the last, so 'ice deeper in the sheet is older'.
Take one step: if deeper ice is older, ice near the top is younger.
So the air in its bubbles was trapped more recently than the air in deep ice. That is certain, not just likely.
A choice such as 'contains more carbon dioxide' needs information the passage doesn't give, so reject it.
worked.answer: It holds air that was trapped more recently than the air in ice deep in the core.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: To infer means to work something out from clues, like a detective.
The passage gives the clues. You put two of them together.
Example: 'All the cadets wear blue. Kim is a cadet.' You can work out that Kim wears blue.
But you can't work out Kim's age or hometown. There are no clues for those.
So for each choice, ask: do the clues PROVE this? Or would I need to guess?
Pick the choice the clues prove, and nothing that needs a guess.
Find the clue sentences
Take one short step
Proven, or just plausible?
Reject outside facts and strong words

visual.caption: One safe step from the text

practice.passage: Fatigue builds gradually, and tired people are poor judges of how tired they are. For that reason, the wing does not leave rest decisions to the individual. A pilot who has flown more than eight hours in a single day may not be placed on the overnight alert roster that evening, whatever the pilot reports about how alert he or she feels. The rule has one exception: during a declared emergency, the commander may assign any qualified pilot to alert duty after reviewing the pilot's hours. On Tuesday no emergency was declared, and Captain Ortiz flew nine hours across three sorties.
practice.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: Captain Ortiz felt too tired to stand alert duty on Tuesday night.
Pilots usually believe they are more rested than they really are.
Captain Ortiz could not be placed on Tuesday night's alert roster.
The commander reviewed Captain Ortiz's flying hours on Tuesday.
Captain Ortiz will be placed on the alert roster on Wednesday night.
practice.explain: Ortiz flew nine hours, more than eight, so the rule bars Ortiz from that evening's alert roster, and the only exception needs a declared emergency, which there wasn't. How Ortiz felt is never stated, and the rule ignores it anyway. Being 'poor judges' of tiredness is not the same as usually overestimating rest, the commander reviews hours only in an emergency and nothing is said about Wednesday.

practice.passage: Fatigue builds gradually, and tired people are poor judges of how tired they are. For that reason, the wing does not leave rest decisions to the individual. A pilot who has flown more than eight hours in a single day may not be placed on the overnight alert roster that evening, whatever the pilot reports about how alert he or she feels. The rule has one exception: during a declared emergency, the commander may assign any qualified pilot to alert duty after reviewing the pilot's hours. On Tuesday no emergency was declared, and Captain Ortiz flew nine hours across three sorties.
practice.stem: The author would most likely agree that
options: a pilot's own sense of alertness is not a reliable guide for scheduling
pilots should never be allowed to fly more than eight hours in a day
the exception for declared emergencies should be removed from the wing's rule
commanders are better judges of fatigue than the pilots themselves are
fatigue affects newer pilots more severely than experienced ones
practice.explain: The author says tired people 'are poor judges of how tired they are' and that the rule applies 'whatever the pilot reports', so self-reported alertness isn't trusted. The rule limits the alert roster, not daily flying, so the second choice is too strong. The author describes the emergency exception without criticizing it, the commander reviews hours rather than judging fatigue and experience is never mentioned.

practice.passage: Radiation fog forms on calm, clear nights. After sunset the ground gives off heat to the open sky, and the air in contact with it cools. If that air cools to its dew point, the temperature at which it becomes saturated, water vapor condenses into droplets that hang near the ground. A light breeze can deepen the fog by mixing more air down to the cold surface, but a stronger wind usually prevents it, because it stirs the cooled layer with warmer air above. Cloud cover also discourages radiation fog, since clouds absorb much of the heat the ground gives off and send some of it back down. Once the sun rises and warms the ground, the fog typically lifts or burns off by midmorning.
practice.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that radiation fog would be LEAST likely to form on a night that is
options: calm and clear after a rainy day
practice.explain: The passage says a strong wind 'usually prevents it' and cloud cover 'also discourages radiation fog', so a night with both is least favorable. Clear, calm skies are exactly the setting the passage describes for fog. A light breeze can even deepen it, and the rainy-day and humid nights still have the clear sky and still air the passage says fog needs.

practice.passage: Radiation fog forms on calm, clear nights. After sunset the ground gives off heat to the open sky, and the air in contact with it cools. If that air cools to its dew point, the temperature at which it becomes saturated, water vapor condenses into droplets that hang near the ground. A light breeze can deepen the fog by mixing more air down to the cold surface, but a stronger wind usually prevents it, because it stirs the cooled layer with warmer air above. Cloud cover also discourages radiation fog, since clouds absorb much of the heat the ground gives off and send some of it back down. Once the sun rises and warms the ground, the fog typically lifts or burns off by midmorning.
practice.stem: Which statement is best supported by the passage?
options: Radiation fog is the most common kind of fog found in most parts of the world today.
A cloudy night is less favorable for radiation fog than a clear night with the same wind.
Radiation fog always burns off completely by the middle of the morning, whatever the season.
A light breeze always makes an existing layer of radiation fog both thicker and deeper.
Fog will form on any night when the ground loses heat to the open sky after sunset.
practice.explain: Clouds 'absorb much of the heat the ground gives off and send some of it back down', so with the wind the same, a cloudy night cools the ground less and is less favorable. The passage says fog 'typically' lifts by midmorning and that a light breeze 'can' deepen it, so 'always' is too strong in both. Fog needs the air to reach its dew point, so it doesn't form whenever the ground cools, and how common radiation fog is never comes up.

practice.passage: For centuries, sailors could find their latitude easily by measuring the height of the sun or the North Star, but longitude was another matter. Because the earth turns 15 degrees every hour, a navigator who knew the time at his home port and the local time aboard ship could calculate how far east or west he had traveled. Local time was simple to find from the sun. The difficulty was carrying home-port time across the ocean: pendulum clocks failed on a rolling deck, and ordinary watches gained or lost minutes a day. In 1714 the British Parliament offered a large prize for a practical solution. John Harrison, a self-taught clockmaker, spent decades building marine timekeepers, and his fourth, tested at sea in the 1760s, lost only seconds on a voyage across the Atlantic.
practice.stem: It can be inferred that a shipboard watch that lost several minutes a day would have caused a navigator to
options: misjudge how far north or south the ship had sailed
be unable to work out the local time aboard ship
need a pendulum clock to replace the faulty watch
misjudge how far east or west the ship had traveled
qualify for the prize offered by Parliament in 1714
practice.explain: East-west position came from comparing home-port time with local time, so a watch carrying the wrong home-port time would give the wrong longitude. Latitude, north or south, came from the sun or the North Star, not from a clock. Local time came from the sun, pendulum clocks failed at sea, and an inaccurate watch is the opposite of what the prize rewarded.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Use the 'so' test.
steps: Read the choice, then try to finish this sentence: 'The passage says ___, so this must be true.'
If you can fill the blank with words from the passage, the inference holds.
If you need 'probably', 'I know that' or 'usually' to finish it, the choice leans on something outside the passage.
Two stated facts often combine: 'All the trainers are on the north ramp' plus 'This aircraft is a trainer' means it's on the north ramp.
Choose the choice that passes the 'so' test in the fewest steps.
The passage says ___
so ___ must be true
Needed 'probably'? Out
Fewest steps wins

example.stem: 'Every member of the honor guard is over six feet tall. Airman Diaz is a member of the honor guard.' What must be true?
steps: The passage says every member is over six feet, and Diaz is a member.
So Diaz is over six feet tall. No guess needed.
'Diaz was chosen because of height' sounds likely but isn't proven: the passage doesn't say why anyone was chosen.
example.answer: Airman Diaz is over six feet tall.

reteach.hook: The passage says ___, so ___.

check.passage: At the academy, any cadet whose grade point average falls below 2.0 is placed on academic probation. Cadets on probation may not hold a leadership position in their squadron. Last term, Cadet Reyes had a grade point average of 1.8.
check.stem: Which statement must be true?
options: Cadet Reyes failed at least one course.
Cadet Reyes will have to leave the academy.
Cadet Reyes was placed on academic probation.
Cadet Reyes was a squadron leader last term.
check.explain: Reyes's 1.8 is below 2.0, and any cadet below 2.0 is placed on probation, so probation is certain. Failing a course and leaving the academy are possible but not stated. Nothing says Reyes was a leader or how other cadets did.

check.passage: At the academy, any cadet whose grade point average falls below 2.0 is placed on academic probation. Cadets on probation may not hold a leadership position in their squadron. Last term, Cadet Reyes had a grade point average of 1.8.
check.stem: It can be inferred that, while on probation, Cadet Reyes
options: would raise the average above 2.0 the next term
could not hold a leadership position in the squadron
had held a leadership position the previous term
was the only cadet in the squadron on probation
was required to attend extra study classes every single week
check.explain: Reyes was on probation, and cadets on probation may not hold a leadership position, so this follows in one step. Whether the average improves, whether Reyes held a post before, how many cadets are on probation and any extra classes are all unstated.

check.passage: Frogs absorb water and oxygen through their thin, moist skin. Because the skin takes in what is around it, pollutants in the water pass easily into a frog's body. For this reason, biologists often treat a sudden drop in a pond's frog population as an early warning that the water may be polluted.
check.stem: The passage suggests that biologists watch frog populations partly because frogs
options: are the most common animals in ponds
are a major cause of pond pollution
can clean pollutants out of water
may show the effects of pollution early
check.explain: Pollutants pass easily into frogs, so a drop in their numbers works as 'an early warning'. Nothing says frogs are the most common pond animal, and they absorb pollution rather than cause or remove it. The passage says frogs take in oxygen through their skin, not that it is their only way to breathe.

check.passage: Frogs absorb water and oxygen through their thin, moist skin. Because the skin takes in what is around it, pollutants in the water pass easily into a frog's body. For this reason, biologists often treat a sudden drop in a pond's frog population as an early warning that the water may be polluted.
check.stem: Which statement is best supported by the passage?
options: A frog's skin leaves it exposed to substances in the water.
Every drop in frog numbers is caused by pollution.
Frogs always avoid ponds that are polluted.
Frogs drink water only through their mouths.
Pollution harms frogs more than it harms any other kind of animal.
check.explain: The skin 'takes in what is around it', so substances in the water reach the frog easily. A drop is treated as a warning that the water 'may be' polluted, not proof that pollution caused it. Avoiding ponds and drinking through the mouth are unstated, and comparing frogs with every other animal goes beyond the passage.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Inferring is working something out from clues.
steps: To infer means to work something out from clues.
The passage gives clues. You put them together.
Example: 'Maya's umbrella is dripping, and her coat is wet.' You can infer it is raining, or was.
But you can't infer where Maya went: there's no clue for that.
Pick the answer the clues point to, and nothing more.

example.stem: 'When the bell rang, the students closed their books and lined up at the door.' What can you infer?
steps: Clues: the bell rang, then the students packed up and lined up to leave.
So the bell signaled that it was time to leave the room.
You can't tell where they were going or what class it was.
example.answer: The bell signaled that it was time to leave.

reteach.hook: Clues in, one step out.

check.passage: The ranger found large paw prints in the mud by the river, and each print showed sharp claw marks. Next to the prints lay the bones of a fish.
check.stem: What can be inferred from the passage?
options: A bear caught a fish in the river.
The ranger was afraid of the animal.
An animal with claws had been by the river.
It had rained for days before.
The animal lives in a cave somewhere near the river.
check.explain: Prints with claw marks show that a clawed animal walked there. The clues don't say what kind of animal it was, so 'a bear' goes too far. The ranger's feelings, rain and a cave are not in the passage.

check.passage: The ranger found large paw prints in the mud by the river, and each print showed sharp claw marks. Next to the prints lay the bones of a fish.
check.stem: The clues best suggest that the animal
options: had no claws on its paws
lives by the river all year
may have eaten a fish there
check.explain: The fish bones lie next to the prints, so the animal may have eaten there; 'may' keeps the inference safe. Large prints don't fit a house cat, the claw marks contradict 'no claws', and nothing suggests it was hunting the ranger or lives there all year.

check.passage: When Ms. Patel arrived on Friday morning, the office lights were off, the computers were shut down and a sign on the locked door read 'Closed today. Back Monday.'
check.stem: What can be inferred from the passage?
options: The workers are away for a month.
The office is closed until Monday.
The office has closed for good.
The whole building has lost its electric power.
Ms. Patel is the office manager.
check.explain: The sign says 'Closed today. Back Monday.', so the office is closed until Monday. A month away and closing for good contradict the sign, and the lights are off because the office is closed, not because of a power cut. Ms. Patel's job is never stated.

check.passage: When Ms. Patel arrived on Friday morning, the office lights were off, the computers were shut down and a sign on the locked door read 'Closed today. Back Monday.'
check.stem: The sign suggests that the workers
options: left the office in a great hurry
check.explain: 'Back Monday' tells you they plan to return then. Nothing suggests they were fired or moved, and 'Back Monday' doesn't mean they work only on Mondays. A locked office with a neat sign doesn't suggest a hurried exit.

units.title: Vocabulary in context
units.objective: Find the meaning a word has in its sentence, and reject its most common meaning when the context points elsewhere.

steps: These questions quote a word: 'As used in the passage, x most nearly means…'. You need its meaning in THAT sentence, which is often not its most familiar one.
The trap is the everyday meaning. Test writers choose words with several senses (check, sound, novel, arrest, sanction) and put the most familiar sense among the choices.
Cover the word and read the sentence. Predict your own replacement from the context, then find the choice closest to your prediction.
Substitute each choice into the sentence. The right one keeps the sentence's meaning and fits its grammar.
Use contrast and example clues: 'although', 'but', 'instead' and 'unlike' signal an opposite; 'such as' and 'for example' show what the word covers.
Don't choose an option just because it's a harder or rarer word. Choose the one that makes the sentence say what the author meant.
teach.formula: Cover → predict → substitute → beware the common meaning

worked.passage: Wildland firefighters seldom try to put out a large blaze directly. Instead they work to check its spread. Crews cut firebreaks, strips of ground cleared down to bare soil, so that the advancing flames run out of fuel. Where the terrain is too steep for crews, aircraft drop retardant ahead of the fire to coat the vegetation it would otherwise consume. These lines rarely stop a fire on their own; they buy time and give the crews a place to hold their ground while the weather changes.
worked.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'check' most nearly means
steps: Cover the word: 'Instead they work to ___ its spread.'
Context: crews don't try to put the fire out; they cut breaks so it 'runs out of fuel' and drop retardant ahead of it.
Your own word: slow or halt. 'Inspect' is the everyday meaning of check, but you don't inspect a fire's spread.
'Halt or slow' fits the sentence and the whole paragraph.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Lots of words have more than one meaning. 'Bank' can be a place for money or the side of a river.
The question wants the meaning the word has in this one sentence.
Find the sentence and read it with the word blanked out.
Ask: what word would I put in the blank? Think of your own word first.
Now look at the choices. The one closest to your word is the answer.
Be careful: the most usual meaning of the word is often there as a trap.
Cover the word
Predict your own word
Substitute each choice
Beware the common meaning

practice.passage: When aluminum first appeared in the nineteenth century, it was so costly to refine that it was treated as a precious metal; the French emperor Napoleon III is said to have served his most honored guests on aluminum plates. The metal itself was not rare, since it is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust. What was rare was a practical way to free it from the minerals that bind it. That changed in 1886, when Charles Martin Hall in the United States and Paul Héroult in France independently discovered an electrolytic process that made refining cheap. Within a few decades the once-exotic metal had become ordinary enough to wrap sandwiches, and its light weight would soon make it the backbone of aircraft construction.
practice.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'free' most nearly means
practice.explain: The sentence speaks of a way to 'free it from the minerals that bind it', meaning to separate the metal out, so extract. Provide at no charge is the most common meaning of free, the classic trap. Exempt and excuse mean to release from a duty, and unfasten suggests undoing a physical fastening, not refining a metal.

practice.passage: When aluminum first appeared in the nineteenth century, it was so costly to refine that it was treated as a precious metal; the French emperor Napoleon III is said to have served his most honored guests on aluminum plates. The metal itself was not rare, since it is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust. What was rare was a practical way to free it from the minerals that bind it. That changed in 1886, when Charles Martin Hall in the United States and Paul Héroult in France independently discovered an electrolytic process that made refining cheap. Within a few decades the once-exotic metal had become ordinary enough to wrap sandwiches, and its light weight would soon make it the backbone of aircraft construction.
practice.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'exotic' most nearly means
practice.explain: The once-exotic metal had been so costly that it was treated as precious, so exotic here means rare and unusual.
