check.explain: Recording the true count and encouraging him is honest and supportive. Recording 40 is a false official record. Asking for a recount you know isn't needed is stalling. Telling everyone shames him publicly, and handing it to another monitor dodges a decision that is yours.

check.passage: You are counting push-ups during a fitness test for a friend from your commissioning class. He does 38 correct push-ups and then stops; he needs 40 to pass that part of the test. He looks up at you and quietly says, 'Come on, call it 40.' The test supervisor is across the gym running another lane, and no one else is watching your lane.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Ask another monitor to take over his count so you don't have to decide.
Ask the test supervisor to recount, even though you are sure you counted correctly.
Record 38 and encourage him to keep training for his retest.
Record 38, then tell everyone at the test what he asked you to do.
Record 40, since two push-ups won't matter and he's a good officer.
check.explain: Recording 40 is the least effective: it falsifies an official test result for a friend. Telling everyone is cruel but honest, and the recount and the hand-off are evasions, but none of them puts a false number on the record. Recording 38 and encouraging him is most effective.

check.passage: After a temporary duty trip, you notice that finance has paid your $400 travel claim twice. Finance hasn't noticed the duplicate, and it could be months before anyone does. A coworker tells you he once kept a duplicate payment for a year before finance caught it and simply took it back from his pay. You have the money in your account now.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Wait until your next travel claim and mention the duplicate then.
Tell finance about the duplicate now and arrange to pay it back.
Set the money aside and repay it only if finance asks for it.
Keep the money, since finance's mistake is finance's problem to find.
Ask a few friends whether people usually bother reporting duplicate payments.
check.explain: Reporting it now and repaying it is honest and closes the matter. Keeping it is keeping money you know isn't yours. Setting it aside until asked is still hiding it. Waiting for the next claim delays for no reason, and polling friends looks for permission to do the wrong thing.

check.passage: After a temporary duty trip, you notice that finance has paid your $400 travel claim twice. Finance hasn't noticed the duplicate, and it could be months before anyone does. A coworker tells you he once kept a duplicate payment for a year before finance caught it and simply took it back from his pay. You have the money in your account now.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Wait until your next travel claim and mention the duplicate then.
Tell finance about the duplicate now and arrange to pay it back.
Set the money aside and repay it only if finance asks for it.
Keep the money, since finance's mistake is finance's problem to find.
Ask a few friends whether people usually bother reporting duplicate payments.
check.explain: Keeping the money is the least effective: you knowingly keep a payment you aren't owed. Setting it aside until asked and waiting for the next claim are poor, but both plan to return it. Polling friends is a stall. Reporting it now and repaying is most effective.

units.title: Chain of command
units.objective: Fix problems at the lowest level that can solve them, keep your supervisor informed, and know when going around a level is justified.

steps: Solve at the lowest level that can fix it. If it is yours, fix it. If a peer, an NCO or another office owns it, go to them first, directly and early.

No surprises up the chain. Tell your supervisor about anything that affects their decisions, their boss or the mission, ideally before they hear it elsewhere. Fixing a problem and then informing is usually stronger than asking permission for something already in your authority.

Don't skip levels without cause. Going over your boss's head is justified when the boss is the problem in a serious matter (harassment, abuse, safety, illegal acts), when the boss can't be reached and time is critical, or when you've raised a serious issue and it still isn't being handled.

Disagree up, then carry out. If you disagree with a lawful order, raise it privately with facts and a better option. If the decision stands, carry it out fully and don't criticize it to your people. An unlawful or clearly unsafe order is different: you don't carry it out, and you raise it.
Conflicting tasks from two bosses: don't silently pick one. Tell the person giving the newer task about the existing one, follow their decision, and inform the other boss.
Respect other people's chains. You don't direct another flight's airmen or settle another unit's problem yourself; you go through their supervisor.
teach.formula: Lowest level that can fix it · No surprises upward · Skip a level only when the boss is the problem, unreachable and time is short, or a serious issue is stalled

worked.passage: Your flight commander, a captain, told you to have your section's quarterly equipment inventory finished by Friday. On Wednesday the squadron operations officer, a major, stops by and tells you to send two of your three inventory technicians to help prepare for a short-notice exercise starting tomorrow. You cannot do both. Your flight commander is on leave until Thursday morning but can be reached by phone.
worked.stem: Which response is the MOST effective? (Responses: send the technicians without telling anyone; refuse the major because your captain's task came first; tell the major about Friday's deadline, follow his decision and phone your captain; ask the squadron commander to decide; have the technicians work overnight to do both.)
steps: Send the technicians and tell no one: the inventory deadline silently slips and your captain is surprised on Thursday. Poor.
Refuse the major: a senior officer's lawful tasking can't simply be refused, and the exercise may matter more. Poor.
Tell the major about the deadline, follow his decision, and call your captain: the person setting the priority knows the cost, and your boss isn't surprised. Best.
Ask the squadron commander to decide: pushes a routine conflict two levels up before talking to the major. Middle.
Have the technicians work overnight to do both: fatigue and safety risk, and it hides the conflict instead of resolving it. A LEAST candidate.
worked.answer: Tell the major about the Friday deadline, follow his decision, and call your flight commander to let him know.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of the chain of command as a ladder. You stand on one rung; your supervisor is on the rung above you.
When a problem comes up, try to fix it on your own rung first.
If you can't, or it's bigger than your job, step up ONE rung: your supervisor.
Jumping several rungs at once, straight to the commander or the Inspector General, is usually a mistake.
The exception: if the person on the rung above you IS the problem, and it's serious, you go to the next rung up.
And whatever you do, tell your supervisor. Bosses hate surprises.
Fix it at your level
Can't? Go one level up
Boss is the problem? Skip
Always keep the chain informed

practice.passage: Your squadron commander has directed every flight to move to a new 12-hour shift schedule starting next month. You believe it will hurt your flight: two of your airmen are single parents whose childcare closes at 1800, and your own error logs show mistakes rising late in long shifts. Your airmen have started complaining to you about the change, and the commander has said she is open to feedback before the start date.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Implement the change as directed, and tell the two parents to raise their childcare problems with the first sergeant.
Ask the commander for a short meeting, show her the childcare and error data, and propose a fix for both.
Keep your flight on the old schedule and report that it has switched, so your airmen are protected.
Encourage your airmen to file complaints with the Inspector General so the commander is forced to reconsider.
Implement the change without comment, since the commander has decided and it isn't your place to question her.
practice.explain: Bringing the commander facts and a proposed fix is exactly how to disagree with a lawful decision, and she has asked for feedback. Passing the parents to the first sergeant shifts your job to someone else. Faking compliance is disobedience plus a false report. Steering airmen to the IG misuses a complaint channel, and staying silent withholds information the commander wants.

practice.passage: Your squadron commander has directed every flight to move to a new 12-hour shift schedule starting next month. You believe it will hurt your flight: two of your airmen are single parents whose childcare closes at 1800, and your own error logs show mistakes rising late in long shifts. Your airmen have started complaining to you about the change, and the commander has said she is open to feedback before the start date.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Implement the change as directed, and tell the two parents to raise their childcare problems with the first sergeant.
Ask the commander for a short meeting, show her the childcare and error data, and propose a fix for both.
Keep your flight on the old schedule and report that it has switched, so your airmen are protected.
Encourage your airmen to file complaints with the Inspector General so the commander is forced to reconsider.
Implement the change without comment, since the commander has decided and it isn't your place to question her.
practice.explain: Staying on the old schedule while reporting the switch is the least effective: it disobeys a lawful order and adds a false report on top. Pushing airmen toward the IG is a poor, manipulative use of the system, but it isn't dishonest. Silent compliance and passing the parents along are weak but legitimate. Meeting the commander with data and an alternative is the most effective.

practice.passage: You are a second lieutenant. A staff sergeant in your section tells you privately, and clearly upset, that your supervisor, a captain, has repeatedly made sexual comments to her and twice blocked the office doorway so she could not leave. She asks you not to tell the captain she came to you. You are new to the unit, and the captain writes your performance report.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Talk to the captain yourself, tell him what was reported to you, and warn him that it has to stop.
Tell her you must take this to the squadron commander, and point her to the Equal Opportunity office so she knows her options.
Advise her to keep a written log of incidents for a few weeks so there is evidence before anyone is told.
Tell her that, as a new officer, you can't get involved in a complaint about your own rater.
Suggest that she ask for a transfer to another section so she no longer has to work with the captain.
practice.explain: When your own supervisor is the alleged problem in a serious matter, going around him to the commander is justified, and pointing her to the Equal Opportunity office makes sure she knows her formal and informal options. Confronting the captain tips him off and exposes her. Waiting weeks to build a log leaves her at risk. Refusing to get involved abandons her, and a transfer moves the victim instead of the problem.

practice.passage: Your flight commander, a captain, is away on temporary duty and told you to make no changes to the flight's schedule while he is gone. On Tuesday the base issues a severe winter storm warning for tomorrow, and the squadron commander's office tells every flight to submit a plan by 1600 that keeps only essential personnel on shift. Your captain has not answered his phone or email since this morning.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Draft the essential-personnel plan, submit it by 1600, and email the captain explaining what you did and why.
Reply to the squadron office that the plan will have to wait until the captain returns next week.
Ask the squadron office for an extension until you can reach the captain to approve a plan.
Have the flight's senior NCO write and submit the plan in his own name so you aren't seen to override the captain.
Submit the plan you think is right, but don't tell the captain, since he can't be reached anyway.
practice.explain: Telling the squadron the plan must wait a week is the least effective: it ignores a time-critical safety tasking from a higher level and leaves the flight with no storm plan. Asking for an extension stalls, passing it to the NCO dodges ownership, and not telling the captain creates a surprise, but each still moves toward a plan. Submitting on time and informing the captain is most effective; the commander's tasking outranks the captain's general instruction.

practice.passage: Your flight commander, a captain, is away on temporary duty and told you to make no changes to the flight's schedule while he is gone. On Tuesday the base issues a severe winter storm warning for tomorrow, and the squadron commander's office tells every flight to submit a plan by 1600 that keeps only essential personnel on shift. Your captain has not answered his phone or email since this morning.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Draft the essential-personnel plan, submit it by 1600, and email the captain explaining what you did and why.
Reply to the squadron office that the plan will have to wait until the captain returns next week.
Ask the squadron office for an extension until you can reach the captain to approve a plan.
Have the flight's senior NCO write and submit the plan in his own name so you aren't seen to override the captain.
Submit the plan you think is right, but don't tell the captain, since he can't be reached anyway.
practice.explain: The squadron commander's time-critical safety tasking outranks the captain's general 'no changes' instruction, and the captain can't be reached, so you act and then inform him in writing. Asking for an extension delays a plan the storm won't wait for. Having the NCO submit it in his name dodges your responsibility. Not telling the captain leaves him surprised, and refusing outright fails the commander and the airmen.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's ask one question for every response: whose rung is this on?
steps: Every problem belongs on a rung of the ladder: yours, a peer's, your boss's, or higher.
If it's on your rung, the best answer fixes it and tells your boss.
If it's on your boss's rung, the best answer takes it to your boss, with facts and a suggestion.
Skipping a rung is right only when the person on that rung IS the problem in a serious matter, or can't be reached when time is short.
Responses that jump several rungs at once, or push your own problem up without trying, sit in the middle. Responses that refuse to deal with it at all sit at the bottom.

example.stem: Your boss told you to stop using a vendor. Another captain now says that vendor is the only approved source for an urgent part. Your boss is down the hall. Whose rung is this on?
steps: You can't overrule your boss's instruction yourself.
The other captain isn't your boss, so he can't overrule it either.
Your boss is available, so it goes to him today with the new facts.
example.answer: Your boss's rung: take the new information to him today and ask how he wants to proceed.

reteach.hook: Find the rung the problem belongs on, then climb one rung at a time.

check.passage: Your flight commander told you last week to stop ordering supplies from a particular vendor after a late delivery. Today the squadron supply officer, a captain from another flight, tells you that vendor is the only approved source for a part your airmen urgently need to return an aircraft to service. Your flight commander is in his office down the hall this afternoon.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Order the part from the vendor without telling your flight commander, since the supply officer has approved it.
Go to your flight commander today, explain the supply officer's point, and ask how he wants you to proceed.
Refuse to order the part, and tell your airmen the delay is the supply officer's fault.
Ask the squadron commander to settle the disagreement between the two captains.
Wait a week to see whether the two captains sort it out between themselves.
check.explain: Your boss is down the hall and the new fact changes his decision, so take it to him today. Ordering without telling him ignores his instruction. Refusing and blaming the supply officer stalls an urgent repair and damages a working relationship. Going to the squadron commander skips your boss, and waiting a week leaves the aircraft down.

check.passage: Your flight commander told you last week to stop ordering supplies from a particular vendor after a late delivery. Today the squadron supply officer, a captain from another flight, tells you that vendor is the only approved source for a part your airmen urgently need to return an aircraft to service. Your flight commander is in his office down the hall this afternoon.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Order the part from the vendor without telling your flight commander, since the supply officer has approved it.
Go to your flight commander today, explain the supply officer's point, and ask how he wants you to proceed.
Refuse to order the part, and tell your airmen the delay is the supply officer's fault.
Ask the squadron commander to settle the disagreement between the two captains.
Wait a week to see whether the two captains sort it out between themselves.
check.explain: Refusing and blaming the supply officer is the least effective: it does nothing to get the aircraft back, never involves your boss, and turns your airmen against another officer. Ordering behind your boss's back and going to the commander are poor chain-of-command choices, and waiting is passive, but none adds blame. Taking it to your flight commander today is most effective.

check.passage: Senior Airman Vance, who works in another flight, tells you that her supervisor, a staff sergeant, regularly makes her stay late to finish his own work and then signs it as his. She says she hasn't told anyone in her own chain because she is afraid of him. She asks you, a lieutenant she trusts from a base volunteer program, for help.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Go to the staff sergeant yourself and order him to stop.
Tell her it isn't your business because she isn't in your flight.
Advise her to write down dates and details for a few weeks first, then decide whether to report it.
Encourage her to take it to her flight chief or first sergeant, and offer to go with her.
Tell her flight commander everything without letting her know you're going to.
check.explain: Encouraging her to use her own chain, with you alongside, gets the problem to the people who can fix it while respecting her trust. Ordering the staff sergeant yourself oversteps into another flight. Saying it isn't your business abandons her. Keeping notes first delays action, and going behind her back breaks the trust that brought her to you.

check.passage: Senior Airman Vance, who works in another flight, tells you that her supervisor, a staff sergeant, regularly makes her stay late to finish his own work and then signs it as his. She says she hasn't told anyone in her own chain because she is afraid of him. She asks you, a lieutenant she trusts from a base volunteer program, for help.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Go to the staff sergeant yourself and order him to stop.
Tell her it isn't your business because she isn't in your flight.
Advise her to write down dates and details for a few weeks first, then decide whether to report it.
Encourage her to take it to her flight chief or first sergeant, and offer to go with her.
Tell her flight commander everything without letting her know you're going to.
check.explain: Telling her it isn't your business is the least effective: an airman who is afraid of her supervisor reached out to an officer, and walking away leaves the misconduct untouched. Confronting the staff sergeant and going behind her back mishandle it, and note-taking delays, but each moves toward a fix. Encouraging her to go to her chain, with you alongside, is most effective.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and draw the ladder.
steps: You are on the bottom rung. Your supervisor is on the next rung up. The commander is above them.
Your ideas and problems go to your supervisor first.
Your supervisor shouldn't be surprised by something you did or something you know.
There is one big exception: if your supervisor is doing something seriously wrong, like something unsafe or abusive, you go to the next rung up.
Doing nothing is never the best answer.

example.stem: You have an idea to make the duty roster fairer. Your captain made the roster. Who do you take it to first?
steps: The captain is your supervisor and owns the roster.
Going to the commander first would skip him.
Complaining to the airmen would fix nothing.

reteach.hook: Ideas and problems go one rung up, unless that rung is the problem.

check.passage: You are a second lieutenant in a flight of 30 airmen. Your supervisor is the flight commander, a captain, and above him is the squadron commander. You've noticed that the same airmen always end up with holiday duty, and you have an idea for a rotating roster that would spread it evenly. The captain built the current roster and is in his office today.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Email the idea straight to the squadron commander.
Take the rotating-roster idea to the captain and offer to draft it.
Post your new roster on the board and let the captain find out about it when he sees it.
Tell the airmen the current roster is unfair and that the captain won't listen.
Keep the idea to yourself to avoid making waves.
check.explain: The captain owns the roster and is in his office, so he gets the idea first, with your offer to do the work. Emailing the commander skips him. Posting your own roster takes his decision. Telling the airmen he won't listen is unfair to him and untrue, since he hasn't heard it, and keeping quiet wastes a good idea.

check.passage: You are a second lieutenant in a flight of 30 airmen. Your supervisor is the flight commander, a captain, and above him is the squadron commander. You've noticed that the same airmen always end up with holiday duty, and you have an idea for a rotating roster that would spread it evenly. The captain built the current roster and is in his office today.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Email the idea straight to the squadron commander.
Take the rotating-roster idea to the captain and offer to draft it.
Post your new roster on the board and let the captain find out about it when he sees it.
Tell the airmen the current roster is unfair and that the captain won't listen.
Keep the idea to yourself to avoid making waves.
check.explain: Telling the airmen the captain won't listen is the least effective: it undermines your boss with something he never said and fixes nothing. Posting your own roster oversteps and going to the commander skips a level, but both at least try to fix the problem. Keeping quiet is passive. Taking it to the captain is most effective.

check.passage: A technical sergeant in your section tells you that twice this month he has seen your supervisor, a captain, drinking alcohol in his car in the parking lot at lunch and then coming back to sign off aircraft maintenance paperwork. He says he hasn't told anyone else. Your squadron commander's office is down the hall, and the captain writes your performance report.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Ask the technical sergeant to write a signed statement before you decide what to do.
Talk to the captain privately and tell him that he needs to stop drinking at lunch.
Report what you've been told to the squadron commander today.
Tell the technical sergeant it's his report to make and point him to the Inspector General.
Do nothing, since a lieutenant reporting a captain will only cause trouble for you.
check.explain: Your supervisor is the problem and aircraft safety is at stake, so going to the commander today is justified and urgent. Talking to the captain yourself leaves a safety issue in the hands of the person causing it. Passing it back to the sergeant or asking for a statement first delays action. Doing nothing to protect yourself is the worst choice.

check.passage: A technical sergeant in your section tells you that twice this month he has seen your supervisor, a captain, drinking alcohol in his car in the parking lot at lunch and then coming back to sign off aircraft maintenance paperwork. He says he hasn't told anyone else. Your squadron commander's office is down the hall, and the captain writes your performance report.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Ask the technical sergeant to write a signed statement before you decide what to do.
Talk to the captain privately and tell him that he needs to stop drinking at lunch.
Report what you've been told to the squadron commander today.
Tell the technical sergeant it's his report to make and point him to the Inspector General.
Do nothing, since a lieutenant reporting a captain will only cause trouble for you.
check.explain: Doing nothing to protect your own career is the least effective: possible impaired sign-offs on aircraft maintenance are a serious safety risk. Talking to the captain, passing it to the sergeant and waiting for a statement are all weaker than reporting, but each does something. Reporting to the commander today is most effective.

units.title: Leading and developing airmen
units.objective: Choose responses that correct in private, find the cause before the consequence, work through NCOs and develop airmen instead of doing their jobs.

steps: Praise in public, correct in private. Criticizing or embarrassing an airman in front of peers is almost always a LEAST candidate, even when the criticism is deserved.
Find the cause before choosing the consequence. A sudden change in a good performer (lateness, withdrawal, mistakes, sleeping on duty) is a signal. Talk privately first, then decide on discipline.

Match the tool to the problem. The usual ladder is verbal counseling, then a Letter of Counseling, then a Letter of Admonishment, then a Letter of Reprimand. Serious misconduct, safety or integrity breaches can start higher, but jumping to the top for a first, minor problem is a poor answer.
Work through your NCOs. The supervisor owns the airman's day-to-day. Coach and back the supervisor; don't take the airman over yourself or overturn the NCO's decisions without talking to them.
Develop, don't do. When an airman struggles, have them taught, set a clear standard and check. Doing the task yourself, or quietly handing it to someone better, fixes tonight and guarantees a repeat.

People and mission together. If an airman may be at risk of suicide, act now: ask directly, stay with them and get them to help (Ask, Care, Escort). Refer personal problems to the first sergeant, chaplain or helping agencies; don't play counselor or wait.
teach.formula: Praise public, correct private · Cause before consequence · Through the NCO · Teach, don't take over · At risk? Ask, Care, Escort

worked.passage: Airman First Class Lee, three months into the job, keeps turning in shift logs with missing entries. His supervisor, a staff sergeant, has corrected him on the spot twice. Tonight Lee's log is incomplete again, and it is due to the squadron by 0700. You could fix it yourself in about 20 minutes. Lee is otherwise hard-working and well liked.
worked.stem: Which response is the MOST effective? (Responses: fix the log yourself tonight and every night; have the supervisor sit with Lee tonight to finish it and set a checklist; give Lee a Letter of Reprimand; remind the flight at roll call, naming Lee; assign the logs to another airman.)
steps: Fix it yourself every night: the log is done, but Lee never learns and the supervisor is cut out. Middle at best.
Supervisor sits with Lee tonight, finishes the log with him and sets a checklist: meets the 0700 deadline, teaches the skill and keeps the NCO in charge. Best.
Letter of Reprimand: far too high a rung for a new airman's training problem. Poor.
Naming Lee at roll call: public embarrassment. A LEAST candidate.
Give the logs to someone else: fixes the symptom, punishes the other airman and leaves Lee untrained. Poor.
worked.answer: Have the supervisor sit with Lee tonight, complete the log together and set a clear checklist and standard.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think about the best boss you ever had. They probably told you when you'd done well in front of others, and told you when you'd messed up quietly, one to one.
That's the first rule: praise in public, correct in private.
Second rule: when someone who's normally good suddenly slips, ask what's wrong before you punish.
Third rule: as an officer, you usually work through the airman's supervisor, the NCO. You back them up; you don't go around them.
Fourth rule: teach people to do the job. Doing it for them doesn't help them grow.
If someone might hurt themselves, everything else stops: stay with them and get them help right away.
Talk privately
Find the cause
Coach through the NCO
Then choose the consequence

practice.passage: During a flight meeting with 20 airmen, Senior Airman Diaz gives a status update that contains two wrong figures; you know because you reviewed the numbers with his supervisor yesterday. Nothing decided in the meeting depends on the figures. Diaz is usually accurate, is up for promotion this cycle, and looks nervous presenting to the whole flight. The meeting still has ten minutes of agenda left.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Interrupt Diaz, point out both errors to the group, and remind everyone that sloppy work costs promotions.
Say nothing to Diaz, and quietly email the correct figures to everyone who attended the meeting.
Tell Diaz's supervisor to give him a Letter of Counseling for presenting inaccurate data to the whole flight.
Let the meeting continue, then speak with Diaz privately, give him the right figures and ask what happened.
Ignore the errors entirely, since the figures didn't affect anything decided in the meeting.
practice.explain: A private word after the meeting corrects the figures, finds out why a usually accurate airman slipped, and spares him in front of the flight. Correcting him publicly and linking it to promotions humiliates him. Emailing corrections fixes the record but skips the feedback. A Letter of Counseling for a first slip is out of proportion, and ignoring it leaves wrong numbers in circulation.

practice.passage: During a flight meeting with 20 airmen, Senior Airman Diaz gives a status update that contains two wrong figures; you know because you reviewed the numbers with his supervisor yesterday. Nothing decided in the meeting depends on the figures. Diaz is usually accurate, is up for promotion this cycle, and looks nervous presenting to the whole flight. options: Interrupt Diaz, point out both errors to the group, and remind everyone that sloppy work costs promotions.
Say nothing to Diaz, and quietly email the correct figures to everyone who attended the meeting.
Tell Diaz's supervisor to give him a Letter of Counseling for presenting inaccurate data to the whole flight.
Let the meeting continue, then speak with Diaz privately, give him the right figures and ask what happened.
Ignore the errors entirely, since the figures didn't affect anything decided in the meeting.
practice.explain: Calling Diaz out in front of 20 peers and tying it to promotions is the least effective: it humiliates a nervous, usually reliable airman and teaches the flight to fear presenting. The Letter of Counseling over-reacts and ignoring the errors under-reacts, but both are private. Emailing corrections without talking to him is incomplete. A private conversation after the meeting is the most effective.

practice.passage: Airman Brooks, a quiet member of your flight, has missed two duty days this month and gave his gaming console to a coworker last week. Today the coworker tells you Brooks said, 'It won't matter after this weekend anyway.' Brooks is at his desk now. His supervisor is at a medical appointment for the rest of the afternoon, and the first sergeant's office is in the next building.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Go to Brooks now, talk with him privately, ask him directly whether he is thinking of suicide, and stay with him while you get help.
Email his supervisor so she can talk with Brooks when she is back tomorrow morning.
Wait to see whether Brooks shows up on Monday, so you don't embarrass him over a passing remark.
Ask the coworker to keep an eye on Brooks over the weekend and call you if anything happens.
Call the first sergeant and ask him to handle it, without speaking to Brooks yourself.
practice.explain: Waiting until Monday is the least effective: giving away belongings, absences and 'it won't matter after this weekend' are warning signs of suicide, and the weekend is the danger. Emailing the supervisor and handing it to the coworker also delay or delegate, but they at least pass the warning on. Calling the first sergeant gets help but leaves Brooks alone. Going to him now, asking directly and staying with him (Ask, Care, Escort) is most effective.

practice.passage: Two airmen in your flight requested the same holiday week off, and only one can be approved. Their supervisor, a technical sergeant, approved Senior Airman Park because Park asked first. Airman Grant, who was turned down, comes to you directly and says the decision is unfair because Park also had the holidays off last year. You check, and Grant is right. The flight has no written holiday leave policy.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Overturn the decision yourself and approve Grant's leave, then let the supervisor know afterward what you decided and why.
Tell Grant he should have gone to his supervisor, and that you'll note the complaint in his records.
Raise last year's leave with the supervisor privately, let him make the call, and help him write a holiday leave policy.
Approve leave for both airmen and cover the shortfall by working the extra shifts yourself.
Tell both airmen to work it out between themselves and come back to you with a decision.
practice.explain: Talking privately with the supervisor gives him the fact he missed, keeps the decision with the NCO and fixes the real cause, the lack of a written policy. Overturning him yourself undercuts his authority in front of his airmen. Threatening to record Grant's complaint punishes him for raising a fair point. Covering the shifts yourself does an airman's job and leaves the cause, and handing it to the two airmen abdicates a supervisory decision.

practice.passage: Two airmen in your flight requested the same holiday week off, and only one can be approved. Their supervisor, a technical sergeant, approved Senior Airman Park because Park asked first. Airman Grant, who was turned down, comes to you directly and says the decision is unfair because Park also had the holidays off last year. You check, and Grant is right. The flight has no written holiday leave policy.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Overturn the decision yourself and approve Grant's leave, then let the supervisor know afterward what you decided and why.
Tell Grant he should have gone to his supervisor, and that you'll note the complaint in his records.
Raise last year's leave with the supervisor privately, let him make the call, and help him write a holiday leave policy.
Approve leave for both airmen and cover the shortfall by working the extra shifts yourself.
Tell both airmen to work it out between themselves and come back to you with a decision.
practice.explain: Threatening to note Grant's complaint in his records is the least effective: it is reprisal for raising a legitimate concern, and it teaches every airman to stay quiet. Overturning the supervisor undercuts him, and leaving it to the airmen abdicates, but neither punishes anyone for speaking up. Covering the shifts yourself is well meant but doesn't fix the cause. Working it through the supervisor and writing a policy is most effective.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Think of yourself as a coach, not a referee and not a substitute player.
steps: A referee only blows the whistle and hands out penalties. On the SJ, jumping straight to punishment is rarely best.
A substitute player runs onto the field and does the job. Doing an airman's work for them is rarely best either.
A coach finds out what went wrong, teaches, sets the standard and checks back, through the team's own leaders (the NCOs).
A coach praises in front of the team and corrects one to one.
Pick the coach answer for MOST. The answer that humiliates someone or punishes them for speaking up is usually LEAST.

example.stem: A new airman made a costly mistake on a form he was never trained on. Referee, substitute or coach: which is the best response?
steps: Referee: give him a letter. Unfair, because the cause was missing training.
Substitute: do his forms yourself. He never learns.
Coach: get him trained this week and check the process catches errors.
example.answer: The coach: arrange the training and fix the process.

reteach.hook: Coach, don't referee, and don't play the position yourself.

check.passage: Airman First Class Silva, new to your flight, filled out a shipping document incorrectly and sent a pallet of parts to the wrong base, costing two days. Silva's supervisor, a staff sergeant, tells you Silva was never trained on that document because the flight's trainer was deployed. Silva is embarrassed and has apologized. Two other new airmen are also waiting for the same training.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Have the supervisor give Silva a verbal counseling for the error, note it, and then move on.
Take over all of the flight's shipping documents yourself until the trainer is back from deployment.
Tell the flight at roll call what Silva did so the others learn from it.
Ignore the error, since it wasn't Silva's fault and it's in the past.
Have the supervisor get all three new airmen trained this week, and add a pre-shipment check.
check.explain: Training all three new airmen and adding a check fixes the real cause and protects the next shipment. A counseling punishes Silva for a training gap. Doing the documents yourself is the substitute-player trap. Naming Silva at roll call humiliates him, and ignoring it leaves two more untrained airmen.

check.passage: Airman First Class Silva, new to your flight, filled out a shipping document incorrectly and sent a pallet of parts to the wrong base, costing two days. Silva's supervisor, a staff sergeant, tells you Silva was never trained on that document because the flight's trainer was deployed. Silva is embarrassed and has apologized. Two other new airmen are also waiting for the same training.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Have the supervisor give Silva a verbal counseling for the error, note it, and then move on.
Take over all of the flight's shipping documents yourself until the trainer is back from deployment.
Tell the flight at roll call what Silva did so the others learn from it.
Ignore the error, since it wasn't Silva's fault and it's in the past.
Have the supervisor get all three new airmen trained this week, and add a pre-shipment check.
check.explain: Naming Silva at roll call is the least effective: it publicly shames an embarrassed new airman for a mistake caused by missing training. Ignoring the problem, counseling him and taking over the work are all weak, but none of them humiliates anyone. Arranging training and adding a check is most effective.

check.passage: Your best NCO, Technical Sergeant Avery, asks you to write a recommendation for a special-duty assignment that would move him to another base. Losing him would hurt your flight in the middle of a busy year, and his likely replacement is untrained. Avery has earned the opportunity, and the recommendation is due to the selection board in two weeks.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Tell him to get his recommendation from the squadron commander instead.
Ask him to wait a year before applying, explaining how much the flight needs him.
Write a strong, honest recommendation and start training his replacement.
Recommend him, but tell him you're disappointed that he wants to leave.
Write a lukewarm recommendation so he's less likely to be selected.
check.explain: An honest, strong recommendation develops a deserving NCO, and starting a successor now protects the flight: service before self applies to you too. Sandbagging him is dishonest. Asking him to wait puts your flight ahead of his career. Guilt-tripping him sours the relationship, and passing it to the commander dodges your job as his supervisor.

check.passage: Your best NCO, Technical Sergeant Avery, asks you to write a recommendation for a special-duty assignment that would move him to another base. Losing him would hurt your flight in the middle of a busy year, and his likely replacement is untrained. Avery has earned the opportunity, and the recommendation is due to the selection board in two weeks.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Tell him to get his recommendation from the squadron commander instead.
Ask him to wait a year before applying, explaining how much the flight needs him.
Write a strong, honest recommendation and start training his replacement.
Recommend him, but tell him you're disappointed that he wants to leave.
Write a lukewarm recommendation so he's less likely to be selected.
check.explain: Deliberately writing a weak recommendation is the least effective: it is dishonest and secretly sabotages an NCO who has earned the chance. Asking him to wait, guilt-tripping him and passing it to the commander are self-serving or evasive, but they're open about it. Writing a strong recommendation and training a successor is most effective.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. Two simple habits cover most leadership questions.
steps: Habit one: say 'well done' where others can hear, and say 'that needs fixing' where nobody else can.
Habit two: if someone who's usually good suddenly isn't, ask them what's going on before anything else.
Work through the airman's supervisor, the NCO, instead of around them.
Teach people to do the job instead of doing it for them.
Embarrassing someone in front of others is almost always the LEAST effective choice.

example.stem: An airman who is always on time is suddenly late three days in a row. What's your first step?
steps: Punishing him first might miss a real problem at home or with his health.
Ignoring it lets it continue.
Asking him privately, ideally through his supervisor, finds the cause.
example.answer: Have a private conversation to find out what's going on.

reteach.hook: Praise where they can hear it; correct where they can't.

check.passage: Airman Ward works on your flight line. During this morning's walk-around, with several airmen nearby, his supervisor tells you that Ward found a small fuel leak on an aircraft that two other crews had missed, and the aircraft was pulled before its sortie. Ward was late to work once last week and was counseled for it.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Say nothing, since finding leaks is part of Ward's job.
Thank Ward later in private so the other airmen don't feel left out.
Ask Ward to start training every crew on leak checks today, on top of all his own work.
Thank Ward in front of the airmen, and make sure the commander hears about his catch.
Tell Ward that one good catch doesn't make up for being late last week.
check.explain: A catch that stopped a leaking aircraft flying deserves public thanks, and passing it up the chain makes the recognition count. Saying nothing wastes the moment. Thanking him only in private misses the chance to show the flight what good looks like. Piling on extra work punishes the good deed, and raising last week's lateness turns praise into criticism.

check.passage: Airman Ward works on your flight line. During this morning's walk-around, with several airmen nearby, his supervisor tells you that Ward found a small fuel leak on an aircraft that two other crews had missed, and the aircraft was pulled before its sortie. Ward was late to work once last week and was counseled for it.

Thank Ward later in private so the other airmen don't feel left out.
Ask Ward to start training every crew on leak checks today, on top of all his own work.
Thank Ward in front of the airmen, and make sure the commander hears about his catch.
Tell Ward that one good catch doesn't make up for being late last week.
check.explain: Bringing up last week's lateness, in front of other airmen, at the moment he should be praised is the least effective: it criticizes publicly and reopens a matter already handled. Saying nothing and private-only thanks are weak, and the extra training load is clumsy, but none of them shames him. Public thanks passed up the chain is most effective.

check.passage: Airman Hughes, normally a hard worker, has fallen asleep at his desk twice this week. His supervisor, a staff sergeant, tells you he is ready to give Hughes a Letter of Counseling today. When you ask what is going on with Hughes, the supervisor admits he hasn't asked him yet. Hughes has no previous discipline problems.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Tell the supervisor to go ahead and issue the Letter of Counseling today as he planned.
Have the supervisor ask Hughes privately what's wrong, then decide the next step.
Wake Hughes loudly the next time it happens so the rest of the section sees.
Move Hughes to the night shift, since he seems to be sleeping through the day anyway.
Talk to Hughes yourself and tell the supervisor to stay out of it.
check.explain: A good worker suddenly falling asleep needs a cause found first, and the supervisor should be the one to ask. Issuing the letter now may punish a medical or family problem. Waking him loudly humiliates him. Moving him to nights changes nothing about the cause, and cutting the supervisor out undercuts the NCO.

check.passage: Airman Hughes, normally a hard worker, has fallen asleep at his desk twice this week. His supervisor, a staff sergeant, tells you he is ready to give Hughes a Letter of Counseling today. When you ask what is going on with Hughes, the supervisor admits he hasn't asked him yet. Hughes has no previous discipline problems.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Tell the supervisor to go ahead and issue the Letter of Counseling today as he planned.
Have the supervisor ask Hughes privately what's wrong, then decide the next step.
Wake Hughes loudly the next time it happens so the rest of the section sees.
Move Hughes to the night shift, since he seems to be sleeping through the day anyway.
Talk to Hughes yourself and tell the supervisor to stay out of it.
check.explain: Waking him loudly for the section to see is the least effective: it publicly humiliates an airman who may have a real problem. The early letter, the shift move and sidelining the supervisor are all poor choices, but they're private. Having the supervisor talk with Hughes first is most effective.

units.title: Peer conflict and communication
units.objective: Handle friction with peers directly, privately and specifically, and communicate early, honestly and through the right channel.

steps: Go to the person first. With a peer, the strong answer is a private, face-to-face talk about the specific behavior and its effect, not an email storm, a complaint to the boss or a word with the group.
Assume good intent and listen. Ask for their side; the peer may be overloaded, unaware or working from different information. Then agree on a fix together.
Escalate only if it continues or the mission is suffering, and normally tell the peer first that you're going to raise it. Escalating before you have even talked to them is usually a middle answer.
Never gossip, retaliate, vent to subordinates or fight in front of airmen. Public conflict between leaders damages the whole unit, and these options are LEAST candidates.
When you settle a dispute between your own people, hear both sides privately, decide if the decision is yours, and set the expectation for how disagreements are handled.

Communicate bad news early and accurately. Tell your boss the moment a deadline or result is at risk, bring options, and never present estimates or old data as if they were current. Use face to face for sensitive matters and writing to document.
teach.formula: Private · Direct · Specific · Listen · Escalate only if it continues · Bad news early, never dressed up

worked.passage: You and Lieutenant Shaw, a peer in your squadron, built a new parts-tracking spreadsheet together over several weekends. At this morning's staff meeting, Shaw presented it as his own work and the commander praised him for it. Afterward, two of your NCOs ask you why your name wasn't mentioned. You and Shaw share an office and will be planning next month's exercise together.
worked.stem: Which response is the MOST effective? (Responses: confront Shaw in front of the NCOs; email the commander to correct the record; talk with Shaw privately and agree how joint work is credited; say nothing but stop sharing work with Shaw; tell the NCOs that Shaw stole the credit.)
steps: Confront Shaw in front of the NCOs: a public fight between officers. A LEAST candidate.
Email the commander: goes around Shaw before you have spoken to him, and looks like score-settling. Middle.

Talk with Shaw privately, say how it came across, and agree on how you'll credit joint work, including correcting it with the commander together if needed: direct, private, fixes it going forward. Best.
Say nothing and stop sharing work: hurts the team and next month's exercise. Poor.
Tell the NCOs that Shaw stole credit: gossip about a peer to subordinates. A LEAST candidate, close behind the public confrontation.
worked.answer: Talk with Shaw privately, explain how the meeting came across and agree how you will credit shared work from now on.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: When a coworker annoys you, the easy things to do are complain to someone else, or say nothing and stew.
The SJ key rewards the harder thing: talk to that person yourself.
Do it privately, not in front of others.
Be specific: 'When the forecast came in late, my order slipped two days', not 'you're always late'.
Then listen. They may have a reason you didn't know about.
Only if it keeps happening do you take it to your boss, and you tell your coworker you're going to.
Talk to them, privately
Say the specific effect
Listen to their side
Agree a fix
Still stuck? Escalate

practice.passage: Lieutenant Ramos, a peer who runs another flight, owes you a parts forecast every Monday so you can place orders by Tuesday. Three of the last four forecasts arrived late, and last week a late order grounded one of your vehicles for two days. Ramos is friendly and seems overloaded. You and Ramos sit in the same building, and your flight commanders get along well.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Ask your flight commander to raise the late forecasts with Ramos's flight commander at their next meeting.
Start placing orders from your own estimates and stop relying on Ramos's forecasts.
Copy the squadron commander on your next email asking Ramos where the forecast is.
Talk with Ramos in person about the effect of the late forecasts and agree on a fix together.
Do nothing for now, since Ramos is overloaded and the problem may fix itself.
practice.explain: A direct, in-person talk about the specific effect, with a joint fix, is the first step with a peer and fits someone who may simply be overloaded. Escalating through the flight commanders skips that conversation. Ordering from your own estimates works around the problem without fixing it. Copying the commander is public pressure, and doing nothing lets vehicles keep getting grounded.

practice.passage: Two of your section chiefs, both master sergeants, disagree about how to share a single maintenance bay. This morning their argument became loud on the shop floor in front of a dozen airmen, and one of them walked out. Both are strong performers who usually work well together, and the bay schedule is your decision as the officer in charge.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Meet both chiefs privately, hear each side, set the bay schedule, and keep disputes off the shop floor.
Tell the airmen who saw the argument that it was unprofessional and that both chiefs will be dealt with.
Ask the first sergeant to mediate between the two chiefs and report back to you.
Split the bay evenly by calendar right away and tell both chiefs to stop arguing about it in front of airmen.
Wait a few days for tempers to cool before raising the subject with either chief.
practice.explain: Telling the airmen that their chiefs will be dealt with is the least effective: it undermines two senior NCOs in front of their people and solves nothing. Handing it to the first sergeant passes off a decision that is yours, and splitting the bay by decree skips hearing them out, but neither damages their authority. Waiting a few days is passive. Meeting both privately and deciding is most effective.

practice.passage: Two of your section chiefs, both master sergeants, disagree about how to share a single maintenance bay. Wait a few days for tempers to cool before raising the subject with either chief.
practice.explain: The bay schedule is your decision, so hearing both chiefs privately, deciding and setting the standard for future disagreements solves the dispute and its public spillover. The first sergeant handles enlisted welfare and discipline, not your scheduling call. Splitting the bay by calendar ignores what each chief actually needs. Waiting leaves the conflict open, and talking to the airmen undercuts the chiefs.

practice.passage: You are leading a small team building a briefing for a visiting general next Thursday. On Monday you learn that a data set from base finance, which the briefing depends on, won't be ready until Friday. Your squadron commander checks in on the project every day and has told you she hates surprises. A peer suggests building the slides with last quarter's numbers and swapping in the real ones if they arrive.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Keep working on the slides and tell the commander on Wednesday if the data still hasn't arrived.
Use last quarter's figures as your peer suggests, and present them as current if new data doesn't arrive.
Call the base finance director yourself and insist on the data by Wednesday, stressing that a general is visiting.
Tell the commander about the delay today, with two options: labeled old figures or partial data by Wednesday.
Ask the commander to postpone the general's visit until the finance data is ready.
practice.explain: Telling the commander today, with workable options, is bad news delivered early and constructively, exactly what a boss who hates surprises needs. Waiting until Wednesday wastes two days she could use. Presenting old figures as current misleads a general. Leaning on the finance director may help but leaves your commander uninformed, and asking to move a general's visit is out of proportion.

Tell the commander about the delay today, with two options: labeled old figures or partial data by Wednesday.

Telling the commander late and pressuring finance are poor communication, and asking to postpone is out of proportion, but none of them is dishonest. Informing the commander today with labeled options is most effective.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Run every peer-conflict response through three checks: who, where and how.
steps: WHO hears about it first? The best answer goes to the person themselves, not their boss, not the group, not your airmen.
WHERE? In private, face to face if you can. Not in a meeting, not in front of airmen, not in a group email.
HOW? Calmly and specifically: what happened, what it caused, and what would work better. Then listen.
Answers that fail all three (complaining to others, in public, with an attack) are LEAST. Answers that pass all three are MOST.
Answers that skip straight to a boss pass 'how' but fail 'who', so they land in the middle.

example.stem: A peer keeps swapping duty shifts with you at the last minute. Who, where and how should you raise it?
steps: Who: the peer, not your boss or the other duty officers.
Where: in person, in private.
How: 'The last two swaps came an hour before the shift and I had to cancel plans. Can we agree on a day's notice?'
example.answer: Talk to the peer privately and agree on how much notice you'll give each other.

reteach.hook: Right person, in private, about the specific effect.

check.passage: You and Lieutenant Kim share a duty-officer roster. Twice this month Kim has swapped shifts with you by sending a text an hour before the shift started, and both times you had to cancel personal plans. Kim is otherwise a good teammate who has covered for you before. You see Kim every day at the squadron.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Refuse all future swap requests from Kim without explaining why.
Complain about Kim to the other duty officers so they're warned.
Ask your flight commander to step in and order Kim to stop making last-minute swaps with you.
Say nothing and keep accepting the swaps to avoid an argument.
Talk with Kim in person about the late swaps and agree on how much notice you'll each give.
check.explain: A private, specific talk with an otherwise good teammate fixes the problem and keeps the relationship. Refusing all swaps without explanation punishes without fixing. Complaining to the others is gossip. Going to the flight commander escalates before you've even talked, and saying nothing lets it continue.

check.passage: You and Lieutenant Kim share a duty-officer roster. Twice this month Kim has swapped shifts with you by sending a text an hour before the shift started, and both times you had to cancel personal plans. Kim is otherwise a good teammate who has covered for you before. You see Kim every day at the squadron.

options: Refuse all future swap requests from Kim without explaining why.
Complain about Kim to the other duty officers so they're warned.
Ask your flight commander to step in and order Kim to stop making last-minute swaps with you.
Say nothing and keep accepting the swaps to avoid an argument.
Talk with Kim in person about the late swaps and agree on how much notice you'll each give.
check.explain: Complaining about Kim to the other duty officers is the least effective: it damages a good teammate's reputation behind his back and doesn't fix the problem. Refusing swaps, escalating early and staying silent are weak, but none of them spreads gossip. Talking with Kim directly is most effective.

check.passage: In a planning meeting with several majors present, Lieutenant Brandt, a peer from another squadron, dismisses your proposal for the exercise schedule as 'obviously unworkable.' You believe your proposal is sound and you have the data to back it up. Brandt's own proposal has a timing conflict he seems to have missed. You will work with Brandt on the exercise for the next two months.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Email the majors after the meeting explaining why Brandt was wrong.
Answer calmly with your data, then ask Brandt afterward to review both plans' timing with you.
Drop your proposal to avoid a public disagreement with a peer.
Interrupt Brandt and tell the room that his own plan shows he doesn't understand the schedule.
Ask your flight commander to raise Brandt's behavior with Brandt's own flight commander later this week.
check.explain: Answering a dismissal with calm facts keeps the discussion on the work, and the private follow-up deals with the timing conflict and the relationship you'll need for two months. Attacking Brandt in the room is a public fight. Dropping your proposal abandons a sound plan. Emailing the majors goes behind his back, and escalating through flight commanders skips talking to him.

check.passage: In a planning meeting with several majors present, Lieutenant Brandt, a peer from another squadron, dismisses your proposal for the exercise schedule as 'obviously unworkable.' You believe your proposal is sound and you have the data to back it up. Brandt's own proposal has a timing conflict he seems to have missed. Drop your proposal to avoid a public disagreement with a peer.
Interrupt Brandt and tell the room that his own plan shows he doesn't understand the schedule.
Ask your flight commander to raise Brandt's behavior with Brandt's own flight commander later this week.
check.explain: A personal attack in front of the majors is the least effective: it turns a disagreement into a public feud with a peer you must work with for two months. Emailing the majors behind his back is poor, and dropping the proposal or escalating are weak, but none of them is a public attack. Calm data plus a private follow-up is most effective.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. One habit fixes most problems with coworkers.
steps: If something a coworker does bothers you, tell them, kindly and privately.
Most people don't know they're causing a problem until someone tells them.
Don't complain about them to others first.
Don't play tricks or get back at them.
If an email isn't working, walk over and talk in person.

example.stem: A coworker's loud phone calls make it hard for you to work. What's the first thing to do?
steps: Complaining to your boss first skips the easy fix.
Moving desks every day avoids the problem without solving it.
Asking the coworker politely gives them the chance to fix it.
example.answer: Ask the coworker, politely and privately, if they could take calls somewhere else.

reteach.hook: Tell them first, kindly and privately.

check.passage: You are a lieutenant on the squadron staff. Staff Sergeant Lopez, who works at the desk next to yours but does not report to you, plays music from a speaker most of the day, and it makes it hard to concentrate on detailed paperwork. You have never mentioned it to her. You both work for the same director of operations.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Complain to the director of operations without saying anything to Lopez.
Unplug her speaker while she's at lunch so the problem goes away.
Ask Lopez politely, in private, if she could turn it down or use headphones.
Put up with it, and take your detailed paperwork to a conference room every day.
Send an email to the whole office about noise and the rules for music.
check.explain: A polite, private request gives Lopez the chance to fix something she may not know bothers you. Going to the director first skips the easy fix. Unplugging her speaker is passive-aggressive. Moving out every day avoids the problem, and a group email singles her out without naming her.

check.passage: You are a lieutenant on the squadron staff. check.explain: Secretly unplugging her speaker is the least effective: it's a sneaky act against a coworker's property that is likely to cause resentment, and it solves nothing for long. Complaining to the director, the group email and moving away are indirect, but none is underhanded. Asking her politely is most effective.

check.passage: You emailed Lieutenant Ross, a peer in another section, three times this week asking for data you need for a report due to the commander tomorrow morning. You have had no reply. Ross's office is one floor up, and you can see on the office calendar that he is in the building today.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Send a fourth email, in capital letters, marked URGENT.
Walk upstairs, ask Ross in person if he got your emails, and explain the deadline.
Copy Ross's commander on the next email to make him respond.
Make up estimates for the missing data so the report is finished on time.
Ask your supervisor to extend the deadline without trying to reach Ross again yourself.
check.explain: When email isn't working and the person is one floor up, going in person is fastest and friendliest. A capitalized email is rude and may also be ignored. Copying his commander escalates before you've spoken. Inventing data falsifies the report, and asking for an extension gives up on an easy fix.

check.passage: You emailed Lieutenant Ross, a peer in another section, three times this week asking for data you need for a report due to the commander tomorrow morning. You have had no reply. Ross's office is one floor up, and you can see on the office calendar that he is in the building today.

options: Send a fourth email, in capital letters, marked URGENT.
Walk upstairs, ask Ross in person if he got your emails, and explain the deadline.
Copy Ross's commander on the next email to make him respond.
Make up estimates for the missing data so the report is finished on time.
Ask your supervisor to extend the deadline without trying to reach Ross again yourself.
check.explain: Making up the data is the least effective: it sends the commander a report built on invented figures. The rude email, copying his commander and asking for an extension are poor communication, but none of them is dishonest. Walking upstairs to talk is most effective.

units.title: Safety and regulations, including money
units.objective: Stop unsafe acts, follow tech data and fix bad rules through channels, and apply the basic rules on government money and property.

steps: Safety is never traded for the schedule. Anyone who sees an unsafe act should stop it on the spot, then tell the person in charge. Letting a hazard continue to avoid a delay is a LEAST candidate.

Follow the technical order, checklist or regulation even when it seems pointless. If it is wrong or wasteful, keep complying and submit a change or waiver request through channels. Local workarounds and 'other bases skip it' are poor answers.
Report mishaps, near misses and hazards. A near miss is free information. Hiding one to protect a safety record ranks very low.

Government money is for its intended purpose only. Funds given for one purpose (say, training) can't be spent on another (furniture) without proper authority, and a purchase can never be split to get under a card limit.

Other money rules the SJ uses: the government travel card is for official travel only; appropriated funds generally can't buy gifts or refreshments for ceremonies; don't commit money you don't have; and when unsure, ask the resource advisor, contracting or legal before acting.
When following a rule seems to collide with the mission, the best response usually keeps the rule, tells the boss the cost, and pursues a legitimate fix.
teach.formula: Stop unsafe acts now · Comply, then fix the rule through channels · Report near misses · Right money, right purpose, no splitting

worked.passage: You are the approving official for your flight's government purchase card. The single-purchase limit is $10,000. Your NCOIC wants to buy $14,000 of shop test equipment before the fiscal year ends in two weeks, and suggests placing it as two $7,000 orders on consecutive days. The equipment is genuinely needed. The contracting office says a formal contract purchase will take at least six weeks.
worked.stem: Which response is the MOST effective? (Responses: approve the two $7,000 orders; decline the split and send the full requirement to contracting while asking the resource advisor how to keep the funds; have the NCOIC buy it personally and claim reimbursement; ask the vendor to send two invoices; drop the purchase.)
steps: Approve two $7,000 orders: splitting one requirement to beat the limit is prohibited, and you are the official who would approve it. A LEAST candidate.
Decline, explain the rule, send the full requirement to contracting and ask the resource advisor about the funds: legal, gets the equipment and tackles the deadline problem honestly. Best.
Buy it personally and claim reimbursement: an unauthorized commitment that sidesteps the same controls. Poor.
Two invoices from the vendor: the same split dressed up differently. Also very low.
Drop the purchase: legal, but abandons equipment the flight genuinely needs without trying. Middle.
worked.answer: Decline the split purchase, send the full requirement to contracting, and ask the resource advisor how the funds can be used in time.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Safety first: if you see someone about to get hurt, or a step being skipped that keeps people safe, you say 'stop' right then.
Being on time never matters more than someone's safety.
Rules and checklists: you follow them even when they seem silly.
If a rule really is silly, you ask for it to be changed the official way. You don't just skip it.
Money: government money has a label on it saying what it's for. You only spend it on that.
And you never chop one purchase into smaller pieces to sneak under a spending limit.
Unsafe? Stop it now
Bad rule? Comply
Then request a change
Money: right purpose only

visual.caption: Safety and rules on the SJ

practice.passage: You are a lieutenant observing a weapons-loading crew that is behind schedule for a launch in 25 minutes. You see a loader begin working on a bomb rack under the wing without first installing the safety pin that the technical order requires for that step. The crew chief, who is responsible for the crew, is busy at the other wing about 30 yards away.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Tell the loader to stop and install the pin before continuing, then let the crew chief know what you saw.
Install the safety pin yourself without saying anything, so the crew isn't slowed down.
Say nothing so the launch isn't delayed, since the crew chief is responsible for the loaders.
Walk over to the crew chief at the other wing, wait for him to finish his step, and tell him what you saw.
Halt the entire loading operation and call the squadron commander out to the flight line.
practice.explain: Saying nothing is the least effective: it lets a munitions hazard continue to protect a schedule, and anyone who sees an unsafe act should stop it. Installing the pin yourself means handling munitions you may not be qualified on, and walking over first delays the stop, but both address the hazard. Halting everything and calling the commander over-reacts. Stopping the loader and telling the crew chief is most effective.

practice.passage: Your maintainers tell you that one step in the technical order for a routine engine inspection takes four hours, because it requires removing a panel that, they say, gives no useful access. A senior NCO says other bases skip the step and nothing bad has happened. Skipping it would let your flight clear a backlog of six engines this week, and your commander has been asking about the backlog.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Bring in maintainers from another flight on overtime to clear the backlog using the full procedure.
Have the senior NCO find out which bases skip the step so you can copy their approach.
Keep following the step, and tell the maintainers that the technical order isn't theirs to question or change.
Allow the crews to skip the step this week only to clear the backlog, then return to the full procedure.
Keep following the step, and have the senior NCO submit a technical order change request with the details.
practice.explain: Complying while submitting a change request keeps the aircraft legal and safe and fixes the step properly if the maintainers are right. Skipping it 'this week only' is still unauthorized deviation from tech data. Copying other bases means copying their violation. Shutting the maintainers down complies but wastes their useful feedback, and borrowing another flight's people on overtime moves the problem rather than solving it.

practice.passage: Your maintainers tell you that one step in the technical order for a routine engine inspection takes four hours, because it requires removing a panel that, they say, gives no useful access. A senior NCO says other bases skip the step and nothing bad has happened. Skipping it would let your flight clear a backlog of six engines this week, and your commander has been asking about the backlog.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Bring in maintainers from another flight on overtime to clear the backlog using the full procedure.
Have the senior NCO find out which bases skip the step so you can copy their approach.
Keep following the step, and tell the maintainers that the technical order isn't theirs to question or change.
Allow the crews to skip the step this week only to clear the backlog, then return to the full procedure.
Keep following the step, and have the senior NCO submit a technical order change request with the details.
practice.explain: Authorizing crews to skip a required step is the least effective: you are directing work that departs from the technical order on engines that will fly. Researching other bases points toward the same violation but hasn't committed one yet. Shutting the maintainers down and borrowing another flight's people are weak but compliant. Following the step and requesting a change is most effective.

practice.passage: With three weeks left in the fiscal year, your resource advisor tells you that your flight has $8,000 left in its training budget, and that money not obligated by 30 September will be lost. Your NCOIC suggests spending it on new office chairs and a television for the break room, which the flight badly wants. Two airmen still need a required certification course that is offered in November.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Buy the chairs and television with the training money, since it will be lost otherwise.
Let the money lapse without doing anything, since it isn't worth the paperwork this late in the year.
Ask the resource advisor to move the money to the furniture budget so the chairs can be bought properly.
Spend the money on online training subscriptions for the whole flight, whether or not anyone needs them.
Ask the resource advisor whether the funds can pay now for the November course, and return the rest.
practice.explain: Asking the resource advisor whether the funds can cover the required November course points the money at a real training need through the person who knows the rules. Training money for chairs breaks the purpose rule. Letting it lapse ignores a real need. Buying subscriptions nobody needs is year-end waste, and asking to move it to furniture puts the flight's wants ahead of required training.

practice.passage: With three weeks left in the fiscal year, your resource advisor tells you that your flight has $8,000 left in its training budget, and that money not obligated by 30 September will be lost. Your NCOIC suggests spending it on new office chairs and a television for the break room, which the flight badly wants. Two airmen still need a required certification course that is offered in November.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Buy the chairs and television with the training money, since it will be lost otherwise.
Let the money lapse without doing anything, since it isn't worth the paperwork this late in the year.
Ask the resource advisor to move the money to the furniture budget so the chairs can be bought properly.
Spend the money on online training subscriptions for the whole flight, whether or not anyone needs them.
Ask the resource advisor whether the funds can pay now for the November course, and return the rest.
practice.explain: Spending training money on chairs and a television is the least effective: it uses funds for a purpose they weren't provided for, a violation you would be personally responsible for. Unneeded subscriptions are wasteful, and letting the money lapse ignores the course, but neither misuses the funds' purpose. Asking to move the money goes through proper channels. Asking about funding the November course is most effective.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Ask the same two questions of every safety or money response.
steps: Question one: does this response let anyone get hurt, or let a hazard keep going? If yes, it's a LEAST candidate.
Question two: does this response break a rule on purpose, or spend money on something it isn't for? If yes, it's also a LEAST candidate.
If a rule is getting in the way of the mission, the best answer keeps the rule AND works on fixing it officially (a change request, a waiver, the resource advisor, legal).
If you don't know whether something is allowed, the best answer asks the right office before doing it.
Being over-cautious (cancel everything, ground everyone) isn't best either; it's usually in the middle.

example.stem: A staff sergeant suggests using the government purchase card to buy a cake and plaque for a retirement. Does it pass both questions?
steps: Question one: no one gets hurt. Pass.
Question two: appropriated funds generally can't buy refreshments or personal gifts for a ceremony. Fail.
So the best answer keeps the ceremony and finds a proper way to pay, such as voluntary contributions.
example.answer: It fails the money question; use voluntary contributions instead.

reteach.hook: Nobody hurt, no rule broken on purpose, money for its purpose.

check.passage: You are the officer in charge on the flight line at night. A thunderstorm is 8 miles away and moving toward the base. Local rules require all outdoor work to stop when lightning is within 5 miles, and weather flight will issue the warning. A crew is refueling an aircraft that must launch in an hour, and the crew chief says they can finish in 15 minutes.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Leave the decision to the crew chief and go back inside the operations building.
Tell the crew to keep refueling even if the lightning warning comes, so the launch stays on time.
Stop all work now and cancel the launch, even though lightning is still 8 miles away.
Let the crew finish while lightning stays beyond 5 miles, and stop work the moment the warning comes.
Tell the crew to hurry so they finish before the storm arrives.
check.explain: Continuing while the rule allows, watching the warnings and stopping at once when lightning reaches 5 miles keeps both safety and the mission. Working through the warning breaks a safety rule on purpose. Cancelling now is more cautious than the rule requires.
