Walking away abdicates your role as officer in charge, and urging them to hurry invites mistakes during refueling.

check.passage: You are the officer in charge on the flight line at night. A thunderstorm is 8 miles away and moving toward the base. Local rules require all outdoor work to stop when lightning is within 5 miles, and weather flight will issue the warning. A crew is refueling an aircraft that must launch in an hour, and the crew chief says they can finish in 15 minutes.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Leave the decision to the crew chief and go back inside the operations building.
Tell the crew to keep refueling even if the lightning warning comes, so the launch stays on time.
Stop all work now and cancel the launch, even though lightning is still 8 miles away.
Let the crew finish while lightning stays beyond 5 miles, and stop work the moment the warning comes.
Tell the crew to hurry so they finish before the storm arrives.
check.explain: Ordering the crew to keep refueling through a lightning warning is the least effective: it deliberately exposes people and a fueling aircraft to lightning to save a schedule. Rushing the crew and walking away are poor, and cancelling now over-reacts, but none of them orders a rule broken. Continuing within the rule and stopping on the warning is most effective.

check.passage: Your flight is holding a retirement ceremony for a respected master sergeant who has served 24 years. A staff sergeant suggests using the flight's government purchase card to buy the cake, decorations and an engraved plaque. You know that appropriated funds generally cannot pay for refreshments or personal gifts at events like this. The ceremony is in two weeks.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Tell the staff sergeant to ask the commander, since it's the commander's decision.
Pay for the cake, decorations and plaque out of your own pocket so no one else has to.
Explain why the card can't be used, and organize voluntary contributions instead.
Cancel the refreshments and the plaque to avoid any possible problem.
Use the purchase card, since it's a small amount for a well-deserved honor.
check.explain: Explaining the rule and organizing voluntary contributions keeps the honor and stays within the rules on appropriated funds and gifts. Using the card misuses government money. Paying for it all yourself is generous but sidesteps teaching the rule and isn't sustainable. Cancelling everything is needlessly harsh, and sending him to the commander passes on a question you can answer.

check.passage: Your flight is holding a retirement ceremony for a respected master sergeant who has served 24 years. A staff sergeant suggests using the flight's government purchase card to buy the cake, decorations and an engraved plaque. You know that appropriated funds generally cannot pay for refreshments or personal gifts at events like this. The ceremony is in two weeks.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Tell the staff sergeant to ask the commander, since it's the commander's decision.
Pay for the cake, decorations and plaque out of your own pocket so no one else has to.
Explain why the card can't be used, and organize voluntary contributions instead.
Cancel the refreshments and the plaque to avoid any possible problem.
Use the purchase card, since it's a small amount for a well-deserved honor.
check.explain: Using the purchase card is the least effective: it knowingly spends appropriated funds on refreshments and a personal gift, and a small amount doesn't make it allowed. Cancelling everything and passing it to the commander are weak, and paying yourself is a half-fix, but none of them misuses government money. Voluntary contributions are most effective.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. Two short rules.
steps: Rule one: if someone is about to get hurt, say 'stop' right now. Not later, not at a meeting next week.
Being on schedule is never worth an injury.
Rule two: government things (money, cards, vehicles) are only for official work.
You never lend a government card or spend government money on personal things, even with a promise to pay it back.
When someone needs help, point them to the right place for help instead of bending a rule.

example.stem: A coworker is about to climb a ladder without anyone holding it, which the shop rules require. What do you do?
steps: Waiting until he's finished means he might fall first.
Telling the safety office later doesn't stop it now.
Saying 'stop, let me hold it' fixes it straight away.
example.answer: Stop him and hold the ladder (or get someone to) before he climbs.

reteach.hook: Hazard? Stop it now. Government money? Official use only.

check.passage: You walk into your section's workshop and see an airman about to use a bench grinder without safety glasses. When you catch his eye, he says, 'It'll only take a second, ma'am.' The safety glasses are hanging on the shelf right behind him. His supervisor is in the break room down the hall, and the shop has had no injuries this year.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Report him to the base safety office immediately.
Tell him to stop and put the glasses on first, then mention it to his supervisor.
Remind the whole section about wearing eye protection at next week's safety meeting.
Let him go ahead this once, since it'll only take a second.
Put the glasses on the bench next to him and say nothing.
check.explain: Stopping him before he starts prevents an eye injury, and a quick word to his supervisor deals with the habit. Letting him go ahead accepts the hazard. A reminder next week is too late for today. Reporting to the base safety office is out of proportion, and silently leaving the glasses there hopes he takes the hint.

check.passage: You walk into your section's workshop and see an airman about to use a bench grinder without safety glasses. When you catch his eye, he says, 'It'll only take a second, ma'am.' The safety glasses are hanging on the shelf right behind him. His supervisor is in the break room down the hall, and the shop has had no injuries this year.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Report him to the base safety office immediately.
Tell him to stop and put the glasses on first, then mention it to his supervisor.
Remind the whole section about wearing eye protection at next week's safety meeting.
Let him go ahead this once, since it'll only take a second.
Put the glasses on the bench next to him and say nothing.
check.explain: Letting him grind without eye protection is the least effective: you see the hazard and allow it. Leaving the glasses on the bench, the late reminder and the formal report are weak or out of proportion, but each at least tries to address it. Stopping him and telling his supervisor is most effective.

check.passage: Your friend, a lieutenant in your flight, is short of money before payday and asks to borrow your government travel card to pay for urgent car repairs. He promises to pay the bill in full before it is due. The travel card is issued in your name for official travel expenses only. He needs the car to get to work next week.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Tell him you can lend him the card only if your commander approves the loan in writing first.
Decline without any explanation and change the subject.
Decline, explain it's for official travel only, and point him to the Air Force Aid Society.
Decline and report him to the commander for asking.
Lend him the card, since he has promised to pay the bill before it's due.
check.explain: Declining with the reason and pointing him to emergency financial help keeps the rule and still helps your friend: the Air Force Aid Society exists for exactly this. Lending the card is misuse whatever he promises. Declining without explanation helps no one. Reporting him for asking is harsh, and no commander can approve personal use of a travel card.

check.passage: Your friend, a lieutenant in your flight, is short of money before payday and asks to borrow your government travel card to pay for urgent car repairs. He promises to pay the bill in full before it is due. The travel card is issued in your name for official travel expenses only. He needs the car to get to work next week.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Tell him you can lend him the card only if your commander approves the loan in writing first.
Decline without any explanation and change the subject.
Decline, explain it's for official travel only, and point him to the Air Force Aid Society.
Decline and report him to the commander for asking.
Lend him the card, since he has promised to pay the bill before it's due.
check.explain: Lending the card is the least effective: it is misuse of a government travel card in your name, whatever the promise of repayment. Asking for a commander's approval shows you don't know the rule, and reporting him or refusing coldly are poor, but none of them misuses the card. Declining and pointing him to the Air Force Aid Society is most effective.

units.title: Initiative vs overstepping
units.objective: Tell when to act on your own, when to bring a recommendation instead, and how to act in an emergency when no one can be reached.

steps: Initiative: when something is clearly in your lane and within your authority, act without waiting to be told, then inform. The key rewards officers who close gaps.

Overstepping: deciding things that belong to someone else, such as another flight, your boss, a specialist office like legal, contracting, security or civil engineering, or committing people and money you don't control.

Ask four questions: Is it my lane? Is it within my authority? Is it time-critical? Will my boss be surprised? Yes, yes and no surprise means act. Not your lane means bring a recommendation, not a decision.
Bring solutions, not just problems. 'Here's the issue, here's what I recommend, and I can pilot it in my flight' beats both doing nothing and announcing a squadron-wide change yourself.
New to a unit: learn why things are done before changing them, and take your idea through whoever approves it. But clear violations of safety or security rules get raised right away, new or not.
Emergencies: when harm is happening now and the decision-maker can't be reached, take the reasonable action that limits the damage, use emergency channels, and inform your boss as soon as you can.
teach.formula: My lane + my authority = act, then inform · Not my lane = recommend · Emergency + boss unreachable = limit the damage, inform fast

worked.passage: You took over a supply flight two weeks ago. You notice that airmen fill out every parts request on paper and then type the same information into a database, which wastes several hours a week. You have built a simple electronic form that would end the double entry. Your NCOs are used to the paper system, and the squadron's records manager must approve any change to an official form.
worked.stem: Which response is the MOST effective? (Responses: roll out your form on Monday; ask the NCOs why the paper step exists, then take your form and their input to the records manager for approval; drop the idea because the NCOs like paper; have airmen use your form unofficially alongside the paper one; send your form to the wing as a best practice.)
steps: Roll it out Monday: changes an official form without the records manager's approval. Overstepping. Poor.
Ask the NCOs why the paper step exists, then take the form and their input to the records manager: learns before changing, involves the people affected and uses the approval path. Best.
Drop the idea: passive, and the wasted hours continue. Middle-low.
Use your form unofficially alongside paper: adds a third copy of the work and creates unofficial records. Poor, the least effective here.
Send it to the wing: skips your own squadron's approval and your NCOs entirely. Poor.
worked.answer: Ask your NCOs why the paper step exists, then take your form and their input to the records manager for approval.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Taking initiative means doing the useful thing nobody told you to do.
But it has to be YOUR thing to do: your job, your people, your authority.
If it belongs to someone else, such as another office or your boss, you don't just do it. You tell them, and suggest what could be done.
Think of it this way: you can tidy your own desk without asking, but you shouldn't rearrange your boss's office.
Emergencies are special. If something bad is happening right now and nobody in charge can be reached, do the sensible thing to stop the damage.
Then tell your boss what you did as soon as you can.
Is it my lane?
Is it my authority?
Is it time-critical?
Act, or recommend
Inform either way

practice.passage: During a base exercise, you notice that the sign directing visitors to your building's temporary entrance has blown over, and visitors are walking straight into a fenced construction zone through a gap in the fence. Setting the sign back up takes two minutes. Civil engineering owns the construction site and its signs, and their office is closed until morning. It is getting dark, and more visitors are expected this evening.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Leave the sign where it is, since it belongs to civil engineering and touching it could create liability.
Call the base commander's office to report the construction hazard tonight.
Set the sign back up, steer visitors away from the gap, and leave civil engineering a message.
Email civil engineering so they can fix the sign when their office opens in the morning.
Close your building's temporary entrance yourself and order everyone to use the main door until further notice.
practice.explain: Setting the sign back up takes two minutes, stops people walking into a hazard now and stays within what anyone can reasonably do, and the message lets the owner fix the fence. Leaving it creates a risk to avoid a non-problem. Calling the base commander's office over a fallen sign is out of proportion. An email alone leaves the hazard all night, and closing the entrance goes beyond your authority.

practice.passage: At a staff meeting your squadron commander says she wants to raise the unit's fitness test pass rate, but she has not decided how. Afterward you draft a plan for mandatory 0600 group workouts for the whole squadron, three days a week. You are a flight commander responsible for 15 of the squadron's 120 airmen, and you are proud of the plan.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Bring your plan to the commander as a recommendation, and offer to pilot it with your own flight first.
Start the 0600 workouts in your own flight on Monday without mentioning them to the commander.
Email the plan to the whole squadron as the new fitness program, starting Monday.
Wait until the commander announces her own plan before doing anything about fitness.
Ask the other flight commanders to adopt your plan in their flights before you show it to the commander.
practice.explain: Offering the plan as a recommendation, with a pilot in your own flight, is initiative inside your lane: the commander keeps the squadron-wide decision and gets a tested option. Starting it in your flight without telling her surprises her on a topic she has just raised. Announcing it squadron-wide claims her authority. Waiting is passive, and lobbying the other flight commanders goes around her.

practice.passage: At a staff meeting your squadron commander says she wants to raise the unit's fitness test pass rate, but she has not decided how. Afterward you draft a plan for mandatory 0600 group workouts for the whole squadron, three days a week. You are a flight commander responsible for 15 of the squadron's 120 airmen, and you are proud of the plan.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Bring your plan to the commander as a recommendation, and offer to pilot it with your own flight first.
Start the 0600 workouts in your own flight on Monday without mentioning them to the commander.
Email the plan to the whole squadron as the new fitness program, starting Monday.
Wait until the commander announces her own plan before doing anything about fitness.
Ask the other flight commanders to adopt your plan in their flights before you show it to the commander.
practice.explain: Announcing a mandatory squadron-wide program is the least effective: you are giving orders to 105 airmen outside your authority, on a decision the commander has said she hasn't made. Starting in your own flight and lobbying peers both go around her, but on a much smaller scale. Waiting is passive. Recommending the plan with a pilot offer is most effective.

practice.passage: You are the senior officer present on a Saturday when a water pipe bursts above your squadron's server room, and water is dripping onto the equipment. The on-call technician says shutting the servers down will take the unit's email offline for the weekend; leaving them on risks destroying the equipment. Your commander is on a flight and unreachable for three hours. The building's water shutoff is in a locked mechanical room controlled by civil engineering, which has a 24-hour emergency line.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Have the servers shut down, call civil engineering's emergency line, and message your commander.
Wait for your commander to land so she can decide whether to take the unit's email offline.
Force open the mechanical room yourself and shut off the building's water.
Cover the servers with plastic sheeting, keep them running, and check on them every hour until she lands.
Phone the wing commander at home to ask permission to take the email offline.
practice.explain: Waiting three hours is the least effective: the equipment is being damaged now, the decision is within what the senior officer present can reasonably make, and the commander can't be reached. Forcing the door oversteps when an emergency line exists, plastic sheeting is a gamble, and calling the wing commander escalates unnecessarily, but each at least tries to limit the damage. Shutting down, calling the emergency line and informing the commander is most effective.

practice.passage: You are the senior officer present on a Saturday when a water pipe bursts above your squadron's server room, and water is dripping onto the equipment. The on-call technician says shutting the servers down will take the unit's email offline for the weekend; leaving them on risks destroying the equipment. Your commander is on a flight and unreachable for three hours. The building's water shutoff is in a locked mechanical room controlled by civil engineering, which has a 24-hour emergency line.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Have the servers shut down, call civil engineering's emergency line, and message your commander.
Wait for your commander to land so she can decide whether to take the unit's email offline.
Force open the mechanical room yourself and shut off the building's water.
Cover the servers with plastic sheeting, keep them running, and check on them every hour until she lands.
Phone the wing commander at home to ask permission to take the email offline.
practice.explain: In an emergency with the commander unreachable, you take the reasonable action that limits the damage, use the owner's emergency channel and inform the boss as soon as you can. Losing email for a weekend is recoverable; losing the servers may not be. Forcing the door takes over civil engineering's job, sheeting leaves powered equipment under water, waiting lets damage continue, and calling the wing commander skips levels for a decision you can make.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Picture your job as a lane on a running track.
steps: Inside your lane, you run hard without asking permission: fix the problem, then tell your boss.
When you see a problem in someone else's lane, you shout across to them. You don't run into their lane and take over.
Security, legal, contracting, civil engineering and your commander's decisions are other people's lanes.
Some things are everyone's lane: reporting a security hole, stopping a hazard, opening a help-desk ticket.
Doing nothing because 'it's not my place' is the LEAST answer when it's something anyone should raise.

example.stem: In your first week you notice the classified safe's combination is three years old, against the rules. Your lane, someone else's lane, or everyone's?
steps: Changing the combination yourself: the security manager's lane.
Raising it: everyone's lane, new officer or not.
So you tell the security manager today.
example.answer: Raising it is everyone's lane; changing it is the security manager's.

reteach.hook: Run hard in your lane; shout across to theirs.

check.passage: You are new to a squadron. In your first week you notice that the flight keeps classified documents in a safe whose combination has not been changed in three years, although the rules require a change whenever someone with access leaves. Several people with access have left since then. The unit security manager works in your building.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Tell the security manager today and ask to have the combination changed now.
Offer to take over the safe yourself and draw up a new access list for the security manager to approve.
Say nothing, since as the newest officer it isn't your place to point out the problem.
Mention it to your flight commander at your next monthly feedback session.
Report the flight to the wing information protection office as non-compliant.
check.explain: The security manager owns the safe and is in your building, so telling them today closes the gap fast through the right lane. Taking over the safe yourself steps into their job; the access list is theirs to decide. Staying silent leaves classified material exposed. Waiting for a monthly session is too slow, and going to the wing skips the unit's own security manager.

check.passage: You are new to a squadron. In your first week you notice that the flight keeps classified documents in a safe whose combination has not been changed in three years, although the rules require a change whenever someone with access leaves. Several people with access have left since then. The unit security manager works in your building.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Tell the security manager today and ask to have the combination changed now.
Offer to take over the safe yourself and draw up a new access list for the security manager to approve.
Say nothing, since as the newest officer it isn't your place to point out the problem.
Mention it to your flight commander at your next monthly feedback session.
Report the flight to the wing information protection office as non-compliant.
check.explain: Saying nothing is the least effective: a classified safe that former members may still be able to open is a security risk, and raising it is everyone's job. Taking over the safe oversteps a newcomer's role, the feedback session is slow, and going to the wing over-escalates, but each brings the problem to light. Telling the security manager today is most effective.

check.passage: Your commander asks you to plan a squadron family day using $2,000 the booster club has raised. A local business offers free inflatable rides for the children if it can hand out flyers advertising its services at the event. You are not sure whether the base allows commercial advertising at official squadron events. The event is a month away.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Accept the offer, since free rides for the families are a good deal.
Turn the business down without checking, just to be safe, and don't mention the offer to anyone else.
Ask your commander to decide on the offer without looking into the rules first.
Ask the base legal office whether the offer is allowed before you answer the business.
Cancel the inflatable rides and spend the whole budget on food instead.
check.explain: You don't know the rule and there's a month to spare, so asking legal first is initiative in the right lane. Accepting without checking risks an improper commercial endorsement. Declining silently may throw away a good offer for nothing. Sending it to the commander without the facts gives her a problem instead of a recommendation, and cancelling the rides solves nothing.

check.passage: Your commander asks you to plan a squadron family day using $2,000 the booster club has raised. A local business offers free inflatable rides for the children if it can hand out flyers advertising its services at the event. You are not sure whether the base allows commercial advertising at official squadron events. The event is a month away.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Accept the offer, since free rides for the families are a good deal.
Turn the business down without checking, just to be safe, and don't mention the offer to anyone else.
Ask your commander to decide on the offer without looking into the rules first.
Ask the base legal office whether the offer is allowed before you answer the business.
Cancel the inflatable rides and spend the whole budget on food instead.
check.explain: Accepting without checking is the least effective: it commits the squadron to a possible ethics problem, letting a business advertise at an official event, when you already suspect there may be a rule. Declining silently, passing the decision up unprepared and dropping the rides are overcautious or weak, but none of them risks a violation. Asking legal first is most effective.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. Two kinds of situations.
steps: Kind one: something simple anyone is allowed to do, like calling the help desk. Just do it. Don't wait for someone else.
Kind two: something that belongs to another person or office, like letting a stranger into a secure room. Check with the right people first.
If you're not sure who's allowed in, check their ID. Rank or hurry doesn't replace an ID check.
Doing nothing and hoping someone else handles it is usually the LEAST effective choice.
Taking over something you're not trained or authorized for is usually poor too.

example.stem: The office coffee machine is broken and a repair request takes two minutes online. Everyone has noticed. Who should submit it?
steps: Anyone is allowed to submit it.
Waiting for someone else is why nobody has.
So you submit it.

reteach.hook: If anyone can do it, you do it. If it's someone else's, check with them first.

check.passage: Your section's only printer has jammed several times a day for two weeks, slowing everyone down. Getting it fixed means calling the base help desk to open a repair ticket, which any member of the section can do in about five minutes. Everyone, including you, has been complaining about it, but nobody has called.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Complain about the printer again at the next staff meeting.
Take the printer apart yourself to try to clear the fault and get it working again.
Wait for someone else to call, since the printer isn't your responsibility.
Buy a new printer with your own money and bring it in.
Call the help desk and open the repair ticket yourself today.
check.explain: Anyone can open the ticket in five minutes, so doing it yourself is simple initiative. Complaining again changes nothing. Taking it apart risks damage and is the technicians' job. Waiting for someone else is why it's still broken, and buying one yourself sidesteps the proper repair route.

check.passage: Your section's only printer has jammed several times a day for two weeks, slowing everyone down. Getting it fixed means calling the base help desk to open a repair ticket, which any member of the section can do in about five minutes. Everyone, including you, has been complaining about it, but nobody has called.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Complain about the printer again at the next staff meeting.
Take the printer apart yourself to try to clear the fault and get it working again.
Wait for someone else to call, since the printer isn't your responsibility.
Buy a new printer with your own money and bring it in.
Call the help desk and open the repair ticket yourself today.
check.explain: Waiting for someone else is the least effective: it's exactly the attitude that has left the printer broken for two weeks, when anyone could fix it in five minutes. Complaining, tinkering and buying your own are poor or wasteful, but each at least tries to deal with it. Calling the help desk yourself is most effective.

check.passage: During a base-wide exercise, you are told to keep your building's secure work area locked. A man in civilian clothes with no visible badge asks you to let him in, saying he is from the wing staff and late for an inspection. You don't recognize him. A phone list for confirming visitors' access is posted by the door.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Let him in, but follow him around closely to keep an eye on him.
Politely ask for his ID and confirm his access on the posted list before letting him in.
Refuse to talk to him and walk away without a word.
Call the security forces emergency line immediately and report an intruder in the building.
Let him in, since wing staff outrank you and he's late for an inspection.
check.explain: Checking his ID and confirming access is exactly what the posted list is for, and it's polite and secure. Letting him in on his word defeats the point of a secure area. Walking away is rude and leaves the question open. Calling an intruder in before even checking is premature, and escorting someone you haven't verified still lets an unknown person in.

check.passage: During a base-wide exercise, you are told to keep your building's secure work area locked. A man in civilian clothes with no visible badge asks you to let him in, saying he is from the wing staff and late for an inspection. You don't recognize him. A phone list for confirming visitors' access is posted by the door.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Let him in, but follow him around closely to keep an eye on him.
Politely ask for his ID and confirm his access on the posted list before letting him in.
Refuse to talk to him and walk away without a word.
Call the security forces emergency line immediately and report an intruder in the building.
Let him in, since wing staff outrank you and he's late for an inspection.
check.explain: Letting him in on his say-so is the least effective: it gives an unverified stranger access to a secure area because he claimed rank and urgency, a classic social-engineering trick. Escorting him is still poor but at least watches him. Walking away and calling security are over- or under-reactions that keep him out. Checking ID is most effective.

units.title: Picking MOST and LEAST
units.objective: Rank all five responses quickly: find the one that acts at the right level, honestly and completely, and the one that lies, endangers, abdicates or humiliates.

steps: Read for four things: your role and rank, who owns the problem, what is at stake (safety, integrity, mission, people) and how much time there is.

Rank all five; don't just hunt for one. Sort them into three piles: good, flawed-but-legitimate, and harmful. The real test asks for both the MOST and the LEAST from the same five, so you need the whole order anyway.

The MOST effective response usually does several things at once: you act yourself, at the lowest level that can fix it, promptly and honestly, privately where people's feelings are involved, and you inform whoever needs to know. It fixes the problem now AND its cause.

The LEAST effective response is usually one of four failures: integrity (lying, falsifying, covering up), safety (letting a hazard continue), abdication (ignoring it, waiting, dumping it on someone else when it is yours) or mistreating people (public humiliation, reprisal, favoritism).

The middle pile is where the traps live: over-escalation (straight to the commander or the Inspector General), doing someone else's job yourself, delaying for 'more information', and partial fixes. They are rarely MOST and rarely LEAST.

If two options both look best, prefer the one that also informs the chain or fixes the cause. If two look worst, prefer the one that breaks integrity or safety. About 40 seconds an item: decide, mark both, move on.
teach.formula: MOST = act + right level + honest + inform · LEAST = lie, endanger, abdicate or humiliate · Middle = escalate, take over, delay, half-fix

worked.passage: You are a new second lieutenant. On Friday afternoon your NCOIC tells you that Airman Cole posted a photo on social media taken in your work area. A whiteboard in the background lists upcoming aircraft maintenance dates, which are controlled information. The post has been up for two hours and has a few dozen views. Cole is off duty until Monday but usually answers his phone.
worked.stem: Rank all five, then pick the MOST and the LEAST effective. (Responses: have his supervisor ask him to remove it when he's next online and discuss it Monday; reach Cole now to get it removed, report the exposure to your security manager and brief your commander; ask the Office of Special Investigations to open a criminal case; send the flight a reminder about social media rules but don't contact Cole until Monday; leave the post alone and say nothing so the flight doesn't look careless.)
steps: What's at stake: controlled information is publicly visible right now, and every hour adds views. Time matters.
Good pile: reach Cole now, get it removed, report to the security manager and brief the commander. It stops the exposure, uses the right channel and leaves no surprises.

Flawed pile: the supervisor asking 'when he's next online' (slow, no security report); the flight reminder with no call to Cole (the post stays up); a criminal case with OSI (over-escalation for a likely careless airman).
Harmful pile: leaving it up and saying nothing to protect the flight's image. That combines a security failure with a cover-up.
So the MOST is reaching Cole now and reporting it, and the LEAST is leaving it and staying quiet.
worked.answer: MOST: reach Cole now, get the post removed, report it to the security manager and brief your commander. LEAST: leave the post up and say nothing.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Each scenario has five responses. Don't look for the answer straight away.
First, give each response a quick grade: good, OK-ish, or bad.
A 'bad' response usually lies, puts someone in danger, ignores the problem, or embarrasses someone in public.
A 'good' response fixes the problem now, at your level, honestly, and tells the right person.
The 'OK-ish' ones overreact, underreact or only half-fix things.
The MOST effective is your best 'good'. The LEAST effective is your worst 'bad'. They can never be the same response.
Read: role, owner, stakes, time
Grade all five
Good · flawed · harmful
MOST = best good
LEAST = worst harmful

practice.passage: During a records check, you find that an airman's government vehicle logbook shows trips to an off-base shopping mall on three weekday lunchtimes. The airman's supervisor, a staff sergeant, tells you he approved the trips because the airman works long shifts and the dining facility closes early. Government vehicles may be used for official purposes only, and the base allows trips to on-base dining facilities.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Report the supervisor and the airman to the squadron commander for misuse of government property.
Let it go, since the trips were short and the supervisor was looking after his airman.
Tell the supervisor to change the logbook entries so the trips show as official business.
Tell the supervisor the trips must stop, explain why, and help him find a proper meal option.
Ban all use of the flight's vehicles during lunch hours, including official trips.
practice.explain: Stopping the trips, explaining the rule and solving the meal problem fixes the misuse and its cause at the lowest level, for a well-meant first mistake. Reporting both to the commander escalates before you've corrected anyone. Letting it go tolerates misuse of government property. Rewriting the logbook is falsification, and a blanket ban punishes official work.

practice.passage: During a records check, you find that an airman's government vehicle logbook shows trips to an off-base shopping mall on three weekday lunchtimes. The airman's supervisor, a staff sergeant, tells you he approved the trips because the airman works long shifts and the dining facility closes early. Government vehicles may be used for official purposes only, and the base allows trips to on-base dining facilities.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Report the supervisor and the airman to the squadron commander for misuse of government property.
Let it go, since the trips were short and the supervisor was looking after his airman.
Tell the supervisor to change the logbook entries so the trips show as official business.
Tell the supervisor the trips must stop, explain why, and help him find a proper meal option.
Ban all use of the flight's vehicles during lunch hours, including official trips.
practice.explain: Directing the supervisor to rewrite the logbook is the least effective: it turns a minor misuse into falsified records, and you would be the one ordering it. Letting it go tolerates the misuse but doesn't make anything false. Over-escalating to the commander and banning official lunchtime trips are clumsy but honest. Stopping the trips and fixing the meal problem is most effective.

practice.passage: You are a lieutenant on a deployment. Your flight commander, a captain, has put you in charge of the night shift. You notice that the captain has given every weekend shift to the same four airmen, all recent arrivals, while the airmen he knows from home station get weekends off. The new airmen have started to grumble, and their work has slipped.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Raise the pattern privately with the captain, and suggest a rotating weekend schedule.
Change the night-shift schedule yourself so weekend duty rotates fairly, without telling the captain.
Tell the new airmen you agree that the captain is playing favorites, but that there's nothing you can do about it.
Report the captain to the Inspector General for unfair treatment of the new airmen.
Volunteer to work some of the weekend shifts yourself to give the new airmen a break.
practice.explain: Agreeing with the airmen that the captain plays favorites, while doing nothing, is the least effective: it undermines your boss in front of his people, feeds the morale problem and fixes nothing. Changing the schedule behind his back and going to the IG are poor (one oversteps, one over-escalates), but each at least tries to fix it. Covering shifts yourself is a half-fix. Raising it privately with the captain is most effective.

practice.passage: You are the officer in charge of an aircrew flight equipment section. At 0500 a technician tells you that a batch of oxygen masks was inspected yesterday by an airman whose certification for that inspection expired last week. The masks have already been issued to aircrews for a 0700 training sortie. The airman's work is usually excellent, and a certified technician can re-inspect the whole batch in about 90 minutes.
practice.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Let the sortie fly, since the airman is skilled and his certification lapsed only a week ago.
Have the same airman re-inspect the batch now, since his skill hasn't changed in a week.
Cancel the sortie yourself and ground the squadron's aircraft until every piece of equipment has been re-checked.
Tell the aircrews about the lapse and let each crew member decide whether to use the masks.
Recall the masks for a certified re-inspection, warn operations of a possible slip, and brief your commander.
practice.explain: Recalling the masks for a certified re-inspection, with 120 minutes to spare for a 90-minute job, closes the safety gap, keeps the sortie likely to fly, and tells operations and your commander. Flying them uninspected accepts the risk. A second uncertified inspection doesn't fix anything. Grounding the squadron is far beyond the problem and your authority, and pushing the decision onto aircrews abdicates your job.

practice.passage: You are the officer in charge of an aircrew flight equipment section. At 0500 a technician tells you that a batch of oxygen masks was inspected yesterday by an airman whose certification for that inspection expired last week. The masks have already been issued to aircrews for a 0700 training sortie. The airman's work is usually excellent, and a certified technician can re-inspect the whole batch in about 90 minutes.
practice.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Let the sortie fly, since the airman is skilled and his certification lapsed only a week ago.
Have the same airman re-inspect the batch now, since his skill hasn't changed in a week.
Cancel the sortie yourself and ground the squadron's aircraft until every piece of equipment has been re-checked.
Tell the aircrews about the lapse and let each crew member decide whether to use the masks.
Recall the masks for a certified re-inspection, warn operations of a possible slip, and brief your commander.
practice.explain: Letting the sortie fly with masks from an uncertified inspection is the least effective: it knowingly accepts a life-support risk when a fix fits in the time available, and it ignores the rule. A repeat uncertified inspection and handing the call to aircrews are poor, but both at least react to the problem. Grounding the squadron over-reacts. Recalling and re-inspecting with a certified technician is most effective.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's sort the five responses into three piles before choosing anything.
steps: Pile one, GOOD: fixes the problem now, at your level, honestly, and tells the right person.
Pile two, FLAWED: tries to help but overreacts (straight to the commander or the IG), underreacts (wait and see), takes over someone else's job, or only half-fixes it.
Pile three, HARMFUL: lies, hides, endangers, ignores, or embarrasses or punishes someone unfairly.
MOST effective = the best of pile one. LEAST effective = the worst of pile three.
If pile three has two items, the one that breaks integrity or safety is usually worse than the one that's merely unkind or lazy.

example.stem: Sort these into piles: (a) change the record so it looks right; (b) report the airman to the commander for a first small mistake; (c) correct the airman privately and fix the record.
steps: (a) Changing the record to look right is falsifying. Harmful.
(b) Reporting a first small mistake to the commander is overreaction. Flawed.
(c) A private correction and an honest record fix it at the right level. Good.

reteach.hook: Good, flawed, harmful: MOST is the best good, LEAST is the worst harmful.

check.passage: You lead a team of six airmen. Airman Ford tells you that another team member, Airman Tate, has been making jokes about Ford's religion in the break room for about a month. Ford says he wants the jokes to stop but doesn't want to get Tate 'in big trouble.' Tate is a solid worker, and the two airmen work side by side every day.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Tell Ford to handle it himself by letting Tate know the jokes bother him.
Talk with Tate privately today, make clear the comments stop, and check back with Ford.
Remind the whole team about respect and professionalism at the next meeting, without speaking to Tate.
File a formal Equal Opportunity complaint on Ford's behalf, against his wishes.
Tell Ford that break-room jokes are part of team life and he shouldn't take them personally.
check.explain: Speaking to Tate privately stops the behavior at the lowest level, respects Ford's wish to avoid a formal case, and the follow-up checks it has worked. Putting it back on Ford leaves him to fix what you're responsible for. A general reminder may not reach Tate. Filing a formal complaint against Ford's wishes over-escalates, and brushing it off dismisses religious harassment.

check.passage: You lead a team of six airmen. Airman Ford tells you that another team member, Airman Tate, has been making jokes about Ford's religion in the break room for about a month. Ford says he wants the jokes to stop but doesn't want to get Tate 'in big trouble.' Tate is a solid worker, and the two airmen work side by side every day.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Tell Ford to handle it himself by letting Tate know the jokes bother him.
Talk with Tate privately today, make clear the comments stop, and check back with Ford.
Remind the whole team about respect and professionalism at the next meeting, without speaking to Tate.
File a formal Equal Opportunity complaint on Ford's behalf, against his wishes.
Tell Ford that break-room jokes are part of team life and he shouldn't take them personally.
check.explain: Telling Ford to put up with religious jokes is the least effective: it dismisses harassment and tells every airman that reporting it is pointless. Putting it back on Ford, the vague reminder and the formal complaint are flawed, but each takes the concern seriously. Talking to Tate privately is most effective.

check.passage: You are responsible for your flight's training records. You find that one airman's required Self-Aid and Buddy Care certification expired two months ago, and he has been working on the flight line, where the certification is required. The airman says he forgot and can take the course next week. His supervisor didn't notice the lapse either.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Change his record to show the certification as current until he takes the course.
Pull him from all of his duties, not just the flight-line tasks that need the certification, until next week's course.
Tell him to take the course whenever he has a free afternoon.
Book the earliest course, keep him off tasks that need it until then, and tell his supervisor how it was missed.
Report his supervisor to the commander for failing to track training.
check.explain: Booking the earliest course, keeping him off work that requires the certification and closing the tracking gap with the supervisor fixes the risk, the record and the cause. Changing the record is falsification. Pulling him from all duties goes further than the requirement. 'Whenever he's free' leaves the lapse open, and reporting the supervisor skips a simple correction.

check.passage: You are responsible for your flight's training records. You find that one airman's required Self-Aid and Buddy Care certification expired two months ago, and he has been working on the flight line, where the certification is required. The airman says he forgot and can take the course next week. His supervisor didn't notice the lapse either.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Change his record to show the certification as current until he takes the course.
Pull him from all of his duties, not just the flight-line tasks that need the certification, until next week's course.
Tell him to take the course whenever he has a free afternoon.
Book the earliest course, keep him off tasks that need it until then, and tell his supervisor how it was missed.
Report his supervisor to the commander for failing to track training.
check.explain: Showing the certification as current is the least effective: it falsifies a training record and hides an airman working without a required qualification. Telling him to go 'whenever' is lax, and pulling him from everything or reporting the supervisor over-react, but none of them is false. Booking the earliest course and restricting his duties is most effective.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. Give each response a thumbs-up, a sideways thumb or a thumbs-down.
steps: Thumbs-down: it's dishonest, unsafe, ignores the problem, or is mean to someone.
Thumbs-up: it's honest, sorts the problem out now, and tells the right person.
Sideways thumb: it's not terrible, but it goes too far, not far enough, or only fixes half the problem.
MOST effective: your best thumbs-up.
LEAST effective: your worst thumbs-down. Lying and danger are the worst of all.

example.stem: You see two airmen shoving each other. Thumbs-up, sideways or down: (a) pretend you didn't see; (b) call the police to arrest one; (c) separate them and find out what happened?
steps: (a) Ignoring it lets it get worse. Thumbs-down.
(b) Calling for an arrest over a shove no one was hurt by goes too far. Sideways.
(c) Separating them and finding out is the sensible fix. Thumbs-up.

reteach.hook: Best thumbs-up for MOST; worst thumbs-down for LEAST.

check.passage: Walking to your car, you see two airmen from your flight arguing loudly in the parking lot. One shoves the other, who stumbles but is not hurt. They stop as soon as they see you. A few other people nearby have stopped to watch. Both airmen are due back at work in ten minutes.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Talk only to the airman who was shoved and tell him to file a complaint.
Shout at both of them in front of the people watching.
Separate them, hear each one privately, and tell their supervisors.
Call security forces and ask them to arrest the airman who shoved.
Pretend you didn't see it, since nobody was hurt.
check.explain: Separating them, hearing each side privately and telling their supervisors stops it and starts the right follow-up. Ignoring it lets a physical fight between your airmen pass. Shouting in public humiliates them. Calling for an arrest over a shove with no injury over-reacts, and hearing only one side is unfair and incomplete.

check.passage: Walking to your car, you see two airmen from your flight arguing loudly in the parking lot. One shoves the other, who stumbles but is not hurt. They stop as soon as they see you. A few other people nearby have stopped to watch. Both airmen are due back at work in ten minutes.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Talk only to the airman who was shoved and tell him to file a complaint.
Shout at both of them in front of the people watching.
Separate them, hear each one privately, and tell their supervisors.
Call security forces and ask them to arrest the airman who shoved.
Pretend you didn't see it, since nobody was hurt.
check.explain: Pretending not to see is the least effective: an officer who ignores airmen shoving each other signals that it's acceptable, and it may escalate. Shouting in public, the arrest and the one-sided talk are poor, but each responds to it. Separating them and finding out is most effective.

check.passage: Your flight commander asks you to sign a memo confirming that all twelve of the flight's vehicles passed their annual safety inspection. You know that two vehicles have not been inspected yet because the inspector was out sick; they are scheduled for tomorrow. The memo is due to the squadron by the end of today.
check.stem: Which response is the MOST effective?
options: Sign it, since the two vehicles will almost certainly pass tomorrow.
Inspect the two remaining vehicles yourself this afternoon so that the memo will be true.
Refuse to sign it without telling the commander why.
Tell the commander which two haven't been inspected, and offer to sign once they are.
Ask another officer in the flight to sign the memo instead.
check.explain: Telling the commander the facts and offering to sign once it's true keeps the memo honest and keeps the commander informed. Signing now certifies something false. Refusing without a reason leaves the commander guessing. You aren't a qualified inspector, so your inspection wouldn't make it true, and passing it to another officer just moves the false signature.

check.passage: Your flight commander asks you to sign a memo confirming that all twelve of the flight's vehicles passed their annual safety inspection. You know that two vehicles have not been inspected yet because the inspector was out sick; they are scheduled for tomorrow. The memo is due to the squadron by the end of today.
check.stem: Which response is the LEAST effective?
options: Sign it, since the two vehicles will almost certainly pass tomorrow.
Inspect the two remaining vehicles yourself this afternoon so that the memo will be true.
Refuse to sign it without telling the commander why.
Tell the commander which two haven't been inspected, and offer to sign once they are.
Ask another officer in the flight to sign the memo instead.
check.explain: Signing is the least effective: you would personally certify a safety inspection you know hasn't happened. Passing it to another officer is close behind but at least isn't your false signature, and refusing silently or inspecting it yourself are poor but honest. Telling the commander and signing once inspected is most effective.

afoqt-ps.title: Physical Science
afoqt-ps.blurb: High-school physics and chemistry at test speed: forces and motion, energy and machines, fluids, heat and gas laws, waves and light, electricity, atoms and reactions, and nuclear, Earth and space basics. Name the principle, then reason or calculate in a line or two.

units.title: Forces, Newton's laws & momentum
units.objective: Apply Newton's three laws with net force, tell mass from weight, conserve momentum, use impulse and work free-fall problems.

steps: First law (inertia): an object keeps its velocity, at rest or moving straight at a steady speed, unless a NET force acts. Constant velocity means the forces are balanced.
Second law: F_net = m × a, using the NET force (push minus friction, thrust minus drag). 1 newton = 1 kg·m/s².
Weight is a force: W = m × g, with g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (often rounded to 10). Mass is the amount of matter and stays the same on the Moon; weight changes with g.
Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on DIFFERENT objects. In a truck-car collision each pushes the other equally hard; the car accelerates more because a = F/m.

Momentum p = m × v is conserved in a collision or explosion when no outside force acts. Impulse F × t = change in momentum, so stretching out the stopping time shrinks the force (air bags, bending your knees).
Free fall from rest with no air: v = g × t and d = ½ × g × t². All objects fall with the same acceleration whatever their mass; air resistance eventually balances weight at terminal velocity.
teach.formula: F_net = ma · W = mg · p = mv · F × t = Δp · free fall: v = gt, d = ½gt²

worked.stem: A 1,200 kg car moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest by its brakes in 4 s. What average braking force acts on it?
steps: Change in momentum: 1,200 × 20 = 24,000 kg·m/s.
Impulse: F × t = Δp, so F = 24,000 ÷ 4 = 6,000 N.
Check with F = ma: a = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m/s², and 1,200 × 5 = 6,000 N ✓.
List every force on the object
Add them with signs: net force
a = net force ÷ mass

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: A force is a push or a pull. Things don't need a force to keep moving; they need one to speed up, slow down or turn.
Push a shopping cart with 30 N while friction pulls back with 10 N, and the cart feels 20 N overall. That overall force is the net force.
The net force decides the acceleration: a heavier cart speeds up less for the same push. That's a = F ÷ m.
Your mass in kilograms is the same everywhere. Your weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, so it is smaller on the Moon.
When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you just as hard. Forces always come in pairs.
Momentum is mass times velocity. In a crash, the total momentum before equals the total after.

practice.stem: An aircraft cruises in a straight line at a constant 250 knots at a constant altitude. What is the net force on it?
options: A forward force equal to its thrust
A force equal to its weight
A small forward force that keeps it moving
A force that grows with distance flown
practice.explain: Constant speed in a straight line means zero acceleration, so by Newton's first and second laws the net force is zero: thrust balances drag and lift balances weight. Thrust and weight are real forces but each is cancelled by another; no extra forward force is needed to keep moving, and nothing in steady flight grows with distance.

practice.stem: A 4 kg block on a level floor is pulled with a horizontal force of 30 N and accelerates at 5 m/s². What is the friction force on the block?
practice.explain: The net force is m × a = 4 × 5 = 20 N, so friction must be 30 − 20 = 10 N. 20 N is the net force, 30 N is the pull, 7.5 N divides the pull by the mass, and 50 N adds the net force to the pull.

practice.stem: A 60 kg astronaut floating at rest throws a 3 kg tool away at 8 m/s. How fast does the astronaut recoil?
practice.explain: Total momentum starts at zero, so the astronaut's momentum must equal the tool's: 3 × 8 = 24 kg·m/s, and 24 ÷ 60 = 0.4 m/s. 8 m/s gives the astronaut the tool's speed, 2.5 divides 60 by 24, 24 is the momentum, not a speed, and about 0.38 divides by 63 kg, wrongly including the tool's mass.

practice.stem: A stone is dropped from rest and falls freely for 4 seconds. Using g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air, how far does it fall during the 4th second alone?
practice.explain: Distance fallen is ½gt²: 80 m after 4 s and 45 m after 3 s, so the 4th second covers 80 − 45 = 35 m. 80 m is the total, 40 m is the speed at 4 s read as a distance, 45 m is the first 3 seconds, and 10 m assumes it falls the same distance every second.

practice.stem: A 0.15 kg ball moving at 40 m/s is caught and brought to rest in 0.02 s. What average force does the catcher's glove exert?
practice.explain: The change in momentum is 0.15 × 40 = 6 kg·m/s, and F = Δp ÷ t = 6 ÷ 0.02 = 300 N. 6 N is the momentum, 0.12 N multiplies by the time instead of dividing, 2,000 N leaves out the mass, and 30 N slips the decimal point.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Let's draw a quick force list every time and let the net force do the talking.
steps: Write each force on the object with its direction: push, pull, friction, weight, lift, drag.
Add forces in the same direction and subtract opposite ones. What's left is the net force.
Zero net force means no change in motion: still at rest, or steady speed in a straight line.
Some net force means acceleration: a = F_net ÷ m.
For collisions and throws, skip forces and use momentum: total m × v before = total m × v after.

example.stem: A 2 kg box is pushed with 14 N against 4 N of friction. What is its acceleration?
steps: Net force: 14 − 4 = 10 N forward.

reteach.hook: List the forces, find the net, then a = F ÷ m.

check.stem: A net force of 24 N acts on an 8 kg mass. What is its acceleration?
check.explain: a = F ÷ m = 24 ÷ 8 = 3 m/s². 192 multiplies, 1/3 divides the mass by the force, 32 adds, and 16 subtracts.

check.stem: A 70 kg pilot goes to the Moon, where g is about 1.6 m/s². What is the pilot's mass there?
check.explain: Mass is the amount of matter and doesn't change: still 70 kg (the weight drops to about 112 N). 112 is the Moon weight in newtons, not a mass; about 11.7 divides by 6; 686 is the Earth weight in newtons; and about 43.8 divides by 1.6.

check.stem: A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg cart, and they stick together. How fast do they move afterward?
check.explain: Momentum before is 2 × 3 = 6 kg·m/s, shared by 3 kg afterward: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s. 3 m/s ignores the extra mass, 1.5 m/s halves the speed, 6 is the momentum, and 1 m/s divides the speed by 3.

check.stem: When a rifle fires a bullet, how does the force on the rifle compare with the force on the bullet?
options: Larger on the rifle, because it is heavier
Larger on the bullet, because it moves faster
Equal in size and opposite in direction
Equal in size and in the same direction
check.explain: Newton's third law: the forces are an equal and opposite pair. The rifle recoils slowly only because its larger mass gives it a smaller acceleration. The forces can't differ in size, can't point the same way, and the recoil shows the rifle does feel a force.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's go back to pushes, pulls and what they do.
steps: A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N).
If all the forces on something cancel out, it carries on doing what it was doing.
If they don't cancel, it speeds up, slows down or changes direction.
Bigger force, bigger acceleration; bigger mass, smaller acceleration: F = m × a.
Weight is gravity's pull on your mass: weight = mass × g, with g about 10 m/s² on Earth.

example.stem: A net force of 20 N acts on a 5 kg cart. What is its acceleration?
steps: a = 4 m/s².

reteach.hook: Unbalanced force → acceleration. F = m × a.

check.stem: Which of these objects must have an unbalanced (net) force acting on it?
options: An aircraft parked on the ramp
An aircraft cruising straight and level at a constant speed
A book resting on a table
An aircraft speeding up on the runway
A puck sliding at a steady speed on frictionless ice
check.explain: Speeding up is acceleration, which needs a net force. The parked aircraft and the book are at rest, and the cruising aircraft and sliding puck move at constant velocity, so their forces are balanced.

check.stem: What net force gives a 10 kg mass an acceleration of 2 m/s²?
check.explain: F = m × a = 10 × 2 = 20 N. 5 divides, 12 adds, 0.2 divides the wrong way, and 8 subtracts.

check.stem: Using g = 10 m/s², what does a 50 kg person weigh on Earth?
check.explain: Weight = m × g = 50 × 10 = 500 N. 50 N confuses mass and weight, 5 N divides, 60 N adds, and 5,000 N multiplies by 100.

check.stem: A ball is dropped from rest. Ignoring air and using g = 10 m/s², how fast is it falling after 2 seconds?
check.explain: v = g × t = 10 × 2 = 20 m/s. 10 m/s is the speed after 1 second, 40 m/s squares the time, 5 m/s divides, and 200 m/s slips a zero.

units.title: Work, energy, power & simple machines
units.objective: Compute work, kinetic and potential energy and power, use energy conservation, and apply mechanical advantage and efficiency to levers, pulleys and ramps.

steps: Work W = F × d, with the force in the direction of motion, in joules (1 J = 1 N·m). Holding a load still, or carrying it level at steady speed, does no work on it against gravity.
Kinetic energy KE = ½mv²: double the speed and KE quadruples. Gravitational potential energy PE = mgh.
Energy is conserved. A falling object trades PE for KE: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh), the same for any mass when air is ignored.
Power = work ÷ time, in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). 1 horsepower ≈ 746 W. Doing the same work faster takes more power, not more energy.
Machines trade force for distance. Ideally work in = work out, and mechanical advantage = output force ÷ input force = input distance ÷ output distance.

Lever: effort × effort arm = load × load arm (distances from the pivot). Pulley system: ideal MA = number of rope segments holding the load. Ramp: MA = length ÷ height. Efficiency = useful work out ÷ work in × 100%, always below 100%.
teach.formula: W = Fd · KE = ½mv² · PE = mgh · P = W ÷ t · effort × effort arm = load × load arm

worked.stem: A motor lifts a 50 kg crate 6 m in 12 s. Using g = 10 m/s², what power does the motor deliver to the crate?
steps: Work against gravity = mgh = 50 × 10 × 6 = 3,000 J.
Power = work ÷ time = 3,000 ÷ 12 = 250 W.
Sanity check: about a third of a horsepower, sensible for a small hoist.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: In physics, work means a force moving something along. Lift a 10 N bag up 2 m and you've done 10 × 2 = 20 J of work.
Energy is the ability to do work. A raised object has stored (potential) energy; a moving object has motion (kinetic) energy.
Drop the bag and its stored energy turns into motion energy as it falls. None is lost if we ignore air.
Power is how fast you do work. Climbing stairs in 10 s instead of 20 s takes the same energy but twice the power.
A lever lets a small force move a big load: put the load close to the pivot and push far from it. You push farther, but more gently.
No machine gives out more work than you put in. Friction always wastes a little, so real efficiency is under 100%.

practice.stem: A 1,000 kg car speeds up from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. By how much does its kinetic energy increase?
practice.explain: KE goes from ½ × 1,000 × 10² = 50,000 J to ½ × 1,000 × 20² = 200,000 J, an increase of 150,000 J. 50,000 J squares the 10 m/s change in speed, 100,000 J assumes doubling the speed doubles KE, 200,000 J is the final KE, and 10,000 J is the change in momentum.

practice.stem: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m. Using g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air, how fast is it moving just before it hits the ground?
practice.explain: mgh = ½mv² gives v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 20) = √400 = 20 m/s. 200 m/s is gh with no root, 400 m/s forgets the square root, about 14 m/s drops the 2 (√200), and 10 m/s is g, not the speed.

practice.stem: A worker uses a 3 m crowbar to lift a 900 N rock. The pivot is 0.5 m from the rock end. What is the least force needed at the far end of the bar?
practice.explain: The effort arm is 3 − 0.5 = 2.5 m, so effort × 2.5 = 900 × 0.5, giving effort = 450 ÷ 2.5 = 180 N. 150 N uses the whole 3 m as the effort arm, 4,500 N swaps the arms, 300 N divides 900 by 3, and 450 N forgets to divide by the effort arm.

practice.stem: A block and tackle has 4 rope segments supporting a 1,200 N load and is 75% efficient. What effort force is needed to lift the load?
practice.explain: Ideal effort = 1,200 ÷ 4 = 300 N, and at 75% efficiency the real effort is 300 ÷ 0.75 = 400 N. 300 N is the frictionless ideal, 225 N multiplies by 0.75 instead of dividing, 1,600 N ignores the pulleys, and 4,800 N multiplies by 4.

practice.stem: A 1,500 kg car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s. Ignoring losses, what is the average power its engine delivers?
practice.explain: The car gains KE = ½ × 1,500 × 20² = 300,000 J, and spreading that over 10 s gives 30,000 W (30 kW). 60,000 W forgets the ½, 300,000 W is the energy in joules, 3,000 W is the accelerating force in newtons, and 600,000 W both forgets the ½ and never divides by the time.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Let's keep an energy account: every joule has to go somewhere.
steps: Write the energy at the start (PE = mgh, KE = ½mv²) and at the end.
With no friction, start total = end total. With friction, the difference became heat.
Work done by a force equals the energy it adds: W = F × d.
Power is energy per second: divide the joules by the seconds.
For any machine, work in ≥ work out. The force you save, you pay back in distance.

example.stem: A 2 kg rock falls 5 m from rest. Using g = 10 m/s² and no air, how fast is it moving at the bottom?
steps: End: all 100 J is KE, so ½ × 2 × v² = 100 and v² = 100.

reteach.hook: Energy in = energy out. Machines trade force for distance.

check.stem: How much work is done pushing a cart 15 m with a steady 40 N force in the direction of motion?
check.explain: W = F × d = 40 × 15 = 600 J. 55 adds, about 2.7 divides, 300 halves as if it were KE, and 6,000 slips a zero.

check.stem: Using g = 10 m/s², what is the potential energy of a 3 kg book on a shelf 2 m above the floor?
check.explain: PE = mgh = 3 × 10 × 2 = 60 J. 6 J forgets g, 30 J adds a ½ that belongs only to KE, and 600 J and 0.6 J slip the decimal point.

check.stem: A frictionless ramp is 10 m long and rises 2 m. What is its ideal mechanical advantage?
check.explain: MA = length ÷ height = 10 ÷ 2 = 5. 20 multiplies, 0.2 divides the wrong way, 8 subtracts, and 12 adds.

check.stem: A machine takes in 400 J of work and puts out 300 J of useful work. What is its efficiency?
check.explain: Efficiency = 300 ÷ 400 = 75%. About 133% divides the wrong way (no machine exceeds 100%), 25% is the share wasted, 100% assumes no losses, and 30% reads the 300 J as a percent.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's start with what physicists mean by work and energy.
steps: Work happens when a force moves something: work = force × distance.
Holding something still, however tiring, does no work on it in the physics sense.
Moving things have kinetic energy; raised things have potential energy.
Power tells you how fast work is done: joules per second, or watts.
A lever balances when force × distance from the pivot is the same on both sides.

example.stem: You lift a 10 N bag 2 m straight up. How much work do you do?
steps: Work = force × distance = 10 × 2.

reteach.hook: Work = force × distance. Power = work ÷ time.

check.stem: Which of these does NO work on the object in the physics sense?
options: Lifting a box onto a shelf
Holding a heavy box still above your head
Pushing a cart across a hangar floor
Pulling a sled up a hill
check.explain: Work needs movement in the direction of the force; a box held still doesn't move, so no work is done on it. Lifting, pushing, pulling and throwing all move the object along the force.

check.stem: A 2 kg ball moves at 4 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
check.explain: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 16 = 16 J. 32 J forgets the ½, 8 J forgets to square the speed (that's the momentum), 4 J halves 8, and 64 J squares the mass too.

check.stem: A hoist does 600 J of work in 3 s. What is its power?
check.explain: Power = 600 ÷ 3 = 200 W. 1,800 multiplies, 600 is the work, not the rate, 0.005 divides the wrong way, and 3 is the time.

check.stem: On a lever, a 20 N effort is applied 3 m from the pivot. What load can it balance 1 m from the pivot on the other side?
check.explain: 20 × 3 = load × 1, so the load is 60 N. 20 N ignores the distances, about 6.7 N divides by 3 instead, 23 N adds, and 40 N multiplies by the difference in distances (3 − 1 = 2).

units.title: Pressure, buoyancy, Pascal & Bernoulli
units.objective: Use P = F/A and depth pressure, apply Pascal's principle to hydraulics, Archimedes' principle to floating, and Bernoulli's principle to lift and flow.

steps: Pressure = force ÷ area (pascals, N/m², or psi). The same force on a smaller area makes more pressure: why a knife edge cuts and snowshoes stop you sinking.
In a fluid at rest, pressure grows with depth: P = ρgh, plus the air pressure on the surface. Fresh water adds about 1 atmosphere (≈ 100 kPa) every 10 m, whatever the container's shape.

Pascal's principle: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is passed on equally everywhere. Hydraulic lift: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂, so a small force on a small piston lifts a large load, but the small piston must move much farther.

Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced. An object floats if it can displace its own weight before it is fully under, which means its average density is less than the fluid's.

Density = mass ÷ volume; water is 1 g/cm³ (1,000 kg/m³). A floating object's submerged fraction = its density ÷ the fluid's density. A steel ship floats because its hollow hull gives it a low average density.

Bernoulli: in a moving fluid, where the speed is higher the pressure is lower. Air flowing faster over a cambered wing gives lower pressure on top and lift; a narrowed pipe (venturi) speeds the flow and drops the pressure.
teach.formula: P = F ÷ A · P = ρgh · F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ · buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced

worked.stem: A hydraulic jack has a small piston of area 2 in² and a large piston of area 50 in². What force on the small piston lifts a 3,000 lb load?
steps: Pressure is the same on both pistons: F₁/2 = 3,000/50.
Trade-off: the area ratio is 25, so the small piston moves 25 times as far as the load.

visual.caption: Same pressure on both pistons: 120 lb on 2 in² lifts 3,000 lb on 50 in²

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Pressure is how concentrated a force is. Stand on one high heel and the floor feels far more pressure than under a flat shoe, even though your weight is the same.
Dive deeper and there is more water stacked above you, so the pressure rises steadily with depth.
Squeeze a sealed bag of water and every part of it feels the squeeze. Hydraulic brakes and lifts use this.
Water pushes up on anything in it. That push equals the weight of the water moved out of the way.
If something weighs less than the water it can push aside, it floats. That's why a big steel ship floats but a steel bolt sinks.
Fast-moving air has lower pressure than still air. Air rushing over the curved top of a wing is what helps lift the aircraft.

practice.stem: A 600 N person stands on snowshoes with a total area of 0.3 m². What pressure do they exert on the snow?
practice.explain: Pressure = force ÷ area = 600 ÷ 0.3 = 2,000 Pa. 180 Pa multiplies instead of dividing, 20,000 Pa uses an area of 0.03 m², 600 Pa is the force, not the pressure, and 200 Pa divides by 3 instead of 0.3.

practice.stem: A 2,000 cm³ block of wood with a mass of 1,200 g floats in fresh water. What volume of the block is below the waterline?
practice.explain: A floating object displaces its own weight: 1,200 g of water, which is 1,200 cm³ (the block's density, 0.6 g/cm³, says 60% is under). 800 cm³ is the part above the water, 2,000 cm³ assumes it is fully under, 720 cm³ applies the 0.6 twice, and 600 cm³ assumes floating objects are always half under.

practice.stem: Which best explains why air pressure on the upper surface of a cambered wing is lower than on the lower surface in flight?
options: The air flows faster over the curved upper surface
Gravity pulls the air on top downward
The air over the top is colder and denser
The wing compresses the air above it
The air slows down as it passes over the top
practice.explain: By Bernoulli's principle, faster-moving air has lower pressure, and the air speeds up over the curved upper surface, so the pressure on top drops and the wing is pushed up. Colder, denser air would not lower the pressure, gravity acts on air above and below alike, compressing air would raise pressure, and slower air would have higher pressure, the opposite of lift.

practice.stem: A diver descends to 25 m in fresh water (density 1,000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²). Air pressure at the surface is 100 kPa. What is the total pressure on the diver?
practice.explain: Water adds ρgh = 1,000 × 10 × 25 = 250,000 Pa = 250 kPa, and the air above adds 100 kPa, for 350 kPa in all. 250 kPa leaves out the air pressure, 125 kPa adds only 1 kPa per meter, 450 kPa counts the air pressure twice, and 35 kPa slips the decimal point.

practice.stem: In a hydraulic lift, the small piston has an area of 0.01 m² and the large piston 0.5 m². A 400 N force pushes the small piston down 0.25 m. How far does the large piston rise?
practice.explain: The fluid volume pushed out equals the volume taken in: 0.01 × 0.25 = 0.0025 m³, which raises the 0.5 m² piston by 0.0025 ÷ 0.5 = 0.005 m = 5 mm (lifting 400 × 50 = 20,000 N). 12.5 m multiplies by the area ratio instead of dividing, 250 mm assumes both pistons move the same distance, and 50 mm and 0.5 mm slip the decimal point.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Let's turn every fluid problem into a question about pressure, which is force shared over area.
steps: Pressure = force ÷ area. Same force, smaller area: more pressure.
Depth: each 10 m of fresh water adds about 100 kPa (one atmosphere). Total pressure includes the air above.
Hydraulics: the pressure is the same on both pistons, so the forces are in the same ratio as the areas.
Floating: the object sinks until the water it pushes aside weighs as much as it does.
Moving fluids: faster flow means lower pressure (Bernoulli).

example.stem: A rock weighs 5 N in air and 3 N when hung fully under water. What is the buoyant force?
steps: The water supports the difference: 5 − 3 = 2 N.
So the rock displaces 2 N of water.

reteach.hook: Pressure is force per area; buoyancy is the weight of water pushed aside.

check.stem: A hydraulic press has a small piston of 2 cm² and a large piston of 60 cm². A 50 N force is applied to the small piston. What force does the large piston exert?
check.explain: The area ratio is 60 ÷ 2 = 30, so the force is 50 × 30 = 1,500 N. 50 N ignores the ratio, about 1.7 N divides by 30, 25 N divides by the small area, and 3,000 N multiplies by the large area instead of the ratio.

check.stem: Why does a steel ship float even though steel is denser than water?
options: Steel becomes less dense when it is shaped
Air pressure on deck holds it up
Its hull displaces its own weight of water
Water pressure is the same at every depth
The ocean's mass is greater than the ship's mass
check.explain: The hollow hull pushes aside a large volume of water, and the ship settles until that water's weight equals its own (its average density is below water's). Shaping doesn't change steel's density, air pressure acts everywhere, water pressure rises with depth, and the ocean's total mass is irrelevant.

check.stem: A metal block weighs 12 N in air and 8 N when fully submerged in water. What is the buoyant force on it?
check.explain: Buoyant force = weight in air − weight in water = 12 − 8 = 4 N. 20 N adds, 8 N and 12 N are the two readings themselves, and 1.5 N divides them.

check.stem: What is the gauge pressure (not counting the air above) 4 m below the surface of fresh water? (density 1,000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²)
check.explain: P = ρgh = 1,000 × 10 × 4 = 40,000 Pa. 4,000 Pa forgets g, 400 Pa and 40 Pa slip zeros, and 140,000 Pa adds the air pressure the question excludes.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's think about pushing on things and things floating.
steps: Pressure is how hard a force presses on each bit of area.
Pressing the same force on a smaller spot makes the pressure bigger.
In water, the deeper you go, the more water is above you, so the pressure rises.
Density is how much mass is packed into each bit of volume. Things less dense than water float.
Squeezing a hose nozzle makes the water speed up, and fast-moving fluid has lower pressure.

example.stem: A 200 N crate rests on a base of 2 m². What pressure does it put on the floor?
steps: Pressure = force ÷ area = 200 ÷ 2.

reteach.hook: Small area, big pressure. Less dense than water, it floats.

check.stem: The same force is applied to a smaller area. What happens to the pressure?
options: It depends only on the force
check.explain: Pressure = force ÷ area, so a smaller area gives a bigger pressure. It can't decrease or stay the same with a smaller divisor, it doesn't vanish, and area matters as much as force.

check.stem: An object has a mass of 300 g and a volume of 400 cm³. What is its density?
check.explain: Density = mass ÷ volume = 300 ÷ 400 = 0.75 g/cm³, so it floats in water. About 1.33 divides volume by mass, 120,000 multiplies, 700 adds, and 100 subtracts.

check.stem: Where is the water pressure greatest in a still lake?
check.explain: Pressure increases with depth, so it is greatest at the bottom. The surface has the least, halfway is in between, it is not uniform, and temperature barely matters compared with depth.

check.stem: Placing a thumb over part of a garden hose's opening makes the water
