The lowered left aileron gives the left wing more lift, which rolls the airplane right, but also more induced drag.
That extra drag pulls the left wing back, so the nose yaws LEFT, away from the turn.
The pilot adds right rudder with the ailerons to keep the turn coordinated.
worked.answer: Right aileron up, left aileron down; the nose yaws left, away from the turn

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Each control surface is a hinged flap. When it moves, the air pushes on it and moves that part of the airplane.
Ailerons, near the wingtips, work as a pair: one up, one down. The wing whose aileron goes up drops.
The elevator is on the flat part of the tail. Pull back and it tilts up, the air pushes the tail down, and the nose comes up.
The rudder is on the upright fin. Push the right pedal and the nose swings right.
A trim tab is a tiny flap on a bigger flap. It moves the opposite way and holds the big one in place so the pilot doesn't have to.
Flaps on the inner wing make extra lift for slow flight. Spoilers on top of the wing spoil lift.
Ailerons: roll
Elevator: pitch
Rudder: yaw
Trim tab: opposite

visual.caption: Each primary control and its job

practice.stem: When the pilot turns the control yoke to the left, the ailerons move so that the
options: left aileron lowers and the right aileron rises.
left aileron rises and the right aileron lowers.
left aileron rises while the right aileron stays neutral.
practice.explain: To roll left, the left wing must lose lift and the right wing gain it: the left aileron rises and the right aileron lowers (PHAK Ch. 6). The reverse would roll right. Ailerons moving the same way together act like flaps or spoilers, not roll controls, and both ailerons always move.

practice.stem: Which high-lift device increases both the camber and the area of the wing?
practice.explain: A Fowler flap slides aft on tracks as it lowers, adding wing area as well as camber, which gives the largest lift increase (PHAK Ch. 6). Plain and split flaps change camber only. A fixed slot raises the critical AOA without changing area, and a spoiler reduces lift.

practice.stem: Frise-type ailerons reduce adverse yaw by
options: making the lowered aileron travel farther than the raised one, adding drag.
moving the rudder automatically into the turn whenever the ailerons deflect.
pushing the raised aileron's leading edge into the airflow to add drag.
adding lift to the raised wing so it rises faster.
reducing the parasite drag on both wings equally.
practice.explain: On a Frise aileron the raised aileron pivots so its leading edge juts below the wing into the airflow, creating drag on the down-going wing that offsets the drag of the lowered aileron (PHAK Ch. 6). Differential ailerons work by making the RAISED aileron travel farther, so 'the lowered aileron travels farther' is reversed. An automatic rudder input describes an aileron-rudder interconnect, not Frise ailerons.

practice.stem: On a stabilator, the antiservo tab
options: moves opposite to the trailing edge to reduce control forces.
moves the same way as the trailing edge, making the stabilator less sensitive.
is a fixed tab that can be adjusted only on the ground.
moves in the same direction as the trailing edge, to reduce the control forces.
works only when the flaps are extended.
practice.explain: The antiservo tab moves the same way as the stabilator's trailing edge, which makes the stabilator less sensitive and gives the pilot control feel; it doubles as a trim tab (PHAK Ch. 6). Moving opposite to reduce forces describes a balance or servo tab. The same-direction option with 'reduce control forces' has the right motion but the wrong effect, and the tab works at all times, not just with flaps.

practice.stem: During the landing roll, ground spoilers are deployed mainly to
options: increase lift to soften the touchdown.
add camber to the wing so it can keep flying more slowly on the rollout.
lower the stall speed for the flare.
reduce lift and put more weight on the wheels for braking.
practice.explain: After touchdown, spoilers dump lift and add drag, transferring weight to the landing gear so the wheel brakes can work (PHAK Ch. 6). Spoilers never increase lift or camber and they raise, not lower, the stall speed. Redirecting engine thrust is the job of thrust reversers.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's follow the push of the air on each surface.
steps: Every surface works by deflecting air, and the air pushes back the other way.
Aileron DOWN: the air pushes that wing UP. Aileron UP: that wing goes down. So the wing you're rolling toward has its aileron up.
Elevator UP: the air pushes the tail DOWN, which levers the nose UP.
A trim tab works the same way on its own surface: tab DOWN pushes the elevator's trailing edge UP. That's why trim moves opposite.
Flaps and slats help the wing fly slowly; spoilers wreck lift on purpose.
Surface deflects air
Air pushes back
Tab down: elevator up
Elevator up: nose up

visual.caption: Follow the push of the air

example.stem: The pilot trims for nose-up. Which way does the elevator trim tab move?
steps: Nose-up needs the elevator held UP.
To hold the elevator up, the air must push its trailing edge up.
So the tab moves DOWN into the airflow.

reteach.hook: Surfaces move air one way; the air moves the airplane the other way.

check.stem: A pilot trims for a nose-up attitude. The elevator trim tab
options: moves up, holding the elevator up.
moves down, holding the elevator down.
moves up, holding the elevator down.
moves down, holding the elevator up.
does not move; the elevator moves directly.
check.explain: Nose-up needs the elevator held up. The trim tab moves opposite its surface, so it goes down and the airflow pushes the elevator up (PHAK Ch. 6). The other combinations either move the tab the same way as the elevator or hold the elevator in the wrong position.

check.stem: Extending flaps on approach mainly lets the pilot
options: fly a steeper descent without increasing airspeed.
reduce drag so the approach can be flown faster.
raise the stall speed to give better control at low speed.
check.explain: Flaps add lift and drag, lowering the stall speed and allowing a steeper approach without picking up speed (PHAK Ch. 6). They increase drag, lower rather than raise the stall speed, slow the airplane, and have nothing to do with adverse yaw.

check.stem: A leading-edge slat increases
options: the wing's stall speed in every configuration.
the parasite drag of the wing only.
check.explain: A slat opens a slot that feeds high-energy air over the top of the wing, delaying separation to a higher critical AOA, so the wing can fly slower before stalling (PHAK Ch. 6). It lowers rather than raises the stall speed, and its purpose is not drag, cruise speed or roll.

check.stem: Differential ailerons reduce adverse yaw because
options: the lowered aileron travels farther than the raised one.
the raised aileron travels farther than the lowered one.
both ailerons move the same way at the same time.
they are mechanically linked to the elevator.
they deflect only at high airspeeds.
check.explain: With differential ailerons the raised aileron moves farther than the lowered one, adding drag on the descending wing to balance the lowered aileron's induced drag (PHAK Ch. 6). Having the lowered aileron travel farther is backwards. Ailerons always move opposite each other, aren't linked to the elevator, and work at all speeds.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. Three controls, three movements.
steps: Ailerons, on the wings, roll the airplane: one wing up, the other down.
The elevator, on the flat tail, moves the nose up and down.
The rudder, on the upright fin, swings the nose left and right.
Pull back on the controls: nose up. Push forward: nose down.
Flaps help you fly slowly. Spoilers spoil lift.

example.stem: Which control swings the nose left and right?
steps: Ailerons roll; the elevator pitches.
Swinging the nose left and right is yaw, and the rudder controls yaw.

reteach.hook: Ailerons roll, elevator pitches, rudder yaws.

check.stem: Pushing the control wheel forward makes the airplane's nose
options: stay level while the speed falls.
check.explain: Forward pressure lowers the elevator, which pushes the tail up and the nose down. Back pressure does the opposite. Yaw is the rudder's job and roll the ailerons'.

check.stem: The rudder is attached to the
check.explain: The rudder is hinged to the vertical stabilizer, or fin (PHAK Ch. 3). The elevator is on the horizontal stabilizer, ailerons and flaps are on the wing's trailing edge, and slats are on its leading edge.

check.stem: Which control surfaces roll the airplane?
check.explain: Ailerons move in opposite directions on each wing, rolling the airplane about its longitudinal axis. The rudder yaws, the elevator pitches, flaps add lift and trim tabs relieve control pressure.

check.stem: Spoilers on top of a wing are used to
options: trim the airplane for level flight.
check.explain: Spoilers rise into the airflow to spoil lift and add drag, for descents, roll control or braking on landing (PHAK Ch. 6). They never increase lift or reduce drag, and yaw and trim belong to the rudder and trim tabs.

units.title: Engines and propellers
units.objective: Explain the four-stroke cycle, ignition, carburetor ice, mixture and abnormal combustion, propellers and left-turning tendencies, and the basic turbine engine.

steps: Four-stroke cycle: intake, compression, power, exhaust; one cycle takes two crankshaft turns. The spark fires near the end of the compression stroke. Two engine-driven magnetos give dual ignition that keeps working if the electrical system fails and burns the charge more completely.

Carburetor ice forms in the venturi from the pressure drop and fuel vaporization, and is most likely below about 70°F with high humidity, though it can form at temperatures up to about 100°F (PHAK Ch. 7). With a fixed-pitch propeller the first sign is a drop in RPM; with a constant-speed propeller it is a drop in manifold pressure. Carb heat richens the mixture (warm air is less dense), so RPM dips first, then rises as the ice melts.

Mixture: as altitude rises the air thins, the mixture gets too RICH, and the pilot leans it. Detonation is the explosive burning of the charge after the spark, caused by too low a fuel grade, high temperatures or too lean a mixture; preignition is the charge lighting early from a hot spot. Never use a lower fuel grade than specified.

Propellers are twisted because the tips travel faster than the roots; the twist keeps the blade's angle of attack nearly the same along its length. A fixed-pitch propeller is a compromise; a constant-speed propeller's governor holds the RPM selected by the prop control, while the throttle sets manifold pressure.

Left-turning tendencies (clockwise propeller): torque rolls the airplane left; spiraling slipstream strikes the left side of the vertical fin, yawing left; P-factor at high AOA gives the descending right-side blade a bigger bite and more thrust, yawing left; gyroscopic precession yaws left when a tailwheel's tail is raised. So climbs and takeoffs need right rudder.

Gas turbines: intake, compression, combustion, expansion through the turbine, exhaust, all continuous. The turbine drives the compressor. Turbojet: all thrust from the jet; turbofan: a fan, with high-bypass fans producing most of the thrust; turboprop: drives a propeller through a reduction gearbox; turboshaft: drives a helicopter rotor. A hot start exceeds the temperature limit; a hung start lights but won't accelerate to idle.
teach.formula: Suck, squeeze, bang, blow · Carb ice: RPM drops (fixed pitch), MP drops (constant speed) · Climb = lean · Turbine drives compressor

worked.stem: A pilot is cruising with a constant-speed propeller in cool, humid air. Carburetor ice begins to form. What will the pilot notice first, and what will happen when carb heat is applied?
steps: Ice narrows the venturi, so less air and fuel reach the cylinders and power falls.
With a constant-speed propeller the governor flattens the blade pitch to hold RPM, so RPM does NOT drop. The first sign is a fall in MANIFOLD PRESSURE.
Carb heat sends warm, less dense air to the carburetor, which richens the mixture and costs a little more power at first.
As the ice melts, airflow returns and manifold pressure rises back toward normal.
worked.answer: A drop in manifold pressure with steady RPM; carb heat first lowers it slightly, then it recovers as the ice melts

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: A piston engine breathes in four steps. Remember 'suck, squeeze, bang, blow'.
Suck: the piston moves down and draws in fuel and air. Squeeze: it moves up and compresses them.
Bang: the spark plug fires and the burning mixture shoves the piston down. Blow: the piston pushes the burnt gas out.
The carburetor mixes fuel with air. When it gets cold and damp inside, ice can grow there and choke the engine.
Carb heat blows warm air in to melt that ice.
A jet engine does the same four jobs, but all at once and nonstop: squeeze the air, burn fuel in it, and let the hot gas spin a turbine and rush out the back.

visual.caption: Compression: both valves closed; the spark fires near the top

practice.stem: In a four-stroke aircraft piston engine, the spark plugs fire near the end of the
options: pause between the exhaust and intake strokes.
practice.explain: The spark ignites the compressed charge just before the piston reaches the top of the compression stroke, which begins the power stroke (PHAK Ch. 7). Firing during intake or exhaust would waste the charge with a valve open. During the power stroke the mixture is already burning, and there is no pause between strokes.

practice.stem: A pilot climbs from sea level to 8,000 feet without touching the mixture control. The fuel/air mixture becomes
options: too lean, because there is less oxygen at altitude.
unchanged, because the carburetor compensates automatically.
too rich, because fuel pressure rises with altitude.
too rich, because the air is less dense.
too lean, because fuel flow increases as the air thins.
practice.explain: The carburetor meters fuel by volume of air, but at altitude that volume weighs less, so the same fuel goes into less air and the mixture becomes too rich; the pilot leans it (PHAK Ch. 7). 'Less oxygen' sounds right but points the wrong way. Most carburetors have no automatic altitude compensation, and fuel pressure does not rise with altitude.

practice.stem: Detonation in a piston engine is most likely to be caused by
options: using fuel of a lower grade than the manufacturer specifies.
using fuel of a higher grade than the manufacturer specifies.
a mixture that is too rich.
operating with the cowl flaps fully open.
a fouled spark plug that fails to fire.
practice.explain: Too low a fuel grade, along with high cylinder temperatures and too lean a mixture, lets the charge explode instead of burning smoothly (PHAK Ch. 7). A richer mixture and open cowl flaps cool the engine and are cures, not causes. A higher grade is the approved substitute when the right one is unavailable, and a fouled plug causes roughness, not detonation.

practice.stem: In a high angle-of-attack climb, an airplane with a clockwise propeller yaws left because of P-factor. The reason is that
options: the ascending blade on the left side has the larger angle of attack and more thrust.
the spiraling slipstream strikes the right side of the vertical fin.
gyroscopic precession acts 90 degrees ahead of the force applied.
the descending blade on the right side has the larger angle of attack and more thrust.
engine torque rolls the airplane to the right.
practice.explain: At high AOA the descending blade, on the right side seen from the cockpit, meets the air at a larger angle and produces more thrust than the ascending left blade, so the thrust center shifts right and the nose yaws left (PHAK Ch. 5). Giving the left blade more thrust reverses it. The slipstream hits the LEFT side of the fin, precession is a separate tendency, and torque rolls the airplane left.

practice.stem: During a turbine engine start, the engine lights off normally but its RPM stays at a low value instead of rising to idle, while temperatures remain within limits. This is a
practice.explain: A hung (or false) start is a normal light-off followed by RPM that stalls below idle (PHAK Ch. 7). A hot start is one that exceeds the exhaust gas temperature limit. A compressor stall is a breakdown of airflow over the compressor blades, a flameout is the fire going out in a running engine, and detonation is a piston-engine problem.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's follow the air through the engine and ask what changes it.
steps: Air enters through the carburetor's venturi, where it speeds up, drops in pressure and cools; fuel evaporating cools it more. That's where carb ice grows.
Less air getting through means less power: RPM falls with a fixed-pitch propeller, manifold pressure falls with a constant-speed propeller.
Climb, and each breath of air weighs less but the fuel stays the same: too rich, so lean.
Warm carb-heat air is also less dense: richer again, so carb heat costs a little power at first.
In a turbine the air path is continuous: compressor, burner, turbine, out. The turbine's job is to drive the compressor.
Venturi: air cools
Ice narrows the throat
Less air: power drops
Carb heat melts it

example.stem: Why does applying carb heat make RPM dip before it recovers?
steps: The warm air is less dense, so the mixture becomes richer and power drops a little.
Then the ice melts and the venturi opens up.
Full airflow returns, so RPM rises.
example.answer: The richer, less dense warm air costs power first; melting ice then restores airflow

reteach.hook: Follow the air: less air in, less power out.

check.stem: In an airplane with a constant-speed propeller, the first sign of carburetor ice is usually
options: rough running with rising manifold pressure.
check.explain: The governor holds RPM by changing blade pitch, so the power loss shows as falling manifold pressure instead (PHAK Ch. 7). A drop in RPM is the first sign with a fixed-pitch propeller. Carb ice doesn't raise oil temperature, RPM, or manifold pressure.

check.stem: Applying carburetor heat
options: leans the mixture, because warm air is less dense.
has no effect on the mixture.
enriches the mixture, because warm air holds more oxygen.
enriches the mixture, because warm air is less dense.
check.explain: Warm air is less dense, so the same fuel goes into less air by weight and the mixture becomes richer, with a small loss of power (PHAK Ch. 7). Less dense air makes it richer, not leaner, and warm air holds less, not more, oxygen per volume.

check.stem: A propeller blade is twisted along its length mainly because
options: its tips travel faster than its roots.
it must clear the engine cowling.
the twist increases torque at low RPM.
the twist lets the blade flex in turbulence.
the twist cancels P-factor in climbs.
check.explain: The tip travels a much bigger circle than the root in the same time, so the blade angle decreases toward the tip to keep the angle of attack nearly the same along the blade (PHAK Ch. 7). Clearance, flex and torque aren't the reason, and twist doesn't remove P-factor.

check.stem: Which type of turbine engine drives a helicopter's rotor through a transmission?
check.explain: A turboshaft delivers its power as shaft output to a transmission, which drives the rotor. A turboprop drives a propeller through a reduction gearbox, a turbojet and a turbofan produce thrust directly, and a ramjet has no turbine at all.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. An engine needs air, fuel and a spark.
steps: Suck: the piston pulls in fuel and air.
Squeeze: it compresses them.
Bang: the spark plug fires and the push drives the piston down.
Blow: the burnt gas is pushed out.
Up high the air is thinner, so the pilot uses less fuel by leaning the mixture.

example.stem: Which stroke comes straight after intake?
steps: Suck, squeeze, bang, blow.
After 'suck' (intake) comes 'squeeze'.

reteach.hook: Suck, squeeze, bang, blow.

check.stem: In the four-stroke cycle, which stroke comes straight after compression?
check.explain: The order is intake, compression, power, exhaust. Ignition is the spark that starts the power stroke, not a stroke of its own, and each stroke happens once per cycle.

check.stem: Aircraft piston engines have two magnetos mainly so that
options: the battery charges faster during flight.
the engine can start without fuel.
ignition continues if one magneto fails.
the cabin lights work during start.
check.explain: Dual ignition means the engine keeps running if one magneto or plug fails, and two sparks burn the mixture more completely (PHAK Ch. 7). Magnetos don't charge the battery, replace fuel, drive the starter or power the lights.

check.stem: As an airplane climbs, the pilot leans the mixture because
options: the fuel gets heavier as it gets colder.
the air is thinner, needing less fuel.
check.explain: Air density falls with altitude, so less fuel is needed to match the air the engine takes in (PHAK Ch. 7). Air gets thinner, not thicker, and the other options don't drive mixture changes.

check.stem: In a jet engine, the turbine's main job is to
check.explain: Hot gas from the combustor spins the turbine, which drives the compressor through a shared shaft (PHAK Ch. 7). Mixing happens in the combustor, and the turbine has nothing to do with steering, fuel storage or cockpit cooling.

units.title: Flight instruments and their errors
units.objective: Know what each instrument senses, how pitot and static blockages show up, the kinds of altitude and airspeed, gyroscopic principles and magnetic compass errors.

steps: Pitot-static: the airspeed indicator uses pitot (ram) AND static pressure; the altimeter and VSI use static only. Pitot inlet blocked with the drain open: airspeed drops to zero. Inlet AND drain blocked: the airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter, reading higher in a climb and lower in a descent. Static port blocked: the altimeter freezes, the VSI reads zero, and airspeed reads low in a climb and high in a descent.

The alternate static source usually vents to the cabin, where pressure is a little lower than outside, so the altimeter reads slightly high, the airspeed reads slightly high and the VSI shows a momentary climb. Airspeed arcs: white = flap range, green = normal range, yellow = caution (smooth air only), red line = never-exceed speed (VNE).

Altitudes: indicated (read off the dial), true (above sea level), absolute (above the ground), pressure (with 29.92 set) and density altitude (pressure altitude corrected for temperature). 'From high to low, look out below': flying into lower pressure or colder air without resetting, the airplane is lower than indicated. About 1,000 feet per inch of mercury.

Gyros: rigidity in space keeps the attitude indicator and heading indicator stable; precession drives the turn coordinator and turn-and-slip indicator. Attitude and heading indicators are usually vacuum-driven, the turn coordinator usually electric. The heading indicator drifts from precession, so reset it to the magnetic compass about every 15 minutes.

Compass errors: variation is the angle between true and magnetic north (east is least, west is best: subtract east, add west); deviation comes from the airplane's own magnetic fields (shown on the compass correction card). Magnetic dip causes turning errors, worst near north and south: Undershoot North, Overshoot South (UNOS); turning from north the compass first shows a turn the OPPOSITE way. Acceleration error, worst on east and west headings: Accelerate North, Decelerate South (ANDS). All for the Northern Hemisphere.
Ball in the turn coordinator: 'step on the ball'. Ball to the inside of the turn = slip (not enough rudder); ball to the outside = skid (too much rudder).
teach.formula: ASI = pitot + static · Altimeter & VSI = static · UNOS · ANDS · High to low, look out below

worked.stem: Ice blocks both the pitot tube's inlet and its drain hole, while the static port stays clear. The pilot then climbs. What does the airspeed indicator show?
steps: With inlet and drain both blocked, the air in the pitot line is trapped at a fixed pressure.
The static side is still open, so static pressure falls normally as the airplane climbs.
The ASI reads the DIFFERENCE between pitot and static pressure. Fixed pitot minus falling static = a growing difference.
So the indicated airspeed rises in the climb, even if the true speed is steady: the ASI is acting like an altimeter.
worked.answer: An increasing airspeed during the climb, like an altimeter

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Two little holes feed the main instruments: the pitot tube, which faces into the wind, and the static port, which sits flush on the side.
The pitot tube feels the push of the air rushing at the airplane. The static port feels the still air pressure around it.
The airspeed indicator compares the two. The faster you go, the bigger the push.
The altimeter only uses the static port: air pressure drops as you climb, and the altimeter turns that into feet.
If a hole gets blocked, the instruments that use it go wrong. Ask: which hole is blocked, and which instruments use it?
The gyro instruments use spinning wheels instead, and the compass uses a magnet.
Pitot + static: airspeed
Static only: altimeter
Static only: VSI
Gyros: attitude, heading

practice.stem: Which instrument uses both pitot pressure and static pressure?
practice.explain: The airspeed indicator measures the difference between pitot (ram) pressure and static pressure (PHAK Ch. 8). The altimeter and VSI use static pressure only. The heading and attitude indicators are gyroscopic instruments with no pitot-static connection.

practice.stem: A pilot checks the heading indicator against the magnetic compass about every 15 minutes because the heading indicator
options: is subject to magnetic dip in turns.
shows acceleration error on east and west headings.
is driven by the pitot-static system.
reads true heading instead of magnetic heading.
practice.explain: Friction in the gyro causes precession, so the heading indicator slowly drifts and must be reset to the compass (PHAK Ch. 8). Dip and acceleration errors affect the magnetic compass itself, not the gyro. The heading indicator is usually vacuum-driven, and it shows whatever heading it was set to, normally magnetic.

practice.stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, a pilot starts a right turn from a heading of north and watches the magnetic compass. During the first part of the turn the compass will
options: lead the turn, showing more heading change than has occurred.
stay on north until the wings are level again.
show a turn toward the south.
briefly show a turn in the opposite direction, toward west.
practice.explain: Magnetic dip makes the compass lag when turning from north: it first swings the opposite way, then catches up (PHAK Ch. 8; Undershoot North). Leading the turn is what happens when turning from SOUTH. The compass doesn't show turns accurately near north or south, doesn't freeze, and a right turn from north is toward east, not south.

practice.stem: A pilot selects the alternate static source, which vents to an unpressurized cabin. Compared with normal readings, the altimeter and airspeed indicator will typically read
practice.explain: Airflow around the cabin makes its pressure a little lower than outside static pressure, so the altimeter reads high and the airspeed indicator reads high (it sees a bigger gap between pitot and static); the VSI momentarily shows a climb (PHAK Ch. 8). The mixed and lower combinations get the pressure change backwards, and a cabin source is never exactly the same as the outside ports.

practice.stem: Ice blocks the pitot tube's ram-air inlet, but its drain hole stays open. The airspeed indicator will
options: act like an altimeter, rising in a climb.
freeze at the speed it showed when the ice formed.
read higher than actual in a descent.
keep reading correctly from static pressure alone.
practice.explain: With the inlet blocked and the drain open, the trapped pressure bleeds out of the drain until the pitot line matches static pressure, so the indicated airspeed drops to zero (PHAK Ch. 8). Acting like an altimeter needs the drain blocked too. Freezing at one value doesn't happen while the drain vents, reading high in a descent is a static-port blockage, and the ASI can't work without pitot pressure.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. For any blockage, ask two questions: which hole, and which instruments use it?
steps: Static port blocked: everything that uses static goes wrong. The altimeter freezes, the VSI reads zero, and the airspeed indicator errs (low in a climb, high in a descent).
Pitot inlet blocked, drain open: only the airspeed indicator uses pitot, so only it fails, and it drops to zero.
Pitot inlet AND drain blocked: the trapped pressure turns the airspeed indicator into an altimeter.
For the compass, ask: turning or speeding up? Turning near north or south: UNOS. Speeding up or slowing on east or west: ANDS.
For altimeter settings: 'high to low, look out below'.
Which hole is blocked?
Which instruments use it?
Static: alt, VSI, ASI
Pitot: ASI only

example.stem: The static port ices over in level cruise. What happens to the VSI?
steps: The VSI uses static pressure only.
With static pressure trapped, it sees no change at all.
So it reads zero, whatever the airplane does.

reteach.hook: Which hole, which instruments?

check.stem: The static port becomes blocked during a climb. The altimeter will
options: freeze at the altitude where it blocked.
keep reading higher than actual altitude.
check.explain: The altimeter needs changing static pressure; with it trapped, the reading freezes at the altitude where the port blocked (PHAK Ch. 8). It can't keep working, has no reason to fall to zero or show a descent, and a frozen reading in a climb is lower than actual, not higher.

check.stem: Which instrument works on the gyroscopic principle of precession?
check.explain: The turn coordinator and turn-and-slip indicator use precession (PHAK Ch. 8). The attitude and heading indicators rely on rigidity in space. The altimeter is a pressure instrument, and the compass uses a magnet.

check.stem: A pilot flies from an area of high pressure into an area of lower pressure without resetting the altimeter. The airplane will be
options: at the altitude the altimeter shows.
higher only if the air is warmer.
check.explain: With the old, higher setting still in, the altimeter over-reads in the lower pressure, so the airplane is lower than indicated: 'high to low, look out below' (PHAK Ch. 8). Temperature has a similar effect of its own, but the pressure error doesn't depend on it or on night.

check.stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, an airplane on a westerly heading slows down. The magnetic compass will indicate
options: a swing only if the heading is north.
check.explain: Acceleration error is greatest on east and west headings: Accelerate North, Decelerate South (ANDS), so slowing shows a turn toward the south (PHAK Ch. 8). North is the acceleration case. The error is real, it doesn't point east, and north headings give turning error, not acceleration error.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. One job per instrument.
steps: Airspeed indicator: how fast you're moving through the air.
Altimeter: how high you are, worked out from air pressure.
Vertical speed indicator: how fast you're climbing or descending.
Attitude indicator: whether the nose and wings are level with the horizon.
Heading indicator and compass: which way you're pointing.

example.stem: Which instrument tells the pilot whether the wings are level?
steps: The altimeter and airspeed indicator show height and speed.
The attitude indicator shows a little airplane against an artificial horizon.

reteach.hook: One instrument, one question answered.

check.stem: The altimeter works by measuring
options: distance to the ground, using a radar signal.
air pressure, which it shows as altitude.
check.explain: A standard altimeter is an aneroid barometer: it senses static air pressure and displays it as altitude (PHAK Ch. 8). Radar altimeters are a separate instrument, and speed, temperature and climb rate are shown elsewhere.

check.stem: Which instrument shows the airplane's pitch and bank relative to the horizon?
check.explain: The attitude indicator shows pitch and bank against an artificial horizon. The heading indicator shows direction, the altimeter height, the VSI climb rate and the airspeed indicator speed.

check.stem: On an airspeed indicator, the red line marks the
check.explain: The red radial line is VNE, the never-exceed speed (PHAK Ch. 8). Stall speeds are at the low ends of the white and green arcs, the flap range is the white arc, and maneuvering and best-climb speeds aren't marked by the red line.

check.stem: The heading indicator is set to agree with
check.explain: The heading indicator has no magnet of its own, so the pilot sets it to the magnetic compass, in steady flight, and rechecks it about every 15 minutes (PHAK Ch. 8). The other instruments don't show heading, and a runway number is only rounded to 10 degrees.

units.title: Airports: runways, markings, signs and lights
units.objective: Number a runway from its heading, read runway and taxiway markings and airport signs, and interpret airport lighting, VASI, PAPI and light-gun signals.

steps: Runway numbers: the magnetic heading of the centerline rounded to the nearest 10°, with the last zero dropped (157° → 16). The two ends differ by 18 (16/34). Parallel runways add L, C or R, which swap at the other end: 22R is the same strip as 04L.

Runway markings are white: designation, threshold, aiming point (two broad stripes about 1,000 feet in), touchdown zone and centerline. A displaced threshold is marked with white arrows; the area before it can be used for taxiing, takeoff and the landing rollout from the other direction, but not for touchdown. Yellow chevrons mark a blast pad or stopway not usable for normal operations. Taxiway markings are yellow.

Runway holding position marking: four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed, across the taxiway. The solid lines are on the side where you hold. At a towered airport you don't cross them without an ATC clearance (AIM 2-3-5).

Signs (AIM 2-3-8 to 2-3-13): mandatory instruction signs are red with white letters (runway holding position, ILS critical area, no entry). Location signs are black with a yellow inscription and yellow border: where you are. Direction and destination signs are yellow with black letters and an arrow: where to go. Runway distance remaining signs are black with a white number in thousands of feet.

Lights: runway edge white (the last 2,000 feet of an instrument runway show yellow), threshold green, runway end red; taxiway edge blue, taxiway centerline green. Beacons (AIM 2-1-9): white and green = lighted civil land airport, white and yellow = water airport, green, yellow and white = heliport, two quick white flashes between greens = military airport.

Glide-path lights (AIM 2-1-2): two-bar VASI: red over white = on glide path; all white = high; all red = low. PAPI (four lights in a row): two white and two red = on path; three white = slightly high; four white = high; three red = slightly low; four red = low. Light gun (AIM 4-3-13), in flight: steady green land, flashing green return for landing, steady red give way and circle, flashing red airport unsafe. On the ground: steady green cleared for takeoff, flashing green cleared to taxi, steady red stop, flashing red taxi clear of the runway, flashing white return to starting point. Alternating red and green: exercise extreme caution.
teach.formula: Runway = magnetic heading ÷ 10 · Ends differ by 18, L and R swap · Red over white, you're all right · PAPI: 2 white + 2 red = on path

worked.stem: You are cleared to land on runway 22R. Roughly what is its magnetic heading, what is the other end called, and what would a PAPI showing three white lights and one red mean on final?
steps: 22 → about 220° magnetic (anywhere from 215° to 224°).
The other end: 22 − 18 = 04. Seen from that end the right-hand runway becomes the LEFT one, so it is 04L.
PAPI: two white and two red is on glide path. Three white and one red means slightly ABOVE it.
So you would reduce your descent slightly until you see two of each.
worked.answer: About 220°; the other end is 04L; three white and one red means slightly high

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Take the runway's compass direction, say 270°. Drop the last zero: runway 27.
Turn around and look the other way: 270° − 180° = 090°, so that end is runway 9.
Paint: runways are white, taxiways are yellow.
Lights: runway edges are white, taxiway edges are blue, taxiway centerlines are green.
Red signs mean 'stop and get permission'. Black signs with yellow writing tell you where you are; yellow signs with black writing tell you where to go.
Approach lights: lots of white means you're high, lots of red means you're low.
4 white: high
3 white 1 red: slightly high
2 white 2 red: on path
3 red 1 white: slightly low
4 red: low

visual.caption: Reading a PAPI on final approach

practice.stem: A runway centerline has a magnetic heading of 157°. That end of the runway is numbered
practice.explain: Round 157° to the nearest 10°, which is 160°, and drop the last zero: runway 16 (AIM 2-3-3). 15 truncates instead of rounding. 34 is the opposite end (337° rounds to 340°), and 33 is the opposite end mis-rounded. Runway numbers never use all three digits.

practice.stem: On final approach, a pilot sees a PAPI showing three red lights and one white light. The aircraft is
practice.explain: On a four-light PAPI, more red means lower: three red and one white is slightly below the glide path, four red is well below, and two of each is on path (AIM 2-1-2). Three white and one red would be slightly above, and four white well above.

practice.stem: Taxiing at a towered airport, a pilot reaches a runway holding position marking with the two solid yellow lines on the pilot's side. The pilot
options: may cross, because the solid lines show the runway side is clear.
may cross if no aircraft can be seen on final approach.
must hold short only at night or in low visibility.
must not cross the marking without an ATC clearance.
should cross and wait on the runway centerline for a clearance.
practice.explain: The solid lines are on the holding side, and at a controlled airport a pilot must not cross them without ATC clearance (AIM 2-3-5). The solid side is where you stop, not a sign the runway is clear. Looking for traffic yourself is the practice at nontowered fields, the rule applies at all times, and waiting on the runway would put you in harm's way.

practice.stem: A runway has a displaced threshold marked with white arrows leading up to it. The paved area before the displaced threshold may be used for
options: taxiing only, and never for a takeoff or a landing rollout.
landing touchdown, but not for takeoff in either direction.
nothing at all; it is closed to every aircraft operation.
takeoff and the landing rollout from the other end, not touchdown.
takeoff only, and then only in an emergency declared to the tower.
practice.explain: The area behind a displaced threshold is available for taxiing, takeoff and the landing rollout from the other direction; you may not touch down on it when landing toward the threshold (AIM 2-3-3). Taxiing only is too narrow, and touchdown is exactly what is forbidden. A paved area closed to everything is marked with yellow chevrons, and no emergency restriction applies.

practice.stem: An airplane is taxiing at a towered airport with a failed radio when the tower aims a flashing red light at it. The pilot should
options: stop and wait for further signals.
taxi clear of the runway in use.
return to the starting point on the airport.
continue, since that signal applies only to aircraft in flight.
practice.explain: To an aircraft on the ground, a flashing red light means taxi clear of the runway in use (AIM 4-3-13). Steady red means stop, flashing white means return to the starting point, and alternating red and green means exercise extreme caution. Flashing red also has a meaning in flight (airport unsafe), but it applies on the ground too.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's turn the airport into colors and numbers.
steps: Numbers: runway = magnetic heading ÷ 10, rounded. The far end is 18 more or less, and L and R swap.
Paint: white on runways, yellow on taxiways.
Signs: red = mandatory, stop and get permission. Black with yellow = you are here. Yellow with black = go this way.
Lights: white runway edges, blue taxiway edges, green taxiway centerlines, green threshold, red runway end.
Glide path: more white = higher, more red = lower.
Red sign: stop, ask
Black + yellow: you are here
Yellow + black: go there
Blue lights: taxiway edge

example.stem: You're on taxiway C and see a black sign with a yellow C, next to a yellow sign with a black B and a left arrow. What does it tell you?
steps: Black with yellow is a location sign: you are on C.
Yellow with black and an arrow is a direction sign: taxiway B is to the left.
example.answer: You are on taxiway C, and taxiway B is to the left

reteach.hook: White runway, yellow taxiway, red means stop.

check.stem: The opposite end of runway 22R is numbered
check.explain: 22 − 18 = 04, and from the other end the right-hand runway becomes the left one, so 22R's opposite end is 04L (AIM 2-3-3). 04R forgets that the letters swap, and 22L is a different, parallel runway.

check.stem: A two-bar VASI shows red over red. The aircraft is
check.explain: Red over red means below the glide path; red over white is on path, and white over white is above (AIM 2-1-2). A VASI shows only vertical guidance, not centerline or speed.

check.stem: A mandatory instruction sign has
options: a black background with yellow letters.
a yellow background with black letters.
a white background with red letters.
a red background with white letters.
a black background with a white number.
check.explain: Mandatory instruction signs, such as runway holding position signs, are red with white inscriptions (AIM 2-3-8). Black with yellow is a location sign, yellow with black a direction or destination sign, and black with a white number a runway distance remaining sign.

check.stem: A rotating beacon showing two quick white flashes between green flashes marks
check.explain: Military airports are identified by dual-peaked white flashes between green (AIM 2-1-9). A civil land airport alternates white and green, a water airport white and yellow, and a heliport green, yellow and white.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. Paint, lights and the tower's light gun.
steps: Runway paint is white. Taxiway paint is yellow.
Lights along taxiway edges are blue. Lights along runway edges are white.
If your radio fails, the tower can aim colored light at you.
Steady green to an aircraft in the air means 'cleared to land'.
On final, a PAPI with more white than red means you're high; more red means you're low.

example.stem: What color paint marks a taxiway centerline?
steps: Runway markings are white.
Taxiway markings, including the centerline, are yellow.

reteach.hook: White for runways, yellow and blue for taxiways.

check.stem: Runway markings are painted
check.explain: Runway markings are white; taxiway markings are yellow (AIM 2-3-1). Blue and green are taxiway light colors, and red is used for mandatory signs and runway end lights.

check.stem: Taxiway edge lights are
check.explain: Taxiway edges are lit blue and taxiway centerlines green (AIM 2-1-10). White lights line runway edges, red marks the runway end, and yellow shows the caution zone at the end of an instrument runway.

check.stem: An aircraft in flight receives a steady green light from the tower. It is
options: told to give way and keep circling.
told not to land because the airport is unsafe.
check.explain: In flight, steady green means cleared to land (AIM 4-3-13). Flashing green means return for landing, steady red give way and keep circling, and flashing red airport unsafe. 'Cleared to taxi' is flashing green to an aircraft on the ground.

check.stem: On a PAPI, four white lights mean the aircraft is
check.explain: All four white is well above the glide path; three white and one red is slightly above, two of each is on path, and more red means lower (AIM 2-1-2).

units.title: Airspace and VFR rules
units.objective: Know the airspace classes and entry requirements, VFR weather minimums, speed limits, cruising altitudes, minimum altitudes and right-of-way rules.

steps: Class A: 18,000 feet MSL up to FL600, IFR only. Class B: around the busiest airports, usually surface to 10,000 MSL in an upside-down wedding cake; VFR pilots need an explicit ATC clearance. Class C: typically a 5 NM core from the surface to 4,000 feet above the airport and a 10 NM shelf from 1,200 feet; you need two-way radio communication first. Class D: towered airports, usually up to 2,500 feet above the airport, two-way radio communication. Class E: all other controlled airspace, including above FL600. Class G: uncontrolled.

VFR minimums (14 CFR 91.155): Class B: 3 SM, clear of clouds. Classes C, D and E below 10,000 MSL: 3 SM; 500 feet below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal ('3-152'). At or above 10,000 MSL (more than 1,200 AGL): 5 SM; 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal. Class G at or below 1,200 AGL by day: 1 SM, clear of clouds. Within the surface area of a towered airport, VFR also needs a 1,000-foot ceiling and 3 SM ground visibility.

Speed limits (91.117): 250 knots indicated below 10,000 MSL; 200 knots at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of the primary airport of Class C or D airspace; 200 knots beneath a Class B shelf or in a VFR corridor through Class B.

VFR cruising altitudes (91.159), above 3,000 feet AGL: magnetic COURSE 0° to 179° = odd thousands plus 500 (3,500, 5,500); 180° to 359° = even thousands plus 500 (4,500, 6,500). It is based on course, not heading.

Right-of-way (91.113): an aircraft in distress has priority over all. Different categories: balloon, then glider, then airship, then airplane or rotorcraft, except that an aircraft towing or refueling another has right-of-way over all other engine-driven aircraft. Same category converging: the aircraft on the right has right-of-way. Head-on: both alter course to the right. Overtaking: the aircraft being overtaken has right-of-way, and you pass well clear on its right. Landing: the lower aircraft has right-of-way but may not cut in.

Minimum altitudes (91.119): over a congested area, 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet horizontally; elsewhere 500 feet AGL; over open water or sparsely populated areas, no closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure. VFR fuel reserve (91.151): 30 minutes by day, 45 minutes at night.
teach.formula: B: clearance · C and D: two-way radio · 3-152 below 10,000 · 0–179° odd + 500, 180–359° even + 500 · Right-of-way: distress, balloon, glider, airship, airplane

worked.stem: A VFR pilot is flying a magnetic course of 135° over terrain about 2,000 feet MSL and wants to cruise near 6,000 feet MSL in Class E airspace. Which altitudes fit the rules, and what cloud clearances apply?
steps: 6,000 MSL over 2,000-foot terrain is about 4,000 AGL, which is above 3,000 AGL, so the cruising-altitude rule applies.
Magnetic course 135° falls in 0° to 179°: odd thousands plus 500. The nearest choices are 5,500 and 7,500 MSL.
Both are below 10,000 MSL in Class E, so the minimums are 3 SM visibility and 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
worked.answer: 5,500 or 7,500 feet MSL; 3 SM visibility and 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Airspace is like rooms with different door rules.
Class A, the top floor (18,000 feet and up), is for instrument flights only.
Class B, around the biggest airports, needs a spoken clearance: 'cleared into the Class Bravo'.
Classes C and D just need you to talk to the controller and hear your call sign back before you enter.
Class E is controlled but has no door rule for VFR pilots, and Class G is uncontrolled.
For cruising heights, think 'east is odd': flying generally east, use odd thousands plus 500; flying west, even thousands plus 500.
Aircraft in distress
Balloon
Glider
Airship
Airplane / rotorcraft

practice.stem: Before entering Class C airspace, a VFR pilot must
options: receive an explicit clearance to enter the airspace.
establish two-way radio communication with ATC.
be flying at least 1,200 feet above the ground.
practice.explain: Class C requires two-way radio communication with ATC before entry, plus a Mode C transponder (AIM 3-2-4). An explicit clearance is the Class B requirement. No flight plan or instrument rating is needed, and Class C starts at the surface around the primary airport, so there's no minimum height to enter.

practice.stem: In Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL, the basic VFR weather minimums are
options: 3 SM visibility; 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
5 SM visibility; 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 1 SM horizontally from clouds.
3 SM visibility; 1,000 feet below, 500 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
practice.explain: Below 10,000 MSL in Classes C, D and E the rule is 3 SM and 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal (14 CFR 91.155). 3 SM and clear of clouds is Class B. The 5 SM figures apply at or above 10,000 MSL. 1 SM and clear of clouds is daytime Class G near the surface, and 1,000 below with 500 above swaps the two distances.

practice.stem: A glider and an airship are converging at about the same altitude, with the airship on the glider's right. Which has the right-of-way?
options: The airship, because it is on the glider's right.
The airship, because it is larger and slower to maneuver.
Neither; both must alter course to the right.
Whichever is at the slightly higher altitude.
practice.explain: Between categories, a glider has the right-of-way over an airship (14 CFR 91.113(d)): balloon, then glider, then airship, then airplane or rotorcraft. The 'on the right' rule applies only within the same category. Both turning right is the head-on rule, and altitude doesn't decide right-of-way.

practice.stem: A VFR pilot is flying a magnetic course of 178° with a 20° wind correction angle to the right, so the magnetic heading is 198°, more than 3,000 feet AGL. An appropriate cruising altitude is
practice.explain: VFR cruising altitudes are based on magnetic COURSE (14 CFR 91.159). 178° falls in 0° to 179°, so the pilot uses odd thousands plus 500: 7,500 feet MSL. 8,500 uses the 198° heading by mistake. Even or odd whole thousands without the 500 are IFR altitudes.

practice.stem: Unless ATC authorizes otherwise, the maximum indicated airspeed at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of the primary airport of Class C airspace is
practice.explain: 14 CFR 91.117 limits aircraft to 200 knots indicated at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 NM of the primary airport of Class C or D airspace. 250 knots is the general limit below 10,000 MSL. 230 knots is a holding-pattern speed, and the other figures are not regulatory limits here.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's think of each class by what you must DO to get in.
steps: Class A: file IFR. VFR pilots can't go in at all.
Class B: hear the words 'cleared into Class Bravo'. Nothing less will do.
Classes C and D: talk to the controller and hear your own call sign back.
Class E and Class G: nothing special for VFR; just meet the weather minimums.
Then pick your height: east-ish (0° to 179° magnetic course) is odd plus 500; west-ish is even plus 500, once you're above 3,000 feet AGL.
A: IFR only
B: explicit clearance
C and D: two-way radio
E and G: weather minimums

example.stem: A VFR pilot calls approach before Class C and hears: 'N123AB, stand by.' May the pilot enter?
steps: Class C needs two-way radio communication.
ATC replied using the aircraft's call sign, so communication is established.
'Stand by' isn't a refusal, so the pilot may enter unless told to remain outside.
example.answer: Yes, because ATC used the aircraft's call sign

reteach.hook: B needs a clearance; C and D need your call sign back.

check.stem: Class A airspace begins at
check.explain: Class A runs from 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL600 (AIM 3-2-2). 14,500 MSL is where Class E begins in many places if lower floors aren't designated, 10,000 MSL is a speed and minimums boundary, and above FL600 is Class E.

check.stem: To enter Class B airspace, a VFR pilot needs
check.explain: Class B requires a clearance to enter, such as 'cleared into the Class Bravo' (AIM 3-2-3). Two-way radio contact alone is enough only for Classes C and D. VFR pilots don't need an instrument rating or flight plan.

check.stem: A VFR pilot flying a magnetic course of 270 degrees more than 3,000 feet AGL should cruise at
options: odd thousands plus 500 feet, such as 7,500.
even thousands plus 500 feet, such as 6,500.
any altitude, because the rule applies only to IFR.
check.explain: Magnetic courses of 180° to 359° use even thousands plus 500 for VFR (14 CFR 91.159). Odd plus 500 is for 0° to 179°. Whole thousands are IFR altitudes, and the rule does apply to VFR above 3,000 feet AGL.

check.stem: Two aircraft are approaching each other head-on. Each pilot should
options: let the faster aircraft give way.
have the higher aircraft climb and the lower one descend.
check.explain: When approaching head-on or nearly so, each pilot alters course to the right (14 CFR 91.113(e)). There is no left-turn, climb, speed or altitude rule for this case.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. A few rules cover most questions.
steps: Class G is uncontrolled airspace.
Classes C and D: talk to the controller before you enter.
An aircraft in trouble always gets the right of way.
Below 10,000 feet, the speed limit is 250 knots.
Meeting another aircraft head-on, both turn right.

example.stem: A balloon and an airplane are converging. Which has the right-of-way?
steps: The less able an aircraft is to maneuver, the higher it ranks.
A balloon can barely steer, so it ranks above everything except an aircraft in distress.

reteach.hook: Distress first, then balloon, glider, airship, airplane.

check.stem: Uncontrolled airspace is
check.explain: Class G is the uncontrolled airspace (AIM 3-3). Classes A, B, C, D and E are all controlled airspace.

check.stem: Before entering Class D airspace, a VFR pilot must
options: establish two-way radio communication with the tower.
receive an explicit clearance from ATC, as for Class B.
do nothing, because Class D is uncontrolled.
check.explain: Class D requires two-way radio communication with the control tower before entry (AIM 3-2-5). An explicit clearance is the Class B rule, no instrument rating is needed, Class D is controlled, and 18,000 feet is Class A.

check.stem: Which has the right-of-way over all other air traffic?
check.explain: An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic (14 CFR 91.113(c)). Balloons, gliders and airships rank in that order only after it, and size gives no priority.

check.stem: Below 10,000 feet MSL, the general maximum indicated airspeed is
check.explain: 14 CFR 91.117 sets 250 knots indicated below 10,000 feet MSL. 200 knots applies near Class C and D primary airports and under Class B shelves.

units.title: Weather
units.objective: Recognize fronts, stable and unstable air, the kinds of fog, structural icing, density altitude and thunderstorm hazards, and estimate cloud bases.

steps: Fronts: a cold front is colder air pushing under warmer air. It is steep and fast, with a narrow band of cumuliform clouds, showers, thunderstorms, gusty winds and a wind shift, then rising pressure, cooler drier air and good visibility behind it. A warm front is warm air sliding up over cold air: a gentle slope, a wide band of stratiform clouds (cirrus, cirrostratus, altostratus, nimbostratus), steady precipitation, low ceilings, poor visibility and fog.

Stable air: stratiform clouds, steady precipitation, smooth air, poor visibility in haze. Unstable air: cumuliform clouds, showers, turbulence, good visibility outside showers. Cloud bases: the temperature/dew point spread in °F ÷ 4.4 × 1,000 feet (or the °C spread ÷ 2.5 × 1,000) estimates the base of cumulus clouds above the ground. Standard lapse rate is 2°C per 1,000 feet.

Fog: radiation fog forms on clear, calm or light-wind nights over low ground. Advection fog is warm, moist air moving over a colder surface, common on coasts, and needs wind. Upslope fog is moist, stable air pushed up rising ground. Steam fog is cold air moving over warmer water. Precipitation-induced fog comes from warm rain falling through cool air.

Structural icing needs visible moisture and an airframe temperature at or below freezing. Clear ice comes from large supercooled drops (cumuliform clouds, freezing rain) and is heavy and hard to remove; rime ice comes from small drops in stratiform clouds and is rough and milky. Freezing rain at the surface means warmer air above. Frost on the wings must be removed before takeoff: it disrupts airflow and raises the stall speed.

Density altitude: high, hot and humid all raise density altitude and cut performance: longer takeoff roll, weaker climb, less engine and propeller output. The indicated airspeed for liftoff stays the same, but the true airspeed and ground speed are higher, so the run is longer.

Thunderstorms need moisture, unstable air and a lifting force. Cumulus stage: updrafts. Mature stage: begins when rain reaches the surface, with updrafts and downdrafts side by side; the most violent stage. Dissipating stage: downdrafts. Avoid severe storms by at least 20 NM. A microburst on approach first gives a headwind (airspeed and performance rise), then a downdraft, then a tailwind (airspeed and lift drop sharply) (AIM 7-1).
teach.formula: Cold front: fast, steep, storms, then clearing · Warm front: slow, layered, steady rain, fog · Ice = visible moisture + at or below 0°C · High, hot, humid = poor performance

worked.stem: A surface report shows a temperature of 86°F and a dew point of 64°F. Estimate the height of the cumulus cloud bases, and say what the moisture tells you.
steps: So the bases are about 5,000 feet above the ground (AGL, not MSL).
A small spread means moist air near saturation; the bigger the spread, the higher the bases. As the spread closes toward zero, expect low clouds or fog.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: A front is the border between two big blobs of air, one cold and one warm.
Cold air is heavy and shoves under warm air like a snowplow: quick, bumpy, stormy, then clear.
Warm air is light and slides up over cold air like a ramp: slow, grey, drizzly and foggy.
Fog is just a cloud on the ground. It forms when air cools until it can't hold its moisture.
Ice sticks to an airplane when it flies through water drops that are colder than freezing.
Hot, high, humid air is thin air, and thin air means the wings and engine work less well.
Cumulus: updrafts
Mature: rain at surface
Mature: up + downdrafts
Dissipating: downdrafts

practice.stem: Which conditions are most favorable for radiation fog?
options: Warm, moist air blowing steadily over a cold ocean surface.
Moist air being pushed up a mountain slope.
Cold air moving over a warmer lake.
Strong, gusty winds under a solid overcast sky through the night.
A clear, calm night with a small temperature/dew point spread.
practice.explain: Radiation fog forms when the ground cools under a clear sky on a calm or nearly calm night and chills the moist air above it to its dew point (PHAK Ch. 12). Moist air over a cold ocean is advection fog, air pushed up a slope is upslope fog, and cold air over warm water is steam fog. Strong wind and overcast both prevent radiation cooling.

practice.stem: Compared with a typical warm front, the passage of a typical cold front usually brings
options: a narrow band of cumuliform clouds and showers, then rapid clearing.
wide areas of stratus clouds and steady drizzle lasting a day or more.
falling pressure and warmer temperatures after it passes.
fog and poor visibility once the front has passed.
warmer, more humid air behind the front.
practice.explain: A cold front's steep slope lifts warm air quickly into a narrow band of cumuliform clouds, showers and sometimes thunderstorms, followed by clearing, rising pressure and cooler, drier air (PHAK Ch. 12). Wide stratus with steady drizzle, fog and warmer, more humid air are typical of a warm front. Pressure rises and temperature falls after a cold front passes.

practice.stem: Freezing rain reported at the surface indicates that
options: the temperature is below freezing at all altitudes above the station.
a cold front passed through several hours earlier.
there is a layer of above-freezing air at a higher altitude.
thunderstorms are certain to be within 5 miles.
the air above is too dry for clouds to form.
practice.explain: Freezing rain falls as liquid from a warmer layer aloft and freezes on contact below, so it signals a temperature inversion with above-freezing air higher up (PHAK Ch. 12). If it were below freezing all the way up, the precipitation would be snow. Freezing rain doesn't prove a recent cold front or nearby storms, and rain needs moist cloud above, not dry air.

practice.stem: On a hot day at a high-elevation airport, compared with a standard day at sea level, an airplane will
options: need a longer takeoff roll, and a higher indicated airspeed to lift off.
need a shorter takeoff roll, because the warm air rises under the wings.
need a longer takeoff roll, but the same indicated airspeed to lift off.
lift off at a lower true airspeed, because the air is thinner.
produce more engine power, because thin air causes less drag.
practice.explain: High density altitude means thin air: the wing needs the same indicated airspeed to lift off, but that is a higher true airspeed and ground speed, and the engine and propeller produce less thrust, so the takeoff roll is longer (PHAK Ch. 11). The indicated liftoff speed doesn't rise, the true speed is higher not lower, and thin air reduces engine power.

practice.stem: An airplane on final approach flies through a microburst. In what order does it usually meet the winds?
practice.explain: The outflow spreading from the microburst first gives a headwind that raises airspeed and performance, then the core's downdraft, then a strong tailwind that cuts airspeed and lift just as the airplane is low (AIM 7-1). The danger is a pilot reducing power in the headwind phase. Reversing the sequence, or adding an updraft, misreads a microburst, which is a downward rush of air.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Most weather questions come down to stable air versus unstable air.
steps: Stable air resists rising. It forms flat, layered clouds (stratus), steady rain or drizzle, smooth air and hazy, poor visibility. Warm fronts bring it.
Unstable air rises on its own. It forms heaped clouds (cumulus), showers, bumps and thunderstorms, with good visibility between showers. Cold fronts trigger it.
Fog is cloud at the surface. Name it by what cooled the air: the ground at night (radiation), a cold surface under moving air (advection), rising ground (upslope).
Ice: big drops (cumulus, freezing rain) give clear ice; small drops (stratus) give rime ice.
Thunderstorms are unstable air at its worst; rain at the surface means the mature, most violent stage.
Stable: stratus, steady rain
Stable: smooth, hazy
Unstable: cumulus, showers
Unstable: bumpy, clear

example.stem: A forecast calls for stratus clouds, steady drizzle and haze. Is the air stable or unstable?
steps: Layered clouds, steady precipitation and poor visibility are the stable-air signature.
Unstable air would give cumulus, showers and good visibility.

reteach.hook: Layers and drizzle: stable. Heaps and showers: unstable.

check.stem: Stable air is typically associated with
options: strong rising thermals and towering clouds.
check.explain: Stable air brings stratiform clouds, steady precipitation, smooth air and fair to poor visibility (PHAK Ch. 12). Cumulus, showers, turbulence, thermals, thunderstorms and good visibility are signs of unstable air.

check.stem: Advection fog forms when
options: the ground cools on a clear, calm night.
warm, moist air moves over a colder surface.
moist air is pushed up a slope.
cold air moves over warmer water.
warm rain falls through cooler air.
check.explain: Advection fog is moist air carried by wind over a colder surface, typical along coasts (PHAK Ch. 12). The other options describe radiation, upslope, steam and precipitation-induced fog.

check.stem: Clear ice is most likely to form
options: from small supercooled droplets in smooth, layered stratus clouds.
from frost on a parked aircraft.
from large supercooled drops, as in cumulus or freezing rain.
check.explain: Large supercooled drops freeze slowly and spread before freezing, forming hard, glossy clear ice; they're found in cumuliform clouds and freezing rain (PHAK Ch. 12). Small droplets in stratus form rime. Very cold clouds hold mostly ice crystals, dry snow doesn't stick, and frost is a separate hazard.

check.stem: The mature stage of a thunderstorm begins when
options: downdrafts take over the whole cell.
rain begins falling at the surface.
the storm moves away from the airport.
check.explain: The start of rain at the surface marks the mature stage, with updrafts and downdrafts side by side (PHAK Ch. 12). The first cumulus is the cumulus stage, and downdrafts taking over mark the dissipating stage.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. Four weather ideas.
steps: A front is where cold air and warm air meet.
Cold fronts are quick and stormy; warm fronts are slow and drizzly.
Ice forms on an airplane when it flies through water drops at or below freezing.
Hot, high, humid air is thin air, and thin air means poorer takeoff and climb.
Thunderstorms are most dangerous in their mature stage.

example.stem: Why does a hot day make an airplane's takeoff run longer?
steps: Hot air is less dense: thin air.
Thin air gives the wings less lift and the engine less power at the same speed.
So the airplane needs a longer run to lift off.
example.answer: Hot air is thin, so the wings and engine work less well

reteach.hook: Hot, high, humid: thin air, long takeoff.

check.stem: A cold front is the leading edge of
options: a warmer air mass replacing colder air.
a colder air mass replacing warmer air.
a jet stream at high altitude.
a sea breeze along the coast.
check.explain: A cold front is where advancing colder air replaces warmer air (PHAK Ch. 12). Warmer air replacing colder air is a warm front, and fog banks, jet streams and sea breezes are not fronts.

check.stem: For structural icing to form, an aircraft needs
options: visible moisture at or below freezing.
strong surface winds and low cloud bases.
check.explain: Structural icing requires visible moisture, such as cloud or rain, and an airframe temperature at or below freezing (PHAK Ch. 12). Dry air leaves nothing to freeze, water above freezing stays liquid, and altitude or wind alone doesn't cause icing.

check.stem: High density altitude makes an airplane's takeoff roll
options: shorter, but only in humid air.
check.explain: High density altitude means thin air: less lift and power at a given speed and a higher true airspeed to lift off, so the takeoff roll is longer (PHAK Ch. 11). Humidity makes it worse, not better, and time of day doesn't change the rule.

check.stem: A thunderstorm is usually most violent in its
options: final stage after the rain ends.
check.explain: The mature stage has the strongest updrafts and downdrafts, heavy rain, hail, lightning and wind shear (PHAK Ch. 12). The cumulus stage is mainly updrafts, and the dissipating stage is mainly weakening downdrafts.

units.title: Helicopter basics
units.objective: Know the four helicopter controls, torque and translating tendency, translational lift, dissymmetry of lift, retreating blade stall, autorotation and settling with power.

steps: Controls (Helicopter Flying Handbook): the collective, in the left hand, changes the pitch of all main-rotor blades together, raising or lowering total lift; it is usually linked to the throttle or a governor to hold rotor RPM. The cyclic, in the right hand, tilts the rotor disc through the swash plate to move the helicopter in any direction. The antitorque pedals change tail-rotor pitch to control heading. The throttle sets engine RPM.

Torque: a main rotor turning counterclockwise from above (most US designs) twists the fuselage clockwise, nose right. More collective means more torque and needs more LEFT pedal; less collective needs right pedal. Translating tendency: the tail rotor's thrust makes the whole helicopter drift right in a hover, countered by a tilted rotor mast or a little left cyclic.

Effective translational lift (ETL) comes in at about 16 to 24 knots, when the rotor moves out of its own downwash and vortices into clean air and becomes much more efficient. Hovering in ground effect, within about one rotor diameter of the surface, needs less power than hovering out of ground effect.

Dissymmetry of lift: in forward flight the advancing blade meets faster relative wind than the retreating blade. Blade flapping (the advancing blade flaps up, the retreating blade down) and cyclic feathering even it out. At high speed, high weight or high density altitude the retreating blade can stall: vibration, nose pitch-up and a roll toward the retreating side (left on a US helicopter). It limits top speed.

Gyroscopic precession: a force applied to the spinning rotor takes effect about 90° later in the direction of rotation, so the cyclic's pitch changes are rigged 90° ahead of where the disc should tilt.

Autorotation: if the engine fails, the freewheeling unit disconnects it and air flowing UP through the rotor keeps it turning. The first action is to lower the collective to keep rotor RPM; near the ground the pilot flares with aft cyclic, then cushions the landing with collective. Settling with power (vortex ring state): a steep or vertical descent below ETL with some power applied lets the rotor fly into its own downwash; recover by moving the cyclic forward to gain airspeed and fly out of it.
teach.formula: Collective = up and down (all blades) · Cyclic = direction (tilts the disc) · Pedals = heading · Engine out: collective DOWN · Precession acts 90° later

worked.stem: A US-design helicopter is hovering. The pilot lowers the collective to descend but does not touch the pedals. Which way does the nose yaw, and what fixes it?
steps: Lowering the collective flattens the blades, so the rotor needs less engine power.
Less power means less torque twisting the fuselage clockwise (nose right).
The tail rotor is still pushing as hard as before, so it now overpowers the reduced torque.
The nose swings LEFT. The pilot adds right pedal to hold the heading.
worked.answer: The nose yaws left; right pedal holds the heading

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: A helicopter pilot uses both hands and both feet.
Left hand, the collective: lift it to go up, lower it to come down. It changes all the blades at once.
Right hand, the cyclic: lean it the way you want to go. It tilts the spinning rotor that way.
Feet, the pedals: they control the little tail rotor, which points the nose left or right.
Why a tail rotor? Spin the big rotor one way and the body wants to spin the other way. The tail rotor stops that.
If the engine quits, the pilot lowers the collective and lets the air rushing up through the rotor keep it spinning, like a sycamore seed.
Collective: up / down
Cyclic: direction
Pedals: heading
Throttle: rotor RPM

practice.stem: Which helicopter control changes the pitch angle of all the main-rotor blades at the same time?
practice.explain: The collective changes the pitch of every main-rotor blade equally, raising or lowering total rotor thrust (Helicopter Flying Handbook). The cyclic changes blade pitch at one point in each turn to tilt the disc. The pedals change tail-rotor pitch, the throttle sets engine RPM, and a rotor brake only stops the rotor after shutdown.

practice.stem: In a helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise as seen from above, increasing the collective in a hover requires
options: more right pedal, to stop the nose yawing left.
more left pedal, to stop the nose yawing left.
no pedal change, because the tail rotor adjusts automatically.
more left pedal, to stop the nose yawing right.
forward cyclic, to stop the nose yawing right.
practice.explain: More collective needs more power, which increases the torque that twists the fuselage clockwise, nose right, so the pilot adds left pedal for more tail-rotor thrust (Helicopter Flying Handbook). Right pedal is what's needed when the collective is lowered. The nose yaws right, not left, the pilot must make the pedal input, and the cyclic doesn't control yaw.

practice.stem: A helicopter gains effective translational lift at about 16 to 24 knots because
options: the tail rotor stops needing to produce thrust at that speed.
the rotor moves out of its own downwash into undisturbed air.
the retreating blade begins to stall.
practice.explain: As speed builds, the rotor outruns its own recirculating downwash and tip vortices and works in clean air, so it produces much more lift for the same power (Helicopter Flying Handbook). The tail rotor keeps working, ground effect depends on height not speed, retreating blade stall is a high-speed problem, and flapping continues in forward flight.

practice.stem: In a helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise as seen from above, retreating blade stall is most likely at
options: low airspeed in a hover; the nose yaws right.
high airspeed; the nose pitches down and it rolls right.
high airspeed; the nose pitches up and it rolls left.
low airspeed; the nose pitches up and it rolls right.
high airspeed; the nose pitches down and it rolls left.
practice.explain: At high forward speed the retreating blade (on the left of a counterclockwise rotor) must fly at a very high angle of attack and can stall; the warning signs are vibration, nose pitch-up and a roll toward the retreating side, which is the left (Helicopter Flying Handbook). It is a high-speed problem, not a hover one. Nose-down or a roll to the right reverses the effects.

practice.stem: A helicopter is descending almost vertically at about 800 feet per minute, below ETL, with about half its available power applied. The rate of descent suddenly increases and the controls feel less effective. The pilot should
options: raise the collective to full power to stop the descent.
apply aft cyclic to raise the nose and slow the descent.
hold the controls still until the descent stops by itself.
apply full right pedal and hold the heading.
move the cyclic forward to gain airspeed and fly out of it.
practice.explain: This is settling with power (vortex ring state): the rotor is descending into its own downwash. Moving the cyclic forward into clean air ends it, and collective can be lowered if altitude permits (Helicopter Flying Handbook). Adding collective deepens the vortex and the sink rate. Aft cyclic slows the helicopter further, holding still lets it continue, and pedal changes heading without fixing the airflow.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's treat the rotor as a spinning wheel that obeys a few rules.
steps: Rule 1, torque: spin the rotor one way and the body spins the other. The tail rotor and pedals fight it; more power means more torque and more left pedal on a US helicopter.
Rule 2, precession: push on a spinning wheel and it reacts 90° later in the direction of rotation.
Rule 3, clean air: once the rotor flies into undisturbed air (ETL, about 16 to 24 knots) it lifts much better; near the ground, ground effect helps too.
Rule 4, uneven blades: in forward flight the advancing blade is faster than the retreating one, so the blades flap to even out lift; too fast and the retreating blade stalls.
Rule 5, autorotation: with no engine, air flowing up through the rotor keeps it turning, but only if the pilot lowers the collective at once.
Torque: body turns back
Precession: 90° later
ETL: clean air lifts
Autorotation: lower it

example.stem: Why are helicopter cyclic controls rigged so the blade pitch changes 90° before the point where the disc should tilt?
steps: A spinning rotor behaves like a gyroscope.
A force applied to it takes effect 90° later in the direction of rotation.
So the pitch change is made 90° early, and the disc tilts where the pilot wants.

reteach.hook: Push a spinning wheel and it answers 90 degrees later.

check.stem: Because of gyroscopic precession, a force applied to a spinning rotor disc takes effect
options: immediately, at exactly the point where it is applied.
about 90 degrees later in the direction of rotation.
about 180 degrees later, on the opposite side.
about 90 degrees earlier, against the rotation.
check.explain: Precession makes the reaction appear about 90° later in the direction of rotation (Helicopter Flying Handbook). It is not immediate, opposite or against the rotation, and it is a property of the spinning main rotor, not only the tail rotor.

check.stem: Dissymmetry of lift in forward flight is caused by
options: the retreating blade moving faster than the advancing blade.
the advancing blade meeting faster relative wind.
check.explain: In forward flight the helicopter's speed adds to the advancing blade's rotational speed and subtracts from the retreating blade's, so the advancing side would make more lift; blade flapping and cyclic feathering even it out (Helicopter Flying Handbook). The retreating blade is the slower one, and tail-rotor thrust, ground effect and torque don't cause it.

check.stem: If the engine fails in flight, the pilot's first action to enter autorotation is to
options: raise the collective to stretch the glide.
check.explain: Lowering the collective at once reduces blade pitch so the rotor keeps its RPM and the upward airflow can drive it (Helicopter Flying Handbook). Raising the collective bleeds rotor RPM fast, full aft cyclic is for the flare near the ground, the throttle can't help a failed engine, and the pedals must stay active.

check.stem: Hovering in ground effect, compared with hovering out of ground effect, requires
options: more power, but only in calm wind.
check.explain: Within about one rotor diameter of the surface, ground effect reduces the downwash and the induced flow through the rotor, so less power is needed to hover (Helicopter Flying Handbook). Out of ground effect, the helicopter needs more power, not less.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. Two hands, two feet.
