steps: The collective, in the left hand, moves the helicopter up and down.
The cyclic, in the right hand, tilts the rotor to move forward, back or sideways.
The pedals, under the feet, point the nose left or right using the tail rotor.
The tail rotor stops the body from spinning the opposite way to the big rotor.
If the engine stops, the pilot lowers the collective and the air keeps the rotor turning.

example.stem: The pilot wants to move forward from a hover. Which control does that?
steps: The collective is for up and down.
The pedals are for heading.
Tilting the rotor forward with the cyclic moves the helicopter forward.

reteach.hook: Collective up and down, cyclic the way you want to go, pedals for the nose.

check.stem: The cyclic control
options: changes the pitch of all the main-rotor blades together.
tilts the rotor disc toward the direction of travel.
check.explain: The cyclic tilts the main-rotor disc, so the helicopter moves in that direction (Helicopter Flying Handbook). The collective changes all blades together, the pedals control the tail rotor, the throttle sets RPM, and the rotor brake stops the rotor.

check.stem: The tail rotor's main job is to
options: counteract main-rotor torque and control heading.
provide most of the helicopter's lift while hovering.
push the helicopter forward in cruising flight.
check.explain: The tail rotor produces sideways thrust that counters the torque reaction and lets the pedals control heading (Helicopter Flying Handbook). The main rotor provides lift and forward thrust, and the engine drives both rotors.

check.stem: To climb vertically from a hover, the pilot
check.explain: Raising the collective increases the pitch of all the blades, adding lift so the helicopter climbs, with left pedal to hold heading on a US helicopter. Cyclic moves it horizontally, lowering the collective makes it descend, and pedal alone only turns it.

check.stem: In an autorotation, the main rotor is kept turning by
options: the engine running at idle power.
air flowing up through the rotor.
check.explain: With the engine disconnected by the freewheeling unit, the upward flow of air through the rotor as the helicopter descends keeps it turning (Helicopter Flying Handbook). The engine is disengaged, and the tail rotor, batteries and pedals don't drive the main rotor.

units.title: Navigation, airspeeds and V-speeds
units.objective: Turn a true course into a compass heading, correct for wind, solve time-speed-distance problems, tell IAS, CAS, TAS, groundspeed and Mach apart, and read the V-speeds and airspeed-indicator arcs.

steps: Courses are drawn on the chart from TRUE north. To get the heading to fly, work in order: true course, then the wind correction angle (WCA) gives the true heading, then variation gives the magnetic heading, then deviation gives the compass heading. Memory aid: TV Makes Dull Children (True, Variation, Magnetic, Deviation, Compass), with the wind fixed first.

Wind correction: point the nose partly into the wind. Wind from the right of course: add the WCA, so the heading is right of the course. Wind from the left: subtract it. A headwind component lowers groundspeed and a tailwind raises it. Winds in written reports and forecasts (winds aloft, METARs, TAFs) are given from TRUE north; winds the tower or ATIS gives you are MAGNETIC.

Variation, read from the chart's isogonic lines, is the angle between true and magnetic north: east is least, west is best, so subtract easterly variation and add westerly variation going from true to magnetic. Deviation, read from the compass correction card, is the airplane's own magnetic error, differs by heading, and is applied last.

Time, speed, distance: distance = groundspeed × time. Work in minutes: groundspeed ÷ 60 = miles per minute, so 120 knots is 2 NM a minute. A knot is one nautical mile per hour, and 1 NM is about 1.15 statute miles (about 6,076 feet). Fuel used = burn rate × time. Always use GROUNDSPEED, never true airspeed, for time en route.

Airspeeds: indicated (IAS) is what the dial shows; calibrated (CAS) is IAS corrected for instrument and position error; true (TAS) is CAS corrected for altitude and temperature, and in thin air TAS is higher than IAS (rule of thumb: about 2 percent per 1,000 feet); groundspeed is TAS corrected for wind. Mach number = TAS ÷ the local speed of sound, which depends on temperature alone and falls as the air gets colder. Subsonic is below Mach 0.75, transonic 0.75 to 1.20, supersonic 1.20 to 5.0, hypersonic above 5.0.

V-speeds and the arcs (PHAK Ch. 8): VSO, stall speed in the landing configuration, is the bottom of the white arc; VS1, stall speed in a specified configuration (usually clean), is the bottom of the green arc; VFE, maximum flap-extended speed, is the top of the white arc; VNO, maximum structural cruising speed, is the top of the green arc and the start of the yellow caution arc (smooth air only); VNE, never exceed, is the red line. VA, design maneuvering speed, is not marked and DROPS as weight drops. VX (best angle of climb) gives the most height over the shortest distance, for obstacles; VY (best rate) gives the most height in the shortest time. VX is slower than VY.
teach.formula: TC ± WCA = TH · TH − east / + west variation = MH · MH ± deviation = CH · Distance = GS × time · Mach = TAS ÷ speed of sound

worked.stem: A pilot plans a true course of 245°. The wind requires a 7° correction to the right, the chart shows 10° east variation, and the compass card says to add 2° on this heading. What compass heading should the pilot fly?
steps: True heading: the wind is from the right, so add the WCA: 245 + 7 = 252°.
Magnetic heading: easterly variation is subtracted ('east is least'): 252 − 10 = 242°.
Compass heading: apply deviation last, as the card says: 242 + 2 = 244°.
Traps: adding the east variation gives 264°; leaving out the wind correction gives 237°.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: The map is drawn from the real North Pole, called true north. Your compass points at the magnetic north pole, which is somewhere else.
The gap between the two, where you are flying, is called variation. The chart prints it for you.
The airplane's own metal and wiring nudge the compass a little more. That's deviation, written on a small card next to the compass.
Wind pushes the airplane sideways, like a river pushing a swimmer. Point the nose a little into the wind and you track straight.
The airspeed dial measures the air flowing past. Up high the air is thin, so you are really moving faster than the dial says.
Distance = speed × time. At 120 knots you cover 2 nautical miles every minute.
True course
± wind correction = true heading
− east / + west variation = magnetic heading
± deviation = compass heading

visual.caption: From the chart to the compass, one correction at a time

practice.stem: The lower end of the green arc on an airspeed indicator marks
options: VSO, the stall speed in the landing configuration.
VS1, the stall speed in a specified configuration, usually flaps up.
VNO, the maximum structural cruising speed.
practice.explain: The green arc runs from VS1 at its bottom to VNO at its top (PHAK Ch. 8). VSO is the bottom of the white arc and VFE is its top. VNO is the top of the green arc, not the bottom, and VA is not marked on the indicator at all.

practice.stem: A pilot's true course is 130°. The wind calls for an 8° correction to the left, and the local magnetic variation is 6° west. What magnetic heading should the pilot fly?
practice.explain: Wind from the left means subtracting the correction: 130 − 8 = 122° true heading; westerly variation is added ('west is best'): 122 + 6 = 128°. 116° subtracts the west variation, 144° adds the left correction, 132° gets both signs backward, and 136° leaves out the wind correction.

practice.stem: An airplane shows 150 knots indicated at 8,000 feet MSL. Using the rule of thumb that true airspeed is about 2 percent higher than indicated airspeed for every 1,000 feet of altitude, its true airspeed is about
practice.explain: 8 × 2 percent = 16 percent, and 150 × 1.16 = 174 knots; TAS is higher because the air up there is thinner. 150 knots ignores altitude, 126 knots subtracts the 16 percent, 166 knots adds 16 knots instead of 16 percent, and 162 knots uses only 1 percent per 1,000 feet.

practice.stem: Right after takeoff, a pilot must clear a line of tall trees close to the end of the runway. Which speed should the pilot fly until clear, and why?
options: VY, because it gives the greatest gain in altitude per unit of time.
VX, because it gives the greatest gain in altitude per unit of time.
VX, because it gives the greatest gain in altitude over the shortest horizontal distance.
VA, because it protects the structure in gusty air near the ground.
VY, because it is slower than VX and gives a steeper climb.
practice.explain: VX, the best angle-of-climb speed, gives the most height for the ground covered, which is what clears a nearby obstacle (PHAK Ch. 11). Most altitude per unit of time defines VY, so pairing that reason with VX is wrong, and flying VY trades obstacle clearance for climb rate. VY is faster than VX, not slower, and VA is a structural limit, not a climb speed.

practice.stem: An airplane holds a constant true airspeed of 480 knots while climbing into steadily colder air. Its Mach number
options: stays the same, because Mach depends only on true airspeed.
decreases, because sound travels faster in thinner air.
increases, because the speed of sound falls as air pressure falls.
increases, because the speed of sound falls as the air gets colder.
decreases, because the indicated airspeed falls as the airplane climbs.
practice.explain: Mach = TAS ÷ speed of sound, and the speed of sound depends on temperature alone: colder air means slower sound, so the same TAS is a higher Mach number. Pressure does not set the speed of sound, so the pressure option has the right result for the wrong reason, and sound is not faster in thin air. Indicated airspeed does fall in the climb, but Mach is based on TAS, and the same TAS against slower sound cannot leave Mach unchanged.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Let's treat the heading problem as a ladder you climb one rung at a time, and keep the speeds in their own family.
steps: Write the ladder down the side of the page: true course, wind correction, true heading, variation, magnetic heading, deviation, compass heading. Fill in each rung before moving on.
Wind rung: wind from the right, turn right (add); wind from the left, turn left (subtract).
Variation rung: east is least (subtract), west is best (add).
Deviation rung: read the compass card for the heading you'll fly and apply it last.
Speeds climb a ladder too: IAS, fix the instrument error to get CAS, fix for altitude and temperature to get TAS, fix for wind to get groundspeed. Time en route always uses groundspeed.

example.stem: True course 300°, wind correction 5° right, variation 4° west, deviation 0°. What compass heading should be flown?
steps: 300 + 5 = 305° true heading (wind from the right, add).
305 + 4 = 309° magnetic heading (west is best, add).
Deviation is 0°, so the compass heading is also 309°.

reteach.hook: TV Makes Dull Children: true, variation, magnetic, deviation, compass, with the wind fixed first.

check.stem: Winds aloft are forecast from 270° at 30 knots. A pilot wants to fly a true course of 360°. To stay on course, the pilot should
options: climb, because heading cannot correct for a crosswind.
turn the nose right of 360°, away from the wind.
hold a heading of exactly 360° and accept the drift.
weave right and then left to average out the drift.
turn the nose left of 360°, into the wind.
check.explain: A wind from 270° blows from the west, the pilot's left on a northbound course, so the nose is turned left into it, to a heading below 360°. Turning right adds to the drift, and holding 360° lets the wind push the airplane east of course. Weaving fixes nothing, and it is heading, not altitude, that corrects for a crosswind.

check.stem: A flight covers 210 NM at a true airspeed of 150 knots into a 10-knot headwind. How long does it take?
check.explain: Groundspeed = 150 − 10 = 140 knots, and 210 ÷ 140 = 1.5 hours, which is 1 hour 30 minutes. 1 hour 24 minutes uses the true airspeed, about 1 hour 19 minutes adds the headwind, 1 hour 50 minutes writes 1.5 hours as if the decimal were minutes, and 40 minutes divides the speed by the distance.

check.stem: Which airspeed is indicated airspeed corrected for instrument and position error?
check.explain: Calibrated airspeed is IAS corrected for instrument and position (installation) error (PHAK Ch. 8). True airspeed is CAS corrected for altitude and temperature, and groundspeed is TAS corrected for wind. Equivalent airspeed corrects CAS for compressibility, and Mach compares TAS with the speed of sound.

check.stem: As fuel burns off and an airplane gets lighter, its design maneuvering speed (VA)
options: stays the same, because it is printed on the airspeed indicator.
decreases only while the flaps are down.
check.explain: VA falls as weight falls, because a lighter airplane is pushed to its load limit more easily by a gust or an abrupt control input (PHAK Ch. 5). VA is not marked on the airspeed indicator at all, it is well below VNE, and it does not depend on flap position.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's go back to what north, heading and speed actually mean.
steps: The map is drawn from the real North Pole: true north. Your compass points to the magnetic north pole, which is somewhere else, and the difference where you are is variation.
The airplane's own metal and wiring push the compass a little more: that's deviation, listed on a card by the compass.
Wind pushes you sideways, like a current pushing a swimmer. Point a little into it and you track straight.
A headwind slows you down over the ground; a tailwind speeds you up.
Distance = speed × time. At 120 knots you cover 2 nautical miles every minute.

example.stem: An airplane's groundspeed is 120 knots. How far does it travel in 25 minutes?
steps: 120 knots = 120 NM per hour = 2 NM per minute.

reteach.hook: East is least, west is best, and the wind gets fixed first.

check.stem: On an airspeed indicator, the white arc shows
options: the caution range, for smooth air only.
check.explain: The white arc runs from VSO to VFE, the speeds at which the flaps may be used. The green arc is the normal range and the yellow arc the caution range for smooth air only. Nothing is marked beyond the red line, and VX and VY are not shown as arcs.

check.stem: An airplane's true heading is 090° and the variation is 5° east. Its magnetic heading is
check.explain: East is least: subtract easterly variation, 090 − 5 = 085° magnetic. 095° adds it, 090° forgets it, 275° turns the heading around, and 080° subtracts it twice.

check.stem: An airplane flies 150 NM in 1 hour 15 minutes. What is its groundspeed?
check.explain: 1 hour 15 minutes is 1.25 hours, and 150 ÷ 1.25 = 120 knots. About 130 knots treats 1:15 as 1.15 hours, 187.5 knots multiplies instead of dividing, 150 knots ignores the extra 15 minutes, and 100 knots uses 1.5 hours.

check.stem: VY, the best rate-of-climb speed, gives
options: the most altitude in a given time.
the most altitude over a given distance.
the highest speed allowed in rough air.
check.explain: VY gives the greatest gain in altitude per unit of time (PHAK Ch. 11). Most altitude over a given distance is VX. Stall speeds are VSO and VS1, the longest glide comes at the best-glide speed, and rough-air limits are set by VA and VNO.

units.title: IFR flight, aircraft lights and airport beacons
units.objective: Tell VFR from IFR and VMC from IMC, pick IFR cruising altitudes, know how the six basic instruments are used without outside references, and read another aircraft's lights and an airport beacon at night.

steps: VFR and IFR are sets of rules; VMC and IMC describe the weather. VMC means visibility and cloud clearance at or above the VFR minimums; IMC means below them. To fly IFR in controlled airspace a pilot needs an instrument rating, an IFR flight plan and an ATC clearance (14 CFR 91.173). Class A airspace, from 18,000 feet MSL, is IFR only.

IFR cruising altitudes (91.179), when ATC has not assigned one: below 18,000 feet MSL, magnetic course 0° to 179° = ODD thousands (3,000, 5,000, 7,000); 180° to 359° = EVEN thousands (4,000, 6,000, 8,000). VFR uses the same odd and even split plus 500 feet, which keeps VFR and IFR traffic 500 feet apart.

The six basic flight instruments: airspeed indicator, attitude indicator and altimeter on the top row; turn coordinator, heading indicator and vertical speed indicator below. In IMC the attitude indicator is the hub of the scan, the only instrument that shows pitch and bank directly, and the others confirm what the airplane is doing. Trust the instruments over body feelings: in a long, gentle turn the inner ear soon senses wings level, and pulling back to stop a descent while still banked tightens a 'graveyard spiral'.

IFR fuel and alternates: carry enough fuel to reach the destination, then the alternate, then fly 45 minutes at normal cruising speed (91.167). An alternate is required unless, from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA, the destination forecast is at least a 2,000-foot ceiling and 3 miles visibility: the 1-2-3 rule (91.169).

Aircraft lights (91.209, sunset to sunrise): position lights are a RED light on the LEFT wingtip, a GREEN light on the RIGHT wingtip and a WHITE light at the tail. The red and green lights shine forward and out to the sides; the white light shines backward. Anti-collision lights (a flashing red beacon or white strobes) must be on whenever they are fitted, unless the pilot turns them off for safety. Landing and taxi lights are white and point forward.

Reading another aircraft at night: red on your RIGHT and green on your LEFT means it is coming head-on. A steady white light alone means you are behind it. Green alone means you see its right side, so it is crossing from your left to your right; red alone means its left side, crossing from your right to your left, and since it is then on your right, you give way. Airport beacons (AIM 2-1-9): white and green = civil land airport, white and yellow = water airport, green, yellow and white = heliport, two quick white flashes between greens = military. A beacon operating in daylight at an airport in a Class B, C, D or E surface area often means the ceiling is below 1,000 feet or the visibility below 3 miles.
teach.formula: IFR: odd thousands 0–179°, even thousands 180–359° · Red left, green right, white tail · Red on your right, green on your left: head-on · See red, give way

worked.stem: At night, ahead and at your altitude, you see another aircraft showing a steady red light and a flashing red beacon, but no green or white light. Which way is it moving, and who has the right-of-way if your paths are converging?
steps: A red light alone is the airplane's LEFT wingtip, so you are off its left side.
Its nose therefore points across your view from right to left.
If you are on its left, it is on your right, and in converging traffic the aircraft on the right has the right-of-way.
So it is crossing from your right to your left, and you must give way.
worked.answer: Crossing from your right to your left; it has the right-of-way, so you give way

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Picture yourself in the cockpit: red light on your left hand, green on your right hand, white on the tail behind you.
Now picture another airplane flying straight at you. Its left hand is on your right, so its red light appears on your right.
If it is flying away from you, you see its tail: a white light.
If you see only one wingtip color, you are looking at its side, and the color tells you which side.
In cloud you can't see the horizon, so the attitude indicator becomes your horizon and the other instruments check it.
Airport beacons are lighthouses for airports: white and green for civilian fields, a double white flash between greens for military ones.
Red on your right, green on your left: head-on
White only: flying away
Green only: crossing left to right
Red only: crossing right to left, give way

visual.caption: What another aircraft's lights tell you at night

practice.stem: An airplane's position lights are
options: green on the left wingtip, red on the right wingtip and white on the tail.
white on both wingtips and red on the tail.
red on the left wingtip, green on the right wingtip and red on the tail.
red on the left wingtip, green on the right wingtip and white on the tail.
red on both wingtips and green on the tail.
practice.explain: Position lights are red on the left wingtip, green on the right and white at the tail, shining backward (91.209). Swapping red and green would reverse the code other pilots use to judge your direction. The tail light is white, not red; a flashing red light is the separate anti-collision beacon.

practice.stem: In uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 feet MSL, an IFR flight in level cruise on a magnetic course of 200° should fly at
practice.explain: Under 91.179 a magnetic course of 180° to 359° calls for an even thousand, such as 6,000 feet. 7,000 and 5,000 feet are odd thousands, for courses of 0° to 179°. 6,500 feet is the VFR altitude for this course, and 7,500 feet is a VFR altitude for easterly courses.

practice.stem: At night you see another aircraft at your altitude showing a steady green light and a flashing red beacon, but no steady red or white light. The other aircraft is
options: crossing your view from right to left.
crossing your view from left to right.
practice.explain: A green light alone is the right wingtip, so you are off the airplane's right side and its nose points across your view from left to right. Head-on would show both red and green, with red on your right, and flying away would show the white tail light. Right to left is what a lone red light shows, and the flashing beacon says nothing about direction or climb.

practice.stem: During the day, a pilot notices the rotating beacon operating at an airport inside a Class D surface area. This often indicates that
options: the control tower has closed for the day.
the airport is a military field.
special VFR clearances are no longer being issued.
the runway edge lights are out of service.
the ground visibility may be below 3 miles or the ceiling below 1,000 feet.
practice.explain: In Class B, C, D and E surface areas, a beacon operating in daylight often means the weather is below basic VFR minimums, a ceiling under 1,000 feet or visibility under 3 miles, though pilots should not rely on it alone (AIM 2-1-9). A closed tower is not signaled this way, and a military field is shown by its double white flash, not by daytime use. The beacon tells you nothing about runway lights or special VFR.

practice.stem: In IMC, a pilot has been in a gentle, coordinated left turn for some time and now feels that the wings are level. The altimeter shows a loss of altitude, and the pilot pulls back on the controls without checking the attitude indicator. The most likely result is
options: a skid to the outside of the turn, with no loss of altitude.
a climb straight ahead, because back pressure always raises the nose.
a wings-level stall, because the turn has already stopped.
a slow return to level flight as the airspeed bleeds off.
a tightening spiral with an increasing rate of descent.
practice.explain: The bank is still there, so back pressure mostly tightens the turn instead of raising the nose, and the airplane winds into a steeper, faster descending spiral: the graveyard spiral (Instrument Flying Handbook). Back pressure raises the nose only with the wings level, and the turn had not stopped, it had only stopped being felt. Airspeed rises in this spiral rather than bleeding off, nothing here causes a skid, and the cure is to level the wings on the attitude indicator first.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Let's sort the rules, the instruments and the lights into three separate boxes.
steps: Box one, rules: VFR and IFR are rule sets; VMC and IMC describe the weather. Flying in IMC means flying IFR, with a rating, a flight plan and a clearance.
IFR altitudes are whole thousands: odd going east (0° to 179°), even going west (180° to 359°). VFR adds 500 feet to the same pattern.

Box two, instruments: the attitude indicator is the hub of the scan, and the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI, heading indicator and turn coordinator confirm it. If your body and the instruments disagree, believe the instruments.
Box three, lights: red left, green right, white tail. The color you see tells you which side of the other airplane you're looking at.
Beacons: white and green civil, white and yellow water, green, yellow and white heliport, a double white flash between greens military.

example.stem: You see another aircraft's red light on your right and its green light on your left. Which way is it heading?
steps: Its red light is its left wingtip, and its left is on your right.
That only happens when its nose points at you.
So it is coming toward you head-on, and both pilots turn right.

reteach.hook: Red left, green right, white behind: the color you see is the side you're looking at.

check.stem: To fly under IFR in controlled airspace, a pilot needs
options: an ATC clearance, but no flight plan when the weather is VMC.
an IFR flight plan, but no clearance below 18,000 feet MSL.
a commercial pilot certificate and an IFR flight plan.
an instrument rating, an IFR flight plan and an ATC clearance.
check.explain: IFR in controlled airspace needs an instrument rating (14 CFR 61.3) and a filed IFR flight plan with an ATC clearance (91.173). The rating alone is not enough, and a clearance is needed at every altitude in controlled airspace, not just above 18,000 feet. A commercial certificate is not required, and good weather does not remove the flight-plan requirement.

check.stem: An IFR flight plan lists an alternate airport. How much fuel must the airplane carry?
options: Enough to reach the destination plus 30 minutes.
Enough to reach the destination plus 45 minutes, ignoring the alternate.
Enough to reach the destination, then the alternate, then 45 minutes at normal cruising speed.
Enough to reach the alternate plus 30 minutes.
Enough to reach the destination, then the alternate, then 30 minutes at normal cruising speed.
check.explain: Under 91.167 an IFR flight must be able to reach the destination, fly on to the alternate, and still have 45 minutes at normal cruising speed. 30 minutes is the daytime VFR reserve (91.151), so every 30-minute option borrows the wrong rule, and leaving out the alternate ignores why it was filed.

check.stem: At night you see only a steady white light ahead at your altitude, plus a flashing beacon, and the light is slowly growing brighter. The other aircraft is
options: crossing your view from left to right.
crossing your view from right to left.
ahead and flying away from you, and you are catching up with it.
on the ground, because tail lights are used only while taxiing.
check.explain: A white light alone is the tail light, so you are behind the aircraft and heading roughly the same way; a light growing brighter means the gap is closing. Head-on shows both red and green, a lone green means a left-to-right crossing and a lone red a right-to-left one. Position lights are used in flight, and the aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way, so you pass well clear on its right.

check.stem: In IMC the pilot feels the airplane turning right, but the attitude indicator and the turn coordinator both show wings level and the heading indicator is steady. The pilot should
options: roll left to cancel the turn the body senses.
climb until the sensation goes away.
trust the sensation, because the vacuum pump may have failed.
keep the wings level by the instruments and disregard the sensation.
turn right to match the sensation, then roll level.
check.explain: Three instruments agree on wings level, so the feeling is spatial disorientation (the leans), and the pilot keeps flying by the instruments (Instrument Flying Handbook). A vacuum failure would not also fool the turn coordinator, which is usually electric, so the cross-check rules it out. Rolling or turning to match the feeling would put the airplane into a real bank, and climbing does nothing for the inner ear.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's start from what a pilot can and can't see.
steps: On a clear day you fly by looking outside: that's VFR, and the weather that allows it is VMC.
In cloud you can't see the ground or the horizon, so you fly by instruments alone: that's IFR, and the weather is IMC.
Without a horizon the inner ear is easily fooled. The attitude indicator is your artificial horizon, so trust it.
At night airplanes show colored lights: red on the left wingtip, green on the right, white on the tail.
Airports have a spinning beacon. Civilian land airports flash white and green.

example.stem: An airplane is on a magnetic course of 090° under IFR in uncontrolled airspace, below 18,000 feet. Should it cruise at an odd or an even thousand feet?
steps: 090° is between 0° and 179°.
Those courses use odd thousands under IFR.
So 3,000, 5,000 or 7,000 feet, for example.
example.answer: An odd thousand, such as 5,000 feet

reteach.hook: IFR: whole thousands. VFR: add 500. Odd going east, even going west.

check.stem: Weather with visibility and cloud clearance below the VFR minimums is called
check.explain: IMC, instrument meteorological conditions, means the weather is below the VFR minimums. VMC is weather at or above them. Class A is a type of airspace, special VFR is a clearance to fly VFR below the basic minimums in a surface area, and VFR on top is a way of flying VFR above a cloud layer.

check.stem: Which light is on an airplane's right wingtip?
check.explain: The right wingtip carries the green position light. Red is the left wingtip, white is the tail, flashing red is the anti-collision beacon, and airplanes don't use yellow position lights.

check.stem: An airport's rotating beacon alternates white and yellow flashes. It marks
check.explain: White and yellow marks a water airport, such as a seaplane base (AIM 2-1-9). White and green is a civil land airport, green, yellow and white is a heliport, and two quick white flashes between greens is military. A closed airport doesn't run its beacon to say so.

check.stem: An IFR flight on a magnetic course of 270° in uncontrolled airspace, below 18,000 feet, should cruise at
check.explain: 270° is a westerly course, between 180° and 359°, so IFR uses an even thousand: 6,000 feet. 5,000 and 7,000 feet are odd thousands, for easterly courses. 6,500 and 5,500 feet are VFR altitudes, with the extra 500 feet.

units.title: USAF aircraft: designations and missions
units.objective: Decode a military aircraft designation and match the main current Air Force aircraft to their missions.

steps: A designation such as KC-46A reads: an optional status prefix (X experimental, Y prototype), a modified-mission letter (K), the basic mission letter (C), a vehicle-type letter if it isn't an ordinary airplane (H helicopter, Q unmanned), then a dash, the design number (46) and the series letter (A, the first version). So the KC-46A is design 46, a cargo-type aircraft modified as a tanker, first series.

Basic mission letters: F fighter, A attack, B bomber, C cargo or transport, E special electronic (radar, command and control, jamming), T trainer, U utility, R reconnaissance. Common modified-mission letters in front: K tanker, M multi-mission (often special operations), R reconnaissance, E electronic, H search and rescue, A attack (the AC-130J gunship), W weather. Vehicle types: H helicopter, Q unmanned. So MQ-9 = multi-mission and unmanned (remotely piloted), and RQ-4 = reconnaissance and unmanned.

Watch for one letter doing two jobs. The E in E-3 is a mission (special electronic); the E in F-15E is only the series letter (a later version of the F-15). In HH-60W the first H means rescue and the second means helicopter. Where a letter sits tells you what it means.

Fighters and attack: F-22A Raptor, a stealth air-superiority fighter; F-35A Lightning II, the Air Force's stealth multirole fighter (the B and C versions are flown by the Marine Corps and Navy); F-15E Strike Eagle, a two-seat dual-role fighter for deep strike; F-15EX Eagle II, the newest F-15, replacing older F-15C/Ds; F-16 Fighting Falcon, a single-engine multirole fighter flown by the Thunderbirds; A-10C Thunderbolt II, the close-air-support jet built around a 30 mm cannon.

Bombers: B-52H Stratofortress, an eight-engine subsonic heavy bomber built in the early 1960s; B-1B Lancer, a supersonic swing-wing bomber, now conventional only; B-2A Spirit, a stealth flying-wing bomber; B-21 Raider, the newest stealth bomber, flying since 2023 and planned to replace the B-1B and B-2A. Mobility: C-5M Super Galaxy, the largest Air Force airlifter; C-17A Globemaster III, a jet strategic airlifter that can also use short airfields; C-130J Super Hercules, a four-turboprop tactical airlifter; KC-135 Stratotanker and the newer KC-46A Pegasus, aerial-refueling tankers.

Support, unmanned and training: E-3 Sentry, the AWACS with the rotating radar dome on its back; MQ-9 Reaper, an armed, remotely piloted hunter-killer and surveillance aircraft; HH-60W Jolly Green II, the combat search-and-rescue helicopter; T-6A Texan II, the turboprop primary trainer; T-38C Talon, the supersonic advanced jet trainer; T-7A Red Hawk, the new jet trainer chosen to replace the T-38C.
teach.formula: [status] [modified mission] BASIC MISSION [type] – design number, series letter · K tanker · M multi-mission · R recon · Q unmanned · H rescue (in front) or helicopter (type)

worked.stem: Decode the designation MC-130J.
steps: Start at the dash: 130 is the design number (the Hercules family) and J is the series, the latest version.
The letter just before the dash, C, is the basic mission: cargo or transport.
The M in front is the modified mission, multi-mission, which on the C-130 means special operations such as infiltration, resupply and refueling helicopters.
So it is a special-operations version of the C-130J transport.
worked.answer: A multi-mission (special operations) version of the C-130J transport

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of the designation as a name tag with a job title on it.
The letter just before the dash is the main job: F fights, B bombs, C carries, T trains.
A letter in front of that is an extra job added on: K for tanker, R for reconnaissance, M for many jobs.
A Q just before the dash means no one is on board: a crew flies it from the ground.
The number is simply which design it is, and the letter after the number is which version.
So a KC-135 is a cargo-type jet turned into a tanker.
Modified mission in front (K, M, R, E, H)
Basic mission (F, A, B, C, E, T, U)
Vehicle type (H helicopter, Q unmanned)
Dash, design number, series letter

visual.caption: Reading a designation from left to right

practice.stem: In the designation KC-46A, the letter K shows that the aircraft
options: is a cargo-type design modified to refuel other aircraft in flight.
is the eleventh version of the C-46 design.
is an experimental aircraft still in flight test.
can be flown remotely without a crew on board.
practice.explain: K is the modified-mission letter for tanker, placed in front of the basic mission C, so the KC-46A is a cargo-type aircraft built for aerial refueling. The version is shown by the series letter after the number, not by K. Experimental aircraft carry an X prefix, electronic aircraft an E, and unmanned ones a Q.

practice.stem: What does the designation MQ-9A tell you about the aircraft?
options: It is a maritime patrol aircraft with a crew of nine.
It is a crewed multirole fighter, the ninth of its series.
It is a reconnaissance-only drone that carries no weapons.
It is a multi-mission aircraft that is remotely piloted.
It is a medical-evacuation helicopter, ninth design.
practice.explain: M is the multi-mission letter and Q marks an unmanned, remotely piloted vehicle; 9 is the design number and A the series. Design numbers never count crew members or versions. A reconnaissance-only unmanned design would carry R, as the RQ-4 does, and a helicopter would carry an H.

practice.stem: The F-15E Strike Eagle and the E-3 Sentry both carry the letter E. What does it mean in each designation?
options: In the F-15E it means electronic warfare; in the E-3 it is the series letter.
In the F-15E it is the series letter; in the E-3 it is the basic mission, special electronic.
It is the series letter in both, marking a fifth version.
In both it stands for escort, a fighter mission.
practice.explain: A letter after the design number is a series letter, so the F-15E is a later version of the F-15; a letter before the dash is a mission letter, so the E-3 is a special-electronic aircraft, the AWACS. Reading both as electronic, or both as series, ignores where the letter sits, and the mixed-up option reverses the two. Escort is not a designation letter.

practice.stem: Which pairing of aircraft and primary mission is correct?
options: KC-135 Stratotanker: airborne warning and control
F-22A Raptor: armed, remotely piloted surveillance
A-10C Thunderbolt II: close air support
practice.explain: The A-10C was built for close air support around its 30 mm cannon. The stealth flying wing is the B-2A, while the B-1B is a supersonic swing-wing bomber. Airborne warning and control is the E-3's job, the turboprop primary trainer is the T-6A (the T-38C is a supersonic jet trainer), and the remotely piloted hunter-killer is the MQ-9, while the F-22A is a crewed air-superiority fighter.

practice.stem: A mission needs one aircraft to refuel a formation of F-35As over the ocean and another to track hostile aircraft at long range with a rotating radar dome. Which pair fits?
practice.explain: The KC-46A is a boom-equipped tanker that refuels Air Force fighters, and the E-3 Sentry is the AWACS with the rotating radar dome. The C-17A is an airlifter, not a tanker, and the RC-135 is a reconnaissance aircraft with no rotating dome. The MQ-9 has no long-range air-search radar, and the HH-60W is a rescue helicopter.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Let's read the designation like a sentence, then hang one picture on each aircraft.
steps: Find the dash. The letter just before it, skipping H or Q for the vehicle type, is the main job.
Letters before that are extra jobs: K tanker, M multi-mission, R recon, E electronic, H rescue, A gunship.
After the dash come the design number and then the version letter. Version letters don't describe the job.
One picture per aircraft: F-22A air superiority, F-35A stealth multirole, A-10C close air support with a big gun, B-2A flying wing, B-52H eight engines, B-1B swing wing, B-21 newest stealth bomber.

Mobility and support: C-5M biggest airlifter, C-17A strategic airlifter for short fields, C-130J turboprop tactical airlifter, KC-135 and KC-46A tankers, E-3 radar dome, MQ-9 remotely piloted, HH-60W rescue, and T-6A, T-38C and T-7A trainers.

example.stem: Decode RC-135.
steps: C just before the dash: the basic mission is cargo or transport (the 135 airframe).
R in front: it has been modified for reconnaissance.
So it is a reconnaissance version of the C-135 family.
example.answer: A reconnaissance version of the C-135 design

reteach.hook: The letter before the dash is the job; the letter after the number is the version.

check.stem: Which aircraft is the Air Force's stealth flying-wing bomber?
check.explain: The B-2A Spirit is the stealth flying wing. The B-1B is a supersonic swing-wing bomber, the B-52H an eight-engine heavy bomber with a conventional tail, the F-15E a two-seat strike fighter, and the E-3 the AWACS radar aircraft.

check.stem: In the designation HH-60W, the two H letters mean
options: hospital and helicopter, because it is unarmed.
search and rescue (the modified mission) and helicopter (the vehicle type).
check.explain: The first H, in the modified-mission position, means search and rescue; the second, just before the dash, is the vehicle type, helicopter. Designations never repeat a letter for emphasis, and heavy, high-altitude, hospital and hunter-killer are not designation meanings.

check.stem: Which aircraft has been chosen to replace the T-38C Talon as the Air Force's advanced jet trainer?
check.explain: The T-7A Red Hawk is the new advanced jet trainer replacing the T-38C. The T-6A is the turboprop primary trainer that students fly before the jet trainer. The F-16 and A-10C are combat aircraft, and the C-130J is a transport.

check.stem: Which aircraft is a four-engine turboprop tactical airlifter?
check.explain: The C-130J has four turboprop engines and is the Air Force's tactical airlifter. The C-5M and C-17A are four-engine jet airlifters, the KC-46A is a twin-jet tanker, and the B-52H is an eight-jet bomber.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's go back to the idea that every Air Force aircraft has a job, and its name tag tells you the job.
steps: Fighters (F) fight other aircraft, and most can strike targets on the ground too.
Bombers (B) carry big loads of weapons a long way.
Cargo aircraft (C) carry people and equipment; tankers (KC) are cargo-type jets that pass fuel to other aircraft in flight.
Trainers (T) teach new pilots.
A Q means nobody is on board: the crew flies it from a ground station.
The number after the dash is just which design it is.

example.stem: What is the basic mission of a C-17A?
steps: The letter just before the dash is C.
C means cargo or transport.
The A at the end means it is the first version.

reteach.hook: F fights, B bombs, C carries, T trains, K refuels, Q has no one on board.

check.stem: The letter B in B-52H means the aircraft is a
check.explain: B is the basic mission letter for bomber. Trainers use T, tankers use the K prefix, and there are no designation letters for battle-damage repair or border patrol.

check.stem: What does the letter T in T-6A tell you?
check.explain: T is the basic mission letter for trainer. Tankers carry a K prefix and transports a C, and test aircraft use prefixes such as X or N. The T-6A does have a turboprop engine, but no designation letter describes engine type.

check.stem: Which aircraft carries a large rotating radar dome on top and serves as an airborne warning and control system?
check.explain: The E-3 Sentry is the AWACS, with its rotating radar dome. The KC-135 is a tanker, the C-5M an airlifter, the B-2A a stealth bomber, and the MQ-9 a remotely piloted strike and surveillance aircraft without a dome.

check.stem: Which of these designations belongs to a remotely piloted aircraft?
check.explain: The Q just before the dash in MQ-9A marks an unmanned, remotely piloted aircraft. The KC-46A tanker, F-35A fighter, HH-60W helicopter and T-38C trainer all carry crews.

units.title: Air-power and USAF history
units.objective: Put the milestones of US military aviation in order, from the Wright brothers to the Space Force, and say why each one mattered.

steps: 17 December 1903: Orville and Wilbur Wright make the first sustained, controlled, powered flight in a heavier-than-air machine, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. On 1 August 1907 the Army Signal Corps sets up its Aeronautical Division, the Air Force's earliest ancestor, and in 1909 it buys its first airplane from the Wrights.

The air arm grows up inside the Army: the Aviation Section of the Signal Corps (1914), the Army Air Service (1918), the Army Air Corps (1926) and the Army Air Forces (June 1941). Billy Mitchell, an air commander in World War I, campaigned for an independent air force; in 1921 his bombers sank the captured German battleship Ostfriesland in tests, and in 1925 he was court-martialed for publicly attacking his superiors' neglect of air power.

World War II: Henry 'Hap' Arnold commands the Army Air Forces, and he remains the only person to hold five-star rank in two services (General of the Army, then General of the Air Force). The Tuskegee Airmen, trained at Tuskegee, Alabama, from 1941, are the first African American military pilots in the US armed forces; the 332nd Fighter Group, the 'Red Tails', escort bombers over Europe. Their commander, Benjamin O. Davis Jr., later becomes the Air Force's first African American general.

18 September 1947: the National Security Act of 1947 creates the US Air Force as a separate service, equal to the Army and Navy. Less than a month later, on 14 October 1947, Captain Chuck Yeager flies the rocket-powered Bell X-1 faster than sound in level flight, over what is now Edwards Air Force Base, California.

The Berlin Airlift, June 1948 to September 1949: when the Soviet Union blockades the roads, railways and canals into West Berlin, US and British transports fly in food and coal for more than two million people, and the Soviets lift the blockade in May 1949. It proved that air power could win a confrontation without fighting. Korea, 1950 to 1953: F-86 Sabres fight MiG-15s over 'MiG Alley' in northwestern North Korea near the Yalu River, the first large-scale jet-versus-jet air war.

20 December 2019: the US Space Force is established as the sixth armed service, organized within the Department of the Air Force, much as the Marine Corps sits within the Department of the Navy. It took over the missions of Air Force Space Command.
teach.formula: 1903 Wrights · 1907 Army aviation · 1941 Army Air Forces and Tuskegee · 18 Sep 1947 USAF · 14 Oct 1947 X-1 · 1948–49 Berlin · 1950–53 MiG Alley · 20 Dec 2019 Space Force

worked.stem: Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier on 14 October 1947. Which service was he flying for, and why is that a neat detail?
steps: The National Security Act made the Air Force a separate service on 18 September 1947.
That is less than a month before Yeager's flight.
So Yeager was already a captain in the brand-new US Air Force, and the first supersonic flight in level flight became one of the young service's first big achievements.
worked.answer: The new US Air Force, which was less than a month old

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of the story in four chapters.
Chapter one, the beginning: the Wright brothers fly in 1903, and the Army starts an aviation office in 1907.
Chapter two, growing up inside the Army: Billy Mitchell argues for a separate air force in the 1920s; Hap Arnold leads the Army Air Forces and the Tuskegee Airmen fly in World War II.
Chapter three, independence: the Air Force becomes its own service in September 1947, and Yeager goes supersonic the next month.
Chapter four, proving itself: the Berlin Airlift in 1948 and 1949, then MiG Alley in Korea from 1950 to 1953.
Epilogue: the Space Force is born in December 2019.
1903: Wright brothers
1907: Army aviation begins
1947: Air Force independent
2019: Space Force

practice.stem: The US Air Force became a separate military service
options: in 1947, under the National Security Act.
in 1926, under the Air Corps Act.
in 1941, when the Army Air Forces were created.
in 1907, when the Signal Corps formed its Aeronautical Division.
in 1949, as a result of the Berlin Airlift.
practice.explain: The National Security Act of 1947 made the Air Force independent on 18 September 1947. 1907, 1926 and 1941 were steps in the Army's own air arm (the Aeronautical Division, the Air Corps and the Army Air Forces), all still part of the Army. The Berlin Airlift began in 1948, when the Air Force already existed, so it could not have created it.

practice.stem: Which lists these events in the order they happened? (1) The Berlin Airlift; (2) the Air Force becomes a separate service; (3) jet fighters battle in MiG Alley; (4) Tuskegee Airmen escort bombers over Europe.
practice.explain: The Red Tails escorted bombers in 1944 and 1945, the Air Force became independent in September 1947, the Berlin Airlift began in June 1948, and MiG Alley belongs to the Korean War, 1950 to 1953. Putting independence first forgets that the Tuskegee Airmen flew in the Army Air Forces in World War II. The airlift came after independence, not before it, and Korea came after Berlin, not before.

practice.stem: The Berlin Airlift is important in air-power history mainly because it
options: was the first large-scale battle between jet fighters.
was the first combat mission flown by the newly independent Air Force's bombers.
showed that airlift alone could supply a blockaded city of over two million people and end a crisis without combat.
proved that bombers could sink a battleship.
led directly to the creation of the Air Force.
practice.explain: For about 15 months US and British transports fed and fueled West Berlin until the Soviets lifted their blockade, a strategic win achieved with cargo aircraft, not weapons. Jet-versus-jet battles came later, in Korea, and sinking a battleship was Billy Mitchell's 1921 test. The airlift was not a combat mission, and the Air Force had already been created in 1947, before the blockade began in 1948.

practice.stem: In 1921 his bombers sank a captured battleship in tests; in 1925 he was court-martialed after publicly accusing Army and Navy leaders of neglecting air power. Who was he, and what was he campaigning for?
options: Hap Arnold, for a larger air corps kept inside the Army
Billy Mitchell, for the Navy to take over all military aviation
Billy Mitchell, for an independent air force
Jimmy Doolittle, for long-range bombers launched from carriers
Benjamin O. Davis Jr., for a racially integrated air arm
practice.explain: Billy Mitchell staged the 1921 bombing tests and was court-martialed in 1925; his goal was a separate air service, which came in 1947, after his death. He wanted aviation out from under both the Army and the Navy, not handed to the Navy. Hap Arnold led the Army Air Forces in World War II, Doolittle led the 1942 carrier-launched raid on Japan, and Davis commanded the Tuskegee Airmen in World War II.

practice.stem: The US Space Force was established on 20 December 2019. Which statement about it is correct?
options: It is a major command inside the US Air Force, like Air Combat Command.
It is part of NASA, staffed by members on loan from the Air Force.
It is a separate armed service organized within the Department of the Air Force.
It is a branch of the Army, which controls missile defense.
It is a reserve component that is activated only in wartime.
practice.explain: The Space Force is the sixth armed service, organized within the Department of the Air Force much as the Marine Corps sits within the Department of the Navy. It took over from Air Force Space Command, which was a major command, but the new service is not a command of the Air Force. NASA is a civilian agency, and the Space Force is neither part of the Army nor a wartime-only reserve.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: Let's hang every fact on a few anchor dates and the one reason each one matters.
steps: 1903 and 1907: flight is invented, and the Army starts flying four years later. The Air Force's roots are in the Army.
The 1920s: Billy Mitchell argues that air power deserves its own service, and is court-martialed for saying so too loudly.
World War II: Hap Arnold leads the huge Army Air Forces, and the Tuskegee Airmen prove their skill in combat.
1947: independence on 18 September, then Yeager's supersonic flight on 14 October.
1948 to 1953: the Berlin Airlift shows air power can win without shooting, and MiG Alley opens the jet age of air combat.
2019: space gets its own service, the Space Force, within the Department of the Air Force.

example.stem: Which came first: Hap Arnold commanding the Army Air Forces, or the Air Force becoming independent?
steps: Arnold led the Army Air Forces from 1941 through World War II.
Independence came in 1947.
So Arnold's command came first, which is why he was a five-star general in the Army before he became General of the Air Force.
example.answer: Hap Arnold's command of the Army Air Forces

reteach.hook: Wrights 1903, Army 1907, independence 1947, Space Force 2019.

check.stem: Who is the only person to have held five-star rank in two US services, the Army and the Air Force?
check.explain: Hap Arnold was made General of the Army in 1944 and General of the Air Force in 1949. Billy Mitchell never reached five stars, Yeager was a test and combat pilot, Spaatz was the first Air Force Chief of Staff as a four-star general, and Davis was the Air Force's first African American general.

check.stem: Chuck Yeager's first supersonic flight in the Bell X-1 came
options: before the Wright brothers' first flight.
less than a month after the Air Force became a separate service.
check.explain: Yeager flew faster than sound on 14 October 1947, less than a month after the Air Force's creation on 18 September 1947. World War II had ended in 1945, the Berlin Airlift began in June 1948, and the Korean War began in 1950.

check.stem: The Tuskegee Airmen are remembered as
options: the first African American military pilots in the US armed forces.
the crews who flew the Berlin Airlift.
the first pilots to fly jets in combat in Korea.
the test pilots of the Bell X-1.
the founders of the Signal Corps' Aeronautical Division.
check.explain: Trained at Tuskegee, Alabama, from 1941, they were the first African American military pilots, and their Red Tails escorted bombers over Europe in World War II. The Berlin Airlift, Korean jet combat, the X-1 and the 1907 Aeronautical Division are separate parts of the story.

check.stem: MiG Alley, where F-86 Sabres fought MiG-15s, was part of which conflict?
check.explain: MiG Alley was in northwestern North Korea, near the Yalu River, during the Korean War of 1950 to 1953. Neither the F-86 nor the MiG-15 fought in World War I or II, Vietnam came later, and the Berlin blockade was beaten by airlift, not air combat.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's just get the big picture straight: first flight, the Army years, independence, and the Space Force.
steps: In 1903 the Wright brothers flew the first powered, controlled airplane, in North Carolina.
For the next 44 years America's military airplanes belonged to the Army.
In 1947 a new law, the National Security Act, made the Air Force its own service.
Right after that the new Air Force did big things: Yeager flew faster than sound, and the Berlin Airlift kept a city alive.
In 2019 the Space Force was created, the newest service.

example.stem: How many years passed between the Wright brothers' first flight and the creation of the Air Force?
steps: First flight: 1903.
Air Force: 1947.

reteach.hook: 1903 first flight, 1947 Air Force, 2019 Space Force.

check.stem: Where did the Wright brothers make their first powered flight in December 1903?
check.explain: The first flights were made near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, chosen for its steady winds and soft sand. Dayton was the Wrights' hometown and workshop, Tuskegee is where the Tuskegee Airmen trained, Edwards is where Yeager broke the sound barrier, and Washington was not involved.

check.stem: Which law created the US Air Force as a separate service in 1947?
options: The National Defense Authorization Act for 2020
check.explain: The National Security Act of 1947 created the independent Air Force. The Air Corps Act of 1926 renamed the Army's air arm but kept it in the Army, and the defense authorization act for 2020 created the Space Force. The Defense Production Act and Selective Service Act deal with industry and the draft.

check.stem: In 1948, when the Soviet Union cut the roads and railways into West Berlin, the United States and Britain responded by
options: bombing the forces enforcing the blockade.
sending ships up the river into the city.
sending jet fighters to break the blockade.
flying in food and fuel by transport aircraft.
check.explain: The Berlin Airlift flew in food and coal for about 15 months until the Soviets gave up the blockade. There was no bombing, fighter battle or airborne assault; avoiding combat was the whole point. Shipping by river was blocked along with the other surface routes.

check.stem: The US Space Force was created in
check.explain: The Space Force was established on 20 December 2019. 1947 is when the Air Force was created, 1958 is when NASA was founded, 1982 is when Air Force Space Command was formed, and 1961 is the year of the first American spaceflight.

afoqt-tbas-uav.title: TBAS: overview & UAV orientation
afoqt-tbas-uav.blurb: What the TBAS is and how it feeds your PCSM score, then the UAV block: a north-up map, a heading-up camera, and a target to find fast. One rule turns the camera; drill it until it's instant.

units.title: The TBAS and your PCSM score
units.objective: Explain what the TBAS measures, who takes it, its blocks, and how it combines with the AFOQT and flight hours into the PCSM score.

steps: The TBAS (Test of Basic Aviation Skills) is the Air Force's computer-based test of the eye, hand and attention skills a pilot uses. You sit it at a test site with a joystick, a throttle and a headset. It is separate from the AFOQT.
Who takes it: rated candidates, meaning pilot, RPA (remotely piloted aircraft) pilot, Combat Systems Officer and Air Battle Manager applicants. Non-rated officer jobs do not need it.

The blocks you practise here: UAV directional orientation (find a target in a drone's camera view), Airplane Tracking (ATT, stick), Vertical Tracking (VTT, throttle), both trackers together (AVTT), and a four-window Multitasking block with spoken radio calls.
Each block is scored on performance, such as accuracy, reaction time or time on target. There is no simple pass mark: the results go into your PCSM score.

PCSM (Pilot Candidate Selection Method) is a score from 1 to 99 built from three things: your TBAS results, your AFOQT Pilot composite (Math Knowledge, Table Reading, Instrument Comprehension and Aviation Information) and your recorded flight hours.

A higher PCSM makes you more competitive for a pilot or RPA pilot slot. The Air Force does not publish the formula or the weights, so nobody can tell you exactly how many points each part is worth. Treat every part as worth raising.
teach.formula: PCSM (1–99) = TBAS results + AFOQT Pilot composite + recorded flight hours · weights not published · higher is more competitive

worked.stem: A pilot candidate has no logged flight hours. Can they still build a competitive PCSM?
steps: List the three parts of the PCSM: TBAS results, the AFOQT Pilot composite and recorded flight hours.
Flight hours are only one of the three. With zero hours, that part adds nothing, but the other two still count in full.
So the candidate raises PCSM by scoring well on the TBAS and on the four Pilot subtests of the AFOQT.
The trap is thinking hours decide everything, or that the TBAS is pass/fail. Neither is true, and the weights aren't published, so you can't write off any part.
worked.answer: Yes: strong TBAS and AFOQT Pilot scores still build a competitive PCSM without flight hours.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of PCSM as one number, from 1 to 99, that a pilot selection board looks at.
That number is made from three ingredients.
Ingredient one: how well you do on the TBAS, the hands-on computer test with a stick and throttle.
Ingredient two: your AFOQT Pilot score, from four of the written subtests.
Ingredient three: how many flight hours you have on record.
Bigger is better. Nobody outside the Air Force knows the exact recipe, so do your best on every ingredient.
TBAS results
AFOQT Pilot composite
Flight hours
PCSM 1–99

practice.stem: Which three things make up the PCSM score?
options: TBAS results, AFOQT Verbal composite, flight hours
TBAS results, AFOQT Pilot composite, commander's rating
AFOQT Pilot composite, flight physical, flight hours
TBAS results, AFOQT Pilot composite, flight hours
TBAS results only, scaled from 1 to 99
practice.explain: PCSM combines TBAS results, the AFOQT Pilot composite and recorded flight hours. The Verbal composite is not the AFOQT part used, the flight physical and commander's ratings are separate parts of an application, and the TBAS alone is only one of three ingredients.

practice.stem: How is a PCSM score reported?
options: 1 to 99, and higher is more competitive
0 to 100 percent, with 70 as a pass
1 to 99, and lower means fewer errors
practice.explain: PCSM runs from 1 to 99 and a higher score makes you more competitive. It is not a percent with a pass mark, not a 1 to 9 scale, and a low number is worse, not better. There is no simple pass/fail.

practice.stem: Which TBAS block is worked with the throttle?
options: None of them; the throttle is unused
practice.explain: In VTT the throttle moves a marker up and down its vertical bar. ATT uses the stick, the UAV block is a find-the-target task, and the radio window is answered by choosing a frequency. The throttle is used, in VTT and in the combined block.

practice.stem: Candidate A has a higher AFOQT Pilot composite than Candidate B. B has the better TBAS results and more flight hours. Who has the higher PCSM?
options: A, because the AFOQT Pilot composite outweighs the rest
B, because B wins two of the three parts
It can't be told from this, as the weights aren't published
A, because flight hours only count for RPA candidates
Neither: each part counts one third, so they tie
practice.explain: The PCSM formula and weights are not published, and we don't know the size of each gap, so the comparison can't be settled. Winning two parts doesn't guarantee a higher total, there is no published equal split, and nothing says the AFOQT part dominates or that hours are RPA-only.

practice.stem: A candidate says: 'The TBAS is pass/fail, so I only need to get through it.' What is wrong with that?
options: The TBAS replaces the AFOQT for pilot candidates
TBAS results feed the PCSM, so every bit of performance counts
Nothing; the TBAS has a fixed pass mark
The TBAS only counts for RPA pilot candidates
Boards see the TBAS score but ignore the PCSM
practice.explain: TBAS results are one of the three ingredients of the PCSM, so a stronger performance raises the score boards look at. The TBAS does not replace the AFOQT, it has no simple pass mark, it counts for pilot as well as RPA candidates, and the PCSM is exactly what boards use.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's sort it by the questions a candidate actually asks.
steps: What is it? The TBAS is a hands-on computer test of aviation skills, with a stick, a throttle and a headset. It is not part of the AFOQT.
Who takes it? Rated candidates: pilot, RPA pilot, CSO and ABM applicants.
What's in it? Here you practise UAV orientation, three tracking blocks (stick, throttle, both) and a four-window multitasking block.
Where does it go? Into the PCSM, a 1 to 99 score built from the TBAS, the AFOQT Pilot composite and recorded flight hours.
How much is each part worth? Not published. So you can't write off any part, and the TBAS is never 'just pass/fail'.

example.stem: Which part of a pilot application is NOT one of the PCSM ingredients: TBAS results, AFOQT Pilot composite, flight hours or college GPA?
steps: Recall the three ingredients: TBAS results, AFOQT Pilot composite, recorded flight hours.
College GPA is not among them. Boards may see it elsewhere in the application, but it doesn't feed PCSM.

reteach.hook: PCSM = Test + Pilot score + Hours: three ingredients, secret recipe.

check.stem: What range does a PCSM score use?
check.explain: PCSM is reported from 1 to 99. The other ranges belong to other kinds of scores or are invented: there is no 0 to 100, 1 to 9, 200 to 800 or 1 to 50 PCSM scale.

check.stem: Who sits the TBAS?
options: Rated candidates: pilot, RPA pilot, CSO and ABM
Only candidates with no flight hours
check.explain: All rated applicants sit the TBAS: pilot, RPA pilot, CSO and ABM. Non-rated officer jobs don't need it, flight hours don't exempt you, it isn't CSO-only, and it isn't an enlisted test.

check.stem: A candidate has zero flight hours. What is true about their PCSM?
options: They can't get a PCSM score at all
Their AFOQT score is doubled to make up for it
Only the TBAS counts for them
TBAS and AFOQT Pilot scores still count in full
check.explain: Flight hours are one ingredient; with none, the TBAS and AFOQT Pilot composite still count. Zero hours doesn't block a score, fix it at 1, drop the AFOQT part, or trigger any published doubling.

check.stem: Why can't you say exactly how many PCSM points a better TBAS result is worth?
options: Because the formula and weights aren't published
Because each part is always one third
Because only flight hours change the score
check.explain: The Air Force doesn't publish the PCSM formula or weights. TBAS results are used, PCSM is a 1 to 99 score not pass/fail, there's no published equal split, and every part can move the score.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's take it one word at a time.
steps: TBAS stands for Test of Basic Aviation Skills.
It's a computer test where you use a stick, a throttle and headphones, a bit like a simple flight game.
PCSM stands for Pilot Candidate Selection Method. It's one number from 1 to 99.
Your PCSM goes up when your TBAS, your AFOQT Pilot score or your flight hours go up.
A higher PCSM is better.

example.stem: Is a PCSM of 80 better or worse than a PCSM of 40?
steps: PCSM runs from 1 to 99.
Higher is more competitive.

reteach.hook: Higher PCSM, better chances.

check.stem: What does TBAS stand for?
check.explain: TBAS is the Test of Basic Aviation Skills. The others swap in words that are close but wrong, such as Air, Tactical, Battlefield or Aptitude Score.

check.stem: Which AFOQT composite feeds the PCSM?
check.explain: The Pilot composite is the AFOQT part of the PCSM. Verbal, Quantitative and Academic Aptitude are other AFOQT composites, and Situational Judgment is another AFOQT measure, none of them PCSM ingredients.

check.stem: Which TBAS block needs the headset?
check.explain: Multitasking has spoken radio calls, so you need to listen. The tracking and UAV blocks are visual, and a headset is used, so 'none' is wrong.

check.stem: Your PCSM moves from 55 to 70. What does that mean?
check.explain: A higher PCSM makes you more competitive. It isn't pass/fail, a rise isn't a fail, and losing flight hours would not raise the score.

units.title: UAV orientation: turning the camera
units.objective: Find any compass target in the heading-up camera view for the eight main headings and the Hard 30° and 60° offsets, quickly and without error.

steps: You see two pictures. The MAP is always north-up and shows the drone with an arrow for its heading. The CAMERA looks straight down at a building with four targets around it: north, east, south and west.
The one rule: the TOP of the camera picture is the way the drone is flying, not north. You are told which target to hit, and you find where it sits in the camera.
Sit in the drone. Ahead is the top of the camera, your right is the right side, your left is the left side, behind you is the bottom. Ask: where is the target from where I'm facing?

Cardinal headings. East: north is on the LEFT, south on the RIGHT, west at the BOTTOM. South: north at the BOTTOM, east on the LEFT, west on the RIGHT. West: north on the RIGHT, south on the LEFT, east at the BOTTOM.

45° headings put every target on a diagonal. Heading northeast: north top-left, east top-right, south bottom-right, west bottom-left. Each 90° turn of the heading moves every target one corner COUNTERCLOCKWISE.

The exact rule, and the one for Hard items (30° and 60° offsets): measure clockwise from the top. Camera angle = target bearing − heading, adding 360 if the result is negative. Heading 060°: north is at 0 − 60 = −60, plus 360 = 300, so 60° LEFT of the top.
The two classic mistakes: reading the camera as north-up (it never is), and turning the wrong way (when the drone turns right, the world in the camera turns left).
Speed: accuracy counts most, but reaction time is scored too. Learn the layouts so the answer comes as a picture, not a calculation. Never trade a correct tap for a faster wrong one.
teach.formula: Camera top = drone heading · camera angle (clockwise from top) = target bearing − heading (+360 if negative)

worked.stem: The drone flies southeast (135°). Where is the north target in the camera picture?
steps: Camera top = southeast. Sit in the drone facing southeast.
Your left points northeast and behind you points northwest. North lies between them: behind you and to the left.
Check with the rule: 0 − 135 = −135, plus 360 = 225. That is 225° clockwise from the top, which is the bottom-left corner.
Traps: north-up thinking puts it at the top, and turning the wrong way (0 + 135 = 135) puts it bottom-right.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Look at the map first. Find the drone's arrow. That direction is now 'up' in the camera.
Imagine picking up the camera picture and turning it until its top points the same way as the drone's arrow.
Example: the drone flies east. Turn the picture so its top points east.
Now ask where north is. If you face east, north is on your left. So the north target is on the left of the camera.
South is on your right, and west is behind you, at the bottom.
Do this for each heading until you can see the answer without turning anything in your head.
Read the heading
Heading = camera top
Target from your seat
Tap it

visual.caption: Map is north-up; camera is heading-up

practice.stem: The drone heads east. Where is the north target in the camera picture?
practice.explain: The top of the camera is east, and facing east, north is on your left (0 − 90 = −90, which is 270°, the left side). The top is the north-up mistake, the right is turning the wrong way, the bottom is where west goes, and top-left would need a 45° heading.

practice.stem: The drone heads southwest. Where is the east target in the camera picture?
practice.explain: 90 − 225 = −135, plus 360 = 225°, the bottom-left corner: facing southwest, east is behind you and to your left. On the right is the north-up mistake, top-left comes from turning the wrong way, and top-right and bottom-right are where west and north go.

practice.stem: The drone heads northwest. Where is the east target in the camera picture?
practice.explain: 90 − 315 = −225, plus 360 = 135°, the bottom-right corner: facing northwest, east is behind you and to your right. On the right is the north-up mistake, top-right comes from turning the wrong way (90 + 315), bottom-left is south and top-left is west.

practice.stem: Hard set: the drone heads 060°. Where is the north target in the camera picture?
practice.explain: 0 − 60 = −60, plus 360 = 300°, which is 60° counterclockwise from the top. 60° right is turning the wrong way, 30° left mixes up the 60° offset with its 30° complement, and the top is the north-up mistake.

practice.stem: Hard set: the drone heads 210°. Where is the west target in the camera picture?
practice.explain: 270 − 210 = 60°, so west is 60° clockwise from the top, upper right. On the left is the north-up mistake, 120° right comes from turning the wrong way (270 + 210 = 480, which is 120°), 60° left flips the side, and 30° right uses the wrong offset.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Forget the map for a moment and sit in the drone's seat.
steps: Ahead of you is the TOP of the camera. Your right hand is the RIGHT side, your left hand the LEFT side, behind you the BOTTOM.
Facing east: north is on your left, south on your right, west behind you.
Facing south: east on your left, west on your right, north behind you.
Facing west: south on your left, north on your right, east behind you.
Facing a diagonal, like northeast: north is ahead-left (top-left) and east is ahead-right (top-right). The other two are behind you on the matching sides.
For 30° and 60° headings, use the rule: target bearing minus heading, plus 360 if negative, measured clockwise from the top.

example.stem: The drone heads south. Where is the east target in the camera?
steps: Sit facing south. Your left hand points east (face south and your left is east).
Check: 90 − 180 = −90, plus 360 = 270, the left side.

reteach.hook: Sit in the seat: ahead is the top, your hands are the sides.

check.stem: The drone heads south. Where is the east target in the camera?
check.explain: Facing south, east is on your left (90 − 180 + 360 = 270). On the right is the north-up mistake, the top and bottom are south and north, and bottom-left would need a diagonal heading.

check.stem: The drone heads west. Where is the north target in the camera?
check.explain: Facing west, north is on your right (0 − 270 + 360 = 90). The top is the north-up mistake, the left is turning the wrong way, the bottom is east, and top-right would need a diagonal heading.

check.stem: The drone heads northeast. Where is the west target in the camera?
check.explain: 270 − 45 = 225, the bottom-left corner: facing northeast, west is behind you and to your left. On the left is the north-up mistake, top-left comes from turning the wrong way, and the other corners belong to north and south or east.

check.stem: Accuracy and reaction time both count in the UAV block. What is the best plan?
options: Drill each heading until it's instant; never trade accuracy for speed
Take as long as you need on every single item
Tap as fast as you can and accept a few misses along the way
Always tap the top of the camera first, then correct
Read the target off the north-up map to save time
check.explain: Accuracy matters most and speed is scored too, so drilled layouts give both. Rushing gives away correct answers, taking forever loses the speed credit, a default tap at the top is a guess, and the map's north-up layout is exactly the mistake to avoid.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's start with a plain compass and turn it one step at a time.
steps: On a normal map, north is up, east is right, south is down and west is left.
The camera is different: its top always points where the drone is flying.
If the drone flies north, the camera matches the map. Easy.
If the drone flies south, the camera is upside down: north at the bottom, east on the left, west on the right.
If the drone flies east, the whole compass has turned a quarter turn: north slides to the left and west slides to the bottom.

example.stem: The drone heads east. Where is the west target in the camera?
steps: East is at the top.
West is the opposite of east, so it's at the bottom.

reteach.hook: Whatever the drone faces goes to the top; its opposite goes to the bottom.

check.stem: The drone heads north. Where is the east target in the camera?
check.explain: Heading north, the camera matches the map, so east is on the right. The left is west, the top is north, the bottom is south, and top-right would be northeast.

check.stem: The drone heads south. Where is the north target in the camera?
check.explain: South is at the top, so north, its opposite, is at the bottom. The top is the north-up mistake, the sides are east and west, and bottom-right would need a diagonal heading.

check.stem: The drone heads east. Where is the west target in the camera?
check.explain: East is at the top, so west, its opposite, is at the bottom. On the left is the north-up mistake, the top is east, the right is south, and bottom-left would need a diagonal heading.

check.stem: Hard set: the drone heads 030°. Where is the east target in the camera?
check.explain: 90 − 30 = 60, so east is 60° clockwise from the top. 30° right mixes in the offset itself, on the right is the north-up mistake, and the left-hand answers put it on the wrong side of the top.

afoqt-tbas-cockpit.title: TBAS: tracking (ATT · VTT · AVTT)
afoqt-tbas-cockpit.blurb: Keep a crosshair and a marker on moving targets with the stick, the throttle, then both at once. Learn how rate controls behave, why small early inputs win, and how to split your attention when two targets jink on their own.

units.title: Stick and throttle tracking
units.objective: Use rate control, aircraft-style stick inputs, throttle inputs and small early corrections to stay on target in ATT and VTT, including through jinks.

steps: ATT (Airplane Tracking): the stick steers a crosshair around the open field to stay on a moving aircraft. VTT (Vertical Tracking): the throttle, a vertical slider on the left of the screen, moves a marker up and down its vertical bar to stay on a target that moves up and down.
Both are RATE controls. How far you push sets how FAST the crosshair or marker moves; centered, it stops where it is. It does not spring back to the middle of the screen.
So to stop on the target, ease off as you arrive. Hold the input and you sail past. To follow a drifting target, keep a small steady input that matches its speed.

The stick works like an aircraft's: push FORWARD and the crosshair goes DOWN, pull BACK and it goes UP. Left and right are normal. The throttle is not flipped: push it forward (up) and the marker goes UP, and holding it there keeps the marker climbing. These stick and throttle conventions come from this app's engine, so read the test's on-screen instructions on test day to confirm, and practise this way until it is automatic.

Targets move in straight lines, speed up in stages through the block and jink without warning: a short burst of speed, often with a change of direction. Jinks come most often just when you are sitting on the target, and a long lock always breaks away.
Technique: small, early corrections beat big, late ones. Lead the target slightly in the direction it's moving. When it jinks, use a firm but not full input, then ease off as you catch it.
Scoring counts time on target most, then how close you stay. Being near the target still earns credit, so never leave the crosshair stranded while you 'reset'.
teach.formula: Push = move · how far = how fast · center = stop · stick forward = crosshair down · throttle up = marker up · small and early beats big and late

worked.stem: In ATT the aircraft is drifting slowly down and to the right. Your crosshair is just above it and level with it left to right. What input do you make?
steps: The crosshair needs to come DOWN onto the target and then keep moving down and right with it.
Aircraft-style stick: down means push FORWARD. Right means stick RIGHT.
Rate control: a gentle forward push brings the crosshair down. As it arrives, ease off to a small forward-and-right input that matches the drift.
Traps: pulling back (the un-inverted habit) climbs away; a full push overshoots; centering and waiting lets the target drift off.
worked.answer: A gentle push forward, easing to a small forward-and-right input that matches the drift

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of the stick as a speed dial for the crosshair, not a pointer.
Push a little and the crosshair creeps. Push a lot and it races. Let go and it stops right where it is.
That means you start braking before you reach the target, just like slowing a car before a stop sign.
Up and down are flipped, as in an airplane: push forward to go down, pull back to go up.
The target will suddenly dart away now and then, often right after you catch it. Expect it, and don't yank the stick.
