The throttle works the same way, but only up and down along its bar on the left: push it up and the marker climbs, pull it back and it sinks.
Small early input
Ease off as you arrive
Match the drift
Expect the jink

practice.stem: In ATT your crosshair is slightly above the aircraft. With the aircraft-style stick, what do you do?
options: Push the stick fully forward and hold
Let go so the crosshair recenters
practice.explain: The crosshair must come down, and with an aircraft-style stick down is forward, so a gentle push. Pulling back is the un-inverted habit, a full push overshoots, the throttle moves the marker on the vertical bar, not the field crosshair, and letting go only stops the crosshair where it is.

practice.stem: You push the stick right and the crosshair is now reaching the target, which is drifting slowly right. What should you do?
options: Ease back to a small right push that matches its drift
Center the stick so the crosshair returns to the middle
Keep the same push until the crosshair passes it
Push hard left to brake the crosshair
Let go and wait for the target to come back
practice.explain: With rate control you ease off as you arrive and keep just enough input to match the drift. Holding the push sails past, the crosshair never returns to the middle, a hard left push overcorrects, and letting go stops the crosshair while the target keeps drifting away.

practice.stem: In VTT the target on the bar jinks down at speed just as you lock on. What is the best response?
options: Hold the throttle fully back until the marker stops on it
Do nothing; it always comes straight back
Push the throttle up to get ahead of its return
A firm pull back on the throttle, easing off as you catch it
practice.explain: Throttle back brings the marker down, a firm but not full input catches the jink, and easing off as you arrive stops you overshooting. Full throttle held until you see a stop overshoots, a jink doesn't reliably reverse, the stick moves the field crosshair, and guessing a return by pushing the throttle up moves you away.

practice.stem: Tracking scores time on target most, then how close you stay. Which habit costs the most points?
options: Leaving the crosshair far off while you reset after a jink
Easing off the input as you arrive
Holding a small steady input to match the drift
practice.explain: Stranding the crosshair throws away both time on target and closeness, so it costs the most. Small corrections, a slight lead, easing off on arrival and matching the drift are all good habits that keep you on or near the target.

practice.stem: In ATT the aircraft is moving up and to the left, and your crosshair is on it. Which stick input keeps you with it?
options: Centered; the crosshair follows by itself
practice.explain: Up means pull back with an aircraft-style stick, and left is left, so back and to the left, gently. Forward and left is the un-inverted mistake, the right-hand inputs go the wrong way across, and a centered stick stops the crosshair while the aircraft moves on.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Think of the controls as speed dials, not pointers.
steps: Pointer: put your hand where you want the dot. That is NOT how the TBAS works.
Speed dial: how far you push sets how fast the crosshair moves. Center the stick and it stops where it is. The throttle drives the marker on the vertical bar the same way.
So steer early and brake early: ease off before you reach the target, then hold just enough input to match its drift.
On the stick, up and down are aircraft-style: forward goes down, back goes up. The throttle is not flipped: up is up.
Later in the block the targets go faster and jink more, especially when you're on them. Expect it and answer with a firm, not full, input.

example.stem: You let go of the stick completely. What does the crosshair do?
steps: The stick is a rate control: no push means no movement.
The crosshair stops where it is; it doesn't return to the middle.

reteach.hook: Push to move, ease to stop, expect the jink.

check.stem: In ATT your crosshair is below the aircraft. What stick input brings it up?
check.explain: Aircraft-style, back means up, and gently avoids overshooting. Forward goes down, a full pull overshoots, the throttle drives the marker on the vertical bar, and letting go only stops the crosshair.

check.stem: You center the stick completely. What does the crosshair do?
options: Jumps back to the middle of the field
Keeps moving at the same speed
check.explain: With a rate control, no input means no movement, so it stops in place. It doesn't spring to the middle, coast on, home in on the target or sink.

check.stem: Late in the block the target is faster. What changes in your technique?
options: Early inputs, more lead, ready for jinks
Wait for it to come to you
check.explain: A faster target needs early inputs and a bit more lead, and jinks come more often. Big late inputs overshoot, jinks don't become rarer, dropping the lead leaves you behind, and waiting loses time on target.

check.stem: Which control drives the marker in Vertical Tracking (VTT)?
check.explain: VTT uses the throttle on the left to move the marker up and down its vertical bar. The stick works the field crosshair in ATT, forward-and-back stick is the up-and-down trap, both controls together is the combined block, and there's no mouse.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's go back to just three facts.
steps: Fact one: push the control and the crosshair moves. Let go and it stops.
Fact two: push further and it moves faster.
Fact three: on the stick, forward is down and back is up.
Now the habit: little pushes, early. Slow down as you get close.

example.stem: The target is just to the right of your crosshair and still. What do you do?
steps: Give a small push right so the crosshair creeps over.
Let go as it lands on the target, so it stops there.
example.answer: A small push right, then let go as you arrive

reteach.hook: Little pushes, early; let go on arrival.

check.stem: The ATT target is still, just left of your crosshair. What do you do?
options: A small push left, letting go as you arrive
check.explain: A small push moves the crosshair over and letting go stops it on the target. Full left overshoots, right goes the wrong way, back moves it up, and doing nothing leaves you off target.

check.stem: You push the stick further. What happens to the crosshair?
options: It jumps to a new place
check.explain: With a rate control, more push means more speed. It doesn't slow, jump, stop or change color because you pushed harder.

check.stem: In ATT you need the crosshair to go DOWN. Which way do you move the stick?
check.explain: Aircraft-style, forward is down. Back is up, left and right move it sideways, and twisting isn't an input here.

check.stem: When is the target most likely to jink?
options: Never; it moves in straight lines
Just when you're sitting on it
Only when the crosshair is far away
Only when you let go of the stick
check.explain: Jinks come most often while you're locked on, and a long lock always breaks away. They aren't limited to the start, they do happen, and they aren't triggered by being far away or letting go.

units.title: Combined tracking: splitting attention
units.objective: Run the stick and throttle together in AVTT with a steady scan, keeping the crosshair and the marker on or close to their targets.

steps: AVTT puts ATT and VTT together: the stick keeps a crosshair on the aircraft in the open field, and the throttle keeps the marker on its target in the vertical bar on the left, at the same time. Both must be on target together for the combined lock-on. It is the hardest block and the closest to flying.

The two targets move and jink independently. Even if you are on each one for a good share of the time, the moments when BOTH are locked together are rare. A low both-on-target figure is normal for everyone.
Scoring is by time on target, then closeness, for each tracker. A tracker you abandon earns almost nothing, so two trackers kept close beat one perfect lock and one left behind.
Split your attention: keep your eyes mostly on the field aircraft, which moves in two directions and is harder. Watch the bar with the edge of your vision and give it quick, regular glances.

Scanning rhythm: field, quick glance at the bar, field. If the bar target is drifting, set a small steady throttle input that matches it, then go back to the field and let that input carry the marker.
Keep your two hands independent. A stick correction should not make your throttle hand twitch, and the other way round. When one target jinks, fix it with one firm input, then check the other.
teach.formula: Eyes on the field · glance at the bar in rhythm · set a matching throttle input and leave it · keep both close, not one perfect

worked.stem: AVTT, late in the block: you're locked on the field aircraft. The bar target is drifting steadily up, away from its marker. What do you do?
steps: Don't drop the field aircraft to stare at the bar: that leaves one tracker earning nothing.
Add a small, steady push up on the throttle that matches the bar target's drift. Rate control means that input keeps the marker moving with it.
Keep your stick hand still and your eyes back on the aircraft.
Glance across again in a second to check, and trim the throttle input if it is too much or too little.
worked.answer: A small, steady push up on the throttle to match the drift, stick hand still, eyes back on the field

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Imagine patting your head and rubbing your belly at once. Each hand has its own job.
Here one hand flies the stick for the aircraft in the field. The other works the throttle for the bar on the left.
Your eyes can only look at one place clearly. Let them rest on the aircraft, because it's the trickier one.
Every second or so, flick your eyes across to the bar. If its target is sliding away, give the throttle a gentle, steady push the same way.
Then look back. The throttle push keeps working while you're not looking.
Nobody keeps both locked all the time. Keeping both close is the goal.

practice.stem: In the combined block (AVTT), which control drives which tracker?
options: Throttle: the field aircraft; stick: the vertical bar
Stick: left and right; throttle: up and down of one crosshair
Stick: the field aircraft; throttle: the vertical bar
Stick: the field aircraft; throttle: how fast the crosshair moves
practice.explain: The stick flies the crosshair on the aircraft in the open field and the throttle moves the marker up and down the vertical bar. Swapping them, one control for both, or splitting one crosshair's axes between the controls all misdescribe the block, and the throttle does not set the field crosshair's speed; it drives its own marker.

practice.stem: Why is the share of time with BOTH trackers on target usually low, even for strong candidates?
options: Each target jinks on its own, so locks rarely overlap
The marker moves only while the stick is centered
The two targets move together, so fixing one disturbs the other
Only one tracker is scored at a time
The bar target pauses whenever you touch the stick
practice.explain: The targets are independent, so a lock on one and a lock on the other must overlap at the same moment, which is rare. Both trackers are scored, the controls work at the same time, the targets don't move together, and nothing pauses.

practice.stem: You're locked on the field aircraft. From the corner of your eye you see the bar target drifting steadily down, away from its marker. What is the best move?
options: Look across and stay on the bar until it is locked
Ignore the bar until the aircraft jinks
Hold the throttle fully back until it's caught
Push the stick forward to drag both down
Add a small, steady pull back on the throttle and keep the stick still
practice.explain: Throttle back brings the marker down, and a small matching input carries it while your eyes and stick hand stay on the aircraft. Staring at the bar abandons the field, ignoring it lets it drift far off, a full pull overshoots, and the stick does not move the marker.

practice.stem: Midway through AVTT the targets speed up and you're losing both. Which plan protects your score best?
options: Lock the aircraft perfectly and let the bar go
Let both go and wait for a calmer stretch
Keep both close, fixing whichever is drifting further off
Waggle both controls so the crosshair and marker sweep through the targets
Put all your attention on the bar, as it has one axis
practice.explain: Each tracker is scored on time on target and closeness, so keeping both near and fixing the worse one first earns from both. Abandoning either tracker, or both, throws its credit away, and waggling the controls keeps both far off most of the time.

practice.stem: Which scanning pattern fits AVTT best?
options: Ten seconds on the field, then ten seconds on the bar
Eyes on the field, a glance at the bar about every second
Look at the bar only after the aircraft jinks
Eyes fixed on the bar; fly the aircraft by feel
Watch the crosshair and marker only, never the targets
practice.explain: Resting on the harder field target with short, regular glances at the bar keeps both under control. Long blocks of time leave one tracker unwatched, the field aircraft can't be flown blind, waiting for a jink makes the glances irregular, and you need to see the targets to lead them.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Think of yourself as a waiter carrying two trays.
steps: Each tray is a tracker. Drop one and you've lost everything on it, however well you hold the other.
Your eyes rest on the heavier tray: the field aircraft, which moves in two directions.
Every second or so, glance at the bar. If its target is sliding, set a small matching throttle push and look back.
Rate control is your friend: that throttle push keeps the marker moving while you look away.
Both trackers locked at once is rare for everybody. Close on both beats perfect on one.

example.stem: You've been staring at the bar for five seconds to get a perfect lock. What's the cost?
steps: The field aircraft has been unwatched for five seconds and has drifted or jinked away.
That tracker earns little time on target or closeness for those seconds.
example.answer: The field tracker has been earning almost nothing

reteach.hook: Two trays: keep both up, not one perfect.

check.stem: Where should your eyes rest most of the time in AVTT?
check.explain: The field aircraft moves in two directions and is harder, so your eyes rest there with glances at the bar. Staring at the bar abandons the field, and the score, the screen edge and your hands tell you nothing about the targets.

check.stem: The bar target drifts steadily up. What input keeps its marker with it while you watch the field?
options: A small, steady push up on the throttle
check.explain: A small steady throttle input matches the drift with rate control. Full throttle overshoots, the stick moves the field crosshair even though back is up on the stick, easing the throttle back goes the wrong way, and nothing follows on its own.

check.stem: Your both-on-target share is low. What does that most likely mean?
options: Nothing unusual; independent targets rarely line up
You should ignore the bar next time
Only the both-on figure is scored
check.explain: Two targets that move and jink on their own rarely let you lock both at once, so a low figure is normal. It doesn't mean the block was done wrong or broken, ignoring the bar would cost more, and each tracker is scored on its own time and closeness.

check.stem: The field aircraft jinks while your bar is drifting a little. What first?
options: Fix the bar first, then deal with the aircraft
Close your eyes and track by feel
Fix the aircraft first, then check the bar
check.explain: The jink will run you off the aircraft fast, so one firm input there first, then a check on the bar, which is only drifting a little. Waiting loses both, full inputs overshoot, and you can't track blind.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's give each hand one job.
steps: One hand: the stick, for the aircraft out in the field.
Other hand: the throttle, for the marker in the vertical bar on the left.
Eyes: mostly on the aircraft, with a quick look across at the bar now and then.
If the bar target is sliding, give one gentle, steady throttle push the same way and look back.

example.stem: Which do you use for the vertical bar: the stick or the throttle?
steps: The bar is the vertical tracker.
The vertical tracker uses the throttle.

reteach.hook: Stick flies the field, throttle rides the bar.

check.stem: In AVTT, what does the throttle move?
options: Both the crosshair and the marker
The marker on the vertical bar
check.explain: The throttle moves the marker up and down the vertical bar. The stick handles the field crosshair, no single control moves both, the gauge belongs to Multitasking, and the throttle doesn't set the crosshair's speed.

check.stem: In AVTT, what does the stick move?
options: The marker on the vertical bar
Both the crosshair and the marker
check.explain: The stick flies the crosshair on the field aircraft. The bar uses the throttle, nothing moves both, and the radio and camera belong to other blocks.

check.stem: How often should you glance at the bar?
check.explain: Short, regular glances, roughly every second, catch drift early. Never or rarely looking lets it drift far off, and the bar doesn't beep for you.

check.stem: What is the goal for the two trackers?
options: Both off target to save effort
check.explain: Each tracker is scored, so keeping both on or close earns the most. Ignoring one, or both, throws its credit away, and picking only the easier one does the same.

afoqt-tbas-multitask.title: TBAS: Multitasking
afoqt-tbas-multitask.blurb: Four windows at once: remember letters, add numbers, keep a gauge out of the red, and change radio frequency only when YOUR callsign is called first. The rules are simple; doing them all together is the test.

units.title: Letters, sums and the gauge
units.objective: Apply the memorization, calculation (carries and the ≥1200 rule) and gauge rules instantly while keeping all four windows going.

steps: Four windows run at once for the whole block: memorization, calculation, gauge and radio. Your score is the average of the four, so a window you ignore costs as much as one you get wrong.

Memorization: a set of six letters shows for a few seconds, then hides. Rehearse it as two chunks of three. Single letters then appear: tap ✓ if it is in the CURRENT set, ✗ if not. When a new set appears, the old one no longer counts. Wrong taps cancel right ones, so blind guessing earns nothing.
Calculation: add two 3-digit numbers. If the sum is 1200 or more, do NOT type it: press the ≥1200 button instead. Typing a big sum is marked wrong even if the number is right.
Fast ≥1200 check: add the hundreds first. 12 or more hundreds means ≥1200. 10 or fewer means below. Exactly 11 means the last two digits decide: if they add to 100 or more, it's ≥1200.

Typing: type the answer the way you would write it, then ✓: 389 + 457 = 846 is typed 8, 4, 6. Give four-digit sums all four digits: 1150 is 1, 1, 5, 0. Watch the carries, because the wrong answers on a real problem are the ones a dropped carry gives. Tap a single box to fix one digit. Unanswered problems time out.

Gauge: the needle drifts from the center through green, then yellow, then red. Tap to re-center it once it is in the YELLOW. Tapping while it's still green counts as early, and reaching red counts as late. Time spent in green also scores.
teach.formula: Letters: current set only · sum ≥ 1200 → press ≥1200 · otherwise type it and ✓ · gauge: tap in yellow, not green, before red

worked.stem: Sum: 645 + 587. What do you press?
steps: Hundreds first: 6 + 5 = 11 hundreds. Exactly 11, so the last two digits decide.
45 + 87 = 132, which is 100 or more. So the sum is 1100 + 132 = 1232.
1232 is 1200 or more, so you do not type it.
Traps: typing 1, 2, 3, 2 (a right number, still marked wrong), or forgetting the carry and typing 1132.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Letters: look at the six letters and say them as two little groups, like 'K R T' and 'B M F'.
When one letter pops up, ask: is it in my groups right now? Yes, tap the tick. No, tap the cross.
Sums: first ask, is this going to be big? Add the front digits. If they make 12 or more, press the 1200 button and you're done.
If it's smaller, type it the way you'd write it, then tap the tick. 846 is 8, then 4, then 6.
Gauge: green is fine, leave it. Yellow means tap it now. Red means you're late.
Then move your eyes on to the next window.
Letters: current set
Sum: ≥1200 or type it
Gauge: tap in yellow
Radio: listen

practice.stem: Sum: 645 + 587. What do you press?
practice.explain: 645 + 587 = 1232, which is 1200 or more, so you press ≥1200 instead of typing. Typing 1232 is marked wrong even though the number is right, 1132 drops the carry from 45 + 87, 1222 drops the carry from 5 + 7, and 1122 drops both.

practice.stem: Sum: 389 + 457. Which keys do you press, in order?
practice.explain: 389 + 457 = 846, below 1200, so type 8, 4, 6, then ✓. 9 + 7 = 16 carries 1 into the tens and 8 + 5 + 1 = 14 carries 1 into the hundreds: 836 drops the first carry, 746 the second and 736 both. ≥1200 is only for sums of 1200 or more.

practice.stem: Sum: 578 + 572. What do you press?
practice.explain: 578 + 572 = 1150, which is below 1200, so you type all four digits: 1, 1, 5, 0, then ✓. Pressing ≥1200 confuses 'four digits' with '1200 or more', leaving off the zero enters 115, 1050 drops the carry into the hundreds and 1140 drops the carry into the tens.

practice.stem: The set was K, R, T, B, M, F. Later a new set, W, H, Q, D, S, P, was shown. Now the letter T appears. What do you tap?
options: ✓, because T was in a set you saw
Nothing, since old-set letters are skipped
✗, because T is not in the current set
✓, because old sets count until the block ends
Nothing, and wait until you're sure
practice.explain: Only the current set counts, and T is not in W, H, Q, D, S, P, so tap ✗. Tapping ✓ uses the old set, and leaving it is a missed probe that earns nothing; nothing is skipped for you.

practice.stem: The gauge needle passes from green into yellow, the zone where a tap re-centres it, while you're halfway through typing a sum. What is the best move?
options: Finish the sum first; the gauge only counts in red
Tap the gauge now, then finish the sum
Wait until it reaches red, then tap it
Tap the gauge over and over from now on
Ignore it, since it drifts back by itself
practice.explain: Yellow is the moment to re-center, and one tap costs a fraction of a second, so tap then return to the sum. Waiting for red is late and loses green time, constant tapping includes early taps in the green, and the needle does not come back on its own.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's turn each window into a single yes/no question.
steps: Letters: is it in the set I'm holding RIGHT NOW? Yes = ✓, no = ✗. A new set replaces the old one.
Sum: will it reach 1200? Add the hundreds: 12 or more, yes. 10 or fewer, no. Exactly 11, check whether the last two digits make 100 or more.
If yes, press ≥1200. If no, type it and tap ✓.
Gauge: is the needle in the yellow? Yes = tap now. Green = leave it. Red = you're late; tap at once.
Ask, act, move on to the next window.

example.stem: Sum: 600 + 600. What do you press?
steps: The rule is 1200 OR MORE, so 1200 counts.

reteach.hook: Letters: now-set only. Sums: 1200 or more, press the button. Gauge: yellow means go.

check.stem: Sum: 600 + 600. What do you press?
check.explain: 1200 is '1200 or more', so press the button. Typing 1200 is marked wrong, 1, 2, 0 enters 120, and 1100 and 200 are adding slips.

check.stem: Sum: 599 + 600. What do you press?
check.explain: 599 + 600 = 1199, just under 1200, so type it: 1, 1, 9, 9, then ✓. Pressing ≥1200 rounds up wrongly, 1099 drops 100, 1, 9, 9 enters 199, and 1100 is a rounding slip.

check.stem: The gauge needle is drifting but still in the green. What do you do?
options: Tap it now to be safe
Leave it and check another window
check.explain: Green is fine, and tapping there counts as early, so leave it and keep scanning. Tapping once or twice now is early, waiting for red is late, and the radio has nothing to do with the gauge.

check.stem: Current set: C, L, N, P, V, Z. The letter N appears. What do you tap?
check.explain: N is in the current set, so ✓. ✗ is for letters not in the set, leaving it is a miss, and the ≥1200 button and the gauge are other windows.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's do the sums first, slowly, then the other two windows.
steps: Add the two numbers as normal. Say the answer to yourself.
Is it 1200 or bigger? Press the ≥1200 button. Done.
Smaller? Type it the way you'd write it, then tap the tick. 734 is 7, 3, 4.
Letters: tick if it's in today's set, cross if not.
Gauge: leave it in green, tap it in yellow.

example.stem: Sum: 712 + 455. What do you type?
steps: That's under 1200, so type it as you'd write it: 1, 1, 6, 7.

reteach.hook: Big sum, press the button; small sum, type it and tick.

check.stem: Sum: 712 + 455. What do you press?
check.explain: 712 + 455 = 1167, under 1200, so type 1, 1, 6, 7, then ✓. Pressing ≥1200 is for 1200 or more, 1157 is an adding slip, 1, 6, 7 enters 167, and 1267 adds an extra hundred.

check.stem: Sum: 734 + 498. What do you press?
check.explain: 734 + 498 = 1232, which is 1200 or more, so press the button. Typing 1232 is marked wrong, 1222 drops the carry into the hundreds, 1132 the carry into the thousands' column, and 1122 both.

check.stem: The gauge needle reaches the red. What do you do?
check.explain: Red is late, but the needle stays pinned until you tap, losing green time, so tap at once. It won't return by itself, and ≥1200 and ✗ belong to other windows.

check.stem: Current set: A, G, J, R, U, Y. The letter H appears. What do you tap?
check.explain: H isn't in the set, so ✗. ✓ is for letters in the set, leaving it is a miss, and the gauge and the radio are other windows.

units.title: Radio calls and the scan
units.objective: Respond quickly and only to calls that start with your own callsign, ignore every distractor, and keep scanning the other windows while you listen.

steps: Before the block you are given a callsign: a word and two digits, such as Heat 24. Memorize it; you won't see it again. Say it to yourself before you start.
Calls sound like: 'Dagger 33, Heat 24, switch to frequency two.' The FIRST callsign is the aircraft being called. The SECOND is the one calling.
Respond only when the first callsign is exactly yours, word AND both digits. Then tap the frequency the call gives, as soon as you hear the number. Quick responses score more than slow ones.

Distractors: your callsign in SECOND place (you are the caller, so ignore it), your word with other digits (Heat 42, Heat 25), and your digits with another word (Viper 24). Any tap that isn't the frequency of a live call to you counts against you.

The radio is by ear, so your eyes can stay busy. Keep a loop going: gauge, radio, letters, sum. When you hear your callsign first, listen to the end of the call, tap the frequency, then carry on with the loop.
There are four frequencies, and a call always gives a different one from the one you are on.
teach.formula: First callsign = who is called · second = who is calling · respond only if FIRST is exactly yours · tap the frequency fast

worked.stem: Your callsign is Heat 24. You hear 'Viper 17, Heat 24, switch to frequency three,' then 'Heat 24, Cobra 51, switch to frequency four.' What do you do?
steps: Call one: the first callsign is Viper 17, so Viper 17 is being called. You are only the caller. Ignore it.
Call two: the first callsign is Heat 24, exactly yours. Cobra 51 is calling you.
Tap frequency four as soon as you hear 'four'.
Traps: switching to three because you heard your callsign, or answering both calls.
worked.answer: Ignore the first call; switch to frequency four on the second

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of a phone call that starts 'Sam, it's Alex.' The first name is the person wanted. The second is the person talking.
Radio calls work the same way. First name: who it's for. Second name: who's speaking.
Your name here is your callsign, like Heat 24. Both the word and the number must match.
If the call is for you, do what it says: tap the frequency number it gives.
If your callsign is the second name, someone else is being called. Do nothing.
If it's a near miss, like Heat 42 or Viper 24, it isn't you. Do nothing.

practice.stem: Call: 'Dagger 33, Heat 24, switch to frequency two.' Your callsign is Heat 24. What do you do?
options: Wait for a repeat, then switch to two
Ignore it: the call is for Dagger 33
Tap your current frequency to acknowledge
practice.explain: The first callsign is the one being called, so this call is for Dagger 33 and Heat 24 is only the caller. Switching to two answers a call that isn't yours, three isn't in the call, there is no repeat to wait for, and any extra tap counts as a false response.

practice.stem: Your callsign is Heat 24. Call: 'Heat 42, Raven 18, switch to frequency one.' What do you do?
options: Ignore it: Heat 42 is not Heat 24
Switch to one, since the word matches
Switch to one, then back if it was wrong
practice.explain: Heat 42 has your word but the digits reversed, so the call is not for you. The word alone doesn't make it yours, switching anywhere is a false response that costs points, and four isn't in the call at all.

practice.stem: Your callsign is Cobra 51. Call: 'Cobra 51, Viper 51, switch to frequency three.' What do you do?
options: Ignore it: the digits appear twice
Wait to hear which callsign comes last
Ignore it: Viper 51 is being called
practice.explain: Cobra 51 is the first callsign, exactly yours, so switch to three. Viper 51 is just the caller with similar digits, the last callsign is the caller not the one called, and one isn't the frequency given.

practice.stem: Your callsign is Hawk 36. Within a few seconds you hear 'Hawk 36, Titan 72, switch to frequency four,' then 'Titan 72, Hawk 36, switch to frequency one.' What should you do?
options: Ignore both: a call to you needs you as caller
Switch to four, then to one
Switch to four, and ignore the second call
Switch to one only, as the latest call
Ignore the first, then switch to one
practice.explain: Only the first call starts with Hawk 36, so switch to four. The second call is for Titan 72, with you as the caller, so switching to one is a false response. Both rules about which callsign matters are reversed in the other options.

practice.stem: You're halfway through a sum when a call begins 'Heat 24...', your callsign. What is the best move?
options: Tap a frequency the moment you hear your callsign
Hear the number, tap it at once, then go back to the sum
Finish and submit the sum, then switch if you recall the number
Wait for the call to be repeated before responding
Tap your current frequency to show you heard
practice.explain: Quick responses score most, so listen to the number, tap it straight away and return to the sum. Tapping before the number is a guess, finishing the sum first makes you slow or forgetful, calls aren't repeated, and tapping your current frequency is a false response.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Picture an envelope: 'To, From, Message'.
steps: Every call is an envelope. The first callsign is TO, the second is FROM, then the message: switch to frequency n.
Only open envelopes addressed TO you, with your exact word and both digits.
From you? Not your envelope. Close match? Not your envelope.
Your envelope? Tap the frequency as soon as you hear the number. Speed scores.
Any tap that isn't for a live call to you costs points, so never tap 'just in case'.

example.stem: Your callsign is Ghost 13. Call: 'Raven 13, Ghost 31, switch to frequency two.' What do you do?
steps: TO: Raven 13. That's not you, even though it has your digits.
FROM: Ghost 31, not you either. Ignore it.

reteach.hook: First is TO, second is FROM; only open mail addressed to you.

check.stem: Your callsign is Heat 24. Call: 'Viper 24, Heat 24, switch to frequency three.' What do you do?
check.explain: Viper 24 is being called; you're the caller, so ignore it. Switching to three answers someone else's call, two isn't in the call, and any tap counts as a false response.

check.stem: Your callsign is Heat 24. Call: 'Heat 24, Heat 42, switch to frequency two.' What do you do?
options: Ignore it, as Heat 42 is a trap
Ignore it, as both say Heat
check.explain: The first callsign is Heat 24, exactly yours, so switch to two. Heat 42 is only the caller, a shared word doesn't cancel the call, four isn't given, and calls aren't repeated.

check.stem: Your callsign is Titan 58. Call: 'Titan 85, Hawk 20, switch to frequency one.' What do you do?
options: Switch to one, as the word matches
check.explain: Titan 85 has your word but swapped digits, so it isn't you; ignore it. Every switching option is a false response, and the word alone never makes a call yours.

check.stem: A call to you ends with 'switch to frequency four'. When should you tap?
check.explain: Quick responses score most, so tap four as soon as you hear it. Waiting for the next call, finishing other work first or waiting for a repeat all cost points, and tapping before the number is a guess.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's just practise the first word of every call.
steps: Your callsign is a word and two numbers, like Heat 24.
Listen only to the FIRST callsign in each call.
If it's exactly yours, tap the frequency number you hear.
If it isn't exactly yours, do nothing at all.

example.stem: Your callsign is Heat 24. Call: 'Heat 24, Ghost 11, switch to frequency one.' What do you do?
steps: The first callsign is Heat 24. That's you.
Tap frequency one.

reteach.hook: First name yours? Tap. Not yours? Nothing.

check.stem: Your callsign is Heat 24. Call: 'Heat 24, Ghost 11, switch to frequency one.' What do you do?
check.explain: Heat 24 comes first, so the call is for you: tap one. Ignoring it misses a call, eleven is Ghost's callsign number not a frequency, two isn't given, and Ghost 11 is the caller, not someone to wait for.

check.stem: In 'Cobra 51, Raven 18, switch to frequency three', who is being called?
check.explain: The first callsign is the one being called: Cobra 51. Raven 18 is the caller, the call is for one aircraft, and the frequency is the instruction, not the address.

check.stem: Your callsign is Raven 17. Call: 'Raven 71, Cobra 33, switch to frequency two.' What do you do?
options: Switch to two, as the word matches
check.explain: Raven 71 has your word with the digits swapped, so it isn't you: ignore it. Any switch is a false response, and seven isn't a frequency in the call.

check.stem: Your callsign is Hawk 36. Call: 'Dagger 40, Hawk 36, switch to frequency four.' What do you do?
check.explain: Dagger 40 is being called and you're only the caller, so ignore it. Switching to four, or to three, answers a call that isn't yours, and any tap is a false response.
